docs.title: Programming the H100: CUDA, CuTe, and CUTLASS from First Principles
docs.text: November 21 corrections: historical executions apply to their archived source hashes. Some current examples have subsequent fixes and require fresh GPU validation; see the repair record. An evidence-verifier pass is an offline consistency check, not a GPU rerun.

docs.title: A Hardware-Level Companion Guide to NVIDIA Hopper
docs.text:
Understand the machine, prove the mapping, build the kernel, then measure the useful result. This book connects Hopper architecture and PTX to safe asynchronous pipelines, Tensor Core programming, application profiling and a complete CuTe/CUTLASS learning sequence.

The thirty-one chapters and the native B200 appendix combine explanatory diagrams, worked calculations, downloadable programs and dated execution records. Follow the foundations in order, or choose a focused route below when a particular kernel or application needs attention.

  • Set up and run

    Getting Started & Installation covers a fresh Ubuntu host, a preconfigured GPU instance and the first verified CUDA program. Reading and website previews need no GPU.

  • Understand Hopper

    Begin with the architecture, then connect data movement, completion, ownership and matrix instructions before assembling a kernel.

  • Learn CuTe and CUTLASS

    Start with CuTe foundations. Progress from coordinate proofs through checked kernels to pipelines, fusion, precision and a capstone.

  • Inspect the actual results

    Read the original-program audit and expanded workshop results. Every result retains its source revision, commands, system and execution scope.

docs.title: How to read this
docs.text:
Build the dependencies from the machine upward. When a profile exposes a bottleneck, return to the layer that explains it.

Prerequisites. Be comfortable with thread/block indexing, launch dimensions, shared-memory lifetime, block synchronization and CUDA error checking. If those are new, begin with NVIDIA's CUDA programming introduction, then follow the first verified run.

Your goal Suggested route What to produce First successful GPU run Getting Started → 1 → 2 A checked result and saved preflight information Understand Hopper data movement 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 Valid descriptors, byte counts and an ownership/completion explanation Design and diagnose a GEMM 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 → 8 → 9 → 10 → 13 Full-output reference checks and a profile tied to the right bottleneck Understand fast attention 3 → 4 → 6 → 7 → 9 → 12 → 30 → 31 → 13 A checked recurrence and a clear account of the design's remaining kernel work Find application stalls 11 → 13 → 14 A bounded timeline and consistently timed useful-result comparison Learn CuTe/CUTLASS progressively 15–19 foundations → 20–24 implementations → 25–29 advanced work → 30–31 attention Coordinate proofs, checked kernels and a reproducible capstone Study distributed GPU work 1 → 2 → 11 → 13 A topology record and a result checked on the required participants

Read each example in three passes. Trace where values live and who owns them. Identify what makes them safe to read and safe to overwrite. Predict the reference result, then compare it with the captured output. Tune performance after those agree.

The CPU coordinate exercises in Chapters 15–19 provide an entry into CuTe without requiring a Hopper instance. Later copy, MMA and pipeline labs reconnect those mappings to the hardware and synchronization chapters. Keep the two routes distinct: calculating an offset on a laptop is useful preparation for a GPU run, not a substitute for it.

The CuTe/CUTLASS chapters use a common learning sequence: define the symbols, read a small worked illustration, follow the matching API call, calculate the intermediate coordinates or values, and check the result before extending the example. Keep the illustration beside the calculation; its labels distinguish logical coordinates, stored values, element offsets and byte addresses.

The companion guides state a goal, explain the mechanisms, provide worked checks and finish with a summary. Open a linked SVG for its full-resolution vector view. Code snippets explain local ideas; complete programs and execution records identify what was actually compiled and run. Use each example's complete command, including its architecture target and required driver, NCCL or cuBLAS linker flags.

docs.title: Execution records and tested scope
docs.text:
Original suite — November 17–18, 2026

Historical evidence covers 26 H100 program revisions and a later revised training program on eight A100 GPUs across the recorded hosts: 26 workloads on H100 and the revised training workload on eight A100 GPUs. The complete audit links the successful program records, stronger Chapter 7 coordinate test and twelve attention-reference cases. The training supplement uses sm_80 and independently checks final weights and per-step losses; it is not an eight-H100 result.

The four barrier-ordering corrections in Chapters 3–5 passed the November 18 two-H100 rerun and memory checks. That host had 2× H100 80GB HBM3, 132 SMs each, NV18 peer topology, Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, driver 580.105.08 and CUDA compiler 12.8.93; the recorded builds used sm_90a, C++17 and -O2.

Expanded workshop — H100, November 18, 2026

The CuTe/CUTLASS workshop record captures eight CUDA compilations, two Python byte-compilations and eleven passing workload invocations, plus two real Nsight Systems reports. CPU-only layout, ownership and format checks retain their stated scope. These additions have their own source identities and records; the original suite is preserved.

The attention extension adds a dated CPU walkthrough and a separate Hopper FMHA collection lab. The CPU record checks the equations. Separate dated H100 captures now cover the complete CUDA reference and all 17 expected FP16 FMHA variant results, including backward, with clean memory checks. These records retain their own scope and do not inherit the earlier workshop's results.

The original single-GPU manifest remains available as historical evidence. Current chapters link exact tested sources, commands, compile/run timestamps, system information and captured outputs beside the relevant examples. Derived arithmetic, architecture specifications and cited paper benchmarks are identified separately from this book's measured results.

What the evidence labels mean

Compiled means the listed complete translation unit built with the recorded command. Executed and passed means the actual workload ran and passed its stated checks. Reference/skeleton means surrounding implementation is still required. A CPU coordinate model, an attention recurrence check and a real GPU kernel validate different scopes; passing one does not establish the others or reproduce a paper benchmark.

Exercises and their worked answers are reasoning aids. A hypothetical timing used to check TFLOP/s arithmetic is not a captured hardware measurement.

A compact glossary — use it while reading Term Meaning in this book Read more SM Streaming multiprocessor: a block of GPU execution resources 1 CTA / thread block Cooperating CUDA threads with a block-local shared-memory lifetime 2 Warp / warpgroup 32 threads / four consecutive warps participating in Hopper WGMMA 2, 6 Cluster / DSMEM Co-scheduled blocks and their distributed shared-memory access 2 Generic / async proxy Distinct memory-access mechanisms that need the right ordering protocol 3 RAW / WAR Read-after-write readiness / write-after-read reuse hazards 3 mbarrier / phase Completion state and the generation being waited on 3, 9 Tensor map / TMA A multidimensional transfer description / Hopper transfer machinery 4, 5 Swizzle A mapping between logical element coordinates and shared-memory byte locations 4 WGMMA / descriptor Hopper warpgroup matrix arithmetic / its shared-memory operand description 6 Commit / wait group Submission of asynchronous arithmetic and waiting for its completion 7 Epilogue Processing after the reduction: conversion, scaling, activation and output storage 7, 9 Stage / empty / full A reusable storage slot and the two directions of its ownership handshake 8, 9 Arithmetic intensity Defined work divided by defined traffic at a stated memory level 8 Stream-K Scheduling based on reduction work, potentially combining partial output tiles 10 TP / PP / DP Tensor, pipeline and data parallelism 11 Online softmax Combining tiles using a running maximum, normalizer and output numerator 12 Replay / occupancy Profiler re-execution / resident execution-resource use; neither alone proves speed 13 CuTe / CUTLASS Tensor/layout and instruction abstractions / the larger CUDA kernel and operator ecosystem 15, 24 Layout / engine / tensor Coordinate-to-offset map / data-access or storage mechanism / their combination 17, 18 size / cosize Logical coordinate count / the layout's codomain extent used for supported storage-sizing calculations 17 Leading dimension / stride Physical spacing in declared units; typed-pointer element offsets and descriptor byte offsets differ 19 Thread/value partition Assignment of logical values to participating threads and per-thread slots 20 Copy / MMA atom An instruction-specific transfer or matrix-operation contract with its participation and value mapping 20, 21 Identity tensor / predicate Coordinate-valued reference view / a validity condition actually applied to the operation 18, 20 Collective / adapter Coordinated mainloop or epilogue / host interface for arguments, workspace and kernel launch 24 Generation Which reuse of a storage slot a readiness/empty event belongs to 25 EVT Epilogue visitor tree: a dataflow expression whose nesting fixes operation order 26 E2M1 / block scale A floating-point nibble codebook / a scale shared by a specified group along a declared axis 27 Makespan / latency / throughput Joined batch duration / time for a defined request / completed work per stated interval 28

docs.title: Read and build locally
docs.text:
From a source checkout, create the documentation environment:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt
mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 on the same machine. Getting Started covers source checkout, Windows activation, remote preview, strict-build checks and the separate GPU prerequisites.

For your own fork, set site_url and repo_url in mkdocs.yml to that repository before publishing. This repository's .github/workflows/ci.yml verifies and deploys changes pushed to main.

Built with Material for MkDocs.

Separate B200 compatibility results distinguish CPU checks, GPU-using programs and architecture exclusions.

docs.title: Lesson 1 Companion Guide — A Deep Dive into Hopper
docs.text:
Architecture introduction years: Volta (2017), Ampere (2020), Hopper (2022), Blackwell (2024). Package drawings are conceptual, not die photographs or scale comparisons.

Validation — November 17, 2026. Architecture reference. SXM product specifications and models are distinguished from the PCIe execution host. Follow-up: the final two-H100 audit records a fresh run of the complete programs. The original dated transcripts below remain available for provenance. Execution system: 1× H100 PCIe, 114 SMs, 80 GB class; Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS; driver 580.105.08; CUDA Toolkit 12.8.93; sm_90a, C++17, -O2. Full system information · CUDA result manifest. Each tested source and captured output is linked beside its example. Diagrams open as original SVGs for zooming.

Target audience: GPU programmers who want to understand the H100 at the hardware level before writing CUDA/PTX kernels. Prerequisites: Basic understanding of parallel computing concepts (threads, memory hierarchy).

Your goal in this chapter

Separate product specifications from a throughput model; identify whether a number is per SM, per GPU, or bidirectional.

No prior Hopper knowledge. Read the installation guide if you want to check the execution host.

What this covers: Every architectural concept in Lesson 1 — the TMA unit, asynchronous execution, Tensor Cores, the memory hierarchy from HBM3 through L2/L1 to registers, the SM microarchitecture (quadrants, warp schedulers, dispatch units, SFUs, LSUs), NVLink 4.0, shared memory banking, swizzling, and how thread blocks are distributed across SMs. Each section includes ASCII diagrams, worked examples with concrete numbers, and practical implications for kernel design.

How to read this chapter. Most sections open with a boxed ASCII diagram or a specification block. Those boxes are the reference material; the prose around them tells you what to look at and why it matters. On a first pass, read the prose and skim the boxes — you can come back for the exact numbers when a later chapter needs them. Nothing here requires you to write code yet.

docs.title: 1 — The Big Picture
docs.text: Before any code, you need a mental picture of what kind of machine this is. This section gives you two things: the H100's raw numbers, and the one idea that separates Hopper from every GPU before it. If you remember nothing else from this chapter, remember §1.2.

docs.title: 1.1 H100 at a Glance
docs.text:
Here is the whole chip on a single card. Don't try to memorise it — skim it now and come back whenever a later section mentions a number you want to place. SKU scope: the specification blocks below describe H100 SXM unless stated otherwise. The November 17, 2026 execution records use a single H100 PCIe; do not apply SXM SM counts, HBM3 bandwidth, NVLink topology, or peak throughput to that machine.

Three lines matter most for kernel work: 132 SMs (how many independent processors you are programming), 3.35 TB/s of HBM3 bandwidth (how fast you can feed them), and 228 KB of shared memory per SM (how much data you can stage right next to the compute).

NVIDIA H100 (Hopper Architecture)
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Released:            September 2022
Process:             TSMC 4N (custom variant of N4)
Transistors:         80 billion
Form factors:        SXM5 (700W)  |  PCIe Gen5 (300W)

Compute:
  SMs:               132 (enabled)
  Tensor Cores:      528 (4 per SM)
  FP32 CUDA Cores:   16,896 (128 per SM)
  FP64 Units:        8,448 (64 per SM)
  INT32 Units:       8,448 (64 per SM)

Memory:
  HBM3:              80 GB @ 3.35 TB/s
  L2 Cache:          50 MB
  Shared Mem/SM:     228 KB (configurable)
  Registers/SM:      256 KB

Interconnect:
  NVLink 4.0:        900 GB/s (18 links)
  PCIe 5.0:          128 GB/s bidirectional

Key Innovation:      Fully asynchronous execution via TMA

docs.title: 1.2 The Generational Leap
docs.text:
Hopper expands the asynchronous programming model with TMA bulk tensor transfers and warpgroup matrix arithmetic. Ampere already supported asynchronous global-to-shared copies with cp.async; overlap did not begin with Hopper. TMA lets an elected thread describe a multidimensional transfer while other threads compute on a previously completed tile. See the Ampere asynchronous-copy contract.

Figure 1.5 — Asynchronous copy is not unique to Hopper; TMA changes how bulk transfers are issued.

This is why pipelined kernels (GEMMs, attention) can approach the theoretical roofline on the H100 — you fetch tile i+1 while computing tile i.

docs.title: 2 — Asynchronous Execution & The TMA
docs.text:
Section 1 claimed the H100 is asynchronous. This section makes that concrete.

The idea in one sentence: Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) requests describe bulk tensor movement, reducing per-thread address generation and allowing computation to overlap a transfer. Earlier GPUs already offered overlap mechanisms, including Ampere asynchronous copies; Hopper adds tensor-aware bulk transfers and their completion protocols.

We build up to it in four steps: what "asynchronous" means for a copy (§2.1), what the TMA actually is (§2.2), a worked comparison of per-thread copying with one tensor-transfer request (§2.3), and the price you pay for all this — bookkeeping (§2.4).

docs.title: 2.1 Synchronous vs Asynchronous Copies
docs.text:
A synchronous copy abstraction requires completion before its consumer proceeds. An ordinary global load is not a promise that every subsequent independent instruction stalls: dependency tracking and scheduling can overlap independent work. The distinction here is explicit asynchronous transfer/completion control, rather than a claim that older load instructions made overlap impossible.

An asynchronous copy only starts the transfer. The issuing thread can immediately continue doing other work — computing on previously loaded data, managing bookkeeping, etc. The thread later uses the operation’s supported completion wait to know when the copy has finished; an ordering fence alone is not a completion wait.

Figure 2.1 — Illustrative scheduling, not a measured utilisation trace.

docs.title: 2.2 The TMA Unit
docs.text:
Each SM in the H100 has a dedicated Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) unit. This is a hardware block — it has its own logic, its own connection to the memory hierarchy, and its own understanding of multi-dimensional tensor layouts.

Figure 2.2 — The transfer request defines the division of work between threads and hardware.

docs.title: 2.3 TMA Descriptor — Concrete Example
docs.text:
The previous section described the TMA in the abstract. Here is the same copy written both ways as conceptual pseudocode. Compare which address-generation and transfer tasks the threads perform; exact instruction counts require inspecting the compiled implementation.

Scenario: Copy a 64×64 tile of BF16 from a [4096, 4096] matrix
starting at row=128, col=256

Traditional approach (per thread, 32 threads in a warp):
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  // Each thread handles 64*64/32 = 128 elements
  for (int i = threadIdx.x; i < 64*64; i += 32) {
      int row = i / 64;
      int col = i % 64;
      int src_offset = (128 + row) * 4096 + (256 + col);  // address math
      smem[row * 64 + col] = global[src_offset];            // load + store
  }
  __syncthreads();  // everyone must finish before compute

  Each lane visits 128 elements in this scalar sketch.
  Thread-level operations are not summed to obtain warp-issued instructions.
  Actual instruction counts depend on vectorisation and compiler lowering.


TMA approach (single thread):
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  // Thread 0 issues one instruction:
  tma_copy_2d(descriptor, /*box_coord=*/{256, 128}, smem_ptr, barrier);
  // Other threads may do independent work; consumers still wait for readiness.

  // The descriptor was set up once at kernel launch:
  //   base_ptr    = &matrix[0][0]
  //   dims        = {4096, 4096}
  //   global_dims = {4096, 4096}   (fastest dimension first)
  //   global_strides = {4096 * 2} (outer stride; inner BF16 size is implicit)
  //   box_size    = {64, 64}
  //   element_sz  = 2 bytes

  One tensor-copy request describes 4,096 BF16 elements = 8 KiB.
  Descriptor setup, issuing-thread election, barriers and waits add instructions.
  Hardware transaction counts depend on the memory layout and request handling.

docs.title: 2.4 The Bookkeeping Cost
docs.text:
The tradeoff for async execution is complexity. You need barriers to know when data is ready:

Figure 2.3 — Never load a new tile over data that a consumer still needs.

docs.title: 3 — 4th Generation Tensor Cores
docs.text:
Almost all of the H100's advertised performance lives in its tensor cores. A CUDA core does one multiply-add at a time; a tensor core does an entire small matrix multiply in one operation, which is where the 10–100× gap comes from.

This section covers what they do (§3.1), the new Hopper unit of work called a warp group (§3.2), the trick of agreeing to skip zeros (§3.3), and the number formats they accept (§3.4). You don't need to write tensor core code yet — Chapters 6 and 7 do that. Here you only need to know what the hardware offers.

docs.title: 3.1 What Tensor Cores Do
docs.text:
Tensor Cores are specialized matrix-multiply-accumulate (MMA) units. While CUDA cores process one FMA (fused multiply-add) per cycle per core, a Tensor Core processes an entire small matrix multiply in one operation.

CUDA Core (FP32):
  1 core does: a × b + c → d     (1 FMA = 2 FLOPs per cycle)
  128 cores/SM × 2 FLOPs = 256 FLOPS/cycle/SM (FP32)

Tensor Core (FP16, 4th Gen):
  1 tensor core does: A[m×k] × B[k×n] + C[m×n] → D[m×n]
  Where m=64, k=16, n=8..256 in steps of 8 (dense FP16/BF16 WGMMA) for wgmma (with warp groups)
  4 tensor cores/SM working together via WGMMA.

  Dense throughput per SM, at the applicable Tensor Core clock:
    FP16/BF16: 4,096 FLOP/cycle/SM
    FP8:       8,192 FLOP/cycle/SM
    (An FMA counts as two FLOPs.)

  H100 SXM Tensor Core peak uses 1.83 GHz, not the 1.98 GHz
  CUDA-core boost clock. Mixing the clock specifications produces
  incorrect noninteger per-cycle rates.
    FP16/BF16: 4,096 × 132 × 1.83 GHz = 989.43 TFLOP/s dense
    FP8:       8,192 × 132 × 1.83 GHz = 1,978.86 TFLOP/s dense
    FP8 sparse effective peak: 3,957.72 TFLOP/s.

  H100 PCIe has 114 SMs and a 1.62 GHz Tensor Core boost:
    FP16/BF16: 4,096 × 114 × 1.62 GHz = 756.45 TFLOP/s dense.
  Actual sustained clocks depend on power, temperature and workload.

Sources: NVIDIA Hopper architecture and NVIDIA’s Tensor Core throughput calculation.

docs.title: 3.2 Warp Group MMA (WGMMA)
docs.text:
The H100 introduces Warp Group operations, where 4 warps (128 threads) cooperate on a single matrix multiply:

Figure 3.1 — Four warps cooperate on one warpgroup-level matrix operation.

docs.title: 3.3 Structured Sparsity
docs.text:
Sparsity is a way of buying throughput by agreeing not to store some of your numbers. The common FP16/BF16/FP8 sparse path uses 2:4 structure: at most two nonzero values per quartet, stored as two retained values plus metadata. TF32 sparse WGMMA instead uses a 1:2 encoding (Chapter 7). Sparse Tensor Core peak is quoted as about twice the dense-equivalent arithmetic rate; total kernel speed also depends on metadata, other operands and memory traffic.

Figure 3.2 — 2:4 structured sparsity stores values plus position metadata.

docs.title: 3.4 Precision Comparison
docs.text:
Lower precision buys throughput: the fewer bits per number, the more numbers a tensor core can chew through per cycle. This table is the menu. The pattern to notice is that halving the bit width roughly doubles the FLOPs — which is the entire reason FP8 exists.

Precision     Bits  Range          Tensor Core FLOPS/cycle/SM*   Use Case
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FP64          64    ±1.8×10^308    ~256                          Scientific
TF32          32**  ±3.4×10^38     2,048                        Training
FP32          32    ±3.4×10^38     (via CUDA cores only, 256)    General
FP16          16    ±65,504        4,096                        Training
BF16          16    ±3.4×10^38     4,096                        Training
FP8 (E4M3)     8    ±448           8,192                        Inference
FP8 (E5M2)     8    ±57,344        8,192                        Gradients
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
* Dense (no 2:4 sparsity), per SM per applicable execution clock.
  The FP16/BF16 and FP8 rows use the Tensor Core clock; do not divide
  their published TFLOP/s peaks by the CUDA-core boost clock.
  Sparse rates are effective dense-equivalent work for supported
  sparse instruction/type combinations; there is no sparse FP64 row.
** TF32 uses 32 bits of storage but a 10-bit mantissa internally.

The Transformer Engine dynamically selects FP8 E4M3 for forward
and E5M2 for backward, auto-scaling to prevent overflow.

docs.title: 4 — The Full GPU Die
docs.text:
Now we zoom out and look at the whole chip as a floor plan. Nearly everything covered in the rest of this chapter is one of the boxes below, so it's worth a minute here to see how the pieces sit relative to each other.

The rough shape: memory around the edges, 132 processors (SMs) in the middle grouped into eight clusters, a large cache shared between them, and a hardware scheduler deciding which processor runs what.

docs.title: 4.1 Top-Level Block Diagram
docs.text:
Read this from the outside in. Data either arrives at the bottom (over PCIe from the CPU) or already lives at the top (in the HBM3 memory stacks). The SMs in the middle are where your code actually runs, and the L2 cache between them is the shared staging area that essentially all traffic passes through.

Figure 1.1 — Logical GH100 organisation. Blocks are schematic, not physical die placement.

On the 132-of-144 figure: the full GH100 die really does have 8 GPCs of 18 SMs each (144 total) [NVIDIA Hopper Architecture whitepaper, GTC22, v1.02]. The SXM5 product binned down to 132 SMs, described in the same whitepaper as "8 GPCs, 66 TPCs" -- 66 TPCs ÷ 8 GPCs is not a whole number, so the 12 disabled SMs are not spread evenly as "1.5 per GPC." NVIDIA does not publish the exact per-GPC enabled-SM breakdown for SXM5; treat the 18-SMs-per-GPC diagram above as the full-die floor plan, not a literal picture of which SMs are switched on in a given chip.

docs.title: 4.2 The GigaThread Engine
docs.text:
The GigaThread Engine is the hardware scheduler that sits at the top of the GPU and manages the entire kernel launch lifecycle:

Figure 4.2 — A logical launch path; exact scheduler implementation is not an ISA contract.

docs.title: 5 — HBM3 Memory System
docs.text:
HBM3 is the GPU's main memory — the 80 GB your tensors live in. It is enormously wide (5,120 bits) and enormously fast in aggregate (3.35 TB/s), and also, relative to the compute, enormously slow: roughly 500 cycles to answer a request.

That tension — huge bandwidth, terrible latency — is the reason the rest of the chip is shaped the way it is. Caches exist to shrink the number of requests that have to travel this far; the TMA exists so you don't have to wait on the ones that do.

docs.title: 5.1 Physical Organization
docs.text:
The part to take away is the bandwidth ladder at the bottom of the diagram: about 33 TB/s GPU-wide modeled shared-memory bandwidth, an illustrative 12 TB/s aggregate L2 rate, and the 3.35 TB/s SXM HBM product peak. The first two are models or workload-dependent estimates, not product guarantees. Every step further from the compute costs you roughly 3×.

HBM3 — High Bandwidth Memory, 3rd Generation
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Total capacity:    80 GB
  Bandwidth:         3.35 TB/s
  Stacks:            6 manufactured, 5 enabled (yield optimization)
  Per stack:         16 GB
  Bus width:         5120 bits total (1024 bits per stack)

  Memory controllers: 10 independent 512-bit controllers
  Each controller manages:
    ├── DRAM protocol timing (activate/precharge/read/write)
    ├── Request reordering (maximize row buffer hits)
    └── Address mapping (channels → banks → rows → cols)

Figure 5.1 — Cache hits can terminate a request before it reaches external memory.

docs.title: 5.2 Why 5120-bit Bus Width Matters for TMA
docs.text:
A number like "5,120-bit bus" only becomes useful once you convert it into how long your tile actually takes to arrive. That's what this does.

Bus width: 5120 bits = 640 bytes (10 × 512-bit memory controllers)
[NVIDIA Hopper Architecture whitepaper, GTC22, v1.02]

The bus width and a TMA transfer's granularity describe different layers.
Dividing 640 bus bytes by 128 does not establish five concurrent TMA requests.

For a 64×64 BF16 tile: 64 × 64 × 2 = 8,192 bytes.
8,192 / 3.35 TB/s ≈ 2.45 ns is an aggregate bandwidth-only lower bound,
not a single-SM tile latency. If 132 SMs shared that bandwidth equally,
one SM's share would be about 25.4 GB/s and 8 KiB would require about
323 ns of bandwidth service. Request latency, cache hits and contention
are additional concerns. This arithmetic does not prove Tensor Cores stay fed.

docs.title: 6 — L2 Cache
docs.text:
The L2 is a 50 MB staging area shared by every SM, and essentially all traffic to and from HBM passes through it.

Two facts about it drive real kernel performance: it is organised into 128-byte lines made of four 32-byte sectors, and it charges you per sector touched, not per useful byte. That single detail is what "coalescing" means, and it is why the same useful payload can generate very different transaction counts. A transaction ratio is not itself a measured runtime ratio.

docs.title: 6.1 Structure and Behavior
docs.text:
Four behaviours are described below. The first two — sectors, and the penalty for scattered access — are the ones you'll actively think about while writing kernels. The last two happen for you, for free.

L2 Cache — 50 MB Unified
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Total size:        50 MB
  Partitions:        2 × 25 MB
  Cache line:        128 bytes
  Sectors per line:  4 × 32 bytes
  Capacity model:    If 50 MiB is assumed, 50 × 2^20 / 128 = 409,600 lines

  Key behaviors:

  1. SECTOR-BASED FILLING
     A cache line is 128 bytes, but consists of 4 × 32-byte sectors.
     A memory request can touch 1-4 sectors of a single line.
     The cache can fill sector-by-sector (no need to load all 128 bytes).

  2. UNCOALESCED ACCESS PENALTY
     A warp of 32 threads issues a memory instruction.
     If threads access scattered addresses:
       Best case:  1 sector  (all 32 threads in same 32B)
       Worst case: 32 sectors (every thread in a different sector)

     Uncoalesced access explodes the number of sectors requested,
     consuming L2 bandwidth and evicting useful cache lines.

  3. CACHE LOCALITY
     L2 is shared across SMs. Address mapping and concurrent traffic affect
     locality and contention; the program cannot assume an SM's working
     set is automatically assigned to a nearby partition.

  4. WRITE COALESCING
     Store transactions and L2 caching affect downstream memory traffic.
     Coalescing is based on lane addresses; cache behavior does not turn
     every scatter/atomic request into a contiguous HBM transfer.

Figure 6.1 — Sector granularity helps explain coalescing and overfetch.

docs.title: 6.2 Worked Example — L2 Sector Math
docs.text:
Same useful payload, two access patterns, an eightfold difference in requested sectors. Work through both by hand — this is probably the most valuable arithmetic in the chapter.

Scenario: A warp of 32 threads each loads a float (4 bytes)
          from consecutive addresses starting at address 0x1000.

Thread  0: loads 4 bytes from 0x1000
Thread  1: loads 4 bytes from 0x1004
Thread  2: loads 4 bytes from 0x1008
...
Thread 31: loads 4 bytes from 0x107C

Total bytes: 32 × 4 = 128 bytes = exactly 1 cache line
Sectors touched: 4 (each sector = 32 bytes, 8 threads per sector)
Requested footprint: four sectors within one cache line

Result: COALESCED — four 32-byte sectors cover the 128 useful bytes.


Bad scenario: 32 threads each load a float with stride 128 bytes

Thread  0: 0x1000
Thread  1: 0x1080  (128 bytes later)
Thread  2: 0x1100
...
Thread 31: 0x1F80

Total bytes still 128, but spread across 32 different cache lines.
Sectors touched: 32 (one sector per thread, all different lines)
Requested footprint: 32 sectors spread across 32 cache lines.

Result: eight times as many sectors (32 versus 4), 1,024 requested bytes
for the same 128 useful bytes. Cache hits affect downstream HBM traffic;
this sector ratio is not a runtime ratio.

docs.title: 7 — GPCs — Graphics Processing Clusters
docs.text:
The enabled SMs are grouped into Graphics Processing Clusters. The full GH100 die has eight GPCs with 18 SMs each; the 132-SM SXM product disables some resources, so its enabled GPCs do not all contain 18 active SMs.

For most of GPU history this grouping was invisible to programmers. On Hopper it stopped being invisible, because thread block clusters — groups of blocks that can read each other's shared memory — only work within a single GPC. This is a short section, but it is the reason cluster sizes cap out where they do.

docs.title: 7.1 GPC Internal Structure
docs.text:
One GPC, drawn out. The pieces to notice: the 18 SMs, their pairing into TPCs, and the DSMEM interconnect that lets SMs read one another's shared memory directly — without going out to L2 and back.

In the full GH100 configuration, one GPC contains 18 SMs organized as nine TPCs of two SMs each. Product configurations enable fewer resources. Clusters provide distributed shared-memory access within a GPC; L2 is a GPU-wide resource.

Figure 7.1 — Full-die schematic: nine texture processing clusters, two SMs per TPC.

docs.title: 7.2 Why GPCs Matter for Kernel Design
docs.text:
Source: NVIDIA Hopper tuning guide cluster and occupancy limits.

The practical consequence of everything above: how large can a cluster be, and what does each size cost you in synchronisation?

Implication for Thread Block Clusters:
═══════════════════════════════════════

  A cluster of thread blocks must all run on SMs within the SAME GPC.
  (Because clusters need DSMEM, and DSMEM only exists within a GPC.)

  Portable maximum: eight blocks, subject to device/configuration limits.
  Larger clusters require nonportable opt-in and actual device support.
  Query cudaOccupancyMaxPotentialClusterSize and cudaOccupancyMaxActiveClusters.

  The 18-SM full-die GPC diagram does not establish a cluster-size limit,
  blocks-per-SM placement rule, active-cluster count or synchronization cost.
  Registers, shared memory, warps, enabled SMs and cluster shape all matter.

docs.title: 8 — NVLink 4.0
docs.text:
Everything so far has been inside a single GPU. NVLink is the wire between GPUs — 900 GB/s aggregate bidirectional on SXM, roughly seven times the bidirectional PCIe 5.0 ×16 link rate. A one-way comparison is 450 versus approximately 64 GB/s before protocol overhead.

You won't program NVLink directly in this chapter (Chapter 11 does that). What matters here is its speed relative to PCIe and HBM, because that ratio is what decides where to put your model once it stops fitting on one card.

docs.title: 8.1 Physical Specifications
docs.text:
The one piece of physics worth knowing is PAM4 signalling: by using four voltage levels on the wire instead of two, each symbol carries two bits instead of one — doubling the data rate without raising the clock.

NVLink 4.0 — GPU-to-GPU Interconnect
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Total bandwidth:     900 GB/s (bidirectional)
  Links:               18 fourth-generation NVLink links
  Per link:            50 GB/s bidirectional
                        (25 GB/s per direction, via 2 differential
                        signal pairs per direction)
  Check:               18 × 50 GB/s = 900 GB/s  ✓
  [NVIDIA Hopper Architecture whitepaper, GTC22, v1.02]

  Signaling:           PAM4 (Pulse Amplitude Modulation, 4 levels)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  NRZ  (NVLink 1.0-3.0): 2 amplitude levels → 1 bit/symbol │
  │  PAM4 (NVLink 4.0+):    4 amplitude levels → 2 bits/symbol│
  │                                                            │
  │  Same baud rate, twice the bits per symbol →              │
  │  2× the data rate per differential pair.                  │
  │  (NVIDIA does not publish exact per-level voltages --      │
  │  only the 4-level/2-bit-per-symbol scheme is public.)      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Direct connections:  Up to 8 GPUs peer-to-peer
  NVSwitch fabric:     Up to 256 GPUs in a switched topology

  TMA integration:
    NVLink connects directly with the TMA unit.
    Within a DGX node, TMA can issue bulk copies to/from
    remote GPU memory without SM intervention.

docs.title: 8.2 Multi-GPU Topology
docs.text:
Eight GPUs, each able to reach every other at full speed. The bandwidth comparison at the bottom is the part to remember.

Figure 1.3 — DGX H100 connects all eight GPUs through a switched NVLink network. NVIDIA HGX H100 platform comparison

docs.title: 9 — The Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)
docs.text:
This is the heart of the chapter. The SM is the unit that actually runs your code: one thread block lands on one SM and stays there until it finishes.

The next several sections take the SM apart layer by layer — the four quadrants inside it (§10), how each quadrant decides which warp to run (§11), the arithmetic units they feed (§12), the shared memory they all share (§13), and the registers each thread owns (§14). The diagram below is the map for all of them.

docs.title: 9.1 SM Overview
docs.text:
The SM is the fundamental execution unit of the GPU. It receives thread blocks from the GigaThread Engine and executes them to completion.

Figure 1.2 — Each SMSP schedules warps and uses a share of the SM’s execution resources.

docs.title: 10 — SM Quadrants (SMSPs)
docs.text:
An SM is not one processor — it is four, and they schedule independently.

Block size affects the available warps, register use and resident blocks. Multiple resident blocks can supply work to the SM’s schedulers, so a block size that is not a multiple of 128 does not by itself imply an idle SMSP. §10.2 uses an illustrative distribution; profile the actual kernel before drawing a utilisation conclusion.

docs.title: 10.1 Quadrant Breakdown
docs.text:
Each SM is divided into 4 identical subdivisions. Each quadrant is an independently scheduling unit:

Figure 10.1 — SMSPs make warp scheduling and register pressure easier to reason about.

docs.title: 10.2 Why 4 Quadrants?
docs.text:
Here is the practical payoff of knowing the SM is four things rather than one.

Figure 10.2 — 256 threads make eight warps of 32 threads each.

The Hopper Tuning Guide specifies the per-SM register and residency limits. Its 64K 32-bit registers are 256 KiB per SM, corresponding to 16,384 registers in each 64 KiB partition shown here.

docs.title: 11 — Warp Schedulers & Dispatch
docs.text:
Threads on a GPU do not run individually. They run in locked groups of 32 called warps, and the hardware's entire latency-hiding strategy is to keep many warps resident and switch between them the moment one stalls.

This section explains what a warp is (§11.1), how the scheduler picks one each cycle (§11.2), and a hardware limit most people never hear about — dispatch ports (§11.3).

docs.title: 11.1 What is a Warp?
docs.text:
Start here if warp is a new word. A warp is simply the granularity at which the hardware thinks: 32 threads that fetch one instruction and execute it together, in lockstep.

Warp = 32 Threads
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Thread block of 256 threads:
    Warp 0: threads   0 -  31
    Warp 1: threads  32 -  63
    Warp 2: threads  64 -  95
    Warp 3: threads  96 - 127
    Warp 4: threads 128 - 159
    Warp 5: threads 160 - 191
    Warp 6: threads 192 - 223
    Warp 7: threads 224 - 255

  Properties:
    ├── Created together from a thread block
    ├── Share a warp scheduler's attention
    ├── Execute the SAME instruction (mostly — divergence aside)
    ├── Each thread has PRIVATE registers
    └── Memory operations coalesce across the 32 threads

  Why 32?
    ├── Matches 32 memory banks in shared memory
    ├── 32 threads × 4 bytes = 128 bytes = 1 cache line
    ├── Good balance between control overhead and parallelism
    └── Hardware sweet spot for SIMT execution

docs.title: 11.2 Warp Scheduler Operation
docs.text:
Five steps, every cycle, in every quadrant. The reason the whole machine is built this way is the sentence at the bottom of the block.

Figure 11.1 — A conceptual dependency-to-execution loop, not a hardware pipeline timing diagram.

docs.title: 11.3 The Dispatch Unit and Dispatch Ports
docs.text:
This is the one part of the SM that no occupancy calculator will show you, and it explains why "the SM has 128 FP32 cores and 64 INT32 units" does not mean a single warp can use both in the same cycle.

Figure 11.2 — An instruction must be issued before an execution unit can do useful work.

docs.title: 12 — Execution Units Deep Dive
docs.text:
The five kinds of arithmetic hardware inside each quadrant, one at a time.

Most of this is reference material — skim it now and come back. The two subsections that will actually change how you write code are §12.2 (integer work runs in parallel with floating-point, so address arithmetic is effectively free) and §12.5 (load/store units, and coalescing).

docs.title: 12.1 FP32 CUDA Cores
docs.text:
The default workhorse. Anything that isn't a matrix multiply ends up here.

FP32 CUDA Cores
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Per SM:        128 (32 per quadrant)
  Total (SXM5):  16,896 (132 SMs × 128)
  Operations:    Standard 32-bit floating point
                 (add, multiply, FMA, comparison, conversion)

  Throughput:    128 FP32 FMA/cycle/SM = 256 FLOPS/cycle/SM
                 (each FMA = 2 FLOPs: multiply + add)

  These are the "default" compute units — used for:
    ├── General-purpose math
    ├── Reduction operations
    ├── Activation functions (when SFU isn't appropriate)
    └── Any FP32 work that doesn't map to tensor cores

docs.title: 12.2 INT32 Units
docs.text:
The important claim here is the one in capitals: integer and floating-point work proceed at the same time, on separate datapaths. This is why the address arithmetic can sometimes overlap floating-point work, subject to issue bandwidth and dependencies.

INT32 Units
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Per SM:        64 (16 per quadrant)
  Total (SXM5):  8,448

  Primary uses:
    ├── Memory address calculations (pointer arithmetic)
    ├── Loop control (counters, comparisons)
    ├── Index math for tiling patterns
    └── General integer arithmetic

  KEY FEATURE: Can execute SIMULTANEOUSLY with FP32 cores.
  The hardware has separate datapaths for INT and FP.

  This means: while the FP32 pipeline computes on data,
  the INT32 pipeline can be computing the next set of
  addresses from another ready warp; address-generation stalls are still possible.

  Typical pattern in a GEMM kernel:
    FP32: compute partial sum  (data path)
    INT32: calculate next tile address  (address path)
    Separate warps may overlap work on the distinct pipelines. A scheduler
    does not issue an INT and an FP instruction from one warp in the same cycle.

docs.title: 12.3 FP64 Units
docs.text:
H100 supports scientific computing as well as machine learning. Its scalar FP64 peak is half the scalar FP32 peak; FP64 Tensor Core throughput is a separate rate.

FP64 Units
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Per SM:        64 (16 per quadrant)
  Total (SXM5):  8,448

  FP64 throughput = exactly HALF of FP32.
  This ratio concerns the scalar datapaths, not a restriction to ML workloads.

  Used for:
    ├── High-precision scientific simulations
    ├── Numerical calculations requiring greater floating-point precision
    └── Numerical methods where FP32 isn't sufficient

  For comparison:
    A100:  FP64 = 1/2 FP32 throughput
    H100:  FP64 = 1/2 FP32 throughput  (same ratio)
    H100 doubles the FP64 execution units per SM relative to A100;
    the SM count and clock also change the chip-wide peak.

docs.title: 12.4 Special Function Units (SFUs)
docs.text:
Special-function hardware accelerates selected elementary operations, but a CUDA source-level function call is not necessarily one SFU instruction. The compiler may combine approximate hardware operations with range reduction, correction and special-case handling. Double-precision functions, standard single-precision functions and fast intrinsics have different implementations and accuracy contracts; compiler flags can also change the lowering.

Source operation             What to verify
expf(x), sinf(x), sqrtf(x)    The documented function error bound and compiled code
__expf(x), __sinf(x)          Fast-intrinsic accuracy/range contract
exp(x) on double             The double-precision implementation, not an FP32 SFU model
--use_fast_math               Which functions and floating-point modes it changes

Do not assume a uniform "22-bit mantissa" accuracy or derive instruction latency from a physical unit count. Throughput, dependent latency and whole-function execution time are different measurements. Check the CUDA mathematical-function accuracy tables, inspect the generated code, and measure the actual input distribution and math mode.

docs.title: 12.5 Load/Store Units (LSUs)
docs.text:
Read this one twice. Coalescing — how well the 32 addresses in a warp merge into cache-line requests — is the single biggest lever on memory performance in most kernels, and this is where it happens.

Load/Store Units (LSUs)
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Per SM:     32 (8 per quadrant)
  Connection: Direct to L1 cache / shared memory

  Operations:
    ├── ld  (load from memory → register)
    ├── st  (store from register → memory)
    ├── atom (atomic read-modify-write)
    └── red  (reduction operations)

  Coalescing (the most important concept for memory performance):
  When a warp executes a load, 32 threads each provide an address.
  The LSU attempts to MERGE these 32 addresses into as few
  cache-line requests as possible.

Figure 12.1 — A warp’s lane addresses determine which sectors it touches.

docs.title: 13 — Unified Shared Memory + L1 Cache
docs.text:
Shared memory is the scratchpad you manage by hand: 228 KB per SM, roughly 100× quicker to reach than HBM, and the place your tiles live while the tensor cores work on them.

This section covers how much of it you get (§13.1), how large to make your tiles (§13.2), the one easy way to accidentally make it 32× slower (§13.3–§13.4), and the fix for that (§13.5).

docs.title: 13.1 The Configurable Split
docs.text:
Shared memory and the L1 data cache are the same 256 KB of silicon, split however you ask for it. More shared memory suits tiled algorithms that stage data deliberately; more L1 suits irregular access patterns you can't predict ahead of time.

Unified Shared Memory / L1 Data Cache
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Total size:     256 KB per SM
  Max shared mem: 228 KB (configurable)
  Bandwidth:      ~0.25 TB/s per SM (32 banks × 4 B/cycle × 1.98 GHz model)
  Banks:          32 banks × 4 bytes (32 bits) wide
  Cache line:     128 bytes
  Sector:         32 bytes (cache fills sector-by-sector)

  The 256 KB is shared between:
    ├── Shared memory (programmer-managed, explicit)
    └── L1 data cache (hardware-managed, automatic)

Figure 13.1 — H100 has a unified 256 KiB resource; supported carveouts are constrained by the product and kernel.

  TRADEOFF:
    More shared memory → better for tiled algorithms (GEMM, attention)
                         but less L1 cache for spill/register pressure
    More L1 cache → better for irregular access patterns
                    but less space for explicit data staging

  Per-thread-block limit: 227 KB (1 KB reserved by CUDA runtime)
  Static __shared__ arrays: limited to 48 KB (compatibility)
  Beyond 48 KB: must use dynamic shared memory (extern __shared__)

docs.title: 13.2 Optimal Tile Sizing
docs.text:
Bigger tiles are not automatically better. Here is how to think about the tradeoff in both directions.

Practical Tile Size Guidelines for GEMMs:
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  The sweet spot is 64-128 KB per thread block.

  Why not use all 228 KB?
    ├── Larger tiles → more data to load before computing
    ├── First iteration has nothing to overlap with
    ├── Higher latency to fill the tile
    └── Fewer thread blocks fit per SM (hurts occupancy)

  Why not tiny tiles (e.g., 8 KB)?
    ├── Tile overhead (setup, sync) amortized over less compute
    ├── Lower compute-to-memory ratio
    └── More tiles needed → more kernel launch overhead

  Example for a BF16 GEMM:
    Tile = 128 × 128 × 2 bytes = 32 KB per matrix
    A tile + B tile = 64 KB ← fits well in shared memory
    Leaves room for double-buffering: 64 KB × 2 = 128 KB
    Still within the 228 KB limit with room for L1 cache

docs.title: 13.3 Bank Conflicts
docs.text:
Shared memory is fast because it is split into 32 independent banks that can all be read in the same cycle. It stops being fast the instant two threads want different addresses that happen to live in the same bank.

Figure 13.2 — For ordinary four-byte words, addresses interleave across 32 banks.

docs.title: 13.4 Worked Example — Bank Conflict
docs.text:
The worst case, worked out. A perfectly reasonable-looking access — read one column of a matrix — collapses to a thirty-second of full speed.

Scenario: 32 threads load column 0 of a 64×64 BF16 matrix
stored row-major in shared memory.

Row layout: 64 elements × 2 bytes = 128 bytes per row

Thread 0 loads: row 0, col 0 → address 0x0000 → bank (0/4)%32 = 0
Thread 1 loads: row 1, col 0 → address 0x0080 → bank (128/4)%32 = 0
Thread 2 loads: row 2, col 0 → address 0x0100 → bank (256/4)%32 = 0
...
Thread 31 loads: row 31, col 0 → address 0x0F80 → bank = 0

ALL 32 THREADS HIT BANK 0!
This is a 32-way bank conflict → takes 32 cycles instead of 1.
That's a 32× performance loss on this access!

Why?
  Row size = 128 bytes = 32 × 4-byte words = exactly 32 banks
  So column 0 of every row maps to the same bank.
  stride (128 bytes) is a perfect multiple of bank width (128 bytes).

This is EXACTLY why swizzling exists.

docs.title: 13.5 Swizzle the 16-byte chunks
docs.text: For the 128-byte TMA swizzle, reason in 16-byte chunks, not independent four-byte bank numbers. A useful aligned-atom mapping XORs the chunk index with row % 8. For the column-0 access above, rows 0–31 then hit banks 0,4,8,12,16,20,24,28 repeated four times. This changes the simplified pattern from a 32-way to a four-way conflict; it does not make every possible access conflict-free. The result depends on element width, lane addresses and the chosen atom. Chapter 4 derives the byte mapping; use the matching descriptor and physical layout together.

docs.title: 14 — Registers
docs.text:
Registers are the fastest storage on the chip and the scarcest: 256 KB per SM, divided among every thread resident there.

The tension running through this section is that using more registers per thread makes each thread faster, but lets fewer threads run at once — and past a certain point that trade goes badly.

docs.title: 14.1 Register File Specifications
docs.text:
The specifications, plus the packing rules. Note that FP16 stores two values per register and FP8 stores four — which is why tensor core operands have to be packed before you hand them over.

Register File
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Per SM:        256 KB (65,536 × 32-bit registers)
  Per quadrant:  64 KB  (16,384 × 32-bit registers)
  Access cost:   Instruction/dependency-dependent, not a one-cycle contract.
  Bandwidth and energy depend on operations and implementation;
                 no universal register/shared/HBM ratio is assumed here.

  Every thread gets a PRIVATE set of registers.
  PTXAS reports the compiled register footprint. Supported warp-specialized
  kernels can redistribute a reserved budget with setmaxnreg; see Chapter 9.

  Base unit: 32-bit slots
    ├── FP32:    1 register per value
    ├── FP64:    2 registers per value (register pair)
    ├── FP16:    2 values packed into 1 register
    ├── BF16:    2 values packed into 1 register
    ├── FP8:     4 values packed into 1 register
    ├── INT32:   1 register per value
    └── Pointers: 2 registers (64-bit address)

docs.title: 14.2 Occupancy Limiting
docs.text:
The tradeoff in numbers. Watch for the cliff: because the compiler allocates registers in fixed-size chunks, two extra registers per thread can cost you an entire warp's worth of occupancy.

Register Pressure — The Silent Performance Killer
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Per quadrant: 16,384 registers
  If your kernel uses R registers per thread:

  Max threads per quadrant = floor(16,384 / R)
    But also capped by other limits (warps, shared mem, etc.)

  Example calculations:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Regs/thread    Max threads/quadrant    Max warps/quadrant
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
      32          512                     16 (max)
      64          256                      8
      96          170                      5
     128          128                      4
     160          102                      3
     192           85                      2
     255           64                      2
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

  CRITICAL CLIFF EFFECT:
    63 registers/thread → floor(16384/63) = 260 → 8 warps
    65 registers/thread → floor(16384/65) = 252 → 7 warps

    That's a 12.5% drop in occupancy from adding 2 registers!

    Register allocation has internal GRANULARITY (typically 8 regs).
    The compiler rounds UP to the next granularity boundary.
    A small change in code can push you over a boundary.

docs.title: 14.3 Register Spilling
docs.text:
What happens when you lose that fight, and how to notice that you have.

What Happens When You Run Out of Registers
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  When the compiler needs more registers than the hardware has,
  it "spills" values to slower memory:

  Priority (best to worst):
    1. Registers          ← thread-local operands; instruction-dependent cost
    2. Shared memory      ← optional supported CUDA 13.0+ spill target
    3. Local memory       ← device-memory-backed address space, potentially cached

  CUDA 13.0 opt-in feature (not used by the CUDA 12.8 examples here):
    In supported whole-program compilation, enable_smem_spilling permits
    PTXAS to use shared memory first, with remaining spills in local memory.
    It is disabled by default and consumes shared-memory capacity; measure
    both spill traffic and occupancy before assuming a performance gain.

  How to detect spilling:
    nvcc --ptxas-options=-v  →  shows "spill loads" and "spill stores"
    If you see any, your kernel is likely register-pressure limited.

  How to reduce register usage:
    ├── __launch_bounds__(maxThreads, minBlocks)
    ├── Recompute values instead of storing them
    ├── Pack compatible FP16 pairs when supported; scalar FP16 alone does
    │   not guarantee half the physical register allocation
    └── Restructure code to reduce live variables

Source: NVIDIA shared-memory register spilling requirements.

docs.title: 14.4 WGMMA Register Layout
docs.text:
A forward reference to Chapters 6 and 7. Tensor cores are particular about where their operands live, and the rules are not symmetric between A, B, and C.

WGMMA Register Layout Requirements
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  For Tensor Core operations (WGMMA):

  Matrix A:
    ├── Can be in shared memory OR registers
    ├── If in registers: must follow specific thread-to-element mapping
    └── FP16/BF16: packed 2 per 32-bit register

  Matrix B:
    ├── MUST be in shared memory (SMEM)
    ├── NEVER in registers
    └── This is a hard architectural constraint

  Matrix C (accumulator):
    ├── Distributed across 4 warps (128 threads)
    ├── Each thread holds a small fragment of the output
    ├── Stays in registers throughout the MMA
    └── FP32 accumulation is standard (higher precision)

  Packing requirements:
    FP16:  2 values per 32-bit register → register.xy = {val0, val1}
    BF16:  2 values per 32-bit register → same packing
    FP8:   4 values per 32-bit register → register.xyzw = {v0,v1,v2,v3}

    WGMMA instructions EXPECT packed data. If your data
    isn't packed correctly, the instruction produces garbage.

docs.title: 15 — Instruction Caches (L0 & L1)
docs.text:
Instructions have to be fetched too, and the same caching logic applies to them as to data. There are two levels.

The only practical takeaway is at the end of §15.1: unrolling a loop too aggressively can push your inner loop out of the tiny L0 cache and cost you more than the unrolling saved.

docs.title: 15.1 L0 Instruction Cache
docs.text:
Hopper's SM diagram shows an L0 instruction cache for each SM partition, behind a shared L1 instruction cache. A compact hot loop can benefit from instruction reuse, but neither every first iteration nor every subsequent fetch is guaranteed to hit a particular level. Data-cache sizes must not be reused as instruction-cache capacities, and an instruction-cache hit is not an instruction-latency guarantee.

The practical issue is code footprint. Unrolling and inlining can remove control or call overhead while expanding the instruction working set. Compare variants with the same workload and inspect instruction-fetch stalls instead of assuming that maximum unrolling is best.

docs.title: 15.2 L1 Instruction Cache
docs.text:
The shared instruction-cache level backs the partition-local instruction caches. Capacity, associativity, replacement and timing details require an appropriate published measurement or specification; this guide does not assign an unsupported fixed capacity or latency to them.

NVIDIA's H100 instruction-cache case study shows how larger instruction working sets can degrade a real workload and how selective unrolling can improve it. Use the profiler to compare instruction-fetch stall evidence with register pressure, occupancy and executed instruction count. A reduction in code size is useful only if the complete kernel gets faster.

docs.title: 16 — Thread Block Distribution
docs.text:
This section closes the loop between the code you write — kernel<<<grid, block>>> — and the hardware you've just been reading about.

Two questions get answered: how one block is placed on an SM and split into warps (§16.1), and how many blocks can share an SM at once (§16.2). That second number is what people mean when they say occupancy.

docs.title: 16.1 How CTAs Land on SMs
docs.text:
Follow one thread block from placement through warp scheduling. Each block remains assigned to an SM; warps can execute independently, so __syncthreads() coordinates all participating threads in that block regardless of the illustrated partition placement.

Figure 16.1 — Resource requirements constrain residency; synchronisation controls correctness.

docs.title: 16.2 Multiple CTAs Per SM
docs.text:
Occupancy in one worked example. Whichever resource runs out first — warp slots, registers, or shared memory — is the one that sets your limit.

Multiple CTAs Running Concurrently on One SM
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  An SM can run MULTIPLE thread blocks simultaneously,
  as long as total resources don't exceed limits.

  Example:
    SM capacity: 64 warps, 256 KB registers, 228 KB shared mem

    Block A: 128 threads (4 warps), 64 regs/thread, 32 KB shared
      Resources: 4 warps, 32 KB regs, 32 KB shared

    How many Block A's fit?
      Warps:  64 / 4 = 16 blocks
      Regs:   256 KB / 32 KB = 8 blocks
      Shared: floor(228 KiB / (32 + 1) KiB) = 6 blocks
      (include CUDA's 1 KiB reserved shared memory per CTA)
      Answer: min(16, 8, 6) = 6 blocks per SM

    With 6 blocks: 24 warps active, 192 KiB registers,
    192 KiB dynamic shared plus 6 KiB reserved.
    That is 24/64 = 37.5% warp occupancy.

  Higher occupancy → more warps to hide latency → usually better.
  But diminishing returns after ~50-60% for compute-bound kernels.

docs.title: 17 — PCIe 5.0 Host Interface
docs.text:
The last link, and by a wide margin the slowest: the connection back to the CPU. There is not much to design here, only one rule to internalise, and the bandwidth comparison below makes it obvious.

PCIe 5.0 — CPU ↔ GPU Connection
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Bandwidth:     128 GB/s bidirectional (64 GB/s per direction)
  Generation:    PCIe Gen 5, x16 lanes

  Primary roles:
    1. Data highway: Transfer data between CPU memory and GPU memory
    2. Kernel launch: CPU sends kernel descriptors to GPU
    3. GPUDirect RDMA: Network cards (NICs) can read/write GPU
       memory directly without CPU involvement

  Bandwidth comparison:
    ├── HBM3:      3,350 GB/s (internal GPU memory bandwidth)
    ├── NVLink:      900 GB/s (GPU-to-GPU)
    ├── PCIe 5.0:    128 GB/s (CPU-to-GPU)
    └── Ethernet:     50 GB/s (400GbE network)

  PCIe is the SLOWEST link in the system.
  This is why:
    ├── Model weights should be loaded once and stay on GPU
    ├── Minimize CPU↔GPU data transfers during inference
    ├── GPUDirect RDMA bypasses CPU for network → GPU transfers
    └── NVLink (not PCIe) is used for multi-GPU communication

docs.title: 18 — Putting It All Together
docs.text:
Everything in this chapter, assembled into the path a single GEMM tile actually takes: from host memory into HBM, up through L2 into shared memory, into registers, through the tensor cores, and back out again.

If the individual sections felt disconnected, this is where they join up.

docs.title: 18.1 Complete Data Flow
docs.text:
Read the five steps in order, then read the note at the bottom — the entire point is that steps 2 and 4 are happening at the same time, for different tiles.

Figure 18.1 — The main loop and epilogue have different dataflow and lifetime requirements.

docs.title: 18.2 Memory Hierarchy Summary
docs.text:
The hierarchy on one card. The right-hand columns are the ones worth internalising: each level down costs roughly an order of magnitude more latency and 10× more energy per access.

H100 Memory Hierarchy — Bandwidth vs Capacity
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Level          Size        Bandwidth/model       Latency (illustrative)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Registers     256 KB/SM    ~128 R/W/cycle   operand access; instruction-dependent
  Shared Mem    228 KB/SM    ~0.25 TB/s/SM      ~20 cycles, varies
  L1 Cache      28–256 KiB    (part of shared) ~30 cycles, varies
  L2 Cache      50 MB        ~12 TB/s agg    ~200 cycles, varies
  HBM3          80 GB        3.35 TB/s       ~500 cycles, varies
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  The ratio:
    HBM3 → L2:    ~3.5×  bandwidth amplification
    L2   → SMEM:  ~2.8× GPU-wide (modeled 33 TB/s SMEM vs illustrative 12 TB/s L2)
    SMEM → Regs: no universal bandwidth ratio; operand width and reuse matter

  Each level filters traffic for the next:
    If L1 hits 90%, only 10% of requests reach L2.
    If L2 hits 80%, only 20% of L2 requests reach HBM.
    Total HBM traffic = 10% × 20% = 2% of original requests.

  This cascading filtering is what makes the hierarchy work.

Figure 1.4 — Capacity, product peak bandwidth and a bank-throughput model are different quantities.

docs.text:
Component            Size        Bandwidth      Line/Sector
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
HBM3                 80 GB       3.35 TB/s      —

docs.title: Key Formulas
docs.text:
Occupancy Limiters:
  Max warps from registers: floor(65536 / regs_per_thread) / 32
  Max warps from shared: floor(228 KB / shared_per_block) × warps_per_block
  Max warps from hardware: 64 per SM (16 per quadrant)
  Actual occupancy = min(all three) / 64

Bank Conflict:
  bank = (byte_address / 4) % 32
  Conflict: 2+ threads access different addresses in same bank
  No conflict: all threads access different banks OR same address

Swizzle:
  128B TMA swizzle XORs the 16-byte chunk index with row_index % 8;
  it is not a bank-index XOR with row modulo 32.

Tensor Core throughput (SXM5, derived from published full-GPU totals):
  FP16/BF16: 4,096 FLOPS/cycle/SM (dense)
  FP8:       8,192 FLOPS/cycle/SM (dense)
  Sparse (2:4): 2× dense throughput

docs.title: The Three Laws of H100 Performance
docs.text:
1. ASYNC EVERYTHING
   Use TMA for all bulk data movement.
   Overlap loads with compute via double-buffering.
   Never block an SM waiting for memory.

2. FEED THE TENSOR CORES
   Tensor cores deliver 10-100× the throughput of CUDA cores.
   If your kernel isn't using tensor cores, you're leaving
   90%+ of the chip's capability on the table.

3. RESPECT THE HIERARCHY
   Registers > Shared Mem > L2 > HBM3
   Every access to a lower level is 10-1000× more expensive.
   Design your data layout to maximize hits at each level.

Pause and explain it. These are worked reasoning exercises, not additional hardware execution claims. Attempt each question before opening its answer.

Self-check 1.1. A GPU link is advertised as 900 GB/s bidirectional. What one-way budget may you use in a simple symmetric model?

Worked answer — 1.1

450 GB/s in each direction. Do not compare the 900 GB/s bidirectional sum with a one-way network rate. An eight-port aggregate is also a different quantity from a four-versus-four bisection.

Self-check 1.2. Assume 32 shared-memory banks, four bytes per bank per cycle and a 1.98 GHz clock. Compute the modeled per-SM rate.

Worked answer — 1.2

32 × 4 × 1.98×10⁹ = 253.44×10⁹ bytes/s, or 253.44 GB/s per SM. Multiplying by 132 SMs gives about 33.45 TB/s GPU-wide. This is an assumed bank-throughput model, not a measured bandwidth guarantee.

You now know what the hardware is. Chapter 2 covers the programming model that reaches it: thread block clusters and distributed shared memory, inline PTX assembly, state spaces, the deep-learning number formats, and the address-conversion instructions (cvta, mapa) that later chapters lean on constantly.

Your goal in this chapter

Explain a cluster lifetime, distinguish generic from shared addresses, and map a byte address to a shared-memory bank.

Start with Chapter 1. The first complete program in this chapter is also the installation guide’s first GPU run.

How to read this chapter. It is long, and it is really three chapters stacked together. Sections 1–3 are about clusters — the new level of the CUDA hierarchy that lets thread blocks read each other's shared memory. Sections 4–6 are about inline PTX — how to drop below CUDA C++ and write GPU assembly by hand. Sections 7–16 are the vocabulary those first two halves assume: state spaces, PTX types, packed formats, byte addressing, and the address-conversion instructions that glue them together.

You do not have to read it in order. If you are here because a CUTLASS kernel threw an asm() block at you, start at §5. If you are here for clusters, read §1–3 and stop. Each section opens with a short orientation like this one, and sections marked ★ are complete runnable programs rather than reference material.
