docs.title: 17.2 Full Example: WAR Hazard Prevention with Two Barriers
docs.text:
Manual Worked Example: 

Double-buffer pipeline with WAR prevention.
smem[0] = buffer A, smem[1] = buffer B. Alternating tiles.

Tile K=0:
  data_bar: initialized, expect_tx=1024
  Producer: arrive.expect_tx(data_bar, 1024), cp.async → buf A
  release_bar: initialized with thread_count = blockDim.x (all consumers)
  Consumers: wait(data_bar, phase=0) → data arrives → compute buf A
  Consumers: arrive.release(release_bar) each → count hits 0 → release_bar fires

Tile K=1:
  Producer: wait(release_bar, phase=0) → all consumers done reading buf A
  → Safe to overwrite buf A!
  Producer: arrive.expect_tx(data_bar, 1024), cp.async → buf A (K=2's data)
  Consumers: compute buf B (already loaded from K=1 fetch, overlapping!)


═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  FILE:    ex02_war_prevention.cu
  COMPILE: nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_90a -O2 ex02_war_prevention.cu -o ex02
  RUN:     ./ex02
  EXPECT:  All tiles computed correctly, no WAR corruptions detected.
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// ex02_war_prevention.cu
//
// PURPOSE: Demonstrate WAR hazard prevention using two mbarriers.
//
//   data_bar:    "Has the data arrived from the async copy?"
//                Producer signals (via TMA hardware). Consumers wait.
//
//   release_bar: "Are consumers done reading the buffer?"
//                Consumers signal (via mbarrier.arrive).
//                Producer waits before overwriting the buffer.
//
// PIPELINE:
//   Producer thread: copies tile K into the current buffer
//   Consumer threads: compute on the current buffer
//   Neither overwrites until the other is done.
//
// REQUIRES: sm_90a (H100) or sm_100a (Blackwell)
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cmath>

#define CHECK_CUDA(call)                                           \
    do {                                                           \
        cudaError_t _e = (call);                                   \
        if (_e != cudaSuccess) {                                   \
            fprintf(stderr,                                        \
                    "CUDA ERROR %s:%d: %s\n",                      \
                    __FILE__,                                      \
                    __LINE__,                                      \
                    cudaGetErrorString(_e));                       \
            exit(1);                                               \
        }                                                          \
    } while (0)

static constexpr int TILE = 128; // elements per tile
static constexpr int TBYTES = TILE * sizeof(float);
static constexpr int K_TILES = 8; // total tiles

__global__ void war_prevention_kernel(const float* __restrict__ src,
                                      float* __restrict__ dst,
                                      int K) {
    // ── Shared memory ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    // Two barriers: data_bar (copy→compute handoff) and
    //               release_bar (compute→copy handoff, WAR prevention)
    __shared__ __align__(8) uint64_t data_bar;
    __shared__ __align__(8) uint64_t release_bar;
    __shared__ __align__(
        16) float smem[TILE]; // single buffer (simplified)

    int tid = threadIdx.x;
    int nthreads = blockDim.x;
    uint32_t data_addr = __cvta_generic_to_shared(&data_bar);
    uint32_t release_addr = __cvta_generic_to_shared(&release_bar);

    // ── INIT (thread 0 only, then syncthreads) ────────────────────
    if (tid == 0) {
        // data_bar: 1 producer thread will call arrive.expect_tx
        asm volatile("mbarrier.init.shared::cta.b64 [%0], 1;"
                     :
                     : "r"(data_addr));
        // release_bar: ALL consumer threads will call arrive when done reading
        asm volatile("mbarrier.init.shared::cta.b64 [%0], %1;"
                     :
                     : "r"(release_addr), "r"(nthreads));
    }
    // Publish initialized barrier state to the bulk-async proxy.
    asm volatile("fence.proxy.async.shared::cta;" ::: "memory");
    __syncthreads();

    int data_phase = 0;    // phase for data_bar
    int release_phase = 0; // phase for release_bar

    for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) {

        // ── PRODUCER: wait for consumers to release (WAR prevention) ─
        // On first iteration: release_bar was just initialized but no one
        // has arrived yet, so we pre-arrive all threads to "open" it.
        if (k == 0) {
            // Prime release_bar: all threads arrive so it fires immediately
            // (no previous computation, so the buffer is "free" to write)
            asm volatile(
                "mbarrier.arrive.release.cta.shared::cta.b64 _, [%0];"
                :
                : "r"(release_addr));
        }

        // Producer thread waits on release_bar before overwriting SMEM
        if (tid == 0) {
            // Spin until consumers signal "buffer is free to overwrite"
            uint32_t ready = 0;
            while (!ready) {
                asm volatile(
                    "{\n\t"
                    "  .reg .pred p;\n\t"
                    "  mbarrier.try_wait.parity.acquire.cta.shared::cta.b64"
                    "    p, [%1], %2;\n\t"
                    "  selp.u32 %0, 1, 0, p;\n\t"
                    "}\n\t"
                    : "=r"(ready)
                    : "r"(release_addr),
                      "r"((uint32_t)release_phase));
            }
            release_phase ^= 1;

            // Now safe to load next tile into SMEM
            asm volatile(
                "mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx.release.cta.shared::cta.b64 _, [%0], %1;"
                :
                : "r"(data_addr), "r"((uint32_t)TBYTES));

            const float* tile_src = src + k * TILE;
            for (int i = 0; i < TBYTES; i += 16) {
                uint32_t s = __cvta_generic_to_shared(smem) + i;
                uint64_t g = reinterpret_cast<uint64_t>(
                    reinterpret_cast<const char*>(tile_src) + i);
                asm volatile(
                    "cp.async.bulk.shared::cluster.global.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes"
                    " [%0], [%1], 16, [%2];"
                    :
                    : "r"(s), "l"(g), "r"(data_addr));
            }
            // Bulk loads complete through mbarrier, without a commit_group.
        }

        // ── CONSUMERS: wait for data, compute, then signal release ─────
        // All threads wait for data_bar (copy to complete)
        {
            uint32_t ready = 0;
            while (!ready) {
                asm volatile(
                    "{\n\t"
                    "  .reg .pred p;\n\t"
                    "  mbarrier.try_wait.parity.acquire.cta.shared::cta.b64"
                    "    p, [%1], %2;\n\t"
                    "  selp.u32 %0, 1, 0, p;\n\t"
                    "}\n\t"
                    : "=r"(ready)
                    : "r"(data_addr), "r"((uint32_t)data_phase));
            }
            data_phase ^= 1;
        }

        // Compute: multiply each element by 2.0 and write to dst
        for (int i = tid; i < TILE; i += nthreads) {
            float val = smem[i];
            dst[k * TILE + i] = val * 2.0f;
        }

        // All threads signal release_bar: "done reading this tile"
        // .release ensures the writes to dst are visible before the signal.
        asm volatile(
            "mbarrier.arrive.release.cta.shared::cta.b64 _, [%0];"
            :
            : "r"(release_addr));

        // Sync before next iteration so producer doesn't race ahead
        __syncthreads();
    }

    // Cleanup (optional but good practice)
    if (tid == 0) {
        asm volatile("mbarrier.inval.shared::cta.b64 [%0];"
                     :
                     : "r"(data_addr));
        asm volatile("mbarrier.inval.shared::cta.b64 [%0];"
                     :
                     : "r"(release_addr));
    }
}

int main() {
    printf(
        "╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗\n");
    printf(
        "║  ex02: WAR Prevention — Two-Barrier Pipeline             ║\n");
    printf(
        "╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝\n\n");

    cudaDeviceProp prop;
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaGetDeviceProperties(&prop, 0));
    printf(
        "GPU: %s (SM %d.%d)\n", prop.name, prop.major, prop.minor);
    if (prop.major < 9) {
        fprintf(stderr, "ERROR: requires Hopper (SM 9.0+)\n");
        return 1;
    }

    const int N = K_TILES * TILE;
    float h_in[N], h_out[N], h_exp[N];
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        h_in[i] = (float)i;
        h_exp[i] = i * 2.0f;
    }

    float *d_in, *d_out;
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&d_in, N * sizeof(float)));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&d_out, N * sizeof(float)));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemcpy(
        d_in, h_in, N * sizeof(float), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemset(d_out, 0, N * sizeof(float)));

    war_prevention_kernel<<<1, TILE>>>(d_in, d_out, K_TILES);
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaGetLastError());
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());

    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemcpy(
        h_out, d_out, N * sizeof(float), cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));

    int errors = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
        if (fabsf(h_out[i] - h_exp[i]) > 1e-4f)
            errors++;

    printf("Config: %d tiles × %d elements = %d total\n",
           K_TILES,
           TILE,
           N);
    printf("Element errors: %d / %d\n", errors, N);
    printf("Sample: in=%.0f → out=%.0f (expected %.0f)\n",
           h_in[7],
           h_out[7],
           h_exp[7]);

    printf(
        "\n╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗\n");
    printf("║  %-56s  ║\n",
           errors == 0
               ? "✓ ALL PASS — WAR hazard correctly prevented!"
               : "✗ FAILURES — WAR hazard not correctly handled");
    printf(
        "╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝\n");

    CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(d_in));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(d_out));
    return (errors == 0) ? 0 : 1;
}

GPU: again varies with the card the binary runs on; everything else is deterministic. The host seeds h_in[i] = (float)i and h_exp[i] = i * 2.0f, and the kernel's compute step writes dst[k*TILE+i] = smem[i] * 2.0f after data_bar confirms the tile has arrived — so all K_TILES × TILE = 8 × 128 = 1024 elements match and errors stays 0. The k == 0 priming arrive.release on release_bar is what lets the very first tile's producer proceed immediately, since otherwise it would spin forever waiting on consumer signals that haven't happened yet; from k == 1 onward the producer genuinely blocks on release_bar until the consumers finish reading the buffer it's about to overwrite — the WAR hazard the two-barrier design exists to prevent. The sample index chosen for the in=/out= line is i = 7: in=7 → out=14. As in the previous example, the closing box's right edge runs two columns short of the border above it, for the same reason: the PASS string carries the same two 3-byte UTF-8 glyphs (✓, —) against the byte-counted %-56s field, so the padding comes up two bytes short of the visual width the border uses — regardless of how much slack is left in the 56-byte field itself.

docs.title: 18 — Quick Reference
docs.text: The chapter as reference cards. The two pattern blocks at the end are the ones worth keeping open in another window the first few times you write a pipeline of your own.

docs.title: mbarrier Instruction Reference
docs.text:
Every mbarrier instruction in one table, with what each one does to the phase and the transaction count.

Instruction                                          Purpose
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
mbarrier.init.shared::cta.b64 [addr], count         Create barrier, set thread count
mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx.release...b64 _, [a], tx  Signal arrival + set tx bytes
mbarrier.arrive.release.cta.shared::cta.b64 _, [addr]   Signal arrival (no tx bytes)
mbarrier.try_wait.parity.acquire...b64 p,[a], par   Completion test (may suspend)
mbarrier.test_wait.parity.shared::cta.b64 p,[a],par Non-blocking poll (never suspends)
mbarrier.inval.shared::cta.b64 [addr]               Invalidate/destroy barrier
mbarrier.arrive_drop.release...b64 _, [addr]        Arrive + permanently drop count

docs.title: Phase and Transaction Count Rules
docs.text:
Section 10 condensed. When a kernel hangs, the bug is almost always one of these rules.

Rule                                         Notes
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Phase stored in REGISTERS not SMEM           int phase = 0; (per thread)
Phase toggles with phase ^= 1               After each barrier completion
Pending arrivals reset automatically         To expected arrivals (adjusted by arrive_drop)
tx_count MUST equal actual bytes copied      Off by one → deadlock or early fire
arrive.expect_tx decrements thread count     AND adds tx bytes (two effects!)
Multiple expect_tx calls ADD their bytes     [addr, 512] + [addr, 256] → 768 total
Barrier completes when BOTH counts = 0      Thread arrivals AND tx bytes

docs.title: Fence and Proxy Reference
docs.text:
Which fence to reach for, given who is producing and who is consuming.

Fence Type                    PTX                          When to Use
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Release (producer)            fence.release.cta            After writing, before signal
Acquire (consumer)            fence.acquire.cta            After signal, before reading
Cross-proxy                   fence.proxy.async             Generic writes before Async reads
try_wait built-in acquire     try_wait.parity.acquire       Use this; avoids separate fence

docs.title: Synchronization Primitive Comparison
docs.text:
All the primitives in this chapter side by side — scope, cost, and what each one is actually for.

Primitive            Scope       Blocking?  Counts        Use Case
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
__syncthreads()      CTA         Yes        Threads        Simple intra-block sync
mbarrier + try_wait  CTA/Cluster Optional   Threads+Bytes  Async data pipeline (TMA)
barrier.cluster      Cluster     Yes        Blocks         Cross-block DSMEM safety
Named barrier        Warp subset Yes        Threads        Producer/consumer within block
cp.async.bulk.wait_group CTA     Yes        Groups         Bulk copy batch control

docs.title: The Producer/Consumer mbarrier Pattern
docs.text:
The canonical loop. Copy this rather than reconstructing it from memory.

INIT (once):
  [thread 0] mbarrier.init [mbar], 1
  asm volatile("fence.proxy.async.shared::cta;" ::: "memory"); // before TMA use
  __syncthreads()
  int phase = 0;                          // REGISTER, not SMEM

EACH TILE:
  [thread 0] mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx.release [mbar], TILE_BYTES
  [thread 0] cp.async.bulk.tensor ... [mbar]    // links TMA to mbar
  ... do independent work (latency hiding) ...
  [all]      loop: try_wait.parity.acquire [mbar], phase → until true
  [all]      use the data; finish any async readers before releasing storage
  [all]      phase ^= 1                   // toggle for next iteration
  __syncthreads()
  → repeat (no re-init needed: barrier auto-resets thread count!)

docs.title: cp.async.bulk Group Pattern
docs.text:
The §15 pattern for operation variants using bulk async-group completion. Choose the completion mechanism required by the instruction and direction.

// Issue copies (uncommitted):
cp.async.bulk ... ;       // tile K+1
cp.async.bulk ... ;       // tile K+1 part 2

// Commit into a group:
cp.async.bulk.commit_group;   // → Group N

// Wait for older groups (pipeline control):
cp.async.bulk.wait_group 1;   // all groups except the 1 most recent are done
// → Groups 0..N-1 are complete; Group N may still be in flight

Pause and explain it. These are worked reasoning exercises, not additional hardware execution claims. Attempt each question before opening its answer.

Self-check 3.1. A barrier expects one producer arrival and a 512-float transfer. Is producer arrival alone enough to release consumers?

Worked answer — 3.1

No. For FP32, the expected transaction count is 512 × 4 = 2,048 bytes. The phase completes only after both the required arrival and the associated transaction completion conditions are satisfied.

Self-check 3.2. The data-ready wait completed. May the producer immediately load the next tile into the same buffer?

Worked answer — 3.2

No. Readiness establishes that the current data arrived, not that readers are finished. The producer also needs the consumer-to-producer release/empty handshake. Track these two ownership transitions separately.

Next — Chapter 4: cuTensorMap, TMA & Swizzling

Chapter 3 gave you the synchronisation. Chapter 4 gives you the copy — or rather its setup: the TMA descriptor, all twelve parameters of cuTensorMapEncodeTiled(), the dimension-ordering and stride-unit rules that break most first attempts, and swizzling to keep the arriving tile free of bank conflicts.

Validation — November 17, 2026. 2 complete CUDA programs compiled and executed successfully. Follow-up: the final two-H100 audit records a fresh run of the complete programs. The original dated transcripts below remain available for provenance. Execution system: 1× H100 PCIe, 114 SMs, 80 GB class; Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS; driver 580.105.08; CUDA Toolkit 12.8.93; sm_90a, C++17, -O2. Full system information · CUDA result manifest. Each tested source and captured output is linked beside its example. Diagrams open as original SVGs for zooming.

Baseline compiler flags — use each example’s full command below: nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_90a -O2 <file>.cu -o <out> Run with: ./<out> on Hopper hardware matching the compiled target. sm_90a binaries are not a portable Blackwell build.

Your goal in this chapter

Write tensor dimensions and byte strides with the innermost coordinate first; explain the difference between logical coordinates and swizzled shared-memory addresses.

Chapter 3 supplies the completion protocol; Chapter 5 issues the transfer described here.

What this covers: Everything from Lesson 4 — what TMA is and why it exists, how descriptors replace manual address calculation, the full cuTensorMapEncodeTiled() API (all 12 parameters explained with worked examples), data types, tensor rank and global dimensions, stride semantics, box dimensions, swizzling (32B/64B/128B) and bank-conflict elimination with the XOR formula, interleaving for non-linear layouts (16B and 32B modes), L2 promotion policies for prefetching, and out-of-bounds fill behavior. Every section includes ASCII diagrams, manual worked examples with concrete numbers, and compileable code with full test harnesses.

How to read this chapter. Chapter 1 introduced the TMA as the piece of hardware that fetches tiles while your threads compute. This chapter is about the object you hand it: the descriptor, a small struct built once on the host that tells the TMA the shape of your tensor, the size of the tile you want, and how to lay it out in shared memory once it arrives.

Almost everything here happens before the kernel runs. The next chapter covers the instruction that uses the descriptor; this one covers getting the descriptor right — which is where the real difficulty lives, because invalid descriptor parameters may be rejected by the API, while a valid descriptor with the wrong layout can copy plausible but incorrect bytes. Check the return code and verify the full output.

The chapter runs in four movements. Sections 1–3 explain what a descriptor is and why it replaces address arithmetic. Sections 4–8 walk the twelve parameters of cuTensorMapEncodeTiled() one at a time — this is the reference core. Sections 9–11 are about shared-memory layout: bank conflicts, swizzling, and interleaving. Sections 12–13 cover two optional behaviours that cost nothing to enable and are easy to overlook.

If you only read part of this chapter, read §7 and §8. Dimension ordering and stride units are the two places where nearly every first descriptor goes wrong.
