The tested listing retains conservative wgmma.fence calls after waits. These calls are unnecessary for reading completed results; the waits provide completion. Its source comments are preserved with the executed artifact.

GPU: identifies the tested SKU. This example uses FP16 inputs and FP16 accumulators: the PTX WGMMA BF16 input variant requires FP32 accumulators. Inputs are rounded to FP16 before the reference is computed. Both complete 64×64 output tiles are checked, including all four stmatrix.x4 slices per warp; checking only positive register sums would miss an incomplete epilogue. The uniform input makes every expected output equal: this catches missing stores and nonfinite values, but cannot detect every transposition or permutation. Before reusing the epilogue with new layouts, add nonuniform inputs and check each logical coordinate against a reference. See the CUDA 12.8 PTX WGMMA specification.

Stronger nonuniform audit test

From the repository root, python3 tools/audit_nonuniform_epilogue.py prepares an audit variant and checks its reference pattern on the CPU. It uses 4,096 distinct, exactly representable FP16 output values to expose coordinate permutations. The device implementation is preserved; only host inputs and coordinate checks change.

python3 tools/audit_nonuniform_epilogue.py --run additionally compiles and executes that variant on a suitable Hopper host, saving separate timestamped source hashes and logs under build/audit/. The follow-up GPU test passed on November 17, 2026: zero coordinate errors across both 64×64 output tiles on an H100 80GB HBM3. See the captured source, commands and output. This checks the implemented shape and layout; it does not establish correctness for arbitrary layouts.

The closing banner repeats Chapter 6's byte-vs-codepoint %-56s quirk, with this chapter's own numbers: ✓ ALL PASS — commit/wait pipeline + stmatrix working! is 53 codepoints but 57 UTF-8 bytes (✓ and — each cost 3 bytes for 1 displayed column, wasting 2 bytes apiece). Since 57 already exceeds the 56-byte field width, printf pads with nothing, and the line prints at its raw length. Measured in the columns a terminal actually draws, that puts the whole bordered line — the fixed "║ " and " ║" margins plus 53 content columns, 59 in total — exactly 1 column short of the 60-column border above it, the same shortfall Chapter 6 hit with a differently-worded message of the same coincidental 53-codepoint length.

docs.title: 19 — Quick Reference
docs.text: The chapter as reference cards. As in Chapter 6, the Common Mistakes card at the end is worth reading even though nothing in it is new — these are the bugs that compile cleanly.

docs.title: wgmma Group API
docs.text:
Commit and wait in one card. Remember that N is how many groups may remain outstanding, not how many to wait for.

Instruction                              Purpose
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
wgmma.commit_group.sync.aligned          Seal pending wgmma ops into a group
wgmma.wait_group.sync.aligned N          Wait until ≤ N groups still pending
wgmma.fence.sync.aligned                 Order prior ordinary register accesses before WGMMA

N=0: drain ALL groups → safe to read d[] for epilogue
N=1: wait for all except 1 → read older groups while newest runs
N>1: keep multiple groups in flight → deep pipeline (rare)

docs.title: stmatrix Reference
docs.text:
The instruction forms, and the reminder that there is no 32-bit variant.

Variant                                        Data    Output      Use Case
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
stmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.x4.shared.b16       FP16x2  16×16      FP16/BF16 accumulator ★
stmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.x2.shared.b16       FP16x2   8×16      Half-tile writes
stmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.x1.shared.b16       FP16x2   8×8       Minimal tile / boundary
stmatrix.sync.aligned.m16n8.x4.trans.shared.b8 8-bit   4×(16×8)   Blackwell-family only (sm_100a+)
stmatrix.sync.aligned.m16n8.x1/x2.trans.shared.b8  8-bit  1-2×(16×8)  Blackwell-family only

CORRECTION: there is no "m8n8 + .b8" stmatrix on Hopper — that combination
is not a documented instruction. The ONLY 8-bit stmatrix shape is m16n8,
it is TRANSPOSE-ONLY (.trans is mandatory, not optional), and it requires
Blackwell-family targets (sm_100a and newer) — not sm_90a. On Hopper, an
INT8 uses s32 accumulators; store them with integer stores or explicitly convert.
FP8 inputs support f16/f32 accumulators; choose the corresponding output path.


FP32 accumulators: stmatrix has NO .f32 variant!
  Option A: cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 to downcast + pack → stmatrix.b16 (lossy)
  Option B: st.shared.f32 directly from d[] registers (correct FP32, manual scatter)

docs.title: FP8 Formats at a Glance
docs.text:
E4M3 and E5M2 side by side — bit layout, range, and which phase each one is for.

Format   Bits  E  M  Max Value  Best For              Notes
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
E4M3     8     4  3  448        Forward pass (weights, acts)  Has NaN, no Inf
E5M2     8     5  2  57344      Backward pass (gradients)     Has Inf and NaN
e4m3x2   16    —  —  —          Conversion/transport pack       2 E4M3 packed
e4m3x4   32    —  —  —          Storage, transport            4 E4M3 packed
e5m2x2   16    —  —  —          cvt output (not a full RS register)  2 E5M2 packed
e5m2x4   32    —  —  —          Storage, transport            4 E5M2 packed

docs.title: FP8 Quantization Instructions
docs.text:
The conversion instructions, with their saturation behaviour.

Instruction                                   Input   Output    Notes
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cvt.rn.satfinite.e4m3x2.f16x2  fp8, fp16x2   f16x2  e4m3x2   2 FP16 → 2 FP8 E4M3
cvt.rn.satfinite.e5m2x2.f16x2  fp8, fp16x2   f16x2  e5m2x2   2 FP16 → 2 FP8 E5M2
cvt.rn.satfinite.e4m3x2.f32    fp8, f32, f32  2×f32  e4m3x2   2 FP32 → 2 FP8 E4M3
.satfinite: out-of-range values clamp to ±max (don't become Inf/NaN)

docs.title: Sparse WGMMA sp-sel and sp-meta Rules
docs.text:
Precision Sparsity K/op sp-sel Metadata per retained position/group TF32 1:2 16 0 or 1, thread pair One 4-bit index per pair: 4 or 14 FP16/BF16 2:4 32 0 or 1, thread pair Two 2-bit indices per quartet FP8 E4M3/E5M2 2:4 64 0, all four threads Two 2-bit indices per quartet INT8/UINT8 2:4 64 0, all four threads Two 2-bit indices per quartet

Update metadata for the actual A tile; no mandatory metadata cycling or loop unrolling follows from these encodings. See the primary-source layout links in §§16–17.

docs.title: wgmma.fence Placement Checklist
docs.text:
Section 5 as a checklist. Run through it when a pipeline produces intermittently wrong results.

  □ BEFORE the first wgmma.mma_async in any new warpgroup sequence
  □ Wait for all groups using d[] before reading it; no post-wait fence needed
  □ AFTER ldmatrix (if A is loaded to registers) and BEFORE wgmma that uses them
  □ After ordinary register updates, before a new WGMMA uses those registers

  Do NOT use wgmma.fence for:
  ✗ Ordering SMEM writes visible to wgmma → use mbarrier.try_wait.acquire
  ✗ Cross-proxy ordering → use fence.proxy.async
  ✗ Ordering global memory operations → use fence.sc.gpu or similar

docs.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
docs.text:
Each entry is a bug that produces wrong numbers rather than an error message. Check here before reaching for a profiler.

Mistake                                    Symptom              Fix
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Missing fence before first wgmma.mma_async Wrong accumulator     Add wgmma.fence before
Fence used instead of completion wait      Pending d[] accesses  Commit and wait for the relevant groups
Reading d[] while group still pending       Race condition         wait_group<0> first
stmatrix.b16 with FP32 d[] registers        Type mismatch compile  cvt to FP16 first
FP8 data in MN-major layout for wgmma      Scrambled results      Stage in K-major SMEM
Using ldmatrix.b8 on Hopper (sm_90a)       Compile error          Use SS or a matching non-transposed ldmatrix.b16 packed-byte load
sp-sel nonzero for FP8 sparse wgmma        Wrong/undefined result Use sp-sel=0 for FP8/INT8
Metadata does not match the current A tile Wrong sparse product Supply correct per-lane metadata
TF32 metadata uses 1-bit indices          Invalid encoding      Pack 4-bit indices 4 or 14
FP8 numerical error exceeds tolerance      Accuracy failure      Test scaling and FP32 two-level accumulation

Pause and explain it. These are worked reasoning exercises, not additional hardware execution claims. Attempt each question before opening its answer.

Self-check 7.1. How many collective stmatrix.x4.b16 stores cover one 64×64 FP16 result?

Worked answer — 7.1

The output contains 64 × 64 × 2 = 8,192 bytes. One warp-collective x4 store writes 512 bytes, so the warpgroup needs 16 such collective stores in total: four calls per warp across four warps. A single call per warp leaves most of the tile unstored.

Self-check 7.2. Why is “all accumulator sums are positive” a weak correctness check?

Worked answer — 7.2

It can pass with permuted values, missing stores, or a partly written output. Check every output against a reference, reject nonfinite values, and use position-dependent inputs to expose layout permutations. The tested pipeline also checks both full stored tiles.

Next — Chapter 8: Kernel Design, Warp Specialization & Pipelining

Part V assembles everything so far into real kernels. Chapter 8 opens with the roofline model — deciding whether a kernel is compute- or memory-bound before optimising it — then covers producer/consumer warp specialisation, setmaxnreg for dynamic register allocation, and multi-stage circular buffering.

Shared-stage lifetime. A committed WGMMA group may still read its shared operands. Wait until the last group using a stage completes before releasing that stage to TMA or another producer. Commit is not release, and waiting solely before the epilogue does not protect a buffer that is overwritten earlier. A 64×256 output slice can be covered by one m64n256k16 instruction per K step; eight m64n32k16 calls are only one possible decomposition, not a hardware requirement.

docs.title: 1.1 Two Roofline Bounds, Then a Measured Bottleneck
docs.text:
The roofline model compares two throughput bounds: the rate at which memory can supply bytes and the rate at which the selected arithmetic units can execute work. The lower bound defines the modeled ceiling. A real kernel can run below both because of dependencies, instruction issue, synchronization, or too little parallel work. Use arithmetic intensity to predict a ceiling, then profile to identify the implementation’s actual bottleneck.

The key quantity is Arithmetic Intensity (AI): how many floating-point operations you perform per byte of data you move between the memory hierarchy and the compute units.

H100 SXM product-peak model. Arithmetic intensity uses useful FLOPs divided by transferred bytes.

The Roofline Model — Visual and Equations
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Arithmetic Intensity (AI):
    AI = Total FLOPs executed / Total bytes moved from/to HBM
    Units: FLOP/Byte

  The Ridge Point (crossover):
    Ridge Point = Peak FLOPS / Peak Bandwidth
    H100 SXM5 example:
      FP16 Tensor Core FLOPS: 989 TFLOPS
      HBM3 Bandwidth:         3.35 TB/s
      Ridge (FP16 Tensor):    989 / 3.35 ≈ 295 FLOP/Byte
      Ridge (FP32 CUDA core): ~67 TFLOPS / 3.35 ≈ 20 FLOP/Byte

  The Roofline Chart:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Performance │                                                   │
  │ (TFLOPS)    │                         ╔══════════════════════   │
  │   989 ──────┼────────────────────────═╝ ← Compute Roof (FP16) │
  │             │              ╔══════════════════                  │
  │             │             /          compute-bound region       │
  │             │            / ← slope = bandwidth (3.35 TB/s)     │
  │             │           /                                       │
  │             │   memory-bound region                             │
  │       0 ────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │             │         ↑               ↑                         │
  │             │      AI=20           AI=295                       │
  │             │  (FP32 ridge)    (FP16 ridge)                     │
  │             └─────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
  │                         Arithmetic Intensity (FLOP/Byte)        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Reading the chart:
    • AI < ridge point → the modeled memory ceiling is lower.
      Throughput ≤ AI × bandwidth.
    • AI > ridge point → the selected arithmetic ceiling is lower.
      Throughput ≤ peak FLOPS.

  KEY INSIGHT: The roofline proposes a limit to investigate.
    Measured bandwidth limit? Reduce traffic (tiling, caching, fusion).
    Measured arithmetic limit? Improve use of the relevant execution units.
    Far below both roofs? Inspect parallelism, dependencies and issue stalls.

docs.title: 1.2 Computing AI for Real Operations
docs.text:
Calculate intensity with an explicit traffic model and instruction family. For the FP16 rows below, count each stored element as two bytes and assume one read per input and one write per output. Cache misses, repeated tile loads, reductions and intermediate arrays can increase actual HBM traffic.

Arithmetic Intensity — Illustrative Whole-Problem Traffic
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Operation                Useful work          Bytes       Intensity
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  FP16 ReLU                N comparisons        4N          0.25 comparison/B
  FP16 bias add            N additions          6N          0.167 FLOP/B
  FP16 GEMM n=4096         2n³                   6n²         1365 FLOP/B
  FP16 GEMM n=256          2n³                   6n²         85.3 FLOP/B
  FP16 GEMM M=1,N=K=4096   2MNK                  2(MK+NK+MN) ≈1 FLOP/B

  Compare only with the appropriate arithmetic roof. For the SXM FP16
  Tensor Core ridge near 295 FLOP/B, the n=256 model lies below the ridge,
  while n=4096 lies above it. A scalar-FP32 implementation has a different
  roof and element width. Comparisons, exponentials and divisions also
  need their own throughput accounting; a FLOP ceiling alone is incomplete.

  Fusion may eliminate an intermediate global read/write, but softmax and
  normalization require reductions. They are not arbitrary pointwise
  epilogues; the fused algorithm must preserve their dependency structure.

  Computing AI for your own kernel:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Method 1: Nsight Compute → "roofline" section → reads AI directly
  Method 2: Calculate manually:
    FLOPs = count arithmetic ops in kernel × number of elements
    Bytes = (reads from global) + (writes to global), each in bytes
    AI = FLOPs / Bytes
  Method 3: Use the formula for GEMM:
    AI_GEMM = 2MNK / (bytes_per_element × (MK + NK + MN))
    For square matrices (M=N=K=n):
      AI = 2n³ / (bytes_per_element × 3n²) = (2/3) × n / bytes_per_element
    (CORRECTED: the general formula's denominator carries the storage
    width as an explicit bytes_per_element factor, not a hidden
    constant — the two worked cases below now agree with each other
    and with the FP16 row in the table above.)
    At n=4096, FP16 (bytes_per_element=2):
      AI = (2/3) × 4096/2 ≈ 1365 FLOP/Byte (matches the ~1370 FP16
      GEMM row in the table above)
    At n=4096, FP32 (bytes_per_element=4):
      AI = (2/3) × 4096/4 ≈ 683 FLOP/Byte

docs.title: ★ Section 1 — Runnable Code: Roofline Profiler
docs.text:
Manual Worked Example:

Let's manually compute AI for the test kernels below.

Kernel A: elementwise_scale (multiply each element by a scalar)
  Input: N=1M float32 values = 4 MB read
  Output: N=1M float32 values = 4 MB write
  Total bytes: 8 MB
  FLOPs: N multiplications = 1M FLOPs
  AI = 1M / 8M = 0.125 FLOP/Byte → heavily memory-bound

Kernel B: matrix_multiply_naive (M=N=K=512)
  Input: A matrix (512×512 × 4 bytes) = 1MB, B matrix = 1MB
  Output: C matrix = 1MB
  Total bytes: 3 MB
  FLOPs: 2 × 512³ = 268M FLOPs
  AI = 268435456 / 3145728 = 85.3 FLOP/byte, above the FP32 ridge.
  This rules out the HBM roof as the tightest ideal roof; it does not
  establish the measured kernel's limiting issue/SMEM dependency.

Expected profiler output:
  elementwise_scale: AI ≈ 0.125 → MEMORY-BOUND
  matrix_multiply:   AI ≈ 85.3    → COMPUTE-BOUND

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  FILE:    ex01_roofline.cu
  COMPILE: nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_90a -O2 ex01_roofline.cu -o ex01_roofline
           (Also works on sm_80 — no Hopper-specific features)
  RUN:     ./ex01_roofline
  EXPECT:  AI values with memory-bound/compute-bound classification,
           measured vs theoretical bandwidth and FLOPS.
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// ex01_roofline.cu
//
// PURPOSE: Measure actual bandwidth and FLOP rate of two kernels
//   to demonstrate the Roofline model in practice.
//
// KERNELS:
//   Kernel A: elementwise_scale  — memory-bound (AI ≈ 0.125)
//   Kernel B: tile_matmul        — compute-bound (AI >> 20)
//
// WHAT TO LOOK FOR:
//   - Kernel A achieves close to peak memory bandwidth
//   - Kernel A is far from peak FLOPS (memory limited)
//   - Kernel B achieves higher FLOPS, limited by compute
//   - Both kernels are described by the roofline
//
// WORKS ON: sm_80, sm_86, sm_89, sm_90a, sm_100a
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cmath>

// For timing
#include <cuda_runtime.h>

#define CHECK_CUDA(call)                                           \
    do {                                                           \
        cudaError_t _err = (call);                                 \
        if (_err != cudaSuccess) {                                 \
            fprintf(stderr,                                        \
                    "CUDA ERROR at %s:%d — %s\n",                  \
                    __FILE__,                                      \
                    __LINE__,                                      \
                    cudaGetErrorString(_err));                     \
            exit(1);                                               \
        }                                                          \
    } while (0)

// ─── Timing helper ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Returns elapsed time in milliseconds between two CUDA events.
// Usage:
//   cudaEvent_t start, stop;
//   cudaEventCreate(&start); cudaEventCreate(&stop);
//   cudaEventRecord(start);
//   ... kernel launch ...
//   cudaEventRecord(stop);
//   cudaEventSynchronize(stop);
//   float ms = elapsed_ms(start, stop);
float elapsed_ms(cudaEvent_t start, cudaEvent_t stop) {
    float ms = 0.0f;
    cudaEventElapsedTime(&ms, start, stop);
    return ms;
}

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// KERNEL A: Elementwise Scale — Memory-Bound
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
//
// Each thread reads one float, multiplies by scale, writes one float.
// AI = 1 multiply / (4+4 bytes) = 0.125 FLOP/Byte
//
// This kernel is entirely limited by HBM bandwidth.
// No matter how fast the FP32 ALUs are, the bottleneck is moving
// the data from HBM to registers and back.
__global__ void elementwise_scale(const float* __restrict__ input,
                                  float* __restrict__ output,
                                  float scale,
                                  int N) {
    int idx = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (idx < N) {
        // One load, one multiply, one store.
        // The __restrict__ qualifier tells the compiler these pointers
        // don't alias, enabling better scheduling.
        output[idx] = input[idx] * scale;
    }
}

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// KERNEL B: Tiled Matrix Multiply — Compute-Bound
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
//
// Computes C = A × B using shared memory tiling.
// For TILE=32, M=N=K=512:
//   FLOPs = 2 × 512³ = 268M
//   Bytes = (512²+512²+512²) × 4 = 3MB
//   AI ≈ 85.3 FLOP/Byte → well above FP32 ridge (~20 FLOP/Byte)
//
// The tiling pattern (load tile to SMEM, compute from SMEM) is
// the classic way to improve AI: each element of A and B is loaded
// TILE times instead of once, multiplying the AI by TILE.
//
// ─── Why AI improves with tiling ────────────────────────────────
// Without tiling: AI = 2K / (K + K) * ...(complex)... ≈ N/2 for square
// With TILE tiling: each element of A is loaded once per K/TILE steps
//   and reused TILE times from SMEM → TILE× better bandwidth efficiency
#define TILE 32

__global__ void tile_matmul(const float* __restrict__ A,
                            const float* __restrict__ B,
                            float* __restrict__ C,
                            int M,
                            int N,
                            int K) {
    // ── Shared memory tiles ─────────────────────────────────────
    __shared__ float As[TILE][TILE];
    __shared__ float Bs[TILE][TILE];

    int row = blockIdx.y * TILE + threadIdx.y;
    int col = blockIdx.x * TILE + threadIdx.x;

    float acc = 0.0f; // accumulator stays in register throughout

    // ── K-loop: load tiles and accumulate ───────────────────────
    // Each iteration loads a TILE×TILE tile of A and B into SMEM,
    // then does TILE² multiply-add operations from SMEM (cheap).
    // After K/TILE iterations, acc holds the full dot product.
    for (int t = 0; t < K / TILE; t++) {
        // Collaborative load: each thread loads one element of A and B
        if (row < M && t * TILE + threadIdx.x < K)
            As[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] =
                A[row * K + t * TILE + threadIdx.x];
        else
            As[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = 0.0f;

        if (col < N && t * TILE + threadIdx.y < K)
            Bs[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] =
                B[(t * TILE + threadIdx.y) * N + col];
        else
            Bs[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = 0.0f;

        __syncthreads(); // wait for all threads to finish loading

// ── Compute from SMEM (cheap, ~10 cycle latency) ────────
// TILE multiply-adds per element, using the shared tile.
// These run from SMEM, not HBM — ~10 cycle vs ~500 cycle.
#pragma unroll
        for (int k = 0; k < TILE; k++) {
            acc += As[threadIdx.y][k] * Bs[k][threadIdx.x];
        }

        __syncthreads(); // wait before loading next tile
    }

    if (row < M && col < N)
        C[row * N + col] = acc;
}

// ─── Main ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
int main() {
    printf(
        "╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗\n");
    printf(
        "║  Roofline Model Demo — Memory vs Compute Bound        ║\n");
    printf(
        "╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝\n\n");

    // ── Get GPU specs ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    cudaDeviceProp prop;
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaGetDeviceProperties(&prop, 0));
    printf(
        "GPU: %s (SM %d.%d)\n", prop.name, prop.major, prop.minor);
    printf("     Peak memory bandwidth (theoretical): %.1f GB/s\n",
           (double)prop.memoryBusWidth / 8.0 *
               prop.memoryClockRate * 2.0 / 1e6);
    printf("     SM count: %d\n\n", prop.multiProcessorCount);

    // ── Kernel A: Elementwise Scale ───────────────────────────────
    printf(
        "════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n");
    printf(
        "KERNEL A: elementwise_scale (expected: MEMORY-BOUND)\n");
    printf(
        "════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n");
    {
        const int N = 64 * 1024 * 1024; // 64M elements = 256MB
        const float SCALE = 2.5f;

        // Theoretical AI = 1 FLOPs / 8 bytes = 0.125 FLOP/Byte
        double ai_theoretical = 1.0 / 8.0;
        double flops_total = (double)N;
        double bytes_total =
            2.0 * N * sizeof(float); // read + write

        printf(
            "  Elements: %dM    Bytes moved: %.0f MB    AI: %.3f FLOP/Byte\n",
            N / (1024 * 1024),
            bytes_total / 1e6,
            ai_theoretical);
        printf(
            "  (Ridge point for FP32 CUDA cores ≈ 20 FLOP/Byte)\n");
        printf("  → AI=%.3f << 20 → MEMORY-BOUND ✓\n\n",
               ai_theoretical);

        float *d_in, *d_out;
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&d_in, N * sizeof(float)));
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&d_out, N * sizeof(float)));
        // Initialize (don't care about values for timing purposes)
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemset(d_in, 0, N * sizeof(float)));

        // Warm up the GPU (avoids one-time initialization in timing)
        elementwise_scale<<<N / 256, 256>>>(d_in, d_out, SCALE, N);
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());

        // ── Timed run ──────────────────────────────────────────
        cudaEvent_t start, stop;
        cudaEventCreate(&start);
        cudaEventCreate(&stop);

        const int REPS = 10;
        cudaEventRecord(start);
        for (int i = 0; i < REPS; i++)
            elementwise_scale<<<N / 256, 256>>>(
                d_in, d_out, SCALE, N);
        cudaEventRecord(stop);
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
        float ms = elapsed_ms(start, stop) / REPS;

        double bw_achieved =
            bytes_total / (ms / 1000.0) / 1e9; // GB/s
        double gflops_achieved =
            flops_total / (ms / 1000.0) / 1e9; // GFLOPS

        printf("  Time: %.3f ms\n", ms);
        printf("  Bandwidth achieved: %.1f GB/s\n", bw_achieved);
        printf("  GFLOPS achieved:    %.1f\n", gflops_achieved);
        printf(
            "  → Kernel is BANDWIDTH limited (not compute limited)\n");

        cudaEventDestroy(start);
        cudaEventDestroy(stop);
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(d_in));
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(d_out));
    }

    // ── Kernel B: Tiled Matrix Multiply ──────────────────────────
    printf(
        "\n════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n");
    printf("KERNEL B: tile_matmul (expected: COMPUTE-BOUND)\n");
    printf(
        "════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n");
    {
        const int M = 512, N = 512, K = 512;

        double flops_total =
            2.0 * M * N * K; // multiply + add per element
        double bytes_total =
            ((double)M * K + (double)K * N + (double)M * N) *
            sizeof(float);
        double ai = flops_total / bytes_total;

        printf(
            "  M=N=K=%d    FLOPs: %.1f M    Bytes: %.1f MB    AI: %.1f FLOP/Byte\n",
            M,
            flops_total / 1e6,
            bytes_total / 1e6,
            ai);
        printf(
            "  → AI=%.1f >> 20 → HIGH-AI: inspect issue/shared-memory/dependency limits\n\n",
            ai);

        float *d_A, *d_B, *d_C;
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&d_A, M * K * sizeof(float)));
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&d_B, K * N * sizeof(float)));
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&d_C, M * N * sizeof(float)));
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemset(
            d_A, 1, M * K * sizeof(float))); // fill with 0x01
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemset(d_B, 1, K * N * sizeof(float)));

        dim3 block(TILE, TILE);
        dim3 grid((N + TILE - 1) / TILE, (M + TILE - 1) / TILE);

        // Warm up
        tile_matmul<<<grid, block>>>(d_A, d_B, d_C, M, N, K);
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());

        cudaEvent_t start, stop;
        cudaEventCreate(&start);
        cudaEventCreate(&stop);

        const int REPS = 20;
        cudaEventRecord(start);
        for (int i = 0; i < REPS; i++)
            tile_matmul<<<grid, block>>>(d_A, d_B, d_C, M, N, K);
        cudaEventRecord(stop);
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
        float ms = elapsed_ms(start, stop) / REPS;

        double gflops_achieved = flops_total / (ms / 1000.0) / 1e9;
        double bw_achieved = bytes_total / (ms / 1000.0) / 1e9;

        printf("  Time: %.3f ms\n", ms);
        printf("  GFLOPS achieved: %.1f\n", gflops_achieved);
        printf(
            "  Effective BW:    %.1f GB/s (not the bottleneck)\n",
            bw_achieved);
        printf(
            "  → AI selects the compute roof; measured bottleneck is not established (bandwidth not saturated)\n");

        cudaEventDestroy(start);
        cudaEventDestroy(stop);
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(d_A));
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(d_B));
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(d_C));
    }

    printf(
        "\n╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗\n");
    printf(
        "║  KEY TAKEAWAY:                                        ║\n");
    printf(
        "║  • elementwise_scale: optimize bandwidth, not FLOPs   ║\n");
    printf(
        "║  • tile_matmul: optimize FLOPs, pipeline depth        ║\n");
    printf(
        "║  • Wrong optimization → wrong results → wasted time   ║\n");
    printf(
        "╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝\n");

    return 0;
}

docs.title: 2.1 The Three Signatures of a Compute-Bound Kernel
docs.text:
An AI above the matching ridge identifies a lower modeled arithmetic ceiling. To call an implementation compute-bound, investigate its execution-pipe demand, achieved throughput, and stalls; low HBM utilization alone is insufficient.

One qualitative signature of imbalance; use counters and timings to confirm it.

Compute-Bound Signatures — What to Look For
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  SIGNATURE 1: High Arithmetic Intensity
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  AI > ridge point (>295 FLOP/Byte for FP16 Tensor on H100)
  The kernel does many arithmetic operations per byte it loads.
  Example: GEMM with large tiles, attention with many heads.

  SIGNATURE 2: Producer/Consumer Warp Imbalance
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  A clue to investigate consumer-side work, not a complete diagnosis.
  When you look at the kernel timeline in Nsight Compute, you see:

  Time →
  Producer warps: [LOAD][LOAD][LOAD][WAIT.....][LOAD][LOAD][WAIT...]
  Consumer warps: [MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA]

  The producer warps are idle (waiting at barriers) while consumer
  warps are 100% busy doing WGMMA.
  Producers waiting for a free stage show that consumers are not releasing
  stages fast enough. The cause may be arithmetic, epilogue work, scheduling,
  dependencies or synchronization. Measure before selecting a fix.

  SIGNATURE 3: High SM Activity, Low Memory Transactions
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Nsight Compute → Memory Workload Analysis:
    "Memory Throughput" = low % of peak
    "Compute Throughput" = high % of peak
  The kernel is not bottlenecked on HBM reads/writes.

  ─── How to Classify Using Nsight ────────────────────────────────
  1. Profile with: ncu --metrics all ./my_kernel
  2. Look for "achieved_occupancy" and "sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak"
  3. Look for "l1tex__t_bytes.sum" and "dram__bytes.sum"
  4. Identify the busy execution pipe and stalls; SM activity alone is not arithmetic saturation

  ─── Common Compute-Bound Kernels ────────────────────────────────
  ├── GEMM with large M,N,K (the king of compute-bound)
  ├── Batched GEMM with sufficient batch size
  ├── Flash Attention 2/3 (for large sequence lengths)
  ├── Convolutions with large channel counts
  └── Any kernel that streams data into tensor cores

  ─── The Key Question for Optimization ───────────────────────────
  "Are my tensor cores busy 100% of the time?"
  If NO → your job is to eliminate everything that prevents this.
    Sources of idle time: barrier stalls, memory stalls, branch divergence,
    producer/consumer imbalance, insufficient pipelining.
  If YES → you're at (or near) the hardware limit. Time to choose
    between better algorithms or accept the limit.

docs.title: 2.2 Optimization Techniques Overview
docs.text:
For compute-bound kernels, there are seven major optimization strategies. Each is covered in depth in the sections that follow.

Compute-Bound Optimization Hierarchy
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Priority  Technique                  Sections  Impact
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1 (HIGH)  Warp Specialization        4-6       Decouples loads & math
  2 (HIGH)  Pipelining (multi-stage)   7-8       Hides memory latency
  3 (HIGH)  mbarrier synchronization   9-10      Efficient producer-consumer
  4 (MED)   Pipeline Architecture      13-14     Ping-pong vs cooperative
  5 (MED)   Cluster TMA multicast      Lesson 2  Reduces HBM bandwidth
  6 (LOW)   Epilogue Fusion            15-16     Eliminates separate kernels
  7 (LOW)   Persistent Scheduling      17-18     Eliminates wave quantization

  ─── What NOT to Optimize for Compute-Bound Kernels ─────────────
  ✗ Bank conflicts (usually not the bottleneck)
  ✗ Global memory coalescing (already high AI means few global reads)
  ✗ Occupancy optimization (more threads may hurt register availability)
  ✓ Reduce unnecessary arithmetic when it preserves the required result

  The goal is simple: keep the tensor cores busy 100% of the time.
  Everything else is in service of that goal.

docs.title: 3.1 The Three Memory-Bound Categories
docs.text:
Memory-bound is not a single condition. The bottleneck can be at three different points in the memory hierarchy, each with different fixes.

Combine timing, traffic, instruction progress and resource constraints.

Three Categories of Memory-Bound Kernels
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ─── Category 1: Bandwidth-Bound ─────────────────────────────────
  Symptom: DRAM throughput near peak (>80% of HBM bandwidth)
  Cause: The kernel moves many bytes relative to its FLOPs.
  Examples: elementwise ops, data type conversions, reductions,
            layer norm, softmax.
  Fix:
    ├── Epilogue fusion — merge the op into an adjacent GEMM
    ├── Operator fusion — combine multiple ops into one kernel
    ├── Vector loads — use float4 instead of float (wider transactions)
    └── Reduce bytes moved — use smaller data types (FP16 vs FP32)

  ─── Category 2: Latency-Bound ───────────────────────────────────
  Symptom: Low DRAM throughput AND low FLOP rate. Hardware is "stuck".
  Cause: Long dependency chains (each operation waits for the previous).
         OR: synchronization overhead (barriers, atomics, fences).
  Examples: Reduction kernels with poor tree structure, kernels with
            many dependent memory accesses (pointer-following).
  Fix:
    ├── Increase thread-level parallelism (more independent operations)
    ├── Software prefetching (issue loads early before data is needed)
    ├── Warp-level primitives instead of shared memory for reductions
    └── Avoid __syncthreads() where possible (use warp intrinsics)

  ─── Category 3: Locality-Bound ──────────────────────────────────
  Symptom: Excess DRAM traffic relative to useful bytes and poor reuse.
           Many cache misses despite seemingly reasonable access patterns.
  Cause: Data accessed in random order, cache thrashing, TLB pressure,
         working set larger than L2 cache.
  Examples: Embedding lookups, sparse ops, gather/scatter.
  Fix:
    ├── Reorder data in memory to match access pattern
    ├── Blocking/tiling to fit working set in cache
    ├── Swizzling (covered in Section 18)
    └── Reduce working set size

  ─── Diagnosis Flowchart ──────────────────────────────────────────

  Start: Is HBM bandwidth > 80% of peak?
    YES → Bandwidth-bound → fuse or reduce bytes
    NO  → Is FLOP rate > 20% of peak?
      YES → partially compute-bound → increase occupancy or AI
      NO  → Is SM utilization > 50%?
        YES → Latency-bound → break dependency chains
        NO  → Check grid size, parallelism, launch geometry and tail effects

docs.title: 3.2 The Epilogue as the Universal Memory-Bound Killer
docs.text:
In a real training pipeline, the operations after GEMM (bias, activation, scaling) are all memory-bound. Instead of running them as separate kernels (3+ HBM round-trips), they are fused into the GEMM epilogue (0 extra HBM round-trips — the data stays in registers).

Without Fusion vs With Fusion — Bandwidth Analysis
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Operation: GEMM → bias → ReLU → layer_norm → write output
  Matrix size: M=N=4096 (output = 4096×4096 × 4 bytes = 64 MB)

  WITHOUT FUSION (4 separate kernels):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Kernel 1 (GEMM):       compute A×B, write 64MB to HBM
  Kernel 2 (bias add):   read 64MB from HBM, add bias, write 64MB
  Kernel 3 (ReLU):       read 64MB from HBM, apply ReLU, write 64MB
  Kernel 4 (layer norm): read 64MB from HBM, normalize, write 64MB

  Total HBM traffic: 64MB + 128MB + 128MB + 128MB = 448MB
  At 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth: 448MB / 3350 GB/s = 0.13ms (JUST bandwidth)
  Plus 4 kernel launches, 4 sets of cache invalidations, etc.

  WITH EPILOGUE FUSION (1 kernel):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Kernel 1 (GEMM+epilogue): compute A×B in registers
    → apply bias IN REGISTERS (0 HBM reads)
    → apply ReLU IN REGISTERS (0 HBM reads)
    → apply layer norm PARTIALLY in registers + SMEM
    → write 64MB final output to HBM

  Total HBM traffic for the fused parts: 64MB (only the final write)
  That's 7× less HBM traffic for the epilogue portion!

  RULE: If an operation runs immediately after a GEMM and its
        output is consumed by a later GEMM, it should be in
        the epilogue, not a separate kernel.

docs.title: 4.1 The Core Concept — Intentional Role Division
docs.text:
On any GPU, an SM hosts many active warps, but only a few can issue instructions each cycle. The default scheduling model lets all warps do the same type of work (e.g., all warps do loads AND math). This creates competition: warps doing math occupy slots that warps needing to do loads could use.

Warp Specialization breaks this competition by giving different warps permanently different jobs for the entire kernel execution. Some warps become dedicated "producers" that only move data. Other warps become dedicated "consumers" that only perform arithmetic.

Dedicated producer and consumer roles can simplify a deep pipeline.

Warp Specialization — Before and After
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ─── WITHOUT Warp Specialization ─────────────────────────────────

  All warps do both load and compute:

  Warp 0:  [LOAD][LOAD]....wait....[MMA][MMA][LOAD][LOAD]....wait....
  Warp 1:  ...[LOAD][LOAD]....wait....[MMA][MMA][LOAD][LOAD]....wait.
  Warp 2:  ......[LOAD][LOAD]....wait....[MMA][MMA][LOAD][LOAD].....
  Warp 3:  .........[LOAD][LOAD]....wait....[MMA][MMA][LOAD]........

  Problems:
  ├── "wait" cycles: memory latency (~500 cycles) blocks math issue
  ├── Register file split: same warp needs regs for BOTH load state
  │   AND math accumulator → half the registers for each → spilling
  └── Compiler can't schedule optimally: mixed dependencies

  ─── WITH Warp Specialization ────────────────────────────────────

  Producer warps (e.g., WG0): ONLY issue loads and manage barriers
  Consumer warps (e.g., WG1, WG2): ONLY issue WGMMA instructions

  WG0 (Producer):  [TMA][TMA][TMA][TMA][TMA][TMA][TMA][TMA][TMA]
  WG1 (Consumer):  [MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA]
  WG2 (Consumer):  [MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA][MMA]

  Results:
  ├── Producer runs ~32 registers (only manages pointers/barriers)
  ├── Consumer runs ~200 registers (holds full output tile)
  ├── Both run SIMULTANEOUSLY on the same SM
  └── Memory latency HIDDEN by overlapping with compute

  ─── The Three Reasons It Works ──────────────────────────────────

  Reason 1 — Resource separation:
    A WGMMA consumer needs ~200 registers/thread for its accumulator tile.
    A TMA producer needs ~32 registers/thread for barrier management.
    A kernel starts with one allocation per thread, determined by its
    maximum live set. Sequential roles do not automatically add their
    register counts. Without reallocation the producer warps reserve
    the same per-thread budget as consumer warps, even while using
    fewer registers. setmaxnreg redistributes this CTA register pool.
    With separation: producer threads commit only ~32 registers/thread
    (128 × 32 = 4,096 total) and consumer threads commit the full
    ~200-232 registers/thread — each role pays only for what it
    actually uses, so the SM's 65,536-register budget stretches
    further across more resident threads.

  Reason 2 — Latency hiding by overlap:
    While WG0 waits for the TMA to fill SMEM (~400 cycles),
    WG1 is executing WGMMA on the PREVIOUS tile's data.
    No SM cycles are wasted — either loads or math is happening.

  Reason 3 — Avoiding SIMT branch divergence:
    If a single warp does if (i_am_producer) { ... } else { ... },
    the warp must execute BOTH branches serially (SIMT divergence).
    With warp specialization: producer warps ONLY execute producer code,
    consumer warps ONLY execute consumer code. Zero divergence.

docs.title: 4.2 Implementing Warp Specialization in Code
docs.text:
The key to implementing warp specialization is determining, at runtime, which warp group the current thread belongs to — and then branching into the appropriate persistent loop.

Warp Specialization Code Pattern
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  How to identify warp group membership:

  // Warp ID within the block (0 to num_warps-1)
  int warp_id = threadIdx.x / 32;

  // Warp GROUP ID (groups of 4 warps, 128 threads each)
  int warpgroup_id = warp_id / 4;

  // Total warpgroups per block
  // If block has 384 threads: 384/128 = 3 warpgroups (WG0, WG1, WG2)

  // Branch based on role
  if (warpgroup_id == 0) {
      // I am a PRODUCER warpgroup
      producer_loop(...);
  } else {
      // I am a CONSUMER warpgroup
      consumer_loop(warpgroup_id - 1, ...);  // consumer index 0 or 1
  }

  ─── The Key Dispatch Pattern ─────────────────────────────────────

  // Typical H100 GEMM warp layout:
  // 384 threads per block = 3 warpgroups:
  //   WG0 (threads 0-127):   Producer  — TMA loads
  //   WG1 (threads 128-255): Consumer0 — WGMMA + epilogue
  //   WG2 (threads 256-383): Consumer1 — WGMMA + epilogue (ping-pong)

  constexpr int THREADS_PER_WARPGROUP = 128;  // 4 warps × 32 threads

  int warpgroup_id = threadIdx.x / THREADS_PER_WARPGROUP;

  if (warpgroup_id == 0) {
      // Producer code path
      // This branch never issues WGMMA instructions
      // It only: waits on empty barriers, issues TMA cp.async.bulk,
      //          signals full barriers, manages pipeline state
  } else {
      // Consumer code path
      // This branch never issues TMA instructions
      // It only: waits on full barriers, issues WGMMA,
      //          signals empty barriers, writes epilogue output
  }

  ─── Why Branches Don't Cause Divergence ─────────────────────────
  Divergence occurs when threads in the SAME WARP take different paths.
  In warp specialization, the branch boundary aligns to WARP GROUP
  boundaries (multiples of 128 threads = 4 warps).
  WG0's warps ALL take the producer branch.
  WG1's warps ALL take the consumer branch.
  No single warp straddles the boundary → zero divergence.

docs.title: ★ Section 4 — Runnable Code: Warp Specialization Demo
docs.text:
Manual Worked Example:

We launch a kernel with 256 threads = 2 warp groups (WG0 and WG1). - WG0 (threads 0-127): "producer" — writes a buffer with values computed from thread index - WG1 (threads 128-255): "consumer" — reads that buffer and doubles the values

Without proper synchronization, WG1 might read before WG0 finishes. We use __syncthreads() here for simplicity (a real pipeline would use mbarrier — covered in Section 9).

Expected data flow:
  WG0 thread 0:  smem[0]   = 0   × 3 + 7 = 7
  WG0 thread 1:  smem[1]   = 1   × 3 + 7 = 10
  WG0 thread 63: smem[63]  = 63  × 3 + 7 = 196
  WG0 thread 127:smem[127] = 127 × 3 + 7 = 388

After sync, WG1 reads and doubles:
  WG1 thread 0 (local_idx=0): output[0] = smem[0]  × 2 = 14
  WG1 thread 1 (local_idx=1): output[1] = smem[1]  × 2 = 20
  WG1 thread 127 (local_idx=127): output[127] = 388 × 2 = 776

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  FILE:    ex02_warp_spec.cu
  COMPILE: nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_90a -O2 ex02_warp_spec.cu -o ex02_warp_spec
           (Also works on sm_80, sm_86, sm_89)
  RUN:     ./ex02_warp_spec
  EXPECT:  All 128 consumer outputs verified as 2×(3×idx+7),
           role assignment report showing clean WG separation.
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// ex02_warp_spec.cu
//
// PURPOSE: Demonstrate warp specialization — intentional role division.
//
// LAYOUT:
//   256 threads per block = 2 warpgroups
//   WG0 (threads   0-127): PRODUCER — fills shared memory buffer
//   WG1 (threads 128-255): CONSUMER — reads buffer, doubles values
//
// WHAT TO LOOK FOR IN OUTPUT:
//   - Role assignment: each warpgroup correctly identifies itself
//   - All 128 consumer outputs match expected: 2 × (3*idx + 7)
//   - No divergence: all producer threads do exactly the same work,
//     all consumer threads do exactly the same work
//
// NOTE: In production kernels, the __syncthreads() between producer
// and consumer is replaced by mbarrier (Section 9). __syncthreads()
// is used here for clarity.
//
// WORKS ON: sm_80+ (no Hopper-specific features)
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdint>

#define CHECK_CUDA(call)                                           \
    do {                                                           \
        cudaError_t _err = (call);                                 \
        if (_err != cudaSuccess) {                                 \
            fprintf(stderr,                                        \
                    "CUDA ERROR at %s:%d — %s\n",                  \
                    __FILE__,                                      \
                    __LINE__,                                      \
                    cudaGetErrorString(_err));                     \
            exit(1);                                               \
        }                                                          \
    } while (0)

// Size of each warpgroup (4 warps × 32 threads = 128 threads)
constexpr int WARPGROUP_SIZE = 128;

// ── Producer function ─────────────────────────────────────────────
// Only called by WG0 threads.
// Fills shared memory with a pattern: value = local_idx * 3 + 7
// This simulates loading data from global memory / TMA.
__device__ void
producer_work(float* smem, int local_idx, int wg_size) {
    // Each producer thread writes its own slot
    float val = local_idx * 3.0f + 7.0f;
    smem[local_idx] = val;

    // In a real pipeline, this is where you'd issue TMA and
    // signal the full barrier. Here, the global __syncthreads()
    // in the main kernel serves as our barrier.
}

// ── Consumer function ─────────────────────────────────────────────
// Only called by WG1 threads.
// Reads from shared memory (written by producer) and doubles it.
// local_idx = thread index within WG1 (0 to 127).
__device__ float consumer_work(const float* smem, int local_idx) {
    // Read from SMEM (populated by producer) and compute
    float val = smem[local_idx];
    return val * 2.0f; // "process" the data
}

// ── Main kernel ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
// 256 threads: WG0 produces, WG1 consumes.
// Shared memory buffer is the communication channel.
__global__ void warp_specialized_kernel(
    float* output,    // output array [128 floats]
    int* role_record) // records which WG each thread belongs to
{
    // Shared buffer: WG0 writes, WG1 reads.
    // Size = 1 warpgroup worth of data (128 floats)
    __shared__ float smem_buffer[WARPGROUP_SIZE];

    // ── Determine role ───────────────────────────────────────────
    // Warpgroup = which group of 128 threads am I in?
    // WG0: threads 0-127   → warpgroup_id = 0 → PRODUCER
    // WG1: threads 128-255 → warpgroup_id = 1 → CONSUMER
    int warpgroup_id = threadIdx.x / WARPGROUP_SIZE;
    int local_idx =
        threadIdx.x % WARPGROUP_SIZE; // 0..127 within WG

    // Record which role this thread has (for verification)
    // Only thread 0 of each WG records to avoid races
    if (local_idx == 0) {
        role_record[warpgroup_id] = warpgroup_id;
    }

    // ── Warp-specialized execution ────────────────────────────────
    // No single warp straddles this if-else boundary.
    // WG0's warps ALL take the if-branch.
    // WG1's warps ALL take the else-branch.
    // → Zero warp divergence.

    if (warpgroup_id == 0) {
        // ── PRODUCER path ──────────────────────────────────────
        // WG0: fill the shared memory buffer
        // Each of the 128 producer threads fills one slot
        producer_work(smem_buffer, local_idx, WARPGROUP_SIZE);

        // After filling, the producer has nothing else to do.
        // In a real kernel, it would loop to load the NEXT tile.
        // Here it just participates in the barrier below.

    } else {
        // ── CONSUMER path ──────────────────────────────────────
        // WG1: wait for producer data, then process it.
        // In a real kernel, we'd wait on an mbarrier here.
        // We fall through to __syncthreads() below.
    }

    // ── Barrier: ensure producer finished before consumer reads ──
    // In a real warp-specialized kernel, this is replaced by mbarrier.
    // __syncthreads() works here because it synchronizes ALL threads
    // in the block, including both WG0 and WG1.
    //
    // Timeline:
    //   WG0: fills smem_buffer ─────────────────────── │syncthreads│ idle
    //   WG1: idle (skips producer code) ──────────────── │syncthreads│ reads smem
    //                                                         ↑
    //                           Both WGs must reach here before either proceeds
    __syncthreads();

    // ── Consumer processes shared memory ─────────────────────────
    // Only WG1 threads do this work.
    // WG0 threads skip (warpgroup_id == 0 → not the else branch).
    if (warpgroup_id == 1) {
        float result = consumer_work(smem_buffer, local_idx);
        // Write result to global output
        // Consumer's local_idx 0..127 maps to output[0..127]
        output[local_idx] = result;
    }
}

// ─── Main ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    // ── Launch: 1 block, 256 threads (2 warpgroups) ──────────────

    CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());

    float h_output[OUTPUT_SIZE];
    int h_roles[2];
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemcpy(h_output,
                          d_output,
                          OUTPUT_SIZE * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemcpy(
        h_roles, d_roles, 2 * sizeof(int), cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));

    // ── Verify role assignment ────────────────────────────────────
    printf("Role Assignment Check:\n");
    printf("  WG0 role recorded: %d (expected 0 = producer)\n",
           h_roles[0]);
    printf("  WG1 role recorded: %d (expected 1 = consumer)\n",

    printf("  Checking all 128 outputs...\n\n");

    // Print first 8 and last 4 for display
    printf("  %-8s %-12s %-12s %-8s\n",
           "Index",

    printf("  %s\n", "────────────────────────────────────────");

    for (int i = 0; i < OUTPUT_SIZE; i++) {

        "\n════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n");
    printf("Results: %d/%d output values correct\n",
           OUTPUT_SIZE - errors,

    bool all_pass = (errors == 0 && roles_ok);
    printf(
        "\n╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗\n");

docs.title: 5.1 The Register Budget Problem
docs.text:
The H100's SM has 65,536 × 32-bit registers, divided among all active threads. A warpgroup running WGMMA needs ~200 registers per thread to hold the output tile accumulators. A producer warpgroup doing TMA loads needs only ~32 registers per thread.

If you launch a kernel naively at 200 registers/thread for everyone, you lose occupancy. If you launch at 32 registers/thread, the consumers can't hold their accumulators and spill to local memory (HBM) — catastrophically slow.

setmaxnreg solves this by letting warpgroups dynamically resize their register allocation at runtime.

setmaxnreg — What It Does and When to Use It
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  PTX instruction: setmaxnreg.inc.sync.aligned.u32 LIMIT;
                   setmaxnreg.dec.sync.aligned.u32 LIMIT;

  .inc = increase to LIMIT (consumer warpgroups call this)
  .dec = decrease to LIMIT (producer warpgroups call this)

  VALID LIMITS: Per the PTX ISA, imm-reg-count must be in the range
  24–256 (both inclusive) and must be a multiple of 8. Common values:
    24  — absolute minimum
    32  — producer warps (TMA + barrier management only)
    40  — small compute tasks
    128 — moderate accumulator
    160 — typical consumer warpgroup
    232 — maximum practical (leaving room for control logic)
    256 — hardware maximum (CORRECTED: not 255 — the PTX ISA's
          imm-reg-count range is 24-256 inclusive, a clean multiple
          of 8 on both ends; 255 is not itself a multiple of 8 and
          was never a legal value here)

  ─── Budget Registers Within the CTA ────────────────────────────

  For one 128-thread producer and one 128-thread consumer:
    producer limit = 32, consumer limit = 232
    final allocation = 128×32 + 128×232 = 33792 registers
    average budget = 33792/256 = 132 registers per thread

  A 64-register initial budget cannot fund that split: decreasing one
  warpgroup releases only 4096 registers, while the other needs 21504 more.
  Select a sufficient initial allocation and check compiler/resource output.
  Register allocation granularity can require rounding above this average.

  setmaxnreg redistributes registers from the CTA's own register pool.
  It does not lend them to another CTA or increase resident block occupancy
  after launch. An increase blocks until enough registers are available;
  newly acquired register contents are undefined and must be initialized.
  All warps in the warpgroup must execute the same instruction, and must
  explicitly synchronize before a subsequent setmaxnreg operation.

  ─── C++ Interface ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  // Use the documented inline-PTX setmaxnreg instruction; __syncwarp is synchronization, not a resizing intrinsic:
  __syncwarp();
  // Decrease (for producers):
  asm volatile("setmaxnreg.dec.sync.aligned.u32 %0;" :: "n"(32));
  // Increase (for consumers):
  asm volatile("setmaxnreg.inc.sync.aligned.u32 %0;" :: "n"(232));

  // The "n" constraint = compile-time constant (required by hardware)
  // The .sync means all threads in the warp must reach this point
  // The .aligned means warpgroup must reach it together (128 threads)

docs.title: ★ Section 5 — Runnable Code: setmaxnreg Demo
docs.text:
Manual Worked Example:

We launch 256 threads. WG0 decreases to 32 registers (producer), WG1 increases to 128 registers (consumer). We verify that: 1. The PTX executes without error 2. After setmaxnreg, threads can still compute correctly 3. The register counts are (conceptually) different between warpgroups

Register allocation timeline for the executable below:
  Launch contract: __maxnreg__(80), two 128-thread warpgroups.
  Budget for this split: 256×80 = 20480 registers.

  WG0 decreases 80→32: releases 128×48 = 6144 registers.
  WG1 increases 80→128: requests 128×48 = 6144 registers.
  Final split: 128×32 + 128×128 = 20480 registers.

  The arithmetic check validates the tested execution; it does not measure
  each thread's live register use or demonstrate an occupancy increase.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  FILE:    ex03_setmaxnreg.cu
  COMPILE: nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_90a -O2 ex03_setmaxnreg.cu -o ex03_maxreg
           NOTE: setmaxnreg is a Hopper (sm_90a+) instruction.
                 Will not compile on sm_80 or earlier.
  RUN:     ./ex03_maxreg
  EXPECT:  Both warpgroups produce correct results after setmaxnreg,
           demonstrating that register resize does not corrupt state.
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// ex03_setmaxnreg.cu
//
// PURPOSE: Demonstrate setmaxnreg — dynamic register resizing.
//
// DESIGN:
//   WG0 (threads 0-127):   calls setmaxnreg.dec(32) → producer registers
//   WG1 (threads 128-255): calls setmaxnreg.inc(128) → consumer registers
//
//   After resizing, both warpgroups perform arithmetic to prove
//   that register state is preserved through the resize operation.
//
// IMPORTANT: setmaxnreg MUST be aligned (all threads in warpgroup
// must execute it simultaneously, hence .aligned variant).
//
// REQUIRES: sm_90a (Hopper) or sm_100a (Blackwell)
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cmath>

#define CHECK_CUDA(call)                                           \
    do {                                                           \
        cudaError_t _err = (call);                                 \
        if (_err != cudaSuccess) {                                 \
            fprintf(stderr,                                        \
                    "CUDA ERROR at %s:%d — %s\n",                  \
                    __FILE__,                                      \
                    __LINE__,                                      \
                    cudaGetErrorString(_err));                     \
            exit(1);                                               \
        }                                                          \
    } while (0)

constexpr int WARPGROUP_SIZE = 128;
constexpr int PRODUCER_REGS =
    32; // minimum for producer (TMA + barriers)
constexpr int CONSUMER_REGS =
    128; // moderate consumer register budget

// ── Kernel ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Tests that setmaxnreg works correctly and doesn't corrupt computation.
//
// Protocol:
//   1. All threads compute an initial value (before setmaxnreg)
//   2. setmaxnreg changes register allocation
//   3. All threads perform MORE arithmetic (uses same registers!)
//   4. We verify that the final result is correct
//
// If setmaxnreg corrupted registers, the second computation would be wrong.
__global__ void __maxnreg__(80)
    test_setmaxnreg(float* output_wg0, float* output_wg1) {
    int warpgroup_id = threadIdx.x / WARPGROUP_SIZE;
    int local_idx = threadIdx.x % WARPGROUP_SIZE;

    // ── Step 1: Compute initial value (before any register resize) ─
    // Both warpgroups do this. The value lives in a register.
    float accumulator =
        (float)(local_idx * 2 + 1);           // 1, 3, 5, 7, ...
    float factor = (float)(warpgroup_id + 1); // WG0: 1.0, WG1: 2.0

    if (warpgroup_id == 0) {
        // ── PRODUCER warpgroup: decrease registers ────────────────
        // setmaxnreg.dec: "I am releasing registers down to PRODUCER_REGS"
        // The .sync means: this thread can't issue instructions after
        //                  this point until ALL threads in the warpgroup reach it.
        // The .aligned means: every thread in the warp group must
        //                     execute this together.
        asm volatile("setmaxnreg.dec.sync.aligned.u32 %0;" ::"n"(
            PRODUCER_REGS));
        // After this point: WG0 has PRODUCER_REGS registers available.
        // The register 'accumulator' and 'factor' STILL EXIST because
        // the compiler arranged them to fit within PRODUCER_REGS.
        // (If they didn't fit, the compiler would spill — check with --ptxas-options=-v)

    } else {
        // ── CONSUMER warpgroup: increase registers ─────────────────
        // setmaxnreg.inc: "I am claiming more registers up to CONSUMER_REGS"
        asm volatile("setmaxnreg.inc.sync.aligned.u32 %0;" ::"n"(
            CONSUMER_REGS));
        // After this point: WG1 has CONSUMER_REGS registers available.
        // The existing registers 'accumulator' and 'factor' are still valid.
        // WG1 now has room for more intermediate results.
    }

    // ── Step 2: More computation AFTER register resize ────────────
    // This tests that setmaxnreg did not corrupt the existing register state.
    // If registers were corrupted, this computation would produce wrong results.
    //
    // We do a small computation that uses the pre-resize values:
    //   result = accumulator * factor + local_idx * 0.5
    //
    // WG0: accumulator = 2*idx+1, factor = 1.0 → result = 2*idx+1 + 0.5*idx = 2.5*idx+1
    // WG1: accumulator = 2*idx+1, factor = 2.0 → result = 2*(2*idx+1) + 0.5*idx = 4.5*idx+2
    float result = accumulator * factor + (float)local_idx * 0.5f;

    // Do a few more ops to stress-test register integrity
    result =
        result * 1.0f + 0.0f; // identity: should not change result
    result = result + 0.0f;

    // ── Step 3: Write results ──────────────────────────────────────
    if (warpgroup_id == 0) {
        output_wg0[local_idx] = result;
    } else {
        output_wg1[local_idx] = result;
    }
}

int main() {
    printf(
        "╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗\n");
    printf(
        "║  setmaxnreg Demo — Dynamic Register Resizing         ║\n");
    printf(
        "╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝\n\n");

    // Check for Hopper
    cudaDeviceProp prop;
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaGetDeviceProperties(&prop, 0));
    printf("GPU: %s (SM %d.%d)\n\n",
           prop.name,
           prop.major,
           prop.minor);
    if (prop.major < 9) {
        fprintf(
            stderr,
            "ERROR: setmaxnreg requires Hopper (SM 9.0+) or Blackwell.\n");
        return 1;
    }

    printf("Register Plan:\n");
    printf(
        "  WG0 (threads   0-127): setmaxnreg.dec → %d regs (producer)\n",
        PRODUCER_REGS);
    printf(
        "  WG1 (threads 128-255): setmaxnreg.inc → %d regs (consumer)\n\n",
        CONSUMER_REGS);

    float *d_wg0, *d_wg1;
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&d_wg0, WARPGROUP_SIZE * sizeof(float)));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&d_wg1, WARPGROUP_SIZE * sizeof(float)));

    test_setmaxnreg<<<1, 256>>>(d_wg0, d_wg1);
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaGetLastError());
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());

    float h_wg0[WARPGROUP_SIZE], h_wg1[WARPGROUP_SIZE];
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemcpy(h_wg0,
                          d_wg0,
                          WARPGROUP_SIZE * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemcpy(h_wg1,
                          d_wg1,
                          WARPGROUP_SIZE * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));

    // Verify WG0 results: result = (2*idx+1)*1.0 + idx*0.5 = 2.5*idx + 1
    printf("WG0 (PRODUCER, %d regs after resize):\n",
           PRODUCER_REGS);
    int errors_wg0 = 0, errors_wg1 = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < WARPGROUP_SIZE; i++) {
        float expected = (2.0f * i + 1.0f) * 1.0f + (float)i * 0.5f;
        if (fabsf(h_wg0[i] - expected) > 1e-4f) {
            errors_wg0++;
            if (errors_wg0 <= 3)
                printf("  FAIL [%d]: got %.4f expected %.4f\n",
                       i,
                       h_wg0[i],
                       expected);
        }
    }
    if (errors_wg0 == 0) {
        printf(
            "  ✓ All %d values correct (registers NOT corrupted by setmaxnreg)\n",
            WARPGROUP_SIZE);
        printf(
            "  Sample: output[0]=%.1f (expect 1.0), output[1]=%.1f (expect 3.5)\n",
            h_wg0[0],
            h_wg0[1]);
    }

    // Verify WG1 results: result = (2*idx+1)*2.0 + idx*0.5 = 4.5*idx + 2
    printf("\nWG1 (CONSUMER, %d regs after resize):\n",
           CONSUMER_REGS);
    for (int i = 0; i < WARPGROUP_SIZE; i++) {
        float expected = (2.0f * i + 1.0f) * 2.0f + (float)i * 0.5f;
        if (fabsf(h_wg1[i] - expected) > 1e-4f) {
            errors_wg1++;
            if (errors_wg1 <= 3)
                printf("  FAIL [%d]: got %.4f expected %.4f\n",
                       i,
                       h_wg1[i],
                       expected);
        }
    }
    if (errors_wg1 == 0) {
        printf(
            "  ✓ All %d values correct (registers NOT corrupted by setmaxnreg)\n",
            WARPGROUP_SIZE);
        printf(
            "  Sample: output[0]=%.1f (expect 2.0), output[1]=%.1f (expect 6.5)\n",
            h_wg1[0],
            h_wg1[1]);
    }

    bool all_pass = (errors_wg0 == 0 && errors_wg1 == 0);
    printf(
        "\n╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗\n");
    if (all_pass) {
        printf(
            "║  ✓ ALL TESTS PASSED                                  ║\n");
        printf(
            "║  setmaxnreg correctly resized registers without      ║\n");
        printf(
            "║  corrupting existing register state.                 ║\n");
    } else {
        printf(
            "║  ✗ FAILURES: WG0=%d errors, WG1=%d errors            ║\n",
            errors_wg0,
            errors_wg1);
    }
    printf(
        "╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝\n");

    CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(d_wg0));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(d_wg1));
    return all_pass ? 0 : 1;
}
