docs.title: 11.1 Placement of launch_dependents in Production Kernels
docs.text:
Where you place griddepcontrol.launch_dependents inside Kernel A critically determines how much overlap you get. Too late: Kernel B's cold-start delay adds to total latency. Too early: both kernels compete for SM resources and can slow each other down.

launch_dependents Placement — Decision Guide
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ─── Non-persistent Kernel A (fixed grid, each block does one tile) ─

  Each thread block writes its output tile to global memory, then
  exits. The signal fires when all blocks have issued it OR retired.

  Correct placement:
    kernel_producer(...) {
        compute tile...
        write output tile to DRAM...
        __threadfence();             // ensure writes complete
        __syncthreads();
        if (threadIdx.x == 0) {
            griddepcontrol.launch_dependents;
        }
        // done — block exits
    }

  This is a conservative after-store trigger per CTA. The scheduler waits for
  ALL CTAs to either fire or retire before dispatching Kernel B.

  ─── Persistent Kernel A (one block processes many tiles in a loop) ─

  The block runs a loop processing tile_0, tile_1, ..., tile_last.
  Signal placement is a performance choice. It can precede pipeline
  completion because the dependent waits before reading producer output.
  The producer must still drain its own async operations before exit.

  CONSERVATIVE — trigger after all tile work including epilogue:
    while (has_more_tiles()) {
        process_tile();         // TMA load → WGMMA → epilogue → store
    }
    griddepcontrol.launch_dependents;  // ← kernel is basically done

  EQUIVALENT AFTER-STORE POINT — final tile's epilogue:
    while (has_more_tiles()) {
        process_tile_mainloop();     // TMA + WGMMA
        process_tile_epilogue();     // stores to output
        if (is_last_tile()) {
            __threadfence();
            if (threadIdx.x == 0) {
                griddepcontrol.launch_dependents;
            }
        }
    }
    // Kernel A now only drains pipeline state; no more output writes.

  ─── With warp specialization (producer/consumer warpgroups) ─────

  Consumer warpgroup owns the epilogue stores.
  Signal should come from the consumer warpgroup AFTER its final
  tma_store commits.

  if (is_consumer_warpgroup && is_last_tile) {
      // after cp.async.bulk.commit_group for final tile:
      __threadfence();
      if (warpgroup_elected_thread) {
          griddepcontrol.launch_dependents;
      }
  }

docs.title: 12.1 Boot and Park: What Happens Before .wait
docs.text:
Kernel B's warps begin executing as soon as the scheduler dispatches their blocks to free SMs. They can run any dependency-free instructions before reaching .wait. This is the overlap window where useful work happens:

Kernel B Execution Before and After .wait
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Timeline for one Kernel B warp after launch_dependents fires:

  WARP STATE:     dispatched → running → PARKED → running → done
                  │           │          │         │
                  │           │          │         └─ Kernel A retired.
                  │           │          │            .wait released.
                  │           │          │            Loads Kernel A output.
                  │           │          │
                  │           │          └─ Reached griddepcontrol.wait.
                  │           │             Hardware parks this warp.
                  │           │             Still occupies SM resources.
                  │           │             Cannot issue global loads.
                  │           │
                  │           └─ Runs dependency-FREE instructions:
                  │              - Register initialization
                  │              - Shared memory setup (__syncthreads)
                  │              - Weight/static tensor prefetch (see §13)
                  │              - Loop counter initialization
                  │
                  └─ SM dispatches the block.
                     Block begins executing.

  ─── What "Parked" Means for Resources ───────────────────────────

  A parked warp:
    ✓ Still holds its allocated registers
    ✓ Still holds its allocated shared memory
    ✓ Counts toward the SM's active warp count
    ✗ Cannot issue any new instructions
    ✗ Does NOT free SM resources for other blocks

  IMPLICATION: If Kernel B's blocks take too many SMs too early,
  they reduce the SMs available to Kernel A's tail. Too much
  overlap = Kernel A slows down = net negative. See Section 14.

  ─── Placement of .wait ──────────────────────────────────────────

  Rule: place .wait as LATE as possible while still guaranteeing
  it precedes any load that reads Kernel A's output.

  WRONG — .wait at top of kernel (wastes all overlap potential):
    __global__ void kernel_consumer(...) {
        griddepcontrol.wait;         // park immediately
        // now everything runs after Kernel A, no overlap at all
        run_setup();
        prefetch_weights();
        load_activations();
    }

  CORRECT — .wait after dependency-free work:
    __global__ void kernel_consumer(...) {
        run_setup();                 // register init, smem setup
        prefetch_weights();          // weights are independent of KernelA
        // NOW park
        griddepcontrol.wait;
        load_activations();          // reads Kernel A's output: safe
    }

docs.title: 13.1 Choose prefetch or transfer deliberately
docs.text: For L2-only prefetch, use the documented cp.async.bulk.prefetch.tensor L2 form, as in Chapter 5. A cp.async.bulk.tensor...shared::cluster.global load instead transfers into shared memory and requires a CUtensorMap address, shared destination and mbarrier. Its transaction bytes belong in the barrier's arrive.expect_tx, not an extra trailing transfer operand. A raw global weight pointer is not a tensor-map descriptor. Do not present an SMEM load as an L2-only prefetch or assume one fixed cache-hit latency.

docs.title: 14.1 The Three-Way Tradeoff
docs.text:
Overlap Tuning — What You're Balancing
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Three competing pressures:

  PRESSURE 1 — Overlap gain:
    Launching Kernel B early hides its cold-start latency.
    Earlier launch → more overlap → smaller total time.
    This pushes toward: fire launch_dependents as early as possible.

  PRESSURE 2 — Resource contention:
    Parked Kernel B warps consume SM slots, register file, SMEM.
    Co-resident work can compete for execution bandwidth and memory.
    A's already-resident CTAs are not evicted by B; inspect the
    actual overlap and resource availability, not an SM-count subtraction.
    This pushes toward: fire launch_dependents as LATE as possible
    (or limit Kernel B's SM count).

  PRESSURE 3 — L2 pressure from prefetch:
    Aggressive weight prefetch fills L2 with weight lines.
    If these evict activation or workspace lines that Kernel A
    still needs to write or Kernel B needs to read → DRAM traffic
    spikes from refills, erasing the prefetch benefit.
    This pushes toward: prefetch only high-reuse tensors,
    limit prefetch to tiles that fit in L2 alongside other working sets.

  ─── Practical Tuning Protocol ────────────────────────────────────

  Step 1: Measure baseline (no GDC, strict serialization).
          Record total time T_base and SM utilization timeline.
          Note: how long is Kernel A's tail? (T_tail)

  Step 2: Enable GDC with no prefetch.
          Measure T_gdc; compare identical useful work against T_base.
          Neither overlap nor a fixed fraction of tail hiding is guaranteed.

  Step 3: Add weight prefetch for one tensor.
          Measure L2 hit rate for that tensor in Kernel B.
          If hit rate improves significantly: keep.
          If hit rate unchanged (tensor too large for L2): remove.
          Measure total time T_pref.

  Step 4: Use hardware counters to find the bottleneck.
          Key counters:
            l2_read_hit_rate         → is prefetch working?
            sm__warps_active         → is Kernel B starving Kernel A?
            memory_l2_read_sectors   → is prefetch causing L2 churn?
            gpu__time_duration       → wall time per kernel

  Step 5: Adjust launch_dependents placement:
          If sm__warps_active drops during Kernel A's tail after
          Kernel B launches → move launch_dependents later.
          If overlap window is small compared to Kernel B's cold-start
          → move launch_dependents earlier (accept more contention).

  ─── Key Guardrails (monitor these) ─────────────────────────────

  l2_read_hit_rate:    should INCREASE for prefetched tensors.
                       If unchanged: prefetch is too large or arrives too late.
  sm__warps_active (Kernel A's tail): should NOT decrease significantly
                       after Kernel B launches. If it does: too much contention.
  memory_l2_read_sectors: should NOT increase vs baseline.
                       If it does: prefetch is evicting needed lines.
  Total wall time:     the only metric that ultimately matters.
                       Measure end-to-end with nsys, not per-kernel.

docs.title: 15 — Putting It All Together — Production Checklist
15.1 Stream-K Deployment Checklist
docs.text:
Stream-K Production Checklist
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  □ 1. MEASURE WAVE QUANTIZATION LOSS FIRST
        Compute: r = num_output_tiles % num_SMs;
    idle_fraction = r ? (num_SMs-r)/(num_SMs*ceil(num_output_tiles/num_SMs)) : 0
        Compare predicted idle time against measured split/fixup costs.
        No fixed 5%/15% threshold establishes a win; small output
        grids are candidates for K splitting, not a mandatory policy.

  □ 2. SIZE THE WORKSPACE CORRECTLY
        workspace_bytes = num_output_tiles × output_tile_size_bytes
        lock_bytes      = num_output_tiles × sizeof(int) × num_barriers
        Allocate contiguously: workspace first, then locks.
        Zero-initialize at kernel launch (cudaMemsetAsync).

  □ 3. CHOOSE DETERMINISTIC OR NON-DETERMINISTIC MODE
        Deterministic: for any workload requiring bit-reproducibility.
        Non-deterministic: for maximum speed in inference / training.
        Default: deterministic.

  □ 4. SET num_groups FOR L2 LOCALITY
        Start with: num_groups = min(problem_blocks_m / cluster_m, 8)
        Profile L2 hit rate. Increase groups if hit rate is low.
        Groups of 1 = no grouping (try if problem_blocks_m ≤ cluster_m).

  □ 5. HANDLE PURE DATA-PARALLEL TILES
        Append data-parallel (non-split) tiles for any work that
        divides evenly into whole tiles beyond the stream-K portion.
        These tiles skip fixup and workspace entirely.

  □ 6. CONSIDER spatial tail subdivision INSTEAD
        If K is small (AI is dominated by M×N, not K):
          spatial tail subdivision avoids fixup overhead entirely.
        If K is large relative to M×N: use Stream-K.

  □ 7. TEST WITH SMALL TILE COUNTS
        Test with num_output_tiles = 1, 2, and num_SMs ± 1.
        These edge cases are where split logic bugs hide.
        All output values must match a CPU reference exactly.

docs.title: 15.2 Dependent-Launch Deployment Checklist
docs.text:
Dependent-Launch Production Checklist
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  □ 1. IDENTIFY THE KERNEL BOUNDARY WORTH OVERLAPPING
        Not all boundaries are worth it. Look for:
          - Kernel A has a significant tail (>10% of total runtime)
          - Kernel B has non-trivial cold-start (large register state)
          - Weight tensors in Kernel B are large and reused

  □ 2. VERIFY THE PRODUCER / DEPENDENT CONTRACT
        Kernel A must complete its own stores and async operations before exit.
        Kernel B must wait before reading prerequisite output.
        A separate release fence is only needed for an additional publication protocol.

  □ 3. PLACE launch_dependents AT THE CORRECT POINT
        Non-persistent: after last write, before block exit.
        Persistent: after last tile's epilogue commits.
        Warp-specialized: from consumer warpgroup after tma_store commit.

  □ 4. PLACE .wait AT THE CORRECT POINT IN KERNEL B
        After all dependency-free work (setup, weight prefetch).
        Before any load that reads Kernel A's output.
        Don't move it earlier "for safety" — it wastes overlap.

  □ 5. ALWAYS USE BOTH griddepcontrol INSTRUCTIONS TOGETHER
        A dependent kernel launched with programmatic serialization
        must establish prerequisite completion before consuming output,
        using .wait or another valid completion protocol.

  □ 6. ALWAYS SET THE HOST ATTRIBUTE
        cudaLaunchAttributeProgrammaticStreamSerialization = 1
        Without this opt-in, the dependent launch retains ordinary
        same-stream ordering. PTX inspection confirms instruction
        emission; a timeline is needed to observe actual overlap.

  □ 7. PROFILE BEFORE AND AFTER WITH nsys
        Measure: total elapsed time (Kernel A start to Kernel B end).
        Check: does Kernel A's tail overlap with Kernel B's startup?
        Watch: sm__warps_active during Kernel A's tail.

  □ 8. TUNE PREFETCH SCOPE
        Start small: prefetch only the first tile of weights.
        Add more prefetch only if L2 hit rate improves.
        Stop before L2 hit rate for other tensors degrades.

docs.title: Stream-K Quick Reference
docs.text:
Key Predicates
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  requires_fixup = (k_tile_count != k_tiles_per_output_tile)
  is_final_split = (K_idx + k_tile_count) == k_tiles_per_output_tile

  Role determination (in priority order):
    !requires_fixup  → Full tile: accumulate + direct epilogue
    K_idx == 0       → First split: write workspace, signal lock
    is_final_split   → Final split: wait, merge, run epilogue
    else             → Middle split: wait, merge, re-signal

  Lock semantics:
    lock[T] = cumulative k-tiles written to workspace[T]
    Wait condition: while (lock[T] < my_K_idx) {}
    Signal: atomicAdd(&lock[T], my_k_tile_count)
    Lock only increases. Never reset during kernel lifetime.

  Workspace sizing:
    workspace_bytes = num_output_tiles × output_tile_bytes
    lock_bytes      = num_output_tiles × 4  (× num_barriers for multi-WG)
    Layout: [workspace | locks] in one contiguous allocation

  Group count:
    num_groups = min(problem_blocks_m / cluster_m, 8)
    output_tile_id = tile_id_in_group × num_groups + group_idx

  spatial tail subdivision vs Stream-K:
    Small K, partial wave in M×N  →  spatial tail subdivision (no workspace, no fixup)
    Large K, small M×N            →  Stream-K (K-split + fixup)

docs.title: GDC / Dependent-Launch Quick Reference
docs.text:
GDC Instruction Summary
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  griddepcontrol.launch_dependents  (in Kernel A — producer)
    → Scheduler gate opens for Kernel B
    → May signal before remaining producer work; dependent still waits
    → First invocation per CTA only; repeated calls no-op
    → No effect unless host set programmaticStreamSerialization=1

  griddepcontrol.wait               (in Kernel B — consumer)
    → Park warp until all prerequisite grids retire
    → Place AFTER dependency-free work (setup, weight prefetch)
    → Place BEFORE any load reading Kernel A's output
    → REQUIRED if Kernel A uses launch_dependents

  Host launch:
    cudaLaunchAttribute attr[1];
    attr[0].id  = cudaLaunchAttributeProgrammaticStreamSerialization;
    attr[0].val.programmaticStreamSerializationAllowed = 1;
    cudaLaunchKernelEx(&cfg, kernel_B, ...);

  Memory ordering:
    Kernel A:  launch_dependents → remaining stores / async completion → exit
    Kernel B:  [prefetch weights] → .wait → load activations

  Overlap anatomy:
    Window A = Kernel A tail duration
    Window B = Kernel B cold-start + weight prefetch duration
    Overlap  = min(Window A, Window B)  [rough upper bound]
    Net gain = Overlap - resource_contention_penalty

  Tuning counters (Nsight Compute):
    l2_read_hit_rate         → prefetch effectiveness
    sm__warps_active         → contention during tail
    memory_l2_read_sectors   → L2 pressure from prefetch
    gpu__time_duration       → wall time (the only real metric)

  Hardware requirement:
    griddepcontrol requires sm_90+ (H100, B100)
    sm_80 (A100): strict serialization only

Pause and explain it. These are worked reasoning exercises, not additional hardware execution claims. Attempt each question before opening its answer.

Self-check 10.1. Divide 90 numbered K tiles among four CTAs using boundaries floor(i×90/4). What are the ranges?

Worked answer — 10.1

The boundaries are 0, 22, 45, 67, 90, giving half-open ranges [0,22), [22,45), [45,67), [67,90). Their lengths are 22, 23, 22, 23 and total 90. Check both coverage and overlap before benchmarking.

Self-check 10.2. Can each split apply ReLU before partial results are combined? Test partial sums −2 and 3.

Worked answer — 10.2

No: ReLU(−2+3)=1, while ReLU(−2)+ReLU(3)=3. Combine partial sums first, then apply nonlinear activation. Bias and other final-only epilogue operations must also follow the intended full-output formula, not be duplicated per split.

Next — Chapter 11: Multi-GPU Systems, NCCL & Distributed Training

The final chapter leaves the single GPU behind: NVLink and NVSwitch topology, the DGX H100 node and the SuperPOD, InfiniBand rail networks, SLURM and PMIx, NCCL's six collective primitives, and the four parallelism strategies — data, tensor, pipeline, and expert.

Tail and dependency checks. For T=133 equal tiles and S=132 workers, the nonempty last wave has one active worker; the idle share over two waves is 131/(2×132) ≈ 49.6%, not 0.8%. For 20 full waves plus eight tiles, it is 124/(21×132) ≈ 4.47%. With 8,512 K-iterations and a ceiling chunk of 65, clip each worker interval to the valid total; the last workers are not all full. Splits are not generally K/2. Redistributing eight 128×256 tail tiles into 64×64 tiles yields 64 small tiles, rather than merely handing the same eight workers smaller work. This arithmetic does not establish a separately named published algorithm.

CUTLASS v4.3.6 emits griddepcontrol.launch_dependents and griddepcontrol.wait through its architecture wrappers; the CUDA runtime API names are related interfaces, not literal calls in those headers. Programmatic dependent kernels can contend for co-resident resources after primary CTAs trigger; this is not a claim that unstarted primary CTAs lose dispatch slots. Trigger placement and overlap require an application-specific measurement, not a guaranteed half-tail speedup.

The two-H100 follow-up audit compiled all three complete programs and executed the corrected peer-transfer benchmark and NCCL AllReduce with full-buffer checks. The revised portable training program subsequently passed on eight A100 GPUs, targeting sm_80, with full final-weight and per-step loss comparisons against a CPU reference. This was not an eight-H100 run. All three programs have successful execution records linked below; earlier raw archives remain downloadable from the validation page. Execution system: 1× H100 PCIe, 114 SMs, 80 GB class; Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS; driver 580.105.08; CUDA Toolkit 12.8.93; sm_90a, C++17, -O2. Full system information · CUDA result manifest. Each tested source and captured output is linked beside its example. Diagrams open as original SVGs for zooming.

docs.title: What You Need to Know First
docs.text:
This guide covers the hardware and software stack that sits above single-kernel optimization. You should be comfortable with:

Prerequisites Checklist
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  From Lessons 2-4:
    ✓ CUDA streams, cudaMemcpy, device pointers
    ✓ Basic kernel launch (<<<grid, block>>>)
    ✓ cudaDeviceSynchronize, cudaEvent timing
    ✓ Arithmetic intensity and bandwidth concepts (Lesson 3, §1)

  New concepts introduced HERE (no prior knowledge needed):
    ★ NVLink / NVSwitch — GPU-to-GPU interconnect topology
    ★ Unified Virtual Addressing (UVA) and peer access
    ★ SLURM workload manager — job scripts and rank identity
    ★ PMIx — exascale process management and KVS
    ★ NCCL — collective communications library
    ★ ncclUniqueId / communicator initialization
    ★ AllReduce, ReduceScatter, AllGather, Broadcast, Reduce, All-to-All
    ★ Data, Tensor, Pipeline, and Expert parallelism
    ★ Sequence parallelism and AllReduce decomposition

  Hardware assumed:
    H100 DGX node (8× SXM5 H100, 4× NVSwitch, 8× ConnectX-7)
    Concepts apply to A100 DGX with appropriate bandwidth numbers
    Single-node examples work on any multi-GPU machine

docs.title: Compile Commands for This Guide
docs.text:
Compile Patterns
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  # Single-node multi-GPU (NVLink P2P)
  nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_90a -O2 example.cu -o example

  # NCCL examples (link against NCCL)
  nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_90a -O2 example.cu \
       -lnccl -o example

  # Multi-process NCCL (run with mpirun or srun)
  nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_90a -O2 example.cu \
       -lnccl -lmpi -o example
  mpirun -np 8 ./example

  # With PMIx (HPC cluster)
  nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_90a -O2 example.cu \
       -lnccl -lpmix -o example
  srun --mpi=pmix -n 8 --gpus-per-task=1 ./example

  # Verify NVLink topology on your system
  nvidia-smi topo -m        # shows NVLink/PCIe topology matrix
  nvidia-smi nvlink -s      # NVLink per-GPU bandwidth status

docs.title: 1.1 The Arithmetic of Scale
docs.text:
Before writing a line of multi-GPU code, understand why it is necessary. The compute requirements of frontier AI are so large that single-GPU training is not just slow — it is astronomically infeasible.

Training a 1T Parameter Model on 10T Tokens — Cost Estimate
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Empirical rule for transformer training:
    FLOPs per token ≈ 6 × num_parameters
    (2× forward pass + 4× backward pass, approximate)

  Total training FLOPs:
    FLOPs = 6 × 1×10¹² params × 1×10¹³ tokens
           = 6×10²⁵ FLOPs

  Theoretical throughput on one H100 (BF16 tensor core):
    Peak: ~989 TFLOPS = ~10¹⁵ FLOP/s
    Realistic MFU (model FLOP utilization): ~40% → ~4×10¹⁴ FLOP/s

  Time on one H100:
    t = 6×10²⁵ / 4×10¹⁴ ≈ 1.5×10¹¹ seconds ≈ 4,755 years

  Time on 1,000 H100s:
    t = 4,755 / 1000 ≈ 4.75 years  (still unacceptable)

  Time on 10,000 H100s (a realistic frontier cluster):
    t = 4,755 / 10,000 ≈ 174 days  (feasible at high cost)

  ─── The Communication Problem ────────────────────────────────────

  It is not enough to have 10,000 GPUs. They must exchange gradients,
  activations, and parameters constantly. If communication is slow,
  GPUs idle waiting for data.

  The entire engineering challenge of multi-GPU training is keeping
  every GPU busy at all times, which requires:
    1. A fast intra-node interconnect (NVLink, 900 GB/s per GPU)
    2. A fast inter-node interconnect (InfiniBand, 400 Gb/s per port)
    3. Software that hides communication behind computation
    4. Schedulers that decompose the model efficiently

docs.title: 2.1 Physical Architecture and Bandwidth
docs.text:
NVLink is NVIDIA's proprietary direct GPU-to-GPU interconnect, bypassing the CPU and PCIe bus entirely. On H100, it provides dramatically higher bandwidth than PCIe Gen 5.

NVLink Gen 4 — H100 Physical Specifications
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Bandwidth:
    900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU
    = 450 GB/s in each direction simultaneously

  PCIe Gen 5 comparison:
    PCIe Gen 5 ×16: ~128 GB/s bidirectional
    NVLink Gen 4:   ~900 GB/s bidirectional
    Ratio:          ~7× faster than PCIe

  Physical implementation:
    18 individual NVLink "links" per H100 GPU
    Each link: 2 high-speed differential pairs (down from 4 in Gen 3)
    → More links in the same physical space (density-optimized)
    → Each link: ~50 GB/s bidirectional
    → 18 links × 50 GB/s = 900 GB/s total

  ─── Why Bypassing PCIe Matters ──────────────────────────────────

  PCIe path (old way):
    GPU A → PCIe bus → CPU/Root Complex → PCIe bus → GPU B
    Latency: ~5-10 µs for a round trip
    Budget: 128 GB/s bidirectional; 64 GB/s per direction

  NVLink path (direct):
    GPU A → NVLink fabric → GPU B
    Latency: ~1-2 µs for a round trip
    Per-GPU budget: 900 GB/s bidirectional; 450 GB/s per direction

  Ideal one-way transfer model for 1 GB (decimal):
    PCIe path: 1 GB / 64 GB/s ≈ 15.6 ms per one-way transfer
    NVLink:    1 GB / 450 GB/s ≈ 2.2 ms per transfer
    These are link-budget lower bounds, not AllReduce runtimes.

  ─── What NVLink Enables ─────────────────────────────────────────

  Unified memory access:
    GPU 0 can load/store to GPU 1's HBM3 memory directly from a kernel.
    The address is a virtual pointer; hardware translates and routes.

  Peer-to-peer DMA:
    cudaMemcpyPeer() moves data GPU-to-GPU over NVLink at full speed.

  In-network reduction (via NVSwitch ALUs):
    The NVSwitch chips on the HGX board contain ALUs. AllReduce is
    performed IN THE SWITCH as data transits, not by the GPUs.
    NVLS can offload supported reductions when the topology and NCCL tuner select it.
    It does not make an eight-GPU AllReduce equal to a one-GPU transfer.

docs.title: 3.1 Full Non-Blocking Fabric
docs.text:
On an 8-GPU HGX board (like in the DGX H100), four NVSwitch chips connect all eight GPUs. Each H100 SXM has a product-peak NVLink budget of 900 GB/s aggregate bidirectional bandwidth, or 450 GB/s per direction. That endpoint budget is shared across its peers; each pair does not receive an independent 900 GB/s allocation. A non-blocking fabric supports simultaneous routes within the endpoint and fabric budgets, while achieved throughput depends on the traffic pattern and software. See NVIDIA’s Hopper architecture description.

NVSwitch Topology — 8 GPUs via 4 NVSwitch Chips
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Physical layout:

  GPU 0 ─── SW0 ─── GPU 1
  GPU 0 ─── SW1 ─── GPU 2
  GPU 0 ─── SW2 ─── GPU 3     Each GPU connects to all 4 switches
  GPU 0 ─── SW3 ─── GPU 4     Each switch connects to all 8 GPUs
  ...

  Connectivity matrix (✓ = switched peer path; shared endpoint budget):
  ┌─────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐
  │     │ G0 │ G1 │ G2 │ G3 │ G4 │ G5 │ G6 │ G7 │
  ├─────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┤
  │ G0  │  ─ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │
  │ G1  │  ✓ │  ─ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │
  │ G2  │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ─ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │  ✓ │
  │ ... │ ..   ...  ...  ...  ...  ...  ...  ... │
  └─────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘

  "Non-blocking" means: GPU 0→GPU 7 at full speed WHILE
  GPU 1→GPU 6, GPU 2→GPU 5, GPU 3→GPU 4 are all also running.
  No link is shared, no packet must wait in line.

  ─── NVSwitch ALUs — In-Network Reduction ────────────────────────

  NVSwitch is not just a crossbar. It contains arithmetic units
  (ALUs) that can perform reductions AS DATA TRANSITS:

  One available path is NCCL NVLS (NVLink SHARP), not every AllReduce:
    Participating GPUs submit data; supported reductions use the fabric.
    For payload D, ideal per-endpoint send volume is about D versus
    2(N-1)D/N for ring AllReduce; receive volumes follow the same convention.
    This suggests at most about 2x bandwidth-bound improvement in that
    simplified model, not N-fold scaling or a guaranteed measured speedup.
    NCCL selects algorithms per collective using size, operation and topology.

  ─── NVLink Switch System (external, for >8 GPUs) ────────────────

  For clusters of 16-256 GPUs, NVIDIA uses NVLink Switch System:
    External trays containing NVSwitch chips.
    Connect up to 256 H100 GPUs at native chip speeds.
    32 DGX H100 servers → one "SuperPOD" with NVLink everywhere.

  ─── 4-5 NVLink ports per switch (HGX board) ─────────────────────

  On the HGX H100 board:
    Each GPU's 18 links are distributed 5/4/4/5 across four NVSwitches.
    Each GPU has 18 total NVLink links → split across 4 switches:
    Across eight GPUs there are 8×18 = 144 GPU-side links.

docs.title: 4.1 Full Hardware Layout and Bandwidth Budget
docs.text:
The DGX H100 is NVIDIA's flagship single-node configuration. Understanding its physical structure tells you exactly where your bandwidth budget comes from and where the bottlenecks are.

DGX H100 Single Node — Complete Hardware Layout
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Compute:
    8× H100 SXM5 GPUs
    Each GPU: 80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth, 989 TFLOPS BF16
    Total node HBM: 640 GB
    Total node BF16 FLOPS: 7.9 PFLOPS

  Intra-node interconnect:
    4× NVSwitch Gen 3 chips
    Each GPU: 900 GB/s bidirectional NVLink bandwidth
    Total node bisection bandwidth: ~3.6 TB/s
    Topology: fully non-blocking all-to-all between 8 GPUs

  Inter-node networking:
    8× NVIDIA ConnectX-7 NICs (one per GPU, dedicated)
    Each NIC: 400 Gb/s (= 50 GB/s) NDR InfiniBand
    (Correction: this is NDR, not HDR -- HDR is the PREVIOUS generation
     at 200 Gb/s per port. ConnectX-7 is NDR-capable at 400 Gb/s.)
    Total node network bandwidth: 3.2 Tb/s = 400 GB/s
    Physical connectors: 4× OSFP cages (twin-port = 2×400Gb per cage)

  CPU:
    2× Intel Xeon Platinum 8480C (DGX H100; OEM HGX configurations vary)
    Primarily manages scheduling; GPUs bypass CPU for data

  Storage:
    Separate PCIe network cards for storage fabric
    Fat-tree or leaf-spine to NFS/Lustre/GPFS storage arrays
    Separate from compute fabric (does not share OSFP cages)

  ─── Bandwidth Hierarchy on one Node ─────────────────────────────

  HBM3 (GPU internal):      3.35 TB/s per GPU   (fastest)
       ↕
  NVLink (GPU-to-GPU):      450 GB/s per direction per GPU
       ↕
  PCIe Gen5 (GPU→CPU):      ~64 GB/s per direction
       ↕
  ConnectX-7 (node→node):   50 GB/s per direction per NIC
       ↕
  InfiniBand (rack→rack):   50 GB/s per NIC                (slowest)

  The ratio between NVLink and ConnectX-7:
    450 / 50 = 9× bandwidth drop when leaving the node.
  This is the most critical engineering constraint in cluster training.
  Everything is designed to minimize inter-node traffic.

  ─── GPU Direct RDMA ─────────────────────────────────────────────

  ConnectX-7 supports GPU Direct RDMA:
    GPU memory ←→ network NIC, BYPASSING CPU and system RAM.
    The NIC reads/writes GPU HBM directly over PCIe.
    CPU is not interrupted; it does not copy data.
    This is how inter-node AllReduce achieves near-theoretical speed.

docs.title: 5.1 The 9× Drop — Engineering the Handoff
docs.text:
Within a DGX H100 node, each GPU shares an NVLink budget of 450 GB/s per direction across its peers. Across nodes, traffic also traverses ConnectX-7 NICs and InfiniBand switches. Compare budgets with the same direction convention and account for the NICs assigned to each GPU; the difference is a link-budget model, not a fixed application slowdown.

The Inter-Node Bandwidth Gap
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Intra-node (NVLink):    900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU
  Inter-node (ConnectX):  100 GB/s bidirectional per GPU (2×50 GB/s NIC)
  Ratio:                  9× slower when crossing node boundary

  For a 128-GPU cluster training a large model:
    AllReduce traffic: gradients × 2×(N-1)/N ≈ 2× gradient size per step
    With 128 GPUs, gradient tensor = 1 GB (typical):
    Inter-node traffic per step ≈ 2 GB per GPU per step

    At 100 GB/s inter-node bandwidth:
      Transfer time ≈ 2 GB / 50 GB/s = 40 ms (per-direction ideal bound) per step
    If forward + backward = 100 ms per step:
      Communication = 20% of total time → significant

  ─── How ConnectX-7 Minimizes the Penalty ────────────────────────

  1. GPU Direct RDMA:
     NIC reads/writes GPU HBM directly, no CPU copy.
     Eliminates: 2× PCIe crossings and 2× memory copies.
     Saves: ~5-10 µs of latency per transfer.

  2. In-network reduction (SHARP):
     The InfiniBand switches themselves perform arithmetic reductions.
     Like NVSwitch ALUs for intra-node, SHARP does it for inter-node.
     Reduces endpoint traffic for supported collectives; aggregate traffic still grows with the number of endpoints (see §7).

  3. Rail alignment:
     GPU 0 from every node connects to the SAME set of switches.
     Traffic from GPU 0→GPU 0 (different nodes) never shares a link
     with GPU 1→GPU 1. Eight isolated planes of connectivity.

  ─── OSFP Cages — Physical Connectors ────────────────────────────

  The DGX H100 has 4 OSFP (Octal Small Form-factor Pluggable) cages.
  Each cage uses twin-port technology: one cage = two 400 Gb/s links.

  4 cages × 2 links = 8 links of 400 Gb/s each
  One link per GPU, one per ConnectX-7 NIC.
  Total: 8 × 400 Gb/s = 3.2 Tb/s aggregate node bandwidth.

  OSFP cages are ONLY for compute fabric.
  Storage traffic uses separate standard PCIe NICs on the back panel.
  This physical separation ensures gradient traffic never competes
  with checkpoint I/O for the same links.

docs.title: 6.1 Cluster-Scale Architecture
docs.text:
The DGX H100 SuperPOD is NVIDIA's reference cluster design for scaling from 8 GPUs to 4,096 GPUs. It is organized into a strict hierarchy of Scalable Units (SUs), each designed around the port counts of standard switch hardware.

SuperPOD Hierarchy — 128 GPUs to 4096 GPUs
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Building block: DGX H100 node
    8 GPUs per node, one ConnectX-7 NIC per GPU

  Scalable Unit (SU):
    32 DGX H100 nodes = 256 GPUs
    Why 32 nodes?
      Each Quantum-2 QM9700 switch has 64 ports.
      32 nodes × 8 GPUs/node = 256 GPU-facing ports needed.
      32 downlink ports (to 32 nodes, one per rail) +
      32 uplink ports (to spine layer) = 64 ports exactly.
      → One QM9700 handles one rail of one SU perfectly.

  Illustrative four-SU configuration:
    4 × 32 nodes = 128 nodes = 1,024 GPUs in a simple capacity model.
    Actual reference configurations reserve management/service capacity;
    four SUs is not a universal minimum deployment size. Check the
    selected NVIDIA SuperPOD reference architecture and port plan.

  SuperPOD with NVLink Switching:
    16 SUs = 512 nodes = 4,096 GPUs (connected across nodes with InfiniBand; not a 4,096-GPU NVLink domain)
    Or: 256 GPUs connected via NVLink Switch System for ultra-fast
    intra-cluster AllReduce before InfiniBand scale-out.

  ─── The Port-Count Design Principle ─────────────────────────────

  32 nodes per SU is not arbitrary:
    Standard InfiniBand switch: 64 ports
    Ports needed per SU per rail: 32 (one port per node, for that rail)
    Remaining ports: 32 → uplinks to spine

  This creates a perfect 1:1 ratio between downlinks and uplinks at
  the leaf layer. The network is "full-bisection bandwidth" within
  one SU — any node can talk to any other node at line rate.

  ─── Why 8 NICs Per Node Matters ─────────────────────────────────

  The SuperPOD is organized around the fact that each DGX node has
  8 separate NICs (one per GPU). This enables the Rail architecture.

  If nodes had only 1 NIC (like commodity servers):
    All 8 GPUs share one 400 Gb/s link → 50 Gb/s per GPU for inter-node
    No rail separation possible → all-or-nothing congestion
    No SHARP per-GPU isolation

  With 8 NICs:
    Each GPU has a DEDICATED 400 Gb/s inter-node link
    → 8 independent communication planes (Rails)
    → SHARP on each rail independently
    → No GPU's gradient traffic interferes with another's

docs.title: 7.1 The Rail Architecture
docs.text:
The "rail" concept is the key architectural decision that enables linear scaling of AllReduce across thousands of GPUs. Each GPU's network traffic travels on its own dedicated, isolated plane of switches.

Rail Architecture — 8 Isolated Communication Planes
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ─── Standard Network (what a commodity cluster looks like) ───────

  Node 1: GPU 0-7 → [single NIC] → [switch] → any destination
  Node 2: GPU 0-7 → [single NIC] → [switch] → any destination

  Problem: all 8 GPUs share one 400 Gb/s link = 50 Gb/s per GPU.
  During AllReduce, GPU 0 competes with GPU 7 for the same wire.
  Congestion is unavoidable.

  ─── Rail Architecture (DGX H100 SuperPOD) ────────────────────────

  Rail 1: [GPU 0, Node 1] ─── [Leaf Switch R1] ─── [GPU 0, Node 2]
                                                 └── [GPU 0, Node 3]
                                                 └── [GPU 0, Node N]

  Rail 2: [GPU 1, Node 1] ─── [Leaf Switch R2] ─── [GPU 1, Node 2]
                                                 └── [GPU 1, Node 3]
                                                 └── [GPU 1, Node N]
  ...
  Rail 8: [GPU 7, Node 1] ─── [Leaf Switch R8] ─── [GPU 7, Node 2]

  Key properties:
    Traffic on Rail 1 physically CANNOT interfere with Rail 2.
    They use different cables, different switches, different ports.
    GPU 0's gradient traffic is completely isolated from GPU 7's.

  NCCL and SHARP can now do:
    GPU 0 AllReduce: entirely within Rail 1 infrastructure.
    GPU 1 AllReduce: entirely within Rail 2 infrastructure.
    Both happening simultaneously at full line rate.

  ─── SHARP — In-Network Computation ─────────────────────────────

  SHARP (Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol):
    Offloads gradient reduction arithmetic INTO the switch ASICs.
    The Quantum-2 switch performs additions on packets in transit.
    SHARPv3 on QM9700 is 32x more capable than the previous generation
    -- confirmed real: NVIDIA's own NVIDIA Quantum-2 announcement states
    SHARPv3 "provides 32x more acceleration engines for AI applications
    compared with the previous generation."

  Ring AllReduce traffic, payload D across N endpoints:
    Sent bytes per endpoint: 2(N-1)D/N, approaching 2D.
    Sum of sent bytes over endpoints: 2(N-1)D, which is O(ND).
    Receiving contributes the same endpoint volume; do not mix conventions.

  In-network reduction can reduce endpoint injection and repeated traffic
  on shared upper links. A simple reduction/broadcast model sends D and
  receives D per endpoint. Aggregate endpoint volume remains O(ND),
  not O(D). Topology, implementation, latency and supported operations
  determine actual performance; this is not a linear-scaling guarantee.

  The ConnectX-7 NIC works with SHARP:
    NIC and switch handshake to create a "reduction tree" in hardware.
    The NIC offloads the AllReduce to the switch fabric.
    GPU sees: enqueue gradient, receive result. No N-way coordination.

docs.title: 8.1 The Three-Layer Fat Tree
docs.text:
For clusters beyond a single SU (>256 GPUs), InfiniBand switches are organized in a fat-tree hierarchy. Traffic between SUs must pass through multiple switch layers.

Three-Layer Fat Tree — Full SuperPOD Network
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ─── Layer 1: Leaf (Connection to Nodes) ─────────────────────────

  Where: physically at the top of each rack, or end-of-row
  What:  QM9700 switches, 64 ports each
  Who talks to whom:
    32 downlink ports → 32 nodes (one port per GPU per rail)
    32 uplink ports   → Spine layer switches

  Within-SU traffic STAYS at the leaf layer:
    GPU 0 (Node 1) → Leaf Switch (Rail 1) → GPU 0 (Node 2)
    Never goes to Spine or Core. Minimal hops = minimum latency.

  Adaptive routing at the leaf (for upward traffic):
    Multiple spine switches available for upward traffic.
    Leaf switch monitors queue depth on each uplink port.
    Per-packet (or per-flow) routing to least congested spine port.
    Avoids hot-spots when multiple nodes send to the same destination.

  ─── Layer 2: Spine (Connection Between SUs) ─────────────────────

  Where: core of the data center, dedicated switch rows
  What:  QM9700 (or larger) switches
  Who talks to whom:
    Downlinks → Leaf switches in multiple SUs
    Provides cross-SU paths for inter-SU AllReduce

  Rail isolation maintained at Spine:
    Spine Group 1 connects ONLY to Leaf switches handling Rail 1.
    Spine Group 2 connects ONLY to Rail 2 leaf switches.
    → Rail 1 gradient traffic NEVER shares a Spine with Rail 2.

  Cross-SU traffic path:
    GPU 0 (SU1, Node 1) → Leaf(SU1, Rail 1) → Spine(Group 1)
    → Leaf(SU2, Rail 1) → GPU 0 (SU2, Node 1)

  Link-failure self-healing (SHIELD; distinct from adaptive routing):
    SHIELD (Self-Healing Interconnect Enhancement for Intelligent Datacenters) is the Quantum-2 hardware fault recovery system.
    If a link fails, SHIELD detects it IN HARDWARE (not software).
    Recovery time: microseconds (vs 5-30 seconds for software) --
    confirmed real: NVIDIA/Mellanox's own SHIELD whitepaper cites
    ~1 microsecond hardware reroute vs. traditional subnet-manager
    recovery of up to 5 seconds (1,000-node clusters) or 30 seconds
    (10,000+-node clusters).
    How: switch checks local routing table for alternative path,
         updates its own table, signals upstream if no path found.
    Without SHIELD: one bad cable can crash a training run.
    With SHIELD: the run sees a brief stall (<1 ms), then continues.

  ─── Layer 3: Core / Super-Spine (Maximum Scale) ─────────────────

  Where: added only for clusters > 4 SUs (> 1,024 GPUs)
  What:  connects Pods (clusters of SUs) together
  Optics: 800G optical transceivers (2 × 400G logical links)
          optical because cable lengths too long for copper

  Traffic path (full 3 layers):
    GPU 0 → Leaf(SU1) → Spine(Group1) → Core → Spine(Group1,Pod2)
    → Leaf(SU5) → GPU 0 (SU5, Node 1)

  Each additional layer adds ~100-300 ns latency.
  Fat-tree bisection bandwidth remains full even at 3 layers.

docs.title: 9.1 Unified Virtual Addressing
docs.text:
Before writing any NCCL code, you need to understand the software layer that makes GPU-to-GPU memory access possible: Unified Virtual Addressing (UVA) and peer access.

UVA and Peer Access — How GPUs See Each Other's Memory
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ─── Before UVA (CUDA < 4.0) ─────────────────────────────────────

  CPU has its own virtual address space: [0x00000000 ... 0x7FFFFFFF]
  GPU 0 has its own: [0x0000000000 ... 0x1FFFFFFFFFF]
  GPU 1 has its own: [0x0000000000 ... 0x1FFFFFFFFFF]  ← SAME RANGE!

  You had to manually track which device a pointer belonged to.
  cudaMemcpy needed explicit src/dst device specification.
  Cross-GPU access was impossible from kernel code.

  ─── With UVA (CUDA 4.0+) ────────────────────────────────────────

  The system partitions the virtual address space:
    CPU RAM:          [0x00000000_00000000 ... 0x00000000_7FFFFFFF]
    GPU 0 HBM:        [0x00000020_00000000 ... 0x00000020_1FFFFFFF]
    GPU 1 HBM:        [0x00000040_00000000 ... 0x00000040_1FFFFFFF]
    GPU 2 HBM:        [0x00000060_00000000 ... ...]
    ...

  Effect:
    A pointer VALUE alone tells you which device it lives on.
    cudaPointerGetAttributes() reveals device, type, etc.
    cudaMemcpy() automatically routes based on pointer values.

  ─── Peer Access ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

  cudaDeviceCanAccessPeer reports address-access capability, not link type.
  Enable the direction used by the kernel: GPU 0 accessing GPU 1 memory.
  Peer traffic may traverse NVLink or PCIe according to the actual topology.
  Record nvidia-smi topo -m (and platform documentation) before labeling a link.

  More blocks can expose more independent memory requests; one block or SM
  does not correspond to one NVLink lane. Kernel copies and cudaMemcpyPeer
  use different execution paths, and either can benefit from sufficient work.
  NCCL selects algorithms/protocols for collectives; it is not merely a DMA
  wrapper, nor does raw peer access inherently prevent fabric saturation.

docs.title: ★ Section 9 — Runnable Code: NVLink P2P Bandwidth
docs.text:
Manual Worked Example:

This example measures three complete-buffer paths and checks every destination byte: 1. GPU 0 → pinned host memory → GPU 1 (staged copy). 2. GPU 0 → GPU 1 using the CUDA peer-copy API. 3. A kernel on GPU 0 reading GPU 1 memory, with one block or an SM-count-sized grid.

Bandwidth is payload bytes divided by elapsed time. Staged timing includes both legs and their synchronization; kernel and peer-copy timings use events on GPU 0. These scopes differ. Peer capability does not establish NVLink presence: record nvidia-smi topo -m and the host configuration before interpreting any number. No fixed speedup or link saturation is promised.

FILE: ex11_nvlink_bandwidth.cu
COMPILE: nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_90a -O2 ex11_nvlink_bandwidth.cu -o ex11_nvlink_bandwidth
RUN: ./ex11_nvlink_bandwidth
EXPECT: Full-buffer verification PASS for each executed path; timings vary.

// ex11_nvlink_bandwidth.cu — complete-buffer P2P audit benchmark.
// Peer capability is not proof of NVLink. Record nvidia-smi topo -m separately.
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <chrono>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>

static inline void
check_cuda_status(cudaError_t status, const char* file, int line) {
    if (status != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr,
                "CUDA %s:%d: %s\n",
                file,
                line,
                cudaGetErrorString(status));
        exit(1);
    }
}

#define CHECK_CUDA(call)                                           \
    check_cuda_status((call), __FILE__, __LINE__)

__global__ void peer_copy_kernel(const float* __restrict__ src,
                                 float* __restrict__ dst,
                                 size_t n) {
    // Every launch covers all n, including the one-block configuration.
    for (size_t i = (size_t)blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
         i < n;
         i += (size_t)blockDim.x * gridDim.x)
        dst[i] = src[i];
}

double rate(size_t bytes, double ms) {
    if (!(ms > 0.0)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Invalid elapsed time\n");
        exit(1);
    }
    return (double)bytes / (ms * 1e6);
}

float elapsed(cudaEvent_t begin, cudaEvent_t end) {
    float ms;
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaEventElapsedTime(&ms, begin, end));
    return ms;
}

// Copy back and inspect every byte outside the timed region.
bool verify(int owner,
            const void* dst,
            unsigned char* host,
            size_t bytes,
            unsigned char expected,
            const char* label) {
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(owner));
    CHECK_CUDA(
        cudaMemcpy(host, dst, bytes, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    size_t errors = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < bytes; ++i) {
        if (host[i] != expected) {
            if (errors < 4)
                fprintf(stderr,
                        "%s byte %zu: got %u expected %u\n",
                        label,
                        i,
                        (unsigned)host[i],
                        (unsigned)expected);
            ++errors;
        }
    }
    printf("  %s full-buffer verification: %s (%zu byte errors)\n",
           label,
           errors == 0 ? "PASS" : "FAIL",
           errors);
    return errors == 0;
}

int main() {
    int count;
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaGetDeviceCount(&count));
    printf("GPUs detected: %d\n", count);
    for (int dev = 0; dev < count; ++dev) {
        cudaDeviceProp p;
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaGetDeviceProperties(&p, dev));
        printf("GPU %d: %s, SM %d.%d, %d SMs\n",
               dev,
               p.name,
               p.major,
               p.minor,
               p.multiProcessorCount);
    }
    if (count < 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Requires at least 2 GPUs\n");
        return 2;
    }
    const int dev0 = 0, dev1 = 1, warmup = 3, iters = 10;
    const size_t n = 32 * 1024 * 1024, bytes = n * sizeof(float);
    float *src0, *dst0, *src1, *dst1;
    unsigned char* host;
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMallocHost(&host, bytes));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(dev0));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&src0, bytes));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&dst0, bytes));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemset(src0, 0x01, bytes));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(dev1));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&src1, bytes));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMalloc(&dst1, bytes));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemset(src1, 0x02, bytes));
    // Complete GPU 1 initialization before GPU 0 can read its peer source.
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());

    int can01 = 0;
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceCanAccessPeer(&can01, dev0, dev1));
    printf(
        "GPU 0 can access GPU 1 memory: %s (does not identify NVLink)\n",
        can01 ? "YES" : "NO");
    printf(
        "Record topology with nvidia-smi topo -m. Payload: %zu bytes\n",
        bytes);
    bool enabled_by_us = false;
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(dev0));
    if (can01) {
        cudaError_t e = cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess(dev1, 0);
        if (e == cudaErrorPeerAccessAlreadyEnabled) {
            (void)
                cudaGetLastError(); // consume the expected already-enabled status
        } else {
            CHECK_CUDA(e);
            enabled_by_us = true;
        }
    }
    cudaEvent_t start, stop;
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaEventCreate(&start));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaEventCreate(&stop));
    bool ok = true;

    // Staged path, GPU 0 -> host -> GPU 1; host timing covers both devices.
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(dev1));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemset(dst1, 0, bytes));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
    double staged_ms = 0;
    for (int i = -warmup; i < iters; ++i) {
        auto begin = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(dev0));
        CHECK_CUDA(
            cudaMemcpy(host, src0, bytes, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(dev1));
        CHECK_CUDA(
            cudaMemcpy(dst1, host, bytes, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
        auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        if (i >= 0)
            staged_ms += std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(
                             end - begin)
                             .count();
    }
    staged_ms /= iters;
    ok &= verify(dev1, dst1, host, bytes, 0x01, "Staged 0->1");
    printf(
        "  Staged complete-transfer time: %.6f ms, payload %.3f GB/s\n",
        staged_ms,
        rate(bytes, staged_ms));

    // Peer-copy API; the runtime chooses the path supported by this system.
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(dev1));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemset(dst1, 0, bytes));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(dev0));
    double peer_ms = 0;
    for (int i = -warmup; i < iters; ++i) {
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaEventRecord(start));
        CHECK_CUDA(
            cudaMemcpyPeerAsync(dst1, dev1, src0, dev0, bytes, 0));
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaEventRecord(stop));
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaEventSynchronize(stop));
        if (i >= 0)
            peer_ms += elapsed(start, stop);
    }
    peer_ms /= iters;
    ok &= verify(dev1, dst1, host, bytes, 0x01, "Peer API 0->1");
    printf(
        "  Peer API transfer time: %.6f ms, payload %.3f GB/s (link unclassified)\n",
        peer_ms,
        rate(bytes, peer_ms));

    if (can01) {
        cudaDeviceProp p;
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaGetDeviceProperties(&p, dev0));
        const int grids[] = {1, p.multiProcessorCount};
        for (int blocks : grids) {
            CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(dev0));
            CHECK_CUDA(cudaMemset(dst0, 0, bytes));
            CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
            double ms = 0;
            for (int i = -warmup; i < iters; ++i) {
                CHECK_CUDA(cudaEventRecord(start));
                peer_copy_kernel<<<blocks, 256>>>(src1, dst0, n);
                CHECK_CUDA(cudaGetLastError());
                CHECK_CUDA(cudaEventRecord(stop));
                CHECK_CUDA(cudaEventSynchronize(stop));
                if (i >= 0)
                    ms += elapsed(start, stop);
            }
            ms /= iters;
            ok &= verify(
                dev0, dst0, host, bytes, 0x02, "Kernel 1->0");
            printf(
                "  Kernel grid %d blocks: %.6f ms, payload %.3f GB/s\n",
                blocks,
                ms,
                rate(bytes, ms));
        }
    } else
        printf(
            "Kernel peer reads skipped: GPU 0 cannot access GPU 1 memory.\n");

    // Events belong to GPU 0; destroy them while their owner is current.
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(dev0));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaEventDestroy(start));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaEventDestroy(stop));
    if (enabled_by_us)
        CHECK_CUDA(cudaDeviceDisablePeerAccess(dev1));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(src0));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(dst0));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaSetDevice(dev1));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(src1));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaFree(dst1));
    CHECK_CUDA(cudaFreeHost(host));
    printf("Full-buffer checks: %s\n", ok ? "PASS" : "FAIL");
    return ok ? 0 : 1;
}
