// Adapted predicate/TiledCopy construction from CUTLASS v4.3.6
// examples/cute/tutorial/tiled_copy_if.cu. This teaching lab uses scalar
// float copies and instrumented ownership counts, not vectorization or MMA.
#include <cute/tensor.hpp>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <limits>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <vector>

using namespace cute;

static void cuda_check(cudaError_t result, char const* call) {
    if (result != cudaSuccess) {
        std::fprintf(
            stderr, "%s: %s\n", call, cudaGetErrorString(result));
        throw std::runtime_error("CUDA operation failed");
    }
}

#define CUDA_CHECK(call) cuda_check((call), #call)

template <class Source, class Destination, class TiledCopy>
__global__ void copy_tile(Source source,
                          Destination destination,
                          TiledCopy tiled_copy,
                          int* writers,
                          int columns) {
    auto logical_shape = shape(source);
    auto coordinates = make_identity_tensor(logical_shape);
    auto predicates =
        cute::lazy::transform(coordinates, [&](auto coordinate) {
            return elem_less(coordinate, logical_shape);
        });
    auto tile_shape = make_shape(Int<4>{}, Int<32>{});
    auto tile_coordinate = make_coord(blockIdx.x, blockIdx.y);
    auto source_tile =
        local_tile(source, tile_shape, tile_coordinate);
    auto destination_tile =
        local_tile(destination, tile_shape, tile_coordinate);
    auto predicate_tile =
        local_tile(predicates, tile_shape, tile_coordinate);
    auto coordinate_tile =
        local_tile(coordinates, tile_shape, tile_coordinate);
    auto thread_copy = tiled_copy.get_thread_slice(threadIdx.x);
    auto thread_source = thread_copy.partition_S(source_tile);
    auto thread_destination =
        thread_copy.partition_D(destination_tile);
    auto thread_predicate = thread_copy.partition_S(predicate_tile);
    auto thread_coordinate =
        thread_copy.partition_S(coordinate_tile);
    copy_if(tiled_copy,
            thread_predicate,
            thread_source,
            thread_destination);
    // Instrumentation proves each valid destination has exactly one owner.
    // The same predicate protects both the copy and the ownership counter.
    for (int i = 0; i < size(thread_predicate); ++i) {
        if (thread_predicate(i)) {
            auto coordinate = thread_coordinate(i);
            atomicAdd(writers + int(get<0>(coordinate)) * columns +
                          int(get<1>(coordinate)),
                      1);
        }
    }
}

static int run_case(int rows, int columns) {
    constexpr int guard = 16;
    constexpr float source_canary = -77777.0f,
                    destination_canary = -54321.0f;
    int source_pitch = columns + 3, destination_pitch = columns + 5;
    std::vector<float> source(guard + rows * source_pitch + guard,
                              source_canary);
    std::vector<float> destination(
        guard + rows * destination_pitch + guard,
        destination_canary);
    auto expected = destination;
    for (int row = 0; row < rows; ++row) {
        for (int column = 0; column < columns; ++column) {
            float value = float(row * columns + column + 1);
            source[guard + row * source_pitch + column] = value;
            destination[guard + row * destination_pitch + column] =
                std::numeric_limits<float>::quiet_NaN();
            expected[guard + row * destination_pitch + column] =
                value;
        }
    }
    float *device_source = nullptr, *device_destination = nullptr;
    int* device_writers = nullptr;
    CUDA_CHECK(
        cudaMalloc(&device_source, source.size() * sizeof(float)));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&device_destination,
                          destination.size() * sizeof(float)));
    CUDA_CHECK(
        cudaMalloc(&device_writers, rows * columns * sizeof(int)));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(device_source,
                          source.data(),
                          source.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(device_destination,
                          destination.data(),
                          destination.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemset(
        device_writers, 0, rows * columns * sizeof(int)));
    auto tensor_shape = make_shape(rows, columns);
    auto source_tensor = make_tensor(
        make_gmem_ptr(device_source + guard),
        make_layout(tensor_shape,
                    make_stride(source_pitch, Int<1>{})));
    auto destination_tensor = make_tensor(
        make_gmem_ptr(device_destination + guard),
        make_layout(tensor_shape,
                    make_stride(destination_pitch, Int<1>{})));
    auto threads = make_layout(make_shape(Int<4>{}, Int<32>{}),
                               make_stride(Int<32>{}, Int<1>{}));
    auto values = make_layout(make_shape(Int<1>{}, Int<1>{}));
    auto tiled_copy = make_tiled_copy(
        Copy_Atom<UniversalCopy<float>, float>{}, threads, values);
    dim3 grid((rows + 3) / 4, (columns + 31) / 32);
    copy_tile<<<grid, 128>>>(source_tensor,
                             destination_tensor,
                             tiled_copy,
                             device_writers,
                             columns);
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetLastError());
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(destination.data(),
                          device_destination,
                          destination.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    std::vector<float> source_after(source.size());
    std::vector<int> writers(rows * columns);
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(source_after.data(),
                          device_source,
                          source.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(writers.data(),
                          device_writers,
                          writers.size() * sizeof(int),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaFree(device_writers));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaFree(device_destination));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaFree(device_source));
    int errors = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < expected.size(); ++i)
        if (destination[i] != expected[i])
            ++errors;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < source.size(); ++i)
        if (source_after[i] != source[i])
            ++errors;
    for (int count : writers)
        if (count != 1)
            ++errors;
    std::printf(
        "copy M=%d N=%d: %d unique values, padding/canaries/source checked, errors=%d\n",
        rows,
        columns,
        rows * columns,
        errors);
    return errors;
}

int main() {
    try {
        int count = 0;
        CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetDeviceCount(&count));
        if (!count) {
            std::printf("BLOCKED: requires one CUDA GPU\n");
            return 2;
        }
        CUDA_CHECK(cudaSetDevice(0));
        int errors = run_case(8, 64);
        errors += run_case(37, 70);
        errors += run_case(1, 1);
        std::printf("COPY %s: 3 cases, errors=%d\n",
                    errors ? "FAIL" : "PASS",
                    errors);
        return errors ? 1 : 0;
    } catch (std::exception const& error) {
        std::fprintf(stderr, "COPY FAIL: %s\n", error.what());
        return 1;
    }
}

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• A tiled copy combines a grid tile, thread/value ownership and separate source/destination layouts; constructing partitions issues no memory transfer.

  • Check complete nonuniform values, unique destination ownership, untouched padding/guards and CUDA completion. Predicate tails before any invalid access.

  • Coalescing and vectorization have different alignment and transaction requirements. Apply the same ownership discipline to MMA fragments.

docs.title: 21. MMA Atoms — Prove Who Owns Every Result
Lesson 21 Companion Guide — Decode the Instruction’s Real Fragment Contract
docs.text:
Your goal in this chapter

Derive a real instruction's thread/value mapping, prove complete output coverage, and distinguish a warp MMA from Hopper WGMMA. Read thread/value copy ownership first; revisit WGMMA for the asynchronous instruction contract.

docs.title: 1 — An atom is more than a tile shape
docs.text:
A statement such as “this instruction computes a 16 × 8 result” omits three essential questions: which threads participate, which values each thread supplies, and where each output register belongs. CuTe connects the instruction wrapper to those answers through MMA_Traits. An MMA_Atom combines the operation and its traits; a TiledMMA repeats and arranges atoms into a larger computation.

The pinned MMA atom tutorial separates these layers. The operation's architecture prefix names its first supported architecture, not a declaration that every later instruction has the same layout. Register counts, precision and participation belong to the exact operation.

We will decode SM75_16x8x8_F32F16F16F32_TN. This is a synchronous, warp-level FP16 multiply with FP32 accumulation, useful for learning fragment ownership. It is not Hopper's asynchronous warpgroup MMA. Reading its traits on the CPU does not execute an MMA instruction or validate a GPU kernel.

docs.title: 2 — Count logical values and physical registers
docs.text:
The operation computes D = A × B + C, with A shaped 16 × 8, mathematical B shaped 8 × 8, and C/D shaped 16 × 8. Its instruction wrapper declares:

Operand Logical values per participating lane Physical register arguments per lane A 4 FP16 values Two packed 32-bit registers B 2 FP16 values One packed 32-bit register C 4 FP32 values Four FP32 registers D 4 FP32 values Four FP32 registers

The accumulator accounting closes exactly: 32 lanes × 4 outputs = 128 = 16 × 8. There is no need to invent duplicated outputs to explain a fictitious eight-value fragment. A four-value fragment is also not necessarily a contiguous 2 × 2 rectangle: its coordinates come from the traits, not from drawing a convenient box.

Do not add C and D's interface counts to predict final compiler register allocation. They name input/output operands of the operation; accumulator storage may be reused. Inspect the compiled kernel's resource report for its actual allocation.

docs.title: 3 — Read the actual CLayout
docs.text:
The pinned SM75 traits encode the C mapping with a nested thread mode (4,8) and value mode (2,2). For lane t and value index v, define:

g = t / 4, q = t % 4, a = v % 2, b = v / 2.

The layout's encoded offset is 32q + g + 16a + 8b. It indexes an M × N logical matrix using the atom's first-mode-fast convention. Decode it as:

row = encoded % 16 = g + 8b

column = encoded / 16 = 2q + a.

Lane v=0 v=1 v=2 v=3 0 (0,0) (0,1) (8,0) (8,1) 1 (0,2) (0,3) (8,2) (8,3) 5 (1,2) (1,3) (9,2) (9,3) 10 (2,4) (2,5) (10,4) (10,5) 31 (7,6) (7,7) (15,6) (15,7)

Thus lane 10 owns two column pairs separated by eight rows. Treating those four outputs as four consecutive rows produces an incorrect epilogue even if every arithmetic instruction itself is valid.

This short CPU-side inspection uses the real pinned type:

using Operation = cute::SM75_16x8x8_F32F16F16F32_TN;
using Traits = cute::MMA_Traits<Operation>;
typename Traits::CLayout mapping;
int lane = 10;
for (int value = 0; value < 4; ++value) {
    int encoded = mapping(cute::make_coord(lane, value));
    int row = encoded % 16;
    int column = encoded / 16;
    // Compare these coordinates with an independently derived table.
}

docs.title: Calculate lane 10 before trusting the printed map
docs.text:
1. Split the lane into g=10/4=2 and q=10%4=2.
  2. For value index 0, a=0,b=0. The trait offset is 32×2+2=66; decode 66%16=2 and 66/16=4, yielding output (2,4).
  3. For value index 1, add 16a=16, obtaining 82. It decodes to (2,5).
  4. For value index 2, add 8b=8 instead, obtaining 74. It decodes to (10,4).
  5. For value index 3, both additions apply: offset 90 decodes to (10,5).

Plot the four results before imagining a rectangular per-thread fragment. The labels r0 through r3 are lane 10's accumulator entries, not stored data values or byte offsets:

Logical C/D tile: 16 rows, 8 columns

                 columns n
                  0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
row m=2          [ .  .  .  . r0 r1  .  . ]
                    ... intervening rows ...
row m=10         [ .  .  .  . r2 r3  .  . ]

Lane 10: g=2, q=2
  value 0 -> encoded 66 -> row 2,  column 4
  value 1 -> encoded 82 -> row 2,  column 5
  value 2 -> encoded 74 -> row 10, column 4
  value 3 -> encoded 90 -> row 10, column 5

encoded = row + 16*column   [atom's logical encoding]
row-major global offset = row*leading_dimension + column
                           [a separate storage mapping]

Read the figure: register-entry order jumps from row two to row ten; dots denote outputs belonging to other lanes, not zeros. Decode the trait's logical encoding first, then map (row,column) to the destination tensor. The real Traits::CLayout inspection is the API check behind this picture. Writing a contiguous 2×2 or 4×1 rectangle from these four entries would store the wrong coordinates.

Expected coordinates: (2,4), (2,5), (10,4), (10,5). The integer quotients use the atom's first-mode-fast logical encoding; they are not byte addresses in a row-major output allocation. Check: compare each result with the independently derived table, then enumerate all lanes for complete coverage. Pitfall: treating offsets 66, 82, 74 and 90 as row-major global offsets would use the correct numbers in the wrong coordinate convention.

The type definitions require the matching atom-traits header; the complete program linked below supplies it.

docs.title: Finish the address chain: a trait offset is not a store offset
docs.text:
The trait names logical ownership; an output tensor separately names storage. To make the second step concrete, choose an illustrative row-major FP32 destination with sixteen rows, eight valid columns and leading dimension ld=12 elements. Each row therefore has four padding elements. This destination is a manual storage example, not an additional GPU kernel in the host fragment oracle.

  1. Start with lane 10, value entry v=2. The real Traits::CLayout gives encoded offset 74.
  2. Decode using the trait's first-mode-fast convention: row=74%16=10, column=74/16=4.
  3. Apply the destination formula, not the trait encoding: row*ld+column=10*12+4=124 FP32 elements.
  4. Convert to bytes once: 124*4=496 bytes from the destination view origin.
  5. Repeat for entries zero, one and three: element offsets 28, 29 and 125; byte offsets 112, 116 and 500.

An illustrative tensor expression for that second map is:

// Excerpt with a valid float* output allocation already supplied.
auto output_view =
    cute::make_tensor(cute::make_gmem_ptr(output),
                      cute::make_layout(cute::make_shape(16, 8),
                                        cute::make_stride(12, 1)));
// Coordinate-to-storage example only, not a complete MMA epilogue:
// output_view(cute::make_coord(10, 4)) names output[124].

The complete host oracle deliberately stops at coordinates: it never executes MMA or writes a GPU output. The expression above shows how a separate destination layout would interpret those coordinates. A real tiled MMA epilogue must use the selected instruction's partition/retile interface and collective participation requirements rather than treating this scalar illustration as a replacement implementation.

Pitfall: an epilogue that stores at output[74] confuses encoded logical position with physical storage. An epilogue that writes four consecutive elements beginning at 28 also fails: the third entry belongs to row ten. Nonuniform numerical values are needed to reveal both mistakes; four identical register values can conceal a permutation.

Exercise: move the origin, preserve the mapping

The same destination tile begins at global row 32, column 16 in a row-major matrix with leading dimension 80. Where does lane 10 entry 2 store?

Answer: Local (10,4) becomes global (42,20). Element offset from the matrix origin is 42*80+20=3380; byte offset is 13520. Equivalently, tile origin offset 32*80+16=2576 plus local 10*80+4=804 gives 3380. The local instruction coordinate did not change when the destination origin moved.

docs.title: 4 — Coverage is a proof obligation
docs.text:
Create a 16 × 8 array of zero counters. Enumerate every (lane,value) pair, reject out-of-range coordinates, and increment its destination counter. Every counter must finish at one. Zero means a missing element; two means overlapping ownership. Keeping only the first owner hides precisely the defect the test should detect.

Also compare the trait mapping with the independently derived formula. A bijection can still be the wrong permutation. Finally, remember what this proves: the documented atom layout was decoded consistently. It does not prove that a custom kernel loaded the right operands or stored the accumulator with the same mapping.

docs.title: 5 — A and B have separate contracts
docs.text:
For this exact FP16 operation, A's four logical values have the same coordinate formula as C, but its second coordinate is K, not N. For B, CuTe names the logical modes (N,K), while mathematical matrix notation writes B[k,n]:

A[g + 8b, 2q + a], for four values;

B[2q + v, g], for two values, with B written here in mathematical (K,N) order.

For lane 7, g=1 and q=3: A supplies (1,6), (1,7), (9,6), (9,7); B supplies (6,1) and (7,1). Four packed A values do not imply four packed B values. Nor do these logical coordinates prescribe how an ldmatrix invocation obtains them: its address/packing contract is another layer that must agree.

docs.title: 6 — Grow an atom into a tiled computation
docs.text:
The pinned API permits constructing a default tiled atom:

auto tiled_mma =
    cute::make_tiled_mma(cute::SM75_16x8x8_F32F16F16F32_TN{});
// In a matching device collective, with sA, sB and gC defined:
// auto thread_mma = tiled_mma.get_slice(threadIdx.x);
// auto thread_A = thread_mma.partition_A(sA);
// auto thread_B = thread_mma.partition_B(sB);
// auto thread_C = thread_mma.partition_C(gC);
// auto accumulator = thread_mma.make_fragment_C(thread_C);

This is an API reading sketch, not a complete kernel. The tensor shapes, memory spaces, participating thread count, data movement and completion protocol must be supplied. partition_C returns a view; make_fragment_C constructs accumulator storage; neither computes a product merely by existing. See mma_atom.hpp and the pinned CuTe GEMM tutorial.

docs.title: Tails do not permit partial instruction participation
docs.text:
The synchronous warp MMA is a collective instruction with an aligned participation contract. All required lanes must execute the same instruction form with the required convergence. A lane whose eventual output lies beyond M or N must not simply skip the MMA while the remaining lanes execute it. Instead, a supported tail path arranges legal input fragments—often by zero-filling invalid logical inputs—and predicates final output stores while preserving the instruction's collective participation. The chosen library kernel supplies its own supported tail machinery.

Check: separate three questions: whether each source access is legal, whether every required lane participates, and whether every valid result is stored to its intended coordinate. Passing one does not imply the other two. The host fragment oracle checks the coordinate map only; it does not exercise convergence or the device instruction's runtime behavior. Follow the pinned PTX warp-MMA contract.

Count K repetitions too. A 64 × 32 warp result has 16 spatial 16 × 8 atoms. Covering a K-depth of 64 with k8 needs eight reduction steps: 128 warp MMA instructions, not sixteen. That accounts for 2 × 64 × 32 × 64 = 262,144 floating-point operations under the conventional FMA-equals-two convention. It predicts work, not instruction latency.

docs.title: 7 — Cross the boundary to Hopper carefully
docs.text:
Hopper WGMMA uses a 128-thread collective, different shapes, shared-memory descriptors and asynchronous completion. The warp formulas above cannot be copied into its epilogue. Use the selected mma_traits_sm90_gmma specialization, then trace TMA arrival, WGMMA register ordering, committed-group completion and source-buffer reuse separately. A thread/value layout is not a substitute for any of those waits.

The full host fragment oracle checks A, B and C coordinates against the pinned traits and verifies bijective coverage. With the source pin and workspace prepared in Chapter 15:

mkdir -p build/advanced
nvcc -std=c++17 -O2 --expt-relaxed-constexpr \
  -I "$CUTLASS_ROOT/include" \
  docs/examples/advanced/cute_fragments.cu -o build/advanced/cute_fragments
./build/advanced/cute_fragments

Expected check: FRAGMENT PASS with 128 C, 128 A and 64 B ownership pairs and zero errors. The actual compilation and host execution are captured in the dated block below, separately from the original book programs. This program launches no GPU kernel.

docs.title: 8 — Exercises with worked answers
docs.text:
Lane 18: locate its four results

Compute g=18/4=4 and q=18%4=2. The outputs are (4,4), (4,5), (12,4) and (12,5). A bounding rectangle would include unowned intervening rows, so store exactly the four mapped coordinates.

A correct count but the wrong mapping

An epilogue writes every output exactly once, but swaps the first and second column of every pair. Can an ownership test catch it?

Bijection alone cannot: coverage still equals one everywhere. The independent coordinate comparison catches the permutation, and a full numerical test with nonuniform inputs checks that the actual computation and stores use the intended mapping. Uniform all-one inputs can hide it.

docs.title: Complete source and captured execution
docs.text:
Executed on November 18, 2026 (UTC). Scope: CPU execution of real CuTe coordinate/trait checks.

Tested source SHA-256: fae8d94ea8f09f4eaf81c4d72bd231b27a51779d64bec93ece4d57278876ecb0. Exact source · System information · Workshop results.

The listing below matches the tested source. Its presentation is formatted at build time; downloads retain the captured bytes.

// Host-only ownership checks against CUTLASS v4.3.6 MMA traits.
// This program never calls an MMA instruction and launches no GPU kernel.
#include <cute/atom/mma_traits_sm75.hpp>
#include <array>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    using Operation = cute::SM75_16x8x8_F32F16F16F32_TN;
    using Traits = cute::MMA_Traits<Operation>;
    typename Traits::ALayout a_layout;
    typename Traits::BLayout b_layout;
    typename Traits::CLayout c_layout;
    std::array<int, 128> a_coverage{}, c_coverage{};
    std::array<int, 64> b_coverage{};
    int errors = 0;
    for (int lane = 0; lane < 32; ++lane) {
        const int group = lane / 4, within = lane % 4;
        for (int value = 0; value < 4; ++value) {
            const int row = group + 8 * (value / 2);
            const int column = 2 * within + value % 2;
            const int expected = row + 16 * column;
            const int a = a_layout(cute::make_coord(lane, value));
            const int c = c_layout(cute::make_coord(lane, value));
            errors += a != expected;
            errors += c != expected;
            if (a < 0 || a >= int(a_coverage.size()))
                ++errors;
            else
                ++a_coverage[a];
            if (c < 0 || c >= int(c_coverage.size()))
                ++errors;
            else
                ++c_coverage[c];
            if (lane == 10)
                std::printf(
                    "lane=10 value=%d C=(%d,%d) trait_offset=%d\n",
                    value,
                    row,
                    column,
                    c);
        }
        for (int value = 0; value < 2; ++value) {
            // The B trait encodes (N,K), while mathematical B is B[k,n].
            const int n = group, k = 2 * within + value;
            const int expected = n + 8 * k;
            const int b = b_layout(cute::make_coord(lane, value));
            errors += b != expected;
            if (b < 0 || b >= int(b_coverage.size()))
                ++errors;
            else
                ++b_coverage[b];
        }
    }
    for (int count : a_coverage)
        errors += count != 1;
    for (int count : b_coverage)
        errors += count != 1;
    for (int count : c_coverage)
        errors += count != 1;
    std::printf(
        "%s: C_pairs=128 A_pairs=128 B_pairs=64 errors=%d\n",
        errors ? "FRAGMENT FAIL" : "FRAGMENT PASS",
        errors);
    return errors ? 1 : 0;
}

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• An MMA atom specifies participating threads, operand packing and result coordinates, not merely an M×N tile size.

  • The pinned warp-level atom assigns four FP32 outputs per lane; independent coordinate checks and bijective coverage catch different mapping errors.

  • Count both spatial atoms and K repetitions, and keep warp MMA distinct from asynchronous Hopper WGMMA. Next, align producers and consumers through shared-memory layouts.

docs.title: 22. Shared Layouts — Banks, Swizzles and Descriptor Agreement
Lesson 22 Companion Guide — Keep Banks, Swizzles and Descriptors in Agreement
docs.text:
Your goal in this chapter

Compute bank indices for a specific warp access, prove a swizzle's mapping, and preserve agreement between generic stores, TMA and WGMMA. Read MMA atoms, TMA descriptors and the proxy-ordering rules.

docs.title: 1 — Three layouts must describe the same tile
docs.text:
A shared tile has a producer, a physical allocation and a consumer. The producer might use ordinary stores, an asynchronous copy atom or TMA. The consumer might use scalar loads, ldmatrix, or WGMMA descriptors. All must agree on which physical location represents a logical coordinate.

A successful tensor-copy operation does not establish that an unrelated WGMMA descriptor interprets its output correctly. Conversely, a beautifully bank-distributed layout can still violate an instruction's supported layout or alignment. Establish correctness first, then measure whether changing the physical arrangement improves the actual access pattern.

The pinned GMMA layout definitions and CuTe swizzle implementation are the source contracts for this chapter. The simple bank examples below are scalar models, not predictions of every matrix instruction's transaction decomposition.

docs.title: 2 — Start with an explicit bank model
docs.text:
For aligned, scalar 32-bit shared-memory accesses, use 32 banks of four bytes each:

word_offset = byte_offset / 4, bank = word_offset % 32.

For a compact row-major 32 × 32 FP32 tile, word_offset(i,j)=32i+j. Suppose one warp accesses one element per lane:

Pattern, lane t Word offset Bank Result in this model Row 0: (0,t) t t Distinct banks Column 0: (t,0) 32t 0 Different words in one bank Broadcast: every lane (0,0) 0 0 Same word; broadcast, not 32 distinct conflicting words

Different addresses in one bank differ from the same address requested by several readers. Likewise, a vector instruction can split into several transactions; apply the bank analysis to the relevant transactions rather than counting all its bytes as one request. FP16 coordinates require conversion to byte/word addresses because two adjacent halves share a four-byte word. Do not blindly use element_offset % 32 for every datatype.

A fixed-column access gives a concrete conflict picture. Every numeric address here is a 32-bit word offset; multiply by four for bytes. The example is not an FP16 bank formula:

One warp, one scalar FP32 read per lane, column j=0

lane  plain word  plain bank  | padded word  padded bank
  0       0           0       |      0            0
  1      32           0       |     33            1
  2      64           0       |     66            2
  3      96           0       |     99            3
  4     128           0       |    132            4
  5     160           0       |    165            5
  6     192           0       |    198            6
  7     224           0       |    231            7
 ...    ...          ...      |     ...          ...
 31     992           0       |   1023           31

plain:  distinct words --all--> bank 0      [conflict]
padded: distinct words -----> banks 0..31   [distributed]
broadcast: every lane reads word 0          [same-word case]

Read the figure: form each lane's word offset, take modulo 32, then compare bank identities while keeping distinct-word and same-word requests separate. A minimal address-map API for the two layouts is:

auto plain = cute::make_layout(
    cute::make_shape(cute::Int<32>{}, cute::Int<32>{}),
    cute::make_stride(cute::Int<32>{}, cute::Int<1>{}));
auto padded = cute::make_layout(
    cute::make_shape(cute::Int<32>{}, cute::Int<32>{}),
    cute::make_stride(cute::Int<33>{}, cute::Int<1>{}));
auto lane7_plain = plain(cute::make_coord(7, 0));   // 224 words
auto lane7_padded = padded(cute::make_coord(7, 0)); // 231 words

These layouts calculate addresses only; no shared load occurs when they are constructed. The pinned CuTe layout contract supplies the shape/stride mapping, while the GPU instruction and bank model determine the memory behavior.

The CUDA shared-memory guidance describes bank conflicts and broadcasts. The model identifies a possible conflict; profiler evidence determines its performance impact.

docs.title: 3 — Padding: a simple improvement with a cost
docs.text:
Keep logical shape (32,32) but use FP32 strides (33,1). Column 0's lane-t word offset becomes 33t; its bank is t. Padding breaks the all-in-one-bank pattern.

Storage sizing changes: the largest referenced offset is 31×33+31=1054, so this positive-stride layout's minimum span is 1,055 floats. Reserving 32 full padded rows uses 1,056 floats. Both exceed the 1,024 useful values; document which allocation convention you use.

Padding is not a universal replacement for a descriptor-compatible operand layout. It can increase shared-memory consumption and reduce residency. A scalar transpose tile may benefit while a WGMMA operand requires a different supported physical arrangement.

docs.title: 4 — XOR swizzling by hand
docs.text:
Consider this word-offset mapping for a 32 × 32 FP32 tile:

swizzled(i,j) = 32i + (j XOR i).

For each fixed row, XOR permutes its 32 column positions. Each element still has a unique location, and XORing by i again restores j. The storage span remains 1,024 words.

Logical coordinate Linear offset 32i+j Swizzled offset Swizzled bank (0,0) 0 0 0 (1,0) 32 33 1 (2,0) 64 66 2 (3,0) 96 99 3 (3,5) 101 102 6

Now a fixed-column warp accesses banks j XOR t, all distinct. A fixed-row warp also visits distinct banks. This is a teaching mapping for those accesses; it is not a promise that an arbitrary tensor-core instruction accepts it.

CuTe can express the XOR composition directly:

auto linear = cute::make_layout(
    cute::make_shape(cute::Int<32>{}, cute::Int<32>{}),
    cute::make_stride(cute::Int<32>{}, cute::Int<1>{}));
auto swizzled = cute::composition(cute::Swizzle<5, 0, 5>{}, linear);
// Word offsets: swizzled(3,5) == 102; linear(3,5) == 101.

Swizzle<5,0,5> XORs the five source bits at positions 5–9 into positions 0–4. Its parameters refer to the index presented to the swizzle. Here that index counts FP32 words. Reinterpreting the same parameters as byte offsets changes the physical mapping.

docs.title: 5 — A bijection can leave conflicts unchanged
docs.text:
Test a tempting alternative:

bad_for_this_access(i,j) = 32 × (i XOR (j >> 2)) + j.

It is a valid permutation over the same 1,024 coordinates, but offset % 32 is still j. Every lane reading a fixed column still targets the same bank. The swizzle changes rows while leaving the low column bits untouched.

CuTe can represent this mapping too: compose the linear layout above with Swizzle<3,2,-3>. The negative shift moves column bits 2–4 left into row bits 5–7. For (3,20), the linear offset is 116 and the transformed offset is 212. Neither representability nor uniqueness proves a bank benefit.

docs.title: Make the counterexample an actual CuTe call
docs.text:
Using the linear layout from §4:

auto bank_unchanged =
    cute::composition(cute::Swizzle<3, 2, -3>{}, linear);
auto offset = bank_unchanged(cute::make_coord(3, 20)); // 212
  1. The unswizzled word offset is 3×32+20=116.
  2. Column 20 has 20>>2=5 in the selected three-bit field.
  3. XOR that field into the row bits: 3 XOR 5=6.
  4. The resulting word offset is 6×32+20=212.
  5. Both 116 and 212 select bank 20 modulo 32. The addresses changed, but the relevant bank bits did not.

Expected result: the mapping remains a permutation, yet a fixed-column warp still sends distinct addresses to one bank. Check: enumerate all 32 lane addresses for the actual fixed column; uniqueness of addresses and uniqueness of banks are separate tests. Pitfall: labeling every XOR composition “bank-conflict free” without examining which bits changed.

This distinction is a useful review habit: ask which address bits select the resource you are trying to distribute? Then enumerate those bits for the actual participating lanes.

docs.title: Compare all three maps with the same lane request
docs.text:
The scalar model has logical coordinates (i,j) in a 32×32 FP32 tile. Lane t requests (i,j)=(t,0). Define word offset w as a count of aligned four-byte words from the shared allocation origin, and bank as w%32. A different origin shifts bank numbers; the conflict relationship still needs the actual effective word addresses.

  1. Plain storage: w=32*i+j. Lane 7 requests 32*7=224, byte offset 896, bank zero. Lane 0 requests a different word zero in that same bank.
  2. Padded storage: w=33*i+j. Lane 7 requests 231, byte offset 924, bank seven. The thirty-two lanes visit distinct banks for this fixed-column request.
  3. XOR storage: w=32*i+(j^i). With j zero, lane 7 also requests 231 and bank seven. This agreement at column zero does not mean the complete padded and XOR layouts are identical.
  4. Distinguish them at (3,5). Plain gives 96+5=101 and bank five. Padding gives 99+5=104 and bank eight. XOR gives 96+(5^3)=96+6=102 and bank six. One coordinate is enough to reject equality of the three maps.
  5. Check storage span and producer agreement. Plain and this XOR permutation use 1024 words. Padded storage's logical view spans 1055 words, or 1056 when reserving complete padded rows. A producer writing plain offsets and a consumer reading XOR offsets disagree even though both stay in bounds.

The actual CuTe composition shown earlier applies Swizzle<5,0,5> to a linear word-index layout. Its input bits 5–9 encode the row for this compact map, and XOR into bits 0–4 changes the stored column. Reusing those parameters on byte offsets mixes different bit positions and defines a different map.

Expected check: enumerate all 1024 logical coordinates and require 1024 unique in-range locations for the XOR map, then compare each against 32*i+(j^i). Separately, enumerate one lane request pattern and count distinct banks. Bijective storage is necessary for independent writes but does not itself establish conflict freedom or a supported matrix-instruction operand.

Exercise: a nonzero fixed column

A warp requests (t,5) for t=0 through 31. Which banks does the XOR map visit? Compare lane 3 with padding.

Answer: XOR visits banks 5^t, a permutation of 0 through 31, so all are distinct in this scalar model. Lane 3 reaches word 102, bank six. Padding reaches word 104, bank eight. Both patterns distribute this request, but use different addresses. This calculation predicts a bank property, not measured latency.

docs.title: 6 — Use the supported Hopper layout atoms
docs.text:
A production WGMMA operand should begin with the pinned type-aware GMMA layout atoms, rather than an invented XOR formula:

using Element = cutlass::half_t;
using Atom = cute::SM90::GMMA::Layout_K_SW128_Atom<Element>;
auto shared_layout = cute::tile_to_shape(
    Atom{}, cute::Shape<cute::_128, cute::_64>{});

This is a layout-construction sketch from the pinned definitions, not a complete kernel. It selects a K-major 128-byte-swizzle atom and tiles it to a particular logical operand shape. The other operand and any MN-major choice require their own supported layouts. The header also defines 32-byte, 64-byte and interleaved alternatives. The aliases carry datatype-aware upcasting and shared-pointer semantics; copying internal bit-level parameters into a manually indexed element array is not an equivalent construction.

A swizzle mode and a full matrix descriptor are different things. The descriptor also contains the matrix start and leading/stride offsets. Follow the selected core-matrix layout when deriving those offsets, not the original global matrix's row stride. Match the TMA tensor-map swizzle and the consuming WGMMA interpretation. Chapter 6 gives the field contract.

docs.title: 7 — Alignment, stages and lifetime
docs.text:
For the documented WGMMA swizzle patterns, zero-base-offset repeating boundaries are 1,024 bytes for 128-byte swizzling, 512 for 64-byte and 256 for 32-byte. These are pattern boundaries, not interchangeable with a 16-byte descriptor-field granularity. Instruction-specific destination alignment still applies. A pointer can satisfy one alignment requirement and fail another.

For a staged allocation, compute each stage's span, rounding and starting address explicitly. A stage stride that packs useful elements tightly may put the next stage at the wrong pattern offset. A larger allocation fixes neither its mapping nor its producer/consumer interpretation. Use the builder's selected storage organization unless you have independently derived a replacement.

Layout agreement also does not order memory accesses:

Handoff Additional obligation Generic shared stores → async reader Applicable proxy publication and participating-thread synchronization TMA load → consumer Matching transaction count, barrier generation and completion wait WGMMA source → overwritten next tile Complete the asynchronous readers before releasing the stage Accumulator → epilogue Wait for the relevant arithmetic groups before ordinary register reads

The Hopper PTX contracts and pipeline chapter connect these requirements. A bank-conflict fix must preserve every one of them.

docs.title: 8 — Exercises and a review checklist
docs.text:
Is the padded tile only 1,024 floats?

Shape (32,32) with strides (33,1) has 1,024 coordinates, but references offset 1,054. Its minimum span is 1,055 floats. Allocate by the actual layout/storage contract, not the useful element count alone.

The XOR mapping has no duplicate addresses. Is it faster?

Not necessarily. The row-XOR counterexample in §5 is bijective but leaves fixed-column banks unchanged. Even the bank-distributing mapping needs a benchmark because instruction transactions, occupancy, extra address arithmetic and other bottlenecks can dominate.

Before a GPU run, enumerate bounds, uniqueness, bank indices and stage starts. During the run, compare the full nonuniform result and use memory-safety checks. During tuning, record actual shared storage, instruction selection, relevant bank metrics and the application timing distribution. These arithmetic examples are worked models; they are not captured Hopper performance measurements.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Derive bank indices from byte addresses and access width. Distinct words in one bank differ from a shared-word broadcast.

  • Padding and XOR permutations can improve particular accesses, but a bijection alone proves neither a bank benefit nor instruction compatibility.

  • Producer layout, allocation, TMA/WGMMA interpretation, alignment and stage lifetime must agree. Use those obligations in the complete tiled GEMM.

docs.title: 23. Build and Validate a Complete Tiled GEMM
Lesson 23 Companion Guide — Build a Complete Reference-Checked SIMT Baseline
docs.text:
Your goal in this chapter

Follow every address and barrier in a complete, bounded GEMM before replacing its scalar arithmetic with a Tensor Core collective. Read CTA indexing, copy ownership and shared layouts first.

docs.title: 1 — Choose a contract small enough to prove
docs.text:
The lab computes batched D = 0.5 * A * B + 0.25 * C using row-major FP32 operands. Each batch has M×K, K×N and M×N mathematical shapes. Physical rows are padded: lda=K+3, ldb=N+5, ldc=N+7. The padding makes a mistaken assumption of compact storage visible.

This is a SIMT shared-memory baseline, not a Tensor Core kernel and not a complete CuTe GEMM. It deliberately makes the scalar address arithmetic explicit. The preceding CuTe chapters teach how to represent the same mappings; the next chapter shows how CUTLASS packages a Tensor Core implementation. A reference implementation can be valuable without being fast.

The full tiled_gemm.cu includes allocation, initialization, launch checks, an independent CPU oracle, input-preservation checks, padding and guards. Its mathematical reference does not call the GPU implementation’s indexing helpers.

The captured harness uses separate allocations for A, B, C and D, with nonoverlapping batch regions within each allocation. This removes input/output aliasing from the contract. Overlapping D with A or B can overwrite a value another block still needs; a block barrier cannot order unrelated blocks. An in-place C/D variant must separately establish compatible layout and aliasing semantics and obtain its own validation; it is not demonstrated by the separate-buffer result. The integer indexing in this small lab is also bounded by its fixed cases, rather than a general interface for arbitrarily large dimensions.

docs.title: 2 — Hand-compute the operation first
docs.text:
Consider

A = [ 1 -2  3 ]    B = [ 2  1 ]    C = [ 2 -4 ]
    [ 4  0 -1 ]        [ 3 -2 ]        [ 6  8 ]
                        [ 1  4 ]

The product is AB=[[-1,17],[7,0]]. Applying the scalars gives D=[[0,7.5],[5,2]]. For example, the top-right element is 0.5*(1*1 + (-2)*(-2) + 3*4) + 0.25*(-4) = 7.5.

This tiny case establishes three conventions before any tiling: B is indexed by reduction coordinate k and output column n; C participates in the epilogue; and beta is applied once after the full reduction. Applying beta to each K tile would add C repeatedly.

docs.title: 3 — One block owns a 16×16 output tile
docs.text:
Use 256 threads in a 16×16 block. Thread (tx,ty) owns the output coordinate

m = blockIdx.y*16 + ty, n = blockIdx.x*16 + tx.

For batched input, blockIdx.z selects the batch. The grid is (ceil(N/16), ceil(M/16), L). Each thread keeps one FP32 accumulator for the entire K loop. Two shared arrays hold a 16×16 A tile and a 16×16 B tile, for 2*16*16*4 = 2048 bytes of explicit operand storage per block.

This is not a prediction of total register count or occupancy. Address variables, loop state, compiler transformations and launch constraints add resources. Inspect the compiler report and the measured kernel after correctness is established.

docs.title: 4 — Cooperative loads use independent predicates
docs.text:
At K origin k0, thread (tx,ty) loads:

  • A coordinate (m,k0+tx) into shared A position (ty,tx).
  • B coordinate (k0+ty,n) into shared B position (ty,tx).

A is valid when m<M && k0+tx<K; B is valid when k0+ty<K && n<N. These are different predicates. False inputs contribute zero to the reduction, so the thread writes zero into its shared slot instead of leaving data from a previous iteration.

The physical offsets include the selected batch and padded leading dimensions. Use a sufficiently wide type for the products: widening only after m*lda has overflowed does not repair the arithmetic. Chapter 19 derives the byte-address chain in detail.

docs.title: 5 — Two barriers protect different hazards
docs.text:
After cooperative loads, every block thread reaches a barrier before any thread consumes the shared arrays. That protects read-after-write readiness. The inner loop then accumulates 16 products. A second barrier prevents the next K iteration from overwriting a shared tile that another thread is still reading.

For each K tile:
  all threads load their A/B elements, or write zero for a false predicate
  all threads rendezvous              // shared operands ready
  each thread accumulates 16 products
  all threads rendezvous              // shared operands reusable

The second barrier is not redundant just because the first exists. On an output tail, a thread with m>=M or n>=N still participates in this protocol. It may skip the final output store, but returning before a block-wide barrier would break collective participation.

These are synchronous CUDA shared-memory loads. They do not require inventing a TMA transaction-count barrier. Conversely, replacing the loads with TMA while retaining only these barriers would not implement the required asynchronous completion contract. Mechanism-specific ordering matters.

docs.title: 6 — Keep the accumulator alive across the whole reduction
docs.text:
Suppose K=41. Three 16-wide K iterations are needed. The last has nine useful reduction positions and seven zero-filled positions. The accumulator is initialized once before all three iterations, updated by each tile, and consumed once afterward.

An accumulator reset inside the K-tile loop retains only the final tile. A kernel may pass an input where the first two tiles contain zeros, so include nonzero contributions across the whole reduction. Nonuniform binary-rational input values in the lab exercise that condition without requiring an arbitrary tolerance.

For K=0, the loop executes zero times and the epilogue becomes D=0.25*C. This case checks that the launch and epilogue do not assume a first operand tile always exists. It does not imply that every Tensor Core library configuration accepts a zero reduction dimension; support is part of each API’s contract.

docs.title: Work one ragged output through all three reduction tiles
docs.text:
Take the actual ragged case M=37,N=29,K=41,L=2. Let batch l=1, block (blockIdx.x,blockIdx.y)=(1,2) and thread (tx,ty)=(12,4). These are logical coordinates, not byte addresses. All offsets below are relative to the operand pointers passed to the kernel, after the 16-element leading guards.

  1. Find the output. m=2*16+4=36, n=1*16+12=28. Both are valid: this thread owns the last logical output of the second batch.
  2. Find the padded rows. The source uses lda=44, ldb=34, ldc=36. Thus A's batch stride is 37*44=1628 elements; B's is 41*34=1394; C/D's is 37*36=1332. Output (1,36,28) is at element offset 1332+36*36+28=2656, or byte offset 10624 for FP32.
  3. Distinguish loading from consuming. At k0=32, this thread's A load names (m,k)=(36,44) and is invalid, so it writes zero to As[4][12]. Its B load names (k,n)=(36,28) and is valid: offset 1394+36*34+28=2646. Its own A load being invalid does not make its output invalid.
  4. Consume the shared tile collectively. To compute its output, it reads As[4][q] and Bs[q][12] for q=0..15. The nine positions q=0..8 represent valid k=32..40; q=9..15 are zero-filled. Other threads supplied many of those inputs. The previous tiles supplied k=0..31.
  5. Apply the epilogue once. After all three tiles, write D[2656]=0.5*acc+0.25*C[2656]. A thread at (tx,ty)=(13,4) owns n=29, so it skips this store but still joins both barriers in every tile.

Check: the block contains 256 threads but only 5*13=65 valid output owners, because rows 32–36 and columns 16–28 remain. Every valid owner must see all 41 reduction terms. Using the actual initialization formulas gives acc=1.125, C=0.5 and D=0.6875 at this coordinate. This hand calculation complements the independently captured executable, which checks every output.

docs.title: See the ragged reduction and the final store together
docs.text:
Read left to right in each row, then top to bottom. k0 is the first reduction coordinate of a shared tile; q is its local coordinate, so k=k0+q. The displayed partial sums use the actual source initialization for output (batch,m,n)=(1,36,28), not arbitrary schematic data.

Output owner: block(x=1,y=2), thread(tx=12,ty=4)
              m=2*16+4=36     n=1*16+12=28

k0     shared q values      global k values     dot contribution
 0     0 .......... 15       0 ........ 15          0.625
16     0 .......... 15      16 ........ 31          0.21875
32     0 .... 8 | 9..15     32 ... 40 | absent       0.28125
                     zero-fill absent inputs          |
                                                     v
acc starts 0 ---> 0.625 ---> 0.84375 ---> 1.125
                                           |
                  alpha=0.5 -------------->* = 0.5625
                  C[2656]=0.5, beta=0.25 --->+  0.125
                                           |
                                           v
                                 D[2656] = 0.6875

Offsets 2656 are FP32 element offsets relative to the guarded kernel view, not offsets from the raw allocation base. In source, this chapter's k0 is named base, and q is named inner. The variable sum persists across the outer base loop, while the inner loop consumes a_tile[ty][inner] * b_tile[inner][tx]. The two barriers bracket each shared tile's ready/read/reuse lifetime.

This owner's cooperative A load at k0=32 uses k=44 and is zero-filled, yet its output still receives nine real final-tile products loaded by the whole block. The diagram distinguishes one thread's load ownership from the operands it consumes for its output. Resetting sum at each arrow would leave only 0.28125 and produce the wrong final value 0.265625.

docs.title: Reproduce the partial sums from the actual initializer
docs.text:
The numeric figure can be reproduced without a GPU or a second tiling implementation. For the chosen batch l=1, row m=36 and column n=28, the source initializer defines

A_k = ((36*3 + k*5 + 1*7)%9 - 4)/8

B_k = ((k*2 + 28*3 + 1*5)%7 - 3)/4.

Here k is the reduction coordinate, not a memory offset. All modulo inputs are nonnegative integers, so the formulas have unambiguous ordinary integer remainders. The fractions are binary-exact. A standalone CPU arithmetic check is:

parts = []
for k0 in (0, 16, 32):
    partial = 0.0
    for k in range(k0, min(k0 + 16, 41)):
        a = ((36*3 + k*5 + 7) % 9 - 4) / 8
        b = ((k*2 + 28*3 + 5) % 7 - 3) / 4
        partial += a * b
    parts.append(partial)
assert parts == [0.625, 0.21875, 0.28125]
assert sum(parts) == 1.125
c = ((36 + 28*2 + 1) % 5 - 2) / 2
assert c == 0.5 and 0.5*sum(parts) + 0.25*c == 0.6875

This snippet reconstructs one known coordinate from the published input contract. It is not a new numerical workload capture and cannot replace the full oracle, which independently checks every output. It does let you connect every intermediate number in the figure to the source rather than accepting a plausible final answer.

To inspect a single product, choose k=32: A is ((275%9)-4)/8=(5-4)/8=0.125; B is ((153%7)-3)/4=(6-3)/4=0.75; their product is 0.09375. Eight other real terms complete the last partial 0.28125. The remaining seven tile positions contribute zeros; they do not create reduction coordinates beyond K=41.

Exercise: diagnose a misplaced accumulator reset

A modified kernel resets sum before every K tile and otherwise uses the same epilogue. What does this output become? What if it instead adds beta*C after each of three tiles while retaining the correct reduction sum?

Answer: Resetting keeps only 0.28125, yielding 0.5*0.28125+0.25*0.5=0.265625. Adding the C term three times yields 0.5*1.125+3*0.25*0.5=0.9375. Both differ from 0.6875, so this nonzero early-tile/nonzero-beta example distinguishes the two bugs.

docs.title: 7 — Store only valid output coordinates
docs.text:
After the reduction, a valid owner reads C and writes D at the padded output offset. Invalid output threads do not access C or D. D’s valid region starts as a NaN sentinel so omitted stores cannot masquerade as correctly computed zeros. Padding and outer guards have separate sentinels and must remain unchanged.

The GPU and CPU implementations use the same mathematical shapes and scalars but different control structure. The CPU loops over each batch/output coordinate and performs a direct full-K reduction in double. Test values are small binary fractions, with short reductions and scalars chosen so the expected result is exactly representable in FP32. Exact equality is justified for these bounded cases; it is not a universal rule for floating-point GEMM.

docs.title: 8 — Test a matrix, not just one square
docs.text:
Case What it exercises M=N=K=16, L=1 A complete output tile and one K tile M=37, N=29, K=41, L=2 Partial M/N/K tiles, batch offsets and padded strides M=7, N=9, K=0, L=1 Empty reduction and nonzero-beta epilogue

Require all case results, complete output equality, intact padding/guards and successful CUDA completion. Sanitizer memcheck supplements these checks. A successful run does not prove performance, races in a different asynchronous implementation or every possible matrix extent.

The workshop collector retains exact source, toolchain and output records. Use those records to distinguish this SIMT baseline from the CUTLASS kernel in Chapter 24. Comparing both on identical supported cases is a correctness cross-check; benchmarking them requires a separate, consistently timed workload.

docs.title: Why the exact-equality test is bounded
docs.text:
The generated A values are integer multiples of 1/8, B values of 1/4, and C values of 1/2. Each product is therefore a multiple of 1/32; for the largest tested K=41, the sum magnitude is bounded by 41*(4/8)*(3/4)=15.375. Multiplication by alpha 1/2 and beta 1/4 retains a small binary-rational result. The integer significands remain far below FP32's 24-bit precision, so both the sequential GPU reduction and double CPU oracle represent these particular results exactly.

This argument depends on the bounded initialization, reduction length and scalars. Keeping D==expected after replacing them with arbitrary decimal or large-magnitude values would impose a different numerical contract. Choose and justify a tolerance for that new experiment, while preserving finite-value, padding and guard checks.

docs.title: 9 — Turn the baseline into a source-reading guide
docs.text:
When reading the official CuTe GEMM tutorial, locate the equivalents of these explicit components: problem/tile shapes, operand views, cooperative partitions, register accumulators, the reduction loop, readiness/reuse synchronization and epilogue. The implementation can replace arithmetic with layout objects and MMA atoms while retaining the same obligations.

Do not transplant one scalar loop into a Tensor Core fragment and assume its elements are row-major. Chapter 21 explains that ownership. Likewise, replacing the scalar loads with an asynchronous atom adds a pipeline state machine rather than removing the need to reason about lifetime.

Can output-tail threads return before the K loop?

Thread (15,15) has an invalid output on a small edge tile. Can it immediately return?

Answer: Not in this cooperative-load design. It owns shared input positions and participates in block-wide barriers. Predicate its memory accesses and final store while preserving collective participation.

Where does beta belong?

There are three K tiles. Should the epilogue add beta*C after each tile?

Answer: No. The defined operation adds it once after the complete reduction. Repeating it changes the mathematical result.

docs.title: Complete source and captured execution
docs.text:
Executed on November 18, 2026 (UTC). Scope: CUDA workload with its stated numerical checks.

Tested source SHA-256: 2e538ea2ead02582618632d764eb54d3420d87ebda007616ff54f5b499eb3c61. Exact source · System information · Workshop results.

The listing below matches the tested source. Its presentation is formatted at build time; downloads retain the captured bytes.

// A deliberately simple SIMT shared-memory GEMM, not Tensor Core or CuTe code.
// D = alpha*A*B + beta*C, row-major padded storage, independent batches.
// Small binary-rational inputs make these bounded reference cases exact in FP32.
#include <cuda_runtime.h>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <limits>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <vector>

static void cuda_check(cudaError_t result, char const* call) {
    if (result != cudaSuccess) {
        std::fprintf(
            stderr, "%s: %s\n", call, cudaGetErrorString(result));
        throw std::runtime_error("CUDA operation failed");
    }
}

#define CUDA_CHECK(call) cuda_check((call), #call)

constexpr int tile = 16;

__global__ void tiled_gemm(float const* a,
                           float const* b,
                           float const* c,
                           float* d,
                           int m,
                           int n,
                           int k,
                           int lda,
                           int ldb,
                           int ldc,
                           int stride_a,
                           int stride_b,
                           int stride_c,
                           float alpha,
                           float beta) {
    __shared__ float a_tile[tile][tile];
    __shared__ float b_tile[tile][tile];
    int tx = threadIdx.x, ty = threadIdx.y;
    int row = blockIdx.y * tile + ty;
    int column = blockIdx.x * tile + tx;
    int batch = blockIdx.z;
    float sum = 0.0f;
    for (int base = 0; base < k; base += tile) {
        int a_k = base + tx, b_k = base + ty;
        a_tile[ty][tx] = row < m && a_k < k
                             ? a[batch * stride_a + row * lda + a_k]
                             : 0.0f;
        b_tile[ty][tx] =
            b_k < k && column < n
                ? b[batch * stride_b + b_k * ldb + column]
                : 0.0f;
        __syncthreads(); // All writers complete before any tile is consumed.
        for (int inner = 0; inner < tile; ++inner)
            sum += a_tile[ty][inner] * b_tile[inner][tx];
        __syncthreads(); // All readers complete before the next tile overwrites.
    }
    if (row < m && column < n) {
        int offset = batch * stride_c + row * ldc + column;
        d[offset] = alpha * sum + beta * c[offset];
    }
}

static int run_case(int m, int n, int k, int batches) {
    constexpr int guard = 16;
    constexpr float canary = -98765.0f;
    constexpr float alpha = 0.5f, beta = 0.25f;
    int lda = k + 3, ldb = n + 5, ldc = n + 7;
    int stride_a = m * lda, stride_b = k * ldb, stride_c = m * ldc;
    std::vector<float> a(guard + batches * stride_a + guard,
                         canary);
    std::vector<float> b(guard + batches * stride_b + guard,
                         canary);
    std::vector<float> c(guard + batches * stride_c + guard,
                         canary);
    std::vector<float> d(c.size(), canary),
        expected(c.size(), canary);
    for (int batch = 0; batch < batches; ++batch) {
        for (int row = 0; row < m; ++row)
            for (int inner = 0; inner < k; ++inner)
                a[guard + batch * stride_a + row * lda + inner] =
                    float((row * 3 + inner * 5 + batch * 7) % 9 -
                          4) *
                    0.125f;
        for (int inner = 0; inner < k; ++inner)
            for (int column = 0; column < n; ++column)
                b[guard + batch * stride_b + inner * ldb + column] =
                    float((inner * 2 + column * 3 + batch * 5) % 7 -
                          3) *
                    0.25f;
        for (int row = 0; row < m; ++row)
            for (int column = 0; column < n; ++column) {
                int offset =
                    guard + batch * stride_c + row * ldc + column;
                c[offset] =
                    float((row + column * 2 + batch) % 5 - 2) *
                    0.5f;
                d[offset] = std::numeric_limits<float>::quiet_NaN();
            }
    }
    // Independent scalar CPU calculation: no shared tiling or GPU fragment map.
    // Products are multiples of 1/32 and bounded short sums remain FP32-exact.
    for (int batch = 0; batch < batches; ++batch)
        for (int row = 0; row < m; ++row)
            for (int column = 0; column < n; ++column) {
                double sum = 0.0;
                for (int inner = 0; inner < k; ++inner)
                    sum += double(a[guard + batch * stride_a +
                                    row * lda + inner]) *
                           double(b[guard + batch * stride_b +
                                    inner * ldb + column]);
                int offset =
                    guard + batch * stride_c + row * ldc + column;
                expected[offset] = float(double(alpha) * sum +
                                         double(beta) * c[offset]);
            }
    float *da = nullptr, *db = nullptr, *dc = nullptr,
          *dd = nullptr;
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&da, a.size() * sizeof(float)));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&db, b.size() * sizeof(float)));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&dc, c.size() * sizeof(float)));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&dd, d.size() * sizeof(float)));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(da,
                          a.data(),
                          a.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(db,
                          b.data(),
                          b.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(dc,
                          c.data(),
                          c.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(dd,
                          d.data(),
                          d.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    dim3 block(tile, tile),
        grid((n + tile - 1) / tile, (m + tile - 1) / tile, batches);
    tiled_gemm<<<grid, block>>>(da + guard,
                                db + guard,
                                dc + guard,
                                dd + guard,
                                m,
                                n,
                                k,
                                lda,
                                ldb,
                                ldc,
                                stride_a,
                                stride_b,
                                stride_c,
                                alpha,
                                beta);
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetLastError());
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(d.data(),
                          dd,
                          d.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    std::vector<float> a_after(a.size()), b_after(b.size()),
        c_after(c.size());
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(a_after.data(),
                          da,
                          a.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(b_after.data(),
                          db,
                          b.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(c_after.data(),
                          dc,
                          c.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaFree(dd));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaFree(dc));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaFree(db));
    CUDA_CHECK(cudaFree(da));
    int errors = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < d.size(); ++i)
        if (!std::isfinite(d[i]) || d[i] != expected[i]) {
            if (errors < 4)
                std::fprintf(stderr,
                             "D storage[%zu]=%.9g expected=%.9g\n",
                             i,
                             d[i],
                             expected[i]);
            ++errors;
        }
    for (size_t i = 0; i < a.size(); ++i)
        if (a_after[i] != a[i])
            ++errors;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < b.size(); ++i)
        if (b_after[i] != b[i])
            ++errors;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < c.size(); ++i)
        if (c_after[i] != c[i])
            ++errors;
    std::printf(
        "SIMT GEMM M=%d N=%d K=%d batches=%d: %d exact outputs, padding/canaries/inputs checked, errors=%d\n",
        m,
        n,
        k,
        batches,
        m * n * batches,
        errors);
    return errors;
}

int main() {
    try {
        int count = 0;
        CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetDeviceCount(&count));
        if (!count) {
            std::printf("BLOCKED: requires one CUDA GPU\n");
            return 2;
        }
        CUDA_CHECK(cudaSetDevice(0));
        int errors = run_case(16, 16, 16, 1);
        errors += run_case(37, 29, 41, 2);
        errors += run_case(7, 9, 0, 1);
        std::printf("TILED GEMM %s: 3 cases, errors=%d\n",
                    errors ? "FAIL" : "PASS",
                    errors);
        return errors ? 1 : 0;
    } catch (std::exception const& error) {
        std::fprintf(stderr, "TILED GEMM FAIL: %s\n", error.what());
        return 1;
    }
}
