docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The SIMT baseline makes batch strides, cooperative loads, padded rows and partial M/N/K tiles explicit before adding Tensor Core abstractions.

  • Two block barriers protect input readiness and safe shared-tile reuse; output-tail threads still participate in the cooperative protocol.

  • Initialize the accumulator once, apply beta once, and check every result plus padding and guards. Then compare the contract with the CUTLASS builder implementation.

docs.title: 24. CUTLASS — Build a Hopper GEMM You Can Verify
docs.text:
Correctness build versus performance build

The archived H100 build reports ptxas C7510: WGMMA instructions were serialized across a function boundary. Its output establishes the stated numerical checks, not representative WGMMA overlap or performance. For a new benchmark, add -DNDEBUG to the complete documented command, inspect the new compiler diagnostics and validate the resulting binary again. No optimized-build timing is inferred from the old capture. Auto schedules depend on toolkit and CUTLASS versions; the recorded plain GEMM selected Cooperative with seven stages under CUDA 12.8. CUDA 12.0 can resolve Auto differently.

docs.title: Lesson 24 Companion Guide — Assemble a Pinned Hopper Kernel and Its Launch Contract
docs.text:
Your goal in this chapter

Construct a reproducible CUTLASS GEMM, explain every operand’s physical layout, and check every output against an independent CPU reference. Read the introductory CuTe sequence, the tiled GEMM baseline, WGMMA and epilogues first.

docs.title: 1 — From a library name to a specific kernel
docs.text:
CUTLASS is a collection of building blocks, kernels, utilities and examples; it is not a single GEMM algorithm. A device adapter accepts arguments and workspace, a kernel schedules tiles, a collective mainloop coordinates copies and MMA, and an epilogue transforms accumulators into output. CuTe supplies much of the layout and instruction-partition vocabulary underneath those layers.

This chapter uses CUTLASS v4.3.6, commit 1afc6d355b8cb992398f17beb4425702f1d57ddd, with the book’s CUDA 12.8 baseline. The C++ API is still commonly called the CUTLASS 3.x GEMM API even though the repository release is 4.x. Python operator APIs and the CuTe DSL have separate entry points. We use the pinned example 49 and GEMM API documentation as references.

The exercises in Chapters 14–29 extend the original 27-program suite and use a separate validation collector. Keep their compilation, execution and profiler records distinct from the original suite. Expected checks stated in the explanation are specifications; actual execution evidence must identify the corresponding source revision, commands, dates and system.

docs.title: 2 — Pin the source and keep the build narrow
docs.text:
Complete Getting Started, including a working driver, CUDA 12.8 and a compatible host compiler. Start in the book repository’s root directory. The helper clones a fresh destination or checks an existing one; it refuses the wrong commit or modified tracked CUTLASS files.

export CUTLASS_ROOT="$HOME/cutlass-v4.3.6"
bash tools/fetch_cutlass.sh "$CUTLASS_ROOT"
git -C "$CUTLASS_ROOT" rev-parse HEAD
mkdir -p build/advanced
nvcc --version
g++ --version
nvidia-smi

The expected commit is the hash above. The original headers are used directly: the book’s GEMM needs no global CUTLASS installation, Python package or prebuilt CUTLASS shared library. Its adapter uses header-only templates, the CUDA runtime and the CUDA driver-library link -lcuda required by this pinned path. The direct command includes both the public headers and tools/util/include, because the small harness uses the repository’s device-allocation and packed-stride utilities.

nvcc -std=c++17 -O2 -lineinfo -arch=sm_90a \
  --expt-relaxed-constexpr \
  -I "$CUTLASS_ROOT/include" \
  -I "$CUTLASS_ROOT/tools/util/include" \
  docs/examples/advanced/cutlass_gemm.cu \
  -o build/advanced/cutlass_gemm -lcuda
./build/advanced/cutlass_gemm

Sm90 in a template is not a compiler flag. The architecture-accelerated Hopper instructions still need sm_90a; that binary is not a portability promise for A100 or B200. The harness checks that device 0 is compute capability 9.0 and returns a nonzero prerequisite failure otherwise.

docs.title: 3 — Define the operation before the types
docs.text:
Our operation is batched D = alpha * A * B + beta * C.

Object Mathematical shape per batch Physical storage Element type A M × K Row-major FP16 B K × N Row-major FP16 C M × N Row-major FP32 D M × N Row-major FP32 Accumulator Output tile Instruction-defined registers FP32

The initial tile is 128 × 128 × 64; the cluster is 1 × 1 × 1. Tile shape is a scheduling choice, not the full problem shape. Small, rectangular and partial-tile problems can behave very differently from a large square GEMM.

The builder alignment arguments count elements, not bytes. Eight FP16 elements or four FP32 elements describe a 16-byte alignment contract. Base addresses, leading dimensions and batch strides must satisfy the selected path’s constraints. An aligned base pointer does not repair an incompatible row stride.

docs.title: Check the nonzero-beta contract on paper
docs.text:
For A=[[1,-2,3],[4,0,-1]], B=[[2,1],[3,-2],[1,4]] and C=[[2,-4],[6,8]], the mathematical product is [[-1,17],[7,0]]. With alpha=0.5 and beta=0.25, D is [[0,7.5],[5,2]]. This small reference establishes B’s reduction/output axes and C’s one-time participation without depending on a template or GPU.

The full harness scales that same contract to aligned, rectangular, batched and partial-tile cases. The initialization patterns differ across operands and batches, and it checks all outputs rather than assuming a constant-valued result proves a layout. At each library boundary, compare mathematical shape, physical strides and the adapter’s logical coordinate convention.

docs.title: Map each builder parameter to a design decision
docs.text:
Parameter group Baseline choice What a change must revalidate Architecture / operator class Sm90 / TensorOp Target flags and instruction availability A/B types and layouts FP16, row-major Packing, precision, stride and alignment Accumulator / output FP32 / FP32 Error policy and conversion points CTA tile 128×128×64 Tail work, reuse and resource use Cluster 1×1×1 Collective scheduling and any multicast assumptions Stage policy Auto with epilogue carveout Actual shared storage and launch validity Schedule pair Compatible Auto choices Mainloop/epilogue interface and performance

None of these parameters is merely decoration. A supported type combination can still have poor performance for a particular shape; a fast configuration can still implement the wrong layout if the host arguments are wrong.

docs.title: 4 — Build the epilogue before choosing stage capacity
docs.text:
An epilogue can reserve shared storage too. Build it first, then account for its SharedStorage size when selecting the mainloop’s stage count:

using StagePolicy =
    cutlass::gemm::collective::StageCountAutoCarveout<
        static_cast<int>(sizeof(Epilogue::SharedStorage))>;

The complete cutlass_gemm.cu supplies matching KernelScheduleAuto and EpilogueScheduleAuto tags. For this Sm90 linear-combination baseline in pinned v4.3.6, the automatic epilogue selects NoSmemWarpSpecialized; the carveout pattern also accounts for epilogues that do use shared storage when choosing an explicit compatible schedule. Auto is a builder heuristic for this release and configuration; it does not benchmark every kernel on the user’s machine. If you later request a specific schedule, select an explicitly compatible pair, as Chapter 25 explains.

The type assembly is:

Element types + layout tags + alignments + tile/cluster shapes
                       |
                CollectiveEpilogue
                       |
        CollectiveMainloop with epilogue carveout
                       |
                 GemmUniversal kernel
                       |
                GemmUniversalAdapter

A builder error can be a failed contract, not a missing include. Reduce it to the first failed static assertion and inspect architecture, layout, alignment, tile and schedule compatibility. Repeatedly changing template tags until compilation succeeds is not a correctness method.

docs.title: Assemble the exact tested aliases in dependency order
docs.text:
The following are excerpts from the complete captured source, not independent translation units. They require its CUTLASS/CuTe headers and belong together at namespace scope. Start by naming the element/layout choices and static scheduling shapes:

using namespace cute;
using Half = cutlass::half_t;
using Row = cutlass::layout::RowMajor;
using CtaTileShape = Shape<_128, _128, _64>;
using Cluster = Shape<_1, _1, _1>;
using Epilogue = cutlass::epilogue::collective::CollectiveBuilder<
    cutlass::arch::Sm90,
    cutlass::arch::OpClassTensorOp,
    CtaTileShape,
    Cluster,
    cutlass::epilogue::collective::EpilogueTileAuto,
    float,
    float,
    float,
    Row,
    4,
    float,
    Row,
    4,
    cutlass::epilogue::collective::EpilogueScheduleAuto>::
    CollectiveOp;

Read the epilogue arguments in groups, checking the pinned builder signature rather than counting unnamed float tokens from memory:

  1. Sm90, OpClassTensorOp select the architecture/operator family.
  2. CtaTileShape, Cluster, EpilogueTileAuto give the CTA/cluster contract and epilogue tiling policy.
  3. The first two float arguments specify accumulator and epilogue compute elements.
  4. float, Row, 4 specify C's source element, layout and alignment in elements.
  5. The next float, Row, 4 specify D's output element, layout and alignment.
  6. EpilogueScheduleAuto selects the supported automatic epilogue path for this pinned baseline. This is not the explicit ReLU schedule in the later fusion lab.

Next build the mainloop, then the kernel and host adapter:

using Mainloop = cutlass::gemm::collective::CollectiveBuilder<
    cutlass::arch::Sm90,
    cutlass::arch::OpClassTensorOp,
    Half,
    Row,
    8,
    Half,
    Row,
    8,
    float,
    CtaTileShape,
    Cluster,
    cutlass::gemm::collective::StageCountAutoCarveout<
        static_cast<int>(sizeof(Epilogue::SharedStorage))>,
    cutlass::gemm::collective::KernelScheduleAuto>::CollectiveOp;
using Kernel = cutlass::gemm::kernel::
    GemmUniversal<Shape<int, int, int, int>, Mainloop, Epilogue>;
using Gemm = cutlass::gemm::device::GemmUniversalAdapter<Kernel>;

The two Half,Row,8 groups describe A and B. Eight half elements correspond to sixteen bytes. The next float selects the accumulator, followed by the same CTA/cluster shapes. Stage policy depends on the epilogue's already defined shared storage. KernelScheduleAuto completes the mainloop policy. Finally, GemmUniversal composes the collectives around a runtime rank-four problem (M,N,K,L); the adapter exposes the host methods used below.

This order explains a common compiler diagnostic: a failure in Mainloop can stem from an unsupported A/B layout or schedule, while a failure in StageCountAutoCarveout can originate in the epilogue's resource contract. Read the first failed assertion and identify its group before changing unrelated types. The pinned mainloop builder and epilogue builder define the API signatures.

Exercise: change output storage, then locate the consequences

If D changes from FP32 to FP16 while C remains FP32, which group describes that change? Can the old full-output reference remain unchanged?

Answer: Change the D element/layout/alignment group, not A/B or the accumulator by accident. A sixteen-byte FP16 alignment would count eight elements rather than four, if that path supports it. The selected builder must accept the new combination. The independent reference must now specify the final FP16 conversion/rounding and compare the resulting output representation; the existing FP32 pass does not validate this unexecuted variant.

docs.title: 5 — Do not transpose B by accident
docs.text:
CUTLASS’s CuTe logical B coordinates are (N,K,L) even though the mathematical matrix in A * B is K × N. The kernel’s StrideB encodes how that logical view names the physical B allocation. The helper must receive the corresponding logical shape:

auto stride_B = cutlass::make_cute_packed_stride(
    Kernel::StrideB{}, cute::make_shape(N, K, L));

In this harness the independent CPU reference reads row-major B with B[(l * K + k) * N + n]. That is deliberate: the oracle follows the mathematical matrix and its physical row-major storage instead of duplicating the library’s CuTe indexing code. A reference that repeats the same wrong layout transform can agree with the kernel while both compute the wrong problem.

Similarly, use StrideA with (M,K,L) and output strides with (M,N,L). Check leading dimensions and batch offsets in elements before converting any quantity to bytes.

docs.title: Substitute a rectangular batch into the runtime contract
docs.text:
Use the illustrative aligned problem M=128,N=256,K=64,L=2, with packed row-major arrays. Here M,N,K,L count matrix rows, columns, reduction positions and independent batches; they are not the CTA tile or cluster shape.

  1. Write the physical offsets first. A(l,m,k)=l*8192+m*64+k, B(l,k,n)=l*16384+k*256+n, and C/D(l,m,n)=l*32768+m*256+n. These formulas are in elements; multiply by two for A/B bytes and by four for C/D bytes.
  2. Translate to CuTe's operand modes. A has logical shape (M,K,L) and stride (64,1,8192). B has logical shape (N,K,L) and stride (1,256,16384). C/D have shape (M,N,L) and stride (256,1,32768). B's reordered logical modes do not transpose the allocated mathematical matrix.
  3. Check one coordinate independently. Mathematical B(l=1,k=7,n=11) is offset 16384+7*256+11=18187. Its CuTe coordinate (n,k,l)=(11,7,1) gives 11*1+7*256+1*16384=18187, the same half element and byte offset 36374.
  4. Construct, then validate. The complete source obtains these strides with make_cute_packed_stride, places them beside their pointers in Gemm::Arguments, and sets args.epilogue.thread.alpha and .beta. can_implement(args) checks the library contract before workspace initialization and launch; pointer alignment alone cannot replace it.
  5. Check the result, not the launch alone. If one independently calculated dot product is acc=-1 and the corresponding C value is 2, alpha 0.5 and beta 0.25 require output zero. This scalar example checks the epilogue expression; the executable's nonuniform reference checks every output of its actual cases.

Pitfall: constructing B with a packed (K,N,L) shape while retaining Kernel::StrideB mixes two coordinate conventions. The dimensions can look plausible in a square example. A rectangular example and the explicit offset equality above expose the mistake before performance tuning.

docs.title: Read mathematical B and CuTe B as the same storage
docs.text:
Read the two upper paths downward into their shared element. Here l=1 selects the second independent batch; all offset labels count FP16 elements, not bytes. This panel uses the rectangular example just derived, M=128,N=256,K=64,L=2.

Mathematical B is K x N          CuTe B modes are (N,K,L)
coordinate (l,k,n)=(1,7,11)      coordinate (n,k,l)=(11,7,1)
         |                                  |
row-major B formula                 stride dot product
l*(K*N) + k*N + n                  n*1 + k*256 + l*16384
         |                                  |
16384 + 1792 + 11                  11 + 1792 + 16384
         +----------------+-----------------+
                          v
                element offset = 18187
                byte offset    = 36374
                          |
                     same B value

For the same example, the view maps supplied beside each pointer are:

Object  Logical coordinate  Element strides         Batch elements
 A         (m,k,l)          (64,1,8192)                  8192
 B         (n,k,l)          (1,256,16384)                16384
 C,D       (m,n,l)          (256,1,32768)                32768

make_cute_packed_stride(Kernel::StrideB{}, make_shape(N,K,L)) supplies the B map in the complete code. It does not physically transpose B or change the CPU oracle's B[(l*K+k)*N+n]. Its role is to present the existing allocation using the kernel's expected logical axes. Check this equality at an interior coordinate, not only (0,0,0), where many wrong stride maps happen to agree.

The example's shape is illustrative; the captured harness's three cases are listed below. A substituted shape becomes execution evidence only after that changed source has been compiled and checked.

Read the figure in two passes. First verify the two B coordinate conventions meet at the same physical element. Then follow the adapter state table downward. can_implement accepts the argument contract; initialize prepares state/workspace; run launches work; CUDA completion and the CPU comparison establish different later facts. A failure must stop that chain rather than being hidden by a final success message.

docs.title: 6 — The host-side launch lifecycle
docs.text:
A successful can_implement checks supported arguments; it does not run the kernel. The harness follows all of these steps and propagates failures:

  1. Initialize distinct, nonuniform A, B and C values.
  2. Allocate/copy the inputs, initialize D to NaN sentinels, and construct shape/stride arguments. An unwritten output must fail even if its expected value is zero.
  3. Call can_implement and reject unsupported arguments.
  4. Obtain get_workspace_size, allocate the workspace and call initialize.
  5. Call run, then check CUDA completion with cudaDeviceSynchronize.
  6. Copy D back and compare every output, including every batch.

can_implement is a kernel-support check, not a general validator for application-owned memory. A success status does not prove that pointers remain live, allocations cover every stride-derived address, data belongs to the intended CUDA device, or overlapping operands obey the operation's aliasing contract. The harness establishes these conditions through its fixed shapes, separate allocations, selected device and synchronized lifetimes. An application wrapper must check its own memory contract before relying on the adapter's support result.

Allocation check: a compact 128×128 FP32 D view needs 128×128=16384 elements, or 65536 bytes. Its last element begins at byte offset (127×128+127)×4=65532 and occupies four bytes. A 16-byte-aligned pointer with only 4096 bytes remaining cannot back this view. Alignment and allocation coverage are different obligations, regardless of the adapter’s support status.

The source includes the full code rather than relying on a library demo’s process exit status. In pinned upstream example 49, unsupported prerequisites and some printed failed cases can still be followed by process exit zero. If you run that example, read every result label and reject any failed/skipped configuration; an exit-only wrapper is insufficient.

docs.title: 7 — Why these reference cases are diagnostic
docs.text:
The three cases are (M,N,K,L) = (128,128,64,1), (256,128,128,2) and (136,264,72,1). The last has partial CTA tiles while retaining the selected alignment requirements. The scalar cases include nonzero beta, so reading C is checked instead of silently testing only A * B.

Inputs are bounded, small binary-rational values. Products and the short reductions fit exactly in FP32 for these cases; the reference accumulates in double and converts the final expression to float. Exact equality is therefore intentional for these inputs and operations. It is not a general FP16 GEMM tolerance policy. Random large-magnitude inputs, long reductions or reduced-precision modes need explicitly justified absolute/relative tolerances and finite-value checks.

Expected checks are three GEMM CASE PASS lines followed by GEMM PASS: 3 full CPU-reference cases, with every error count zero. No timing or TFLOP/s claim follows from this small correctness harness. Its CPU reference would also be inappropriate for timing a large production GEMM.

The tests cover selected dimensions, batching, C participation and partial tiles. They do not establish every supported datatype, leading dimension, split-K mode or fusion. Add a separate test before extending one of those contracts.

docs.title: Extend one contract at a time
docs.text:
The current adapter launches GemmUniversalMode::kGemm with a rank-four (M,N,K,L) problem and packed independent batches. Do not infer that a different universal mode, arbitrary padded strides, overlapping batches or aliased C/D pointers were tested. The raw SIMT lab deliberately covers padded rows and K=0; those cases do not transfer automatically to this Tensor Core kernel.

Before changing the packed helper to explicit strides, write all four operand offset formulas and allocation extents, check alignment at each row/batch origin, and retain a CPU oracle that uses the physical allocation contract independently. For a zero-sized problem, define whether the application skips the launch or requires a supported library operation; can_implement is necessary but does not replace a numerical case or completion check.

docs.title: 8 — Collect revision-specific execution evidence
docs.text:
The collector first verifies the exact CUTLASS commit and records the system, compiler and GPU topology. It prepares the CuTe host oracles, GPU copy/GEMM/overlap programs and CPU reference scripts, requires their explicit pass markers and saves each current source copy/hash with commands, UTC times and logs. An output directory must be fresh.

python3 tools/run_advanced_validation.py \
  --cutlass "$CUTLASS_ROOT" \
  --output "$HOME/h100-advanced-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)" \
  --execute --profiles

For a plan-only run, omit both --execute and --profiles; no compiler, GPU or profiler is launched. --profiles is accepted only with --execute, additionally requires Nsight Systems and saves both serial/overlap reports; profiler capture is separate from numerical correctness. Preserve the complete directory before shutting down the instance. Hardware-backed transcripts can then be published with their actual date and software stack.

For an additional memory-safety check, run the compiled GEMM under the toolkit’s compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --error-exitcode 1. A zero-error report supplements the numerical oracle; it does not prove every possible pipeline schedule is race-free.

Self-check: a 16-byte alignment parameter?

For FP16 inputs, should the builder’s element alignment be 16?

Answer: A 16-byte contract corresponds to 8 FP16 elements. The element count, actual pointer alignment and stride constraints must agree.

Self-check: does successful initialization establish correctness?

can_implement, initialize and run return success. Can you report a verified GEMM?

Answer: Not yet. Check asynchronous CUDA completion and the actual output against the defined reference. The collector requires both.

docs.text:
Executed on November 18, 2026 (UTC). Scope: CUDA workload with its stated numerical checks.

Tested source SHA-256: c906aff6157e1759ebe1b7287bc75b78eeb5b35d4e7ef0751f5001c29d568de3. Exact source · System information · Workshop results.

The listing below matches the tested source. Its presentation is formatted at build time; downloads retain the captured bytes.

// A pinned CUTLASS v4.3.6 Hopper GEMM with an independent full CPU oracle.
#include <cute/tensor.hpp>
#include <cutlass/cutlass.h>
#include <cutlass/epilogue/collective/collective_builder.hpp>
#include <cutlass/gemm/collective/collective_builder.hpp>
#include <cutlass/gemm/device/gemm_universal_adapter.h>
#include <cutlass/gemm/kernel/gemm_universal.hpp>
#include <cutlass/util/device_memory.h>
#include <cutlass/util/packed_stride.hpp>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <vector>
using namespace cute;
using Half = cutlass::half_t;
using Row = cutlass::layout::RowMajor;
using CtaTileShape = Shape<_128, _128, _64>;
using Cluster = Shape<_1, _1, _1>;
using Epilogue = cutlass::epilogue::collective::CollectiveBuilder<
    cutlass::arch::Sm90,
    cutlass::arch::OpClassTensorOp,
    CtaTileShape,
    Cluster,
    cutlass::epilogue::collective::EpilogueTileAuto,
    float,
    float,
    float,
    Row,
    4,
    float,
    Row,
    4,
    cutlass::epilogue::collective::EpilogueScheduleAuto>::
    CollectiveOp;
using Mainloop = cutlass::gemm::collective::CollectiveBuilder<
    cutlass::arch::Sm90,
    cutlass::arch::OpClassTensorOp,
    Half,
    Row,
    8,
    Half,
    Row,
    8,
    float,
    CtaTileShape,
    Cluster,
    cutlass::gemm::collective::StageCountAutoCarveout<
        static_cast<int>(sizeof(Epilogue::SharedStorage))>,
    cutlass::gemm::collective::KernelScheduleAuto>::CollectiveOp;
using Kernel = cutlass::gemm::kernel::
    GemmUniversal<Shape<int, int, int, int>, Mainloop, Epilogue>;
using Gemm = cutlass::gemm::device::GemmUniversalAdapter<Kernel>;

void cuda_check(cudaError_t s) {
    if (s != cudaSuccess)
        throw std::runtime_error(cudaGetErrorString(s));
}

void cutlass_check(cutlass::Status s) {
    if (s != cutlass::Status::kSuccess)
        throw std::runtime_error(cutlassGetStatusString(s));
}

bool test(int M,
          int N,
          int K,
          int L,
          float alpha,
          float beta,
          cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo hardware) {
    std::vector<Half> A(size_t(L) * M * K), B(size_t(L) * K * N);
    std::vector<float> C(size_t(L) * M * N), D(C.size());
    for (size_t i = 0; i < A.size(); ++i)
        A[i] = Half(float(int(i % 13) - 6) / 8);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < B.size(); ++i)
        B[i] = Half(float(int(i % 17) - 8) / 8);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < C.size(); ++i)
        C[i] = float(int(i % 19) - 9) / 16;
    cutlass::device_memory::allocation<Half> da(A.size()),
        db(B.size());
    cutlass::device_memory::allocation<float> dc(C.size()),
        dd(D.size());
    cuda_check(cudaMemcpy(da.get(),
                          A.data(),
                          A.size() * sizeof(Half),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    cuda_check(cudaMemcpy(db.get(),
                          B.data(),
                          B.size() * sizeof(Half),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    cuda_check(cudaMemcpy(dc.get(),
                          C.data(),
                          C.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    // IEEE FP32 all-one bits are NaN: an omitted output store cannot pass
    // merely because its reference value happens to be zero.
    cuda_check(
        cudaMemset(dd.get(), 0xff, D.size() * sizeof(float)));
    auto sa = cutlass::make_cute_packed_stride(Kernel::StrideA{},
                                               make_shape(M, K, L));
    auto sb = cutlass::make_cute_packed_stride(Kernel::StrideB{},
                                               make_shape(N, K, L));
    auto sc = cutlass::make_cute_packed_stride(Kernel::StrideC{},
                                               make_shape(M, N, L));
    auto sd = cutlass::make_cute_packed_stride(Kernel::StrideD{},
                                               make_shape(M, N, L));
    Gemm::Arguments args{cutlass::gemm::GemmUniversalMode::kGemm,
                         {M, N, K, L},
                         {da.get(), sa, db.get(), sb},
                         {{}, dc.get(), sc, dd.get(), sd},
                         hardware};
    args.epilogue.thread.alpha = alpha;
    args.epilogue.thread.beta = beta;
    Gemm gemm;
    cutlass_check(gemm.can_implement(args));
    cutlass::device_memory::allocation<unsigned char> workspace(
        Gemm::get_workspace_size(args));
    cutlass_check(gemm.initialize(args, workspace.get()));
    cutlass_check(gemm.run());
    cuda_check(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
    cuda_check(cudaMemcpy(D.data(),
                          dd.get(),
                          D.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    size_t errors = 0;
    for (int l = 0; l < L; ++l)
        for (int m = 0; m < M; ++m)
            for (int n = 0; n < N; ++n) {
                double sum = 0;
                for (int k = 0; k < K; ++k)
                    sum +=
                        double(
                            float(A[(size_t(l) * M + m) * K + k])) *
                        double(
                            float(B[(size_t(l) * K + k) * N + n]));
                size_t i = (size_t(l) * M + m) * N + n;
                float expected = float(alpha * sum + beta * C[i]);
                // These bounded binary-rational inputs make the sum exact in FP32.
                errors += !std::isfinite(D[i]) || D[i] != expected;
            }
    std::printf(
        "%s M=%d N=%d K=%d L=%d alpha=%.2f beta=%.2f checked=%zu errors=%zu\n",
        errors ? "GEMM FAIL" : "GEMM CASE PASS",
        M,
        N,
        K,
        L,
        alpha,
        beta,
        D.size(),
        errors);
    return errors == 0;
}

int main() {
    try {
        cudaDeviceProp p{};
        cuda_check(cudaSetDevice(0));
        cuda_check(cudaGetDeviceProperties(&p, 0));
        if (p.major != 9 || p.minor != 0) {
            std::fprintf(
                stderr,
                "Requires Hopper compute capability 9.0; found %d.%d\n",
                p.major,
                p.minor);
            return 2;
        }
        cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo hw{};
        hw.device_id = 0;
        hw.sm_count = p.multiProcessorCount;
        bool ok = test(128, 128, 64, 1, 1, 0, hw);
        ok = test(256, 128, 128, 2, 0.5f, 0.25f, hw) && ok;
        ok = test(136, 264, 72, 1, 0.5f, 0.25f, hw) && ok;
        std::puts(ok ? "GEMM PASS: 3 full CPU-reference cases"
                     : "GEMM FAIL");
        return ok ? 0 : 1;
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::fprintf(stderr, "GEMM ERROR: %s\n", e.what());
        return 1;
    }
}

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The collective builder assembles a specific mainloop, epilogue, kernel and adapter from explicit types, layouts, alignments and compatible schedules.

  • Construct logical B strides deliberately, reserve epilogue storage when choosing stages, and preserve every adapter status and asynchronous completion check.

  • Only full-output independent reference checks establish the tested numerical result. Follow the selected kernel into its pipeline and scheduling protocol.

docs.title: Lesson 25 Companion Guide — Trace Readiness, Reuse and the Cost of More Stages
docs.text:
Your goal in this chapter

Trace one tile through a real Hopper mainloop, identify the readiness/reuse protocol, and make one controlled tuning change without breaking the numerical contract. Complete the verified-GEMM exercise first.

docs.title: 1 — A source-reading route with a purpose
docs.text:
Start from the pinned collective-builder example 49, then follow the selected dispatch policy to the kernel and collective. Do not begin by reading every template header from top to bottom.

Layer What to find Connection to earlier chapters Device adapter Arguments, workspace, initialization and launch Host launch/error-checking contract Kernel Tile scheduling, warp roles and shared storage Warp specialization and persistent work, Chapters 8–10 Collective mainloop TMA descriptors, operand stages and tiled MMA Chapters 3–6 Pipeline Empty/full generations and participant counts RAW/WAR ownership, Chapters 3 and 9 Collective epilogue Accumulator partition, conversion, fusion and stores Chapters 7 and 9

Read one operand tile’s full lifetime before comparing schedule variants. Write down who produces it, which barrier proves arrival, who reads it and which event makes it reusable. The abstraction is useful because those obligations are repeated systematically, not because a template makes them disappear.

docs.title: 2 — Build only the upstream examples you need
docs.text:
The book’s harness compiles directly with nvcc. CMake is useful when exploring upstream examples. On the Ubuntu GPU host, install cmake and ninja-build if absent. Configure only Hopper and disable the library/profiler/tests for this first build:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y cmake ninja-build
cmake -S "$CUTLASS_ROOT" -B build/cutlass-examples -G Ninja \
  -DCUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS=90a \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_LIBRARY=OFF \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_PROFILER=OFF \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_TESTS=OFF \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_EXAMPLES=ON
cmake --build build/cutlass-examples --target 49_collective_builder -j 2
./build/cutlass-examples/examples/49_hopper_gemm_with_collective_builder/49_collective_builder \
  --m=512 --n=512 --k=512 --l=2 --alpha=1 --beta=0.5

Use the pinned source path and target spelling; the introductory comment in an upstream example can lag its directory name. Start with low parallel build concurrency because template compilation can consume substantial memory. Increase it only after observing memory use. The recorded large-memory host can support more build jobs; that is not a safe default for a small machine.

Example 49 prints seven configuration results in this revision. Check all seven and their actual pass/fail labels. Its process exit alone is not an aggregate numerical oracle. This exploratory upstream run is separate from the book collector’s three-case, full-output CPU-reference GEMM.

docs.title: 3 — Schedule tags are algorithm choices
docs.text:
The pinned example demonstrates these compatible explicit pairings:

Mainloop schedule Epilogue schedule Reading focus KernelTma NoSmemWarpSpecialized TMA without the same warp-specialized pipeline KernelTmaWarpSpecialized NoSmemWarpSpecialized Separate producer/consumer roles KernelTmaWarpSpecializedPingpong TmaWarpSpecialized Persistent ping-pong organization KernelTmaWarpSpecializedCooperative TmaWarpSpecializedCooperative Cooperative organization and compatible epilogue

The mainloop tags above live in cutlass::gemm; epilogue tags in cutlass::epilogue. The Auto tags used by the builders live in their collective namespaces. Names alone do not describe every supported tile/cluster/datatype combination. Inspect the specialization selected by the pinned builder.

Do not change only one side from Auto to an explicit schedule and assume compatibility. Likewise, do not call every persistent kernel “Stream-K.” Persistent residency, the distribution of output tiles, and splitting reduction work are distinct decisions. Example 49 separately supplies a tile-scheduler type when demonstrating Stream-K.

docs.title: Read the two consumer timelines
docs.text:
Use the pinned kernel headers, not schedule names alone, to identify ownership.

Interval Ping-pong consumer 0 Ping-pong consumer 1 Cooperative consumers A MMA for output tile 0 Wait for MMA turn Both compute disjoint row slices of tile 0 B Epilogue tile 0 MMA for output tile 1 Both finish tile 0 and its epilogue C MMA for output tile 2 Epilogue tile 1 Both advance to tile 1

Ping-pong gives each math warpgroup its own output tile. Ordered math and epilogue barriers alternate the phases; two MMA phases are not promised to execute simultaneously. Cooperative divides one CTA tile between the math warpgroups, sharing staged operands. The producer stages operands ahead of consumers in both organizations. Inspect the selected header for exact thread counts rather than treating all schedule tags as one fixed CTA geometry.

Step through one stage: (1) producer_acquire waits until the slot is empty; its elected leader also calls arrive_and_expect_tx(transaction_bytes) on the full barrier. (2) TMA submits the transfer and later completes its byte count. (3) consumer_wait establishes readiness. (4) MMA consumes the slot. (5) Wait for asynchronous MMA reads before consumer_release. Acquisition and submission are different edges; do not arm the expected bytes twice.

Producer warps can donate registers with setmaxnreg.dec; math warps request more with .inc. Check the launch allocation and CTA register pool together. PersistentTileSchedulerSm90 assigns subsequent output tiles to resident CTAs; raster order and swizzle alter reuse, not the GEMM equation. StreamKScheduler also partitions K and needs compatible workspace/fixup logic (Chapter 10).

The Python workbook checks slot/generation arithmetic only: its serial state assignments do not validate concurrent ready/read/release protocols or phase safety. Its 15 cases do not include the three-stage/eight-tile walkthrough. Use the source-level pipeline edges above and GPU race/memory checks for that stronger claim. The archived PASS label is retained as historical output.

The optional profiler's first two-job build was terminated; the later successful capture used eight jobs. A small job count reduces memory pressure but is not a promise of a short full-profiler build.

docs.title: 4 — Follow the stage state machine
docs.text:
The implementation in sm90_pipeline.hpp is the contract to read. PipelineAsync, PipelineTmaAsync and PipelineTmaStore describe different producer/completion mechanisms. They are not interchangeable barrier wrappers.

For the common TMA-load pipeline, the conceptual lifetime is:

Stage event Producer obligation Consumer obligation Empty available Acquire the correct stage/generation Finish all prior readers before releasing it Transfer submitted An elected leader sets the expected transaction bytes and issues the intended TMA work Wait for the matching full generation Full available Do not overwrite the tile Use the correct layout and issue MMA Reads finished Wait for the next acquire before reuse Release only after asynchronous MMA reads are safe

In the pinned implementation, make_producer_start_state<Pipeline>() starts the producer state at phase 1; a default consumer state starts at phase 0. Copying one initial state into both roles is not a harmless simplification. The stage index wraps and the phase distinguishes generations of the same storage slot.

num_consumers counts participating threads, not warps. transaction_bytes must match the actual TMA-completed byte contract. is_leader must elect the intended single producer issuer. Initialization also needs the implementation’s required visibility and cluster synchronization before any participant uses the pipeline.

One subtle point: PipelineTmaAsync::producer_commit is effectively a no-op outside its pipeline unit-test path in this revision. Calling it does not manufacture TMA arrival. The asynchronous copy’s completion mechanism signals full readiness. Conversely, consumer_wait proves data arrival, not completion of every later asynchronous WGMMA read. Releasing the source too soon recreates the WAR hazard from Chapter 3.

These are reasons to start with a working collective builder. Customizing the raw pipeline requires a new ownership proof and targeted tests, not simply replacing the barrier calls in a tutorial loop.

docs.title: Trace prologue, steady state and drain
docs.text:
Consider three reusable stages and eight actual K tiles. Tile number t uses stage t % 3, but the same stage belongs to a new generation whenever t advances by three. For the pinned initial state conventions, the producer and consumer phase bits below belong to their respective empty/full waits; they are not two values that must be equal.

Tile t Stage Generation Producer phase Consumer phase 0 0 0 1 0 1 1 0 1 0 2 2 0 1 0 3 0 1 0 1 4 1 1 0 1 5 2 1 0 1 6 0 2 1 0 7 1 2 1 0

In the prologue, issue only the tiles that exist, up to the permitted in-flight capacity. During steady state, a consumer waits for its next actual tile while producers reuse only released stages. During the drain, consumers finish the remaining tiles and asynchronous readers/stores complete; producers do not fabricate new work merely to fill all stages.

K shorter than pipeline depth is an important test. If there is one K tile and three storage stages, waiting for a full event on all three stages deadlocks because two transfers never existed. K=0 requires the API/kernel’s explicit supported behavior; the scalar baseline handles it, while a selected library path may reject it. Do not inherit that support across implementations.

The CPU indexing workbook checks slot/generation arithmetic for 15 small depth/tile-count combinations; it does not validate concurrent state transitions. It does not simulate the GPU memory model or validate concurrent TMA/WGMMA behavior. The actual library kernel and sanitizer records supply separate evidence.

docs.title: Walk one stage reuse without confusing readiness and release
docs.text:
Use the three-stage/eight-tile model above. Let the operand tile be 128*128*64 with FP16 A/B, so each K tile contains 16384+16384=32768 raw operand bytes. The actual collective supplies its own transaction count, padding and participant contract; this arithmetic is a simple model, not a replacement for that implementation.

  1. Acquire slot 0 for tile 0. The producer state is (index=0,phase=1). producer_acquire waits for the slot's empty condition before a producer starts a new transfer into that storage.
  2. Publish the real transfer. Issue the supported TMA operation using the collective's full barrier and expected transaction bytes. In this pinned pipeline, calling producer_commit alone does not complete or substitute for the transfer.
  3. Wait as the consumer. Consumer state (0,0) waits for tile 0's full condition. Arrival permits reads of that generation; it says nothing about whether subsequent asynchronous MMA reads have finished.
  4. Release only after the reads are safe. The selected mainloop follows its WGMMA completion protocol before releasing slot 0. This is the edge that prevents a producer from overwriting operands still used by an asynchronous instruction.
  5. Wrap to tile 3. After slots 1 and 2, tile 3 maps to slot 3%3=0, generation floor(3/3)=1. The producer phase is now 0 and the consumer phase 1. An old full signal for tile 0 must not satisfy the wait for tile 3.
  6. Drain exactly the actual work. Tile 7 maps to slot 1, generation 2. There is no tile 8. Finish pending reader/store obligations and release the actual occupied slots; do not issue or await an imaginary transfer merely to visit every slot once more.

Check: slot sequence 0,1,2,0,1,2,0,1 and generation sequence 0,0,0,1,1,1,2,2 must match the earlier table. Halving K until only one tile exists should remove seven transfers, not add waits for unused stages. This is a manual trace beyond the workbook's limited serial arithmetic checks; actual concurrent ordering remains the GPU implementation's responsibility.

docs.title: Draw the generation change at one physical slot
docs.text:
Read this diagram downward. All three rows name the same shared-memory slot 0; the tile and generation identify different contents. P/C label the producer/consumer phase conventions from the earlier table, not two phase values that must be equal.

slot 0, generation 0, tile 0    P=1 / C=0
  acquire empty -> issue TMA -> wait full -> MMA reads -> safe release
       |                                                   |
       +------------ storage cannot be reused ------------+
                                                           |
                 tiles 1 and 2 use slots 1 and 2            |
                                                           v
slot 0, generation 1, tile 3    P=0 / C=1
  acquire empty -> issue TMA -> wait full -> MMA reads -> safe release
                                                           |
                 tiles 4 and 5 use slots 1 and 2            v
slot 0, generation 2, tile 6    P=1 / C=0
  acquire empty -> issue TMA -> wait full -> MMA reads -> safe release

A full event answers “have this generation's operand bytes arrived?” A safe release answers “may a producer overwrite this storage?” These are distinct dependency edges. consumer_wait cannot prove that asynchronous reads launched afterward have finished. The selected mainloop's WGMMA completion protocol must establish that second fact before release.

For eight K tiles, tile 7 still uses slot 1 of generation 2; slot 2 has no generation-2 tile. Drain the actual operations instead of waiting on a third transfer that never existed. Locate producer_acquire, TMA issue, consumer_wait, the asynchronous-reader completion and consumer_release in the selected pinned mainloop; this panel is a lifetime model, not replacement pipeline code.

docs.title: Turn the picture into an explicit lifetime model
docs.text:
Name the model's variables before reading it: S=3 is the number of allocated slots, T=8 is the number of actual K tiles, t is a tile index, s=t%S is a slot index, and g=t//S is its generation. Each slot retains its identity while its contents change. The following is a sequential ownership model, not compilable CUTLASS code or a simulation of the GPU memory model. Its descriptive verbs are not additional API names:

MODEL: each slot begins EMPTY, with next generation 0
for each actual tile t from 0 through T-1:
    s = t modulo S; g = floor(t / S)
    require slot s is EMPTY and belongs to generation g
    acquire s; issue the real transfer for tile t
    wait until this tile's transfer is complete; mark s FULL
    read s for the matrix operation; mark s READING
    wait until every asynchronous reader of s is safe
    release s; mark s EMPTY with next generation g+1
finish only after all issued readers and required stores complete
  1. At t=0, the model selects (s,g)=(0,0). A ready event authorizes the consumer's reads of tile zero, not the next producer's overwrite.
  2. After tile zero's readers finish, slot zero can advance to generation one. That permission is necessary even if the consumer has already issued its arithmetic.
  3. At t=3, the same physical slot zero holds a different tile. Both tile identity and generation matter; retaining only s=0 loses the distinction.
  4. At t=7, slot one reaches generation two. The loop stops because T is eight. There is no transfer for tile eight and no corresponding full event to await.

The deliberately sequential model makes the proof easy to follow. A real pipeline overlaps producer/consumer progress and uses the selected implementation's barriers, elected issuers, phases and completion operations. Substituting this loop for that protocol would discard concurrency and omit mechanism-specific requirements. Use the actual producer_acquire, consumer_wait and consumer_release contracts located in the selected mainloop; match their state progression to this ownership explanation rather than inventing a universal constructor.

Exercise: K=129, BK=64 and S=3

How many K tiles exist? Which waits disappear compared with the eight-tile model?

Answer: ceil(129/64)=3: tiles start at K=0,64,128. The final tile has one valid reduction position and 63 neutral positions under a zero-fill policy. Slots 0,1,2 each have generation-zero contents, and no generation-one transfer exists. Do not wait for tiles 3 through 7 or infer empty-reduction support from this example.

docs.title: Locate the actual mechanisms in the source
docs.text:
Starting from the selected mainloop, find its SharedStorage, pipeline type, producer start state, consumer state and transaction-byte calculation. Then locate the TMA copy operation, consumer wait, WGMMA group completion and consumer release. Follow tail/drain calls in the actual selected specialization, including any cluster barrier and epilogue store pipeline.

Write the dependency edges explicitly: generic producer stores require the appropriate proxy publication; TMA arrival establishes the load’s completion; WGMMA’s register fence is not its completion wait; and a completed shared-to-global source read is different from final destination completion. A synchronization primitive is meaningful only with its participant, memory-space, proxy and generation scope.

docs.title: 5 — Count resources before adding stages
docs.text:
More stages can hide more latency but reserve more shared memory and bookkeeping. They can reduce block residency or leave too little shared storage for the epilogue. A larger CTA tile can reuse operands better while increasing register pressure or wasting work on a small problem’s edges.

Record at least the operand types, CTA tile, cluster shape, selected schedule, stage policy and epilogue storage. Compare the compiler’s resource report and Nsight Compute results with the full application timeline. Occupancy alone is not the objective; a lower-occupancy kernel can win through reuse or better overlap, while an oversized tile can lose on tail work.

Change one variable at a time, rerun the full reference checks, then measure several representative shapes. A 4096-square result does not establish a win for a tall-skinny batched problem.

docs.title: A concrete shared-memory budget
docs.text:
For an FP16 operand tile of M=128, N=128, K=64, the raw A tile is 128*64*2=16,384 bytes and B is another 16,384 bytes. One operand stage is therefore 32,768 bytes before padding or metadata. Three raw stages use 98,304 bytes; six use 196,608 bytes. Neither number includes every barrier, alignment gap or epilogue allocation in a real kernel.

Against H100’s shared-memory resource limits, an extra stage can remove the possibility of two resident CTAs even before registers or threads become limiting. Conversely, too few stages may expose load latency. Use the actual sizeof(SharedStorage), configured shared-memory limit and compiler report, then measure. The raw arithmetic is a design estimate, not a launch-validity certificate.

docs.title: Check a byte budget without confusing it with stage validity
docs.text:
Take a hypothetical 128-KiB budget for this exercise, rather than treating it as an H100 per-block specification. The budget is 128×1024=131072 bytes. Reserve 16384 bytes for an epilogue and estimate 32768 raw operand bytes per stage:

  1. Three raw stages use 98304 bytes. With the epilogue, the subtotal is 114688 bytes, leaving 16384 for other storage.
  2. Four raw stages alone use the entire 131072-byte budget. Adding the epilogue already exceeds it, even before barriers and alignment.
  3. The three-stage estimate still does not certify a launch: compare the actual shared-storage type, alignment and selected device limits. Registers, threads and cluster scheduling can impose additional constraints.

Pitfall: subtracting useful matrix bytes from a hardware limit and declaring the remainder “free stages” ignores the actual layout and collective's metadata. Arithmetic is an early rejection test; the selected implementation and launch checks complete the contract.

docs.title: 6 — Epilogue fusion is a computation graph
docs.text:
The Chapter 24 baseline computes alpha * accumulator + beta * C. A fused epilogue might add a bias and apply an activation before the final store. That can avoid a separate launch and an intermediate write/read, but it also changes arithmetic, live values, shared storage and the numerical reference.

Pinned example 49 demonstrates both a predefined fusion operation and an epilogue visitor tree (EVT). An EVT describes dataflow: accumulator/source fetches, scalar/vector broadcasts, computations and stores. The nesting determines which values feed which operation; it is not merely a list of operations to perform in any order.

For example, activation(alpha * acc + beta * C + bias) is generally different from alpha * activation(acc) + beta * C + bias. Also decide where rounding/conversion occurs. FP32 intermediate computation followed by one FP16 conversion need not match several FP16 intermediate conversions. The fusion operation tags and Hopper callback implementations expose those contracts.

An implementation exercise is to add a supported bias/activation fusion, update the CPU oracle to the exact operation order and rounding policy, and add beta-zero, beta-nonzero, negative-input and edge-tile cases. It becomes verified only after those new sources and outputs are captured; the baseline’s pass does not transfer automatically.

docs.title: 7 — Use a narrow profiler build
docs.text:
The CUTLASS profiler is a separate tool from Nsight Systems and Compute. It instantiates many candidate kernels and measures supported operations. Compiling every kernel, precision, architecture and instantiation level is unnecessary for this chapter.

Start with one actual kernel name from the pinned generator rather than a whole family. Even a single-kernel build compiles common reference-provider support. The recorded configuration uses FP16 A/B, FP32 C and D, beta 0.5, and the cooperative no-shared-memory epilogue schedule. It differs from the small correctness harness; it is a separate configuration, not a timing of that harness.

kernel="cutlass3x_sm90_tensorop_gemm_f16_f16_f32_f32_f32_256x128x64_1x2x1_0_nnn_align8_warpspecialized_cooperative_epi_nosmem"
cmake -S "$CUTLASS_ROOT" -B build/cutlass-profiler \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS=90a \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_LIBRARY=ON \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_PROFILER=ON \
  -DCUTLASS_LIBRARY_OPERATIONS=gemm \
  -DCUTLASS_LIBRARY_KERNELS="$kernel" \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_CUBLAS=ON \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_EXAMPLES=OFF \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_TESTS=OFF
cmake --build build/cutlass-profiler --target cutlass_profiler -j 2
build/cutlass-profiler/tools/profiler/cutlass_profiler --help
build/cutlass-profiler/tools/profiler/cutlass_profiler \
  --mode=enumerate --operation=Gemm

Require exactly the intended matching operation before interpreting a benchmark. If none appears, inspect the generator filter, architecture and instantiation policy; a compatible API combination is not necessarily instantiated by the generator. An empty result is not a fast kernel. Avoid all or maximum instantiation as a first response. The captured host used eight build jobs after checking available RAM; two jobs above is a conservative starting point.

mkdir -p reports
build/cutlass-profiler/tools/profiler/cutlass_profiler \
  --operation=Gemm --kernels="$kernel" \
  --m=512 --n=512 --k=512 --alpha=1 --beta=0.5 \
  --providers=cutlass --verification-enabled=true \
  --verification-required=true --verification-providers=reference_device \
  --warmup-iterations=5 --profiling-iterations=20 \
  --output=reports/cutlass-hopper

Read the pinned profiler documentation and local help. The tool appends an operation-specific CSV suffix; inspect the file actually produced. The following is an abbreviated transcription of the 18 November 2026, 14:38:47 UTC run on the H100 PCIe system described in the workshop record:

Verification: reference_device: Passed
CSV rows: 1
Disposition: passed
Status: success
m=512, n=512, k=512, alpha=1, beta=0.5
Runtime (ms): 0.0566496

Download the exact command and timestamps, raw console log and one-row CSV. This is a bounded tool check, not a representative benchmark distribution or a claim of tuned performance. The tool's FLOP convention includes additional work; use the declared count when comparing rates.

Walk through the acceptance decision. First confirm the kernel name and input types. Next require one actual CSV row, then passed/success, then a provider that explicitly says Passed. Only after these checks should you read the runtime. A zero process exit, a verification flag or a CSV header without a row proves none of those steps by itself.

The pinned profiler has a separate cuBLAS reporting limitation: its verification loop can overwrite a cuBLAS disposition with Not run when a later reference-provider lookup is unavailable. The captured diagnostics showed actual cuBLASLt calls, but this book does not label that provider as passed. The reproducible command above requires the device reference and records its explicit pass. See the pinned verification loop when diagnosing provider results.

docs.title: 8 — Measure the optimization that users receive
docs.text:
For dense GEMM’s conventional work count, report 2MNKL floating-point operations per invocation and state what the timer includes. Sparse dense-equivalent rates, fused non-GEMM work and integer operation counts need their own conventions. State whether allocations, workspace initialization, transfers, graph setup or CPU reference work are excluded.

Keep a record containing the exact CUTLASS commit, source hash, compiler/flags, driver, device, tile/cluster/schedule, shape/layout/strides, alpha/beta, warmup, repetitions, verification result and timing distribution. Then use Systems to determine whether the selected kernel matters to the application’s critical path, and Compute for the kernel’s detailed limiting resources.

Do not put a large CUTLASS profiler sweep under a full Compute metric set. First select one configuration and kernel. Profilers can replay or perturb work; compare like-for-like captures and retain unprofiled timings.

Self-check: can producer_commit repair missing TMA completion?

A custom pipeline calls producer_commit but its consumer never becomes ready. Is adding more commits the solution?

Answer: Not for PipelineTmaAsync. Inspect the elected issuer, transfer, barrier address, phase and expected byte count. TMA completion supplies the relevant arrival; the method name is not a substitute.

Self-check: fusion versus a faster GEMM?

A fused GEMM is slower than the unfused GEMM alone. Should it be rejected?

Answer: Compare the complete unfused sequence with the fused operation, using the same numerical contract and useful-result boundary. Removing another launch and memory pass may still reduce application time.

docs.text: Chapter 26 develops a complete fused ReLU variant and its independent reference. Chapter 27 separates format, scale-layout and kernel error. Chapter 28 defines a reproducible comparison, and Chapter 29 closes the sequence with staged labs and worked answers.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Read one selected tile’s complete lifetime: acquire the correct generation, establish transfer completion, consume it, finish asynchronous readers and release storage.

  • Pipeline types and schedule pairs have distinct contracts. Prologue, steady state and drain must reflect the tiles that actually exist.

  • More stages or larger tiles trade latency hiding against shared storage, registers, residency and tails. Validate each change before measuring fusion or other optimizations.

docs.title: 26. Epilogue Fusion — Preserve the Operation, Remove a Pass
docs.text:
Correctness build versus performance build

The archived H100 build reports ptxas C7510: WGMMA instructions were serialized across a function boundary. Its output establishes the stated numerical checks, not representative WGMMA overlap or performance. For a new benchmark, add -DNDEBUG to the complete documented command, inspect the new compiler diagnostics and validate the resulting binary again. No optimized-build timing is inferred from the old capture. Auto schedules depend on toolkit and CUTLASS versions; the recorded plain GEMM selected Cooperative with seven stages under CUDA 12.8. CUDA 12.0 can resolve Auto differently.

docs.title: Lesson 26 Companion Guide — Preserve Numerical Semantics While Removing a Memory Pass
docs.text:
Your goal in this chapter

Translate a mathematical epilogue into a compatible CUTLASS fusion operation, validate its exact semantics and compare complete workloads. Read the builder and pipeline ownership first.

docs.title: 1 — State the graph before writing a tag
docs.text:
The baseline computes Z = alpha*AB + beta*C. The executable fusion lab computes D = ReLU(Z), with ReLU(x)=max(0,x) for the finite values used by its test. All operands, accumulator and scalar conventions remain explicit: FP16 A/B, FP32 accumulation, FP32 C and output, and scalar alpha/beta applied once.

That ordering matters. For accumulator value −1, alpha −2 and beta zero, ReLU(alpha*acc)=2, while alpha*ReLU(acc)=0. A compiler fusion is correct only when it implements the operation you requested, not an intuitively similar rearrangement. The reference must also preserve the specified conversion points; rounding before activation can differ from rounding only at the final store.

The supplied tutorial’s broad advice to fuse epilogues becomes useful once the graph, layouts, numerical contract and verification are concrete. This chapter builds on the pinned fusion operation tags and Hopper callback implementations.

docs.title: 2 — Three boundaries of an epilogue
docs.text:
An accumulator fragment is distributed across threads according to the MMA implementation. It is not an ordinary contiguous M×N array in one thread. The epilogue must connect three boundaries:

Boundary Obligation Fragment to logical output Every (m,n,l) maps to the intended accumulator value Compute expression Scalars, C, bias/residual and activation use the specified order and precision Logical output to storage Valid destinations are stored once with correct strides and edge predicates

An elementwise expression may be simple while its store path is complicated. A TMA epilogue can also have shared-memory staging and an asynchronous store lifecycle. A fused activation tag does not make those costs or ownership obligations disappear.

docs.title: 3 — Use a supported predefined fusion first
docs.text:
The complete cutlass_gemm_relu.cu uses the pinned predefined operation:

using Fusion = cutlass::epilogue::fusion::LinCombEltAct<
    cutlass::epilogue::thread::ReLu,
    float,
    float,
    float>;

Here the type parameters select the activation functor, output, compute and C-source element types. The chosen scalar type defaults to the compute type in this release. This is a type-level description; the runtime alpha and beta still come from the kernel arguments.

The example chooses an explicit compatible mainloop/epilogue pair: KernelTmaWarpSpecializedPingpong and TmaWarpSpecialized. Both are changed deliberately rather than mixing an explicit epilogue with an unconstrained Auto mainloop. The mainloop stage policy reserves the selected epilogue’s shared storage, as in Chapter 24. In this pinned Sm90 implementation, EpilogueScheduleAuto has a static assertion restricting its fusion to the supported linear combination; it does not select a ReLU implementation automatically. The explicit supported TMA epilogue is therefore an API requirement for this example, not merely a tuning preference. See the pinned Sm90 epilogue builder.

The original linear GEMM remains a separate source and executable. Its pass does not substitute for the fused variant’s numerical tests. Each has its own source hash, compiler record and actual output.

docs.title: Compile the complete fused variant
docs.text:
From the repository root, with the pinned CUTLASS_ROOT and build/advanced prepared in Chapter 15:

nvcc -std=c++17 -O2 -lineinfo -arch=sm_90a \
  --expt-relaxed-constexpr \
  -I "$CUTLASS_ROOT/include" -I "$CUTLASS_ROOT/tools/util/include" \
  docs/examples/advanced/cutlass_gemm_relu.cu \
  -o build/advanced/cutlass_gemm_relu -lcuda
./build/advanced/cutlass_gemm_relu

The driver link is deliberate. A successful CUDA compile stage does not imply a successful executable link; preserve both diagnostics and the final process status.

docs.title: 4 — Follow the runtime arguments
docs.text:
The device adapter takes the same problem shape, operand pointers and strides as before. The epilogue thread arguments carry alpha and beta. The underlying supported fusion supplies the activation during epilogue execution, after forming the requested linear combination.

The host lifecycle is unchanged in principle: check can_implement, allocate workspace, initialize, launch, check asynchronous completion, then validate all output values. A new supported fusion does not justify removing those checks. Changing schedules can change shared-memory demand, available stages and launch constraints even when the mathematical shape is identical.

Do not copy the argument aggregate of an unrelated EVT. Some predefined fusion operations expose flat named fields; custom trees can require nested argument structures that mirror their nodes. Inspect the selected operation and callback definitions in the pinned release.

docs.title: 5 — Read an epilogue visitor tree as dataflow
docs.text:
The scalar arithmetic below is conceptual; the pinned predefined visitor has a ReLU compute node above one Sm90LinearCombination node:

MMA accumulator, C, alpha, beta
             │
Sm90LinearCombination: homogeneous_multiply_add(beta, C, alpha*acc)
             │
     Sm90Compute<ReLU>
             │
       convert/store D

Nodes describe fetch, broadcast, computation or storage. Child order and operation type determine the expression. A multiply_add node with the wrong child order can compile while implementing a different formula. A cast in a child node can also move rounding earlier in the graph.

Pinned example 49 contains a custom tree implementing the linear combination. Start by matching that tree against its scalar formula and argument structure, then identify how a supported activation is attached. Do not write a new callback merely to reproduce a predefined operation that already matches the contract.

docs.title: Evaluate the fusion tree one node at a time
docs.text:
Start with the small matrices from Chapter 23, whose independently computed AB=[[-1,17],[7,0]] and C=[[2,-4],[6,8]]. Choose the lab's operation D=ReLU(0.5*AB+0.25*C). This is a manual semantic example, not a transcript of the larger executable's initialization.

  1. Fetch the completed accumulator. At (m,n)=(0,1), the entire K reduction is acc=17. Do not apply the epilogue to each partial K tile.
  2. Apply alpha. The accumulator branch produces 0.5*17=8.5 in the selected FP32 compute type.
  3. Fetch and scale C. The source branch reads C[0,1]=-4 and produces 0.25*(-4)=-1. This is the C operand, not an accumulator register with the same index.
  4. Join the branches. The linear combination is Z=8.5+(-1)=7.5. Apply ReLU after this addition, so D[0,1]=7.5.
  5. Repeat across the output. The intermediate Z is [[0,7.5],[5,2]]; all entries survive ReLU. To test that activation really occurs, change only the illustrative C[0,0] to -2: Z[0,0]=0.5*(-1)+0.25*(-2)=-1, so the fused output there must be zero. A purely positive test would not distinguish a missing activation.
  6. Connect the API. LinCombEltAct<ReLu,float,float,float> names the activation/output/compute/source contract; args.epilogue.thread.alpha and .beta provide the runtime scalars. The explicit supported mainloop/epilogue schedules implement the storage and synchronization path around this expression.

Check: compare the fused output to the independently evaluated Z followed by activation, not to the unfused output Z itself. The example's binary fractions are exactly representable; a general low-precision output needs an explicit conversion/rounding policy too. If a future bias is added, write its coordinate and insert its addition at the intended node before changing any callback types.

docs.title: Trace the two branches into one activated output
docs.text:
Read each branch left to right; join only at the addition node. Numbers are FP32 values for the manual (m,n)=(0,1) example, after the complete K reduction. Array coordinates and scalar values play different roles: C's coordinate chooses a source value, while beta scales that value.

MMA accumulator at (0,1): 17 -- multiply alpha 0.5 -- 8.5 --+
                                                           |
C source at (0,1):       -4 -- multiply beta 0.25 -- -1.0 ---+
                                                           |
                                                    add: Z=7.5
                                                           |
                                                    ReLU: max(0,Z)
                                                           |
                                                 FP32 D(0,1)=7.5

Negative boundary check at (0,0), illustrative changed C=-2:
  acc=-1 -> alpha*acc=-0.5 --+
  C=-2   -> beta*C=-0.5 ----+--> Z=-1 --> ReLU --> D=0

The complete source expresses this graph through LinCombEltAct<ReLu,float,float,float> and runtime args.epilogue.thread.alpha/beta. The supported collective maps its distributed accumulator to output coordinates and stores the resulting float. The picture does not require that every arithmetic node become a separate instruction: fusion and multiply-add contraction must preserve the specified numerical contract.

The lower path makes a missing ReLU observable. The upper path alone would pass even if activation were omitted. NaN-initialized output separately makes a missing store observable, including when the correct activated output is zero. Together, graph-value checks and storage sentinels test different failure modes.

docs.title: Connect the scalar numbers to the existing API fields
docs.text:
In the complete fused program, args is already a Gemm::Arguments object with matching problem shape, pointers, strides and fusion types. The following is a configuration excerpt after that construction, not an independent kernel:

args.epilogue.thread.alpha = 0.5f;
args.epilogue.thread.beta = 0.25f;
  1. 0.5f supplies the runtime alpha value; it does not choose an output element type. The LinCombEltAct template selected the compute/source/output contract earlier.
  2. 0.25f supplies beta for the C-source branch. Its presence does not allocate C or specify C's coordinate map; those belong to the surrounding arguments.
  3. At the manual coordinate (0,1), the source value −4 becomes −1 through beta, while accumulator 17 becomes 8.5 through alpha.
  4. The activation sees their sum 7.5. Reading a partial accumulator, selecting the wrong C coordinate, or activating each branch independently changes the operation even though these assignments are correct.

Check: use a nonzero-beta case and independently computed C values. Pitfall: a correct template tag cannot repair an argument object that points C at the wrong buffer. Keep argument construction and numerical graph validation in the same review.

docs.title: 6 — Bias and residuals need a coordinate contract
docs.text:
The executable lab adds activation, not bias. A bias extension must define its broadcast axis explicitly. For D[m,n,l]=activation(Z[m,n,l]+bias[n,l]), a length-N vector is shared across M rows. A length-M vector represents a different operation.

Term Logical indexing What changes across output rows? Per-column bias bias[n] Nothing for a fixed n Per-row bias bias[m] The bias value Batched column bias bias[l*N+n] Batch selection, not row selection Residual matrix R[(l*M+m)*ldr+n] Both row and column can change

An implementation can encode a broadcast with a zero stride in the broadcast mode, but the fusion API still needs its supported layout/argument type. A zero-stride source view is useful for replicated reads; using it for independent output writes creates aliases. Add rectangular and multi-batch tests so an accidental row/column swap is visible.

docs.title: Exercise: a rectangular bias distinguishes its axis
docs.text:
This is a paper extension, not an additional operation executed by the ReLU lab. Let the completed product be P=[[-1,17,2],[7,0,-5]], alpha 0.5, beta zero, and a per-column bias [1,-2,3]. Define D[m,n]=ReLU(0.5*P[m,n]+bias[n]).

  1. The first row's scaled product is [-0.5,8.5,1]; adding bias gives [0.5,6.5,4].
  2. The second row's scaled product is [3.5,0,-2.5]; adding the same column bias gives [4.5,-2,0.5].
  3. Apply ReLU last: D=[[0.5,6.5,4],[4.5,0,0.5]].

Worked check: a length-three vector matches N=3, not M=2. A row-bias implementation would need a different vector and produce a different operation. To implement this extension, select a supported bias callback, add its runtime pointer/stride contract and independently test those axes; the existing no-bias executable's result does not validate it.

docs.title: 7 — Make the reference stronger than a checksum
docs.text:
The lab reuses three aligned, batched and partial-tile problem shapes, with mixed-sign nonuniform values and nonzero beta in two cases. D begins as NaNs; any missing store therefore fails the finite/full-output check even when an expected value happens to be zero.

The CPU reference performs the complete reduction independently, forms alpha/beta/C in the defined order, then applies ReLU. Inputs and scalars are bounded binary fractions, so the chosen reductions are exactly representable in FP32; this justifies exact equality for this test matrix. The reference checks every output rather than only a sum or selected positions.

These finite-input cases do not establish NaN propagation, signed-zero policy, overflow behavior, low-precision output rounding or gradients at zero. If those are part of an application’s contract, test the selected activation/conversion implementation against that contract. Framework defaults are not interchangeable specifications.

docs.title: 8 — Count the memory pass you actually remove
docs.text:
For a separate FP32 activation after GEMM, the intermediate Z is written once, read once and the final D is written once. A fused output stores D directly. Ignoring other unchanged traffic, fusion avoids 8*M*N*L bytes: one four-byte write and one four-byte read per intermediate element.

For M=N=2048,L=1, that is 33,554,432 bytes, or 32 MiB. This is a traffic accounting example, not a measured saving in DRAM traffic or elapsed time. C reads, A/B traffic, cache residency, epilogue staging and the changed kernel schedule still matter.

A fused kernel can take longer than the unfused GEMM alone while beating GEMM plus activation. Compare the full operation, including any extra packing/conversion, and check the application’s useful-result boundary in Nsight Systems. A larger epilogue can reduce stages or residency enough to offset an avoided memory pass.

docs.title: Keep activation coverage separate from storage coverage
docs.text:
A complete fused test needs outputs on both sides of zero and at zero. Positive outputs distinguish correct magnitudes; negative preactivation values distinguish ReLU from the identity; zero values exercise the boundary. NaN sentinels separately detect omitted stores, including a missing store whose expected activated output is zero. None of these checks alone establishes the activation's NaN or signed-zero behavior.

When extending the lab, count these categories from the independently computed preactivation values before applying ReLU. If an input change removes a category, restore a targeted case rather than relying on the initialization looking mixed-sign. For a bias or residual extension, keep those categories on output tails and across batches too; a correct interior activation does not prove a correct broadcast or store predicate.

docs.title: Count a tiny unfused sequence before extrapolating it
docs.text:
For a two-by-three FP32 output, one complete matrix occupies 2×3×4=24 bytes. An unfused GEMM writes Z (24 bytes), activation reads Z (24) and writes D (24): 72 bytes of these output/intermediate operations. A fused path writes D once: 24 bytes. The difference is 48 bytes, equal to 8MN for this single batch.

This comparison deliberately holds the rest of the operation fixed. It does not count A/B/C traffic, assert that every byte reaches HBM, or prove that a changed schedule wins. For the larger 2048-square example, apply the same accounting rule rather than inferring a speedup from the byte ratio alone.

docs.title: 9 — A controlled extension exercise
docs.text:
After the existing ReLU variant passes, choose one additional supported operation. Write its scalar formula and explicit types, modify the independent reference, add shape/stride cases that distinguish its broadcast axes, and retain the old result as a regression check. Run the memory sanitizer after any change to the store path or shared-memory staging.

Then measure the complete fused and unfused sequences under the same warmup, allocation and timing policy. Report both the resource change and the latency change. A failed optimization is still useful when the result explains which cost moved onto the critical path.

Can the original GEMM oracle validate a fused activation?

The linear GEMM passes. The activation output looks plausible. Is that enough?

Answer: No. The mathematical output changed. Compare the fused result against an independently computed reduction, linear combination and activation in the specified order.

Does bias belong to M or N?

A 37×29 output uses a 29-element bias. Which coordinate selects it?

Answer: n for a per-column bias, shared across the 37 rows. A per-row bias would require 37 elements and represent a different contract.
