// A complete fused ReLU variant of the pinned Hopper GEMM with a full CPU oracle.
#include <cute/tensor.hpp>
#include <cutlass/cutlass.h>
#include <cutlass/epilogue/collective/collective_builder.hpp>
#include <cutlass/epilogue/fusion/operations.hpp>
#include <cutlass/epilogue/thread/activation.h>
#include <cutlass/gemm/collective/collective_builder.hpp>
#include <cutlass/gemm/device/gemm_universal_adapter.h>
#include <cutlass/gemm/kernel/gemm_universal.hpp>
#include <cutlass/util/device_memory.h>
#include <cutlass/util/packed_stride.hpp>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <vector>
using namespace cute;
using Half = cutlass::half_t;
using Row = cutlass::layout::RowMajor;
using CtaTileShape = Shape<_128, _128, _64>;
using Cluster = Shape<_1, _1, _1>;
using Fusion = cutlass::epilogue::fusion::LinCombEltAct<
    cutlass::epilogue::thread::ReLu,
    float,
    float,
    float>;
using Epilogue = cutlass::epilogue::collective::CollectiveBuilder<
    cutlass::arch::Sm90,
    cutlass::arch::OpClassTensorOp,
    CtaTileShape,
    Cluster,
    cutlass::epilogue::collective::EpilogueTileAuto,
    float,
    float,
    float,
    Row,
    4,
    float,
    Row,
    4,
    cutlass::epilogue::TmaWarpSpecialized,
    Fusion>::CollectiveOp;
using Mainloop = cutlass::gemm::collective::CollectiveBuilder<
    cutlass::arch::Sm90,
    cutlass::arch::OpClassTensorOp,
    Half,
    Row,
    8,
    Half,
    Row,
    8,
    float,
    CtaTileShape,
    Cluster,
    cutlass::gemm::collective::StageCountAutoCarveout<
        static_cast<int>(sizeof(Epilogue::SharedStorage))>,
    cutlass::gemm::KernelTmaWarpSpecializedPingpong>::CollectiveOp;
using Kernel = cutlass::gemm::kernel::
    GemmUniversal<Shape<int, int, int, int>, Mainloop, Epilogue>;
using Gemm = cutlass::gemm::device::GemmUniversalAdapter<Kernel>;

void cuda_check(cudaError_t s) {
    if (s != cudaSuccess)
        throw std::runtime_error(cudaGetErrorString(s));
}

void cutlass_check(cutlass::Status s) {
    if (s != cutlass::Status::kSuccess)
        throw std::runtime_error(cutlassGetStatusString(s));
}

bool test(int M,
          int N,
          int K,
          int L,
          float alpha,
          float beta,
          cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo hardware) {
    std::vector<Half> A(size_t(L) * M * K), B(size_t(L) * K * N);
    std::vector<float> C(size_t(L) * M * N), D(C.size());
    for (size_t i = 0; i < A.size(); ++i)
        A[i] = Half(float(int(i % 13) - 6) / 8);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < B.size(); ++i)
        B[i] = Half(float(int(i % 17) - 8) / 8);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < C.size(); ++i)
        C[i] = float(int(i % 19) - 9) / 16;
    cutlass::device_memory::allocation<Half> da(A.size()),
        db(B.size());
    cutlass::device_memory::allocation<float> dc(C.size()),
        dd(D.size());
    cuda_check(cudaMemcpy(da.get(),
                          A.data(),
                          A.size() * sizeof(Half),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    cuda_check(cudaMemcpy(db.get(),
                          B.data(),
                          B.size() * sizeof(Half),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    cuda_check(cudaMemcpy(dc.get(),
                          C.data(),
                          C.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    // IEEE FP32 all-one bits are NaN: an omitted output store cannot pass
    // merely because its reference value happens to be zero.
    cuda_check(
        cudaMemset(dd.get(), 0xff, D.size() * sizeof(float)));
    auto sa = cutlass::make_cute_packed_stride(Kernel::StrideA{},
                                               make_shape(M, K, L));
    auto sb = cutlass::make_cute_packed_stride(Kernel::StrideB{},
                                               make_shape(N, K, L));
    auto sc = cutlass::make_cute_packed_stride(Kernel::StrideC{},
                                               make_shape(M, N, L));
    auto sd = cutlass::make_cute_packed_stride(Kernel::StrideD{},
                                               make_shape(M, N, L));
    Gemm::Arguments args{cutlass::gemm::GemmUniversalMode::kGemm,
                         {M, N, K, L},
                         {da.get(), sa, db.get(), sb},
                         {{}, dc.get(), sc, dd.get(), sd},
                         hardware};
    args.epilogue.thread.alpha = alpha;
    args.epilogue.thread.beta = beta;
    Gemm gemm;
    cutlass_check(gemm.can_implement(args));
    cutlass::device_memory::allocation<unsigned char> workspace(
        Gemm::get_workspace_size(args));
    cutlass_check(gemm.initialize(args, workspace.get()));
    cutlass_check(gemm.run());
    cuda_check(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
    cuda_check(cudaMemcpy(D.data(),
                          dd.get(),
                          D.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    size_t errors = 0;
    for (int l = 0; l < L; ++l)
        for (int m = 0; m < M; ++m)
            for (int n = 0; n < N; ++n) {
                double sum = 0;
                for (int k = 0; k < K; ++k)
                    sum +=
                        double(
                            float(A[(size_t(l) * M + m) * K + k])) *
                        double(
                            float(B[(size_t(l) * K + k) * N + n]));
                size_t i = (size_t(l) * M + m) * N + n;
                float expected = float(alpha * sum + beta * C[i]);
                expected = expected < 0.0f ? 0.0f : expected;
                // These bounded binary-rational inputs make the sum exact in FP32.
                errors += !std::isfinite(D[i]) || D[i] != expected;
            }
    std::printf(
        "%s M=%d N=%d K=%d L=%d alpha=%.2f beta=%.2f checked=%zu errors=%zu\n",
        errors ? "FUSED GEMM FAIL" : "FUSED GEMM CASE PASS",
        M,
        N,
        K,
        L,
        alpha,
        beta,
        D.size(),
        errors);
    return errors == 0;
}

int main() {
    try {
        cudaDeviceProp p{};
        cuda_check(cudaSetDevice(0));
        cuda_check(cudaGetDeviceProperties(&p, 0));
        if (p.major != 9 || p.minor != 0) {
            std::fprintf(
                stderr,
                "Requires Hopper compute capability 9.0; found %d.%d\n",
                p.major,
                p.minor);
            return 2;
        }
        cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo hw{};
        hw.device_id = 0;
        hw.sm_count = p.multiProcessorCount;
        bool ok = test(128, 128, 64, 1, 1, 0, hw);
        ok = test(256, 128, 128, 2, 0.5f, 0.25f, hw) && ok;
        ok = test(136, 264, 72, 1, 0.5f, 0.25f, hw) && ok;
        std::puts(ok ? "FUSED GEMM PASS: 3 full CPU-reference cases"
                     : "FUSED GEMM FAIL");
        return ok ? 0 : 1;
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::fprintf(stderr, "FUSED GEMM ERROR: %s\n", e.what());
        return 1;
    }
}

docs.title: 27. Precision, Block Scaling and the Hopper–Blackwell Boundary
Lesson 27 Companion Guide — Separate Stored Codes, Scale Layouts and Executed Arithmetic
docs.text:
Your goal in this chapter

Decode E2M1 and packed nibbles, identify the reduction-axis scale contract, and separate representation error from kernel error. Read GEMM contracts and epilogue precision first.

A low-bit GEMM has two independent questions: what numbers do the stored bits represent, and what instructions execute the multiplication? A four-bit allocation answers neither question completely. This chapter separates representation, quantization, scale layout and accumulation so a storage experiment cannot accidentally become a claim about native Tensor Core support.

The executed CUTLASS GEMM labs in this track use FP16 operands and FP32 accumulation. Hopper also supports BF16, but changing these labs to BF16 requires a separate build and numerical validation. The CPU exercise below explores E2M1 representation with exact floating-point block scales. It is a format reference, not an NVFP4 kernel or an implementation of NVIDIA's complete quantization recipe.

docs.title: Hopper FP8 before Blackwell FP4
docs.text:
Hopper supports FP8 E4M3 (largest finite magnitude 448; no infinity) and E5M2 (largest finite magnitude 57344; infinity available). Both are floating point, not evenly spaced integer codes. INT8 is another supported GEMM input family; its quantization and accumulation contracts differ.

For per-tensor scaling define q = quantize(x/s) and reconstruct x ≈ s*q. If x=[1,2,4,8] and s=2, the values before rounding are [0.5,1,2,4]; multiplying back by 2 reconstructs this particular example exactly. Real values generally round. Choose s to manage overflow and underflow; scaling does not add mantissa bits. Delayed per-tensor scaling uses a previous step's reduced amax, not an unavailable future maximum.

Hopper also has software/library blockwise-scaled FP8 GEMM. In pinned CUTLASS, read examples 67 (single GEMM) and 68 (grouped GEMM), and KernelTmaWarpSpecializedCooperativeFP8Blockwise. For each K block t, accumulate sA[m,t]*sB[n,t]*dot(qA[m,t],qB[n,t]) in the output's higher-precision accumulation. With two block dot products 3 and -1, and scale products 2 and 8, the reconstructed sum is 23 + 8(-1) = -2. Applying one final scale to the unscaled sum 2 is generally wrong because the block scales differ.

The KernelTmaWarpSpecialized*FP8FastAccum policies make a distinct precision/ throughput choice. Promoting partial results and fast tensor-core accumulation are not interchangeable error contracts; compare against a higher-precision reference on the actual input distribution. These are source-reading and worked-arithmetic examples, not new GPU execution claims. Blackwell's native NVFP4 scale/storage contract below is a separate architecture feature.

docs.title: 1 — Write the numerical contract before the datatype
docs.text:
Start with logical operands A[M,K] and B[K,N], then state which matrix is actually multiplied. If quantization reconstructs A_hat and B_hat, a low-bit kernel approximates A_hat @ B_hat; comparing only against the original A @ B mixes quantization error with implementation error.

Use two references. A representation reference decodes the exact stored codes and scales. An arithmetic reference multiplies those decoded values with an explicitly chosen accumulator. Comparing the kernel with this second result diagnoses the kernel. Comparing the second result with the original higher-precision product diagnoses the representation's effect on the workload. A large error in either deserves investigation, but the remedies differ.

Record input format, scale format, scale direction, rounding, finite-value policy, accumulator precision, output conversion and alpha/beta. “FP4 GEMM” leaves nearly all of these unspecified. A reference must also reproduce whether scaling occurs before multiplication, during block accumulation or in the epilogue: mathematically equivalent rearrangements can round differently.

docs.title: 2 — E2M1 is a floating-point codebook
docs.text:
The positive E2M1 magnitudes are:

Low three bits Magnitude Low three bits Magnitude 000 0 100 2 001 0.5 101 3 010 1 110 4 011 1.5 111 6

Bit three supplies the sign, including negative zero. The gaps between values grow with magnitude. Signed two's-complement INT4, whose usual range is −8 through 7, has a different interpretation of the same nibble. Sign-extending an E2M1 nibble as an integer therefore produces the wrong value even when the byte packing is correct.

The exercise defines nearest-representable rounding with ties to an even code least-significant bit and saturation of finite magnitudes above six. It rejects NaN and infinity. That explicit policy is part of this reference; it does not imply every conversion API defaults to identical behavior. Transformer Engine's precision primer explains E2M1 and the distinction between low-precision formats.

docs.title: 3 — Scaling changes the represented number
docs.text:
For one illustrative block, reconstruct an element as

x_hat[i] = scale[block] * q[i], where q[i] is one of 0, ±0.5, ±1, ±1.5, ±2, ±3, ±4, ±6.

An exact-scale teaching quantizer can choose s_b = amax(block) / 6, then round x_i / s_b to that codebook. Dividing by amax and rounding to integers instead produces mostly −1, 0 and 1; clamping that result to seven does not recover the missing precision.

For an all-zero block, choose a documented harmless scale, such as one, and emit signed zero codes. Adding an arbitrarily small epsilon is not a robust substitute: 1e-12 becomes zero in FP16, so a zero block can still produce 0 / 0. Check finite inputs and scale underflow explicitly. A real quantizer must additionally define clipping, very small scales and the precision used to calculate amax.

NVIDIA NVFP4 uses E2M1 values, E4M3 block scales shared over 16 elements and a second, per-tensor FP32 scale. Quantizing the scale introduces another rounding step. Our exact-scale example omits that step deliberately; its errors cannot be reported as the errors of the complete NVFP4 recipe. See Transformer Engine's NVFP4 description.

docs.title: 4 — Scale along the reduction axis
docs.text:
For A[M,K], K-block scaling naturally yields logical scales S_A[M,ceil(K/16)]. For B[K,N], K-block scaling yields S_B[ceil(K/16),N]. Quantizing contiguous groups from each row of a row-major B instead groups along N and changes the representation.

One simple reference transposes B into a logical B_T[N,K], quantizes its rows, and retains that orientation for the packed payload. The consumer must then interpret B as [N,K] storage, not silently reuse [K,N] indexing. This distinction is why a matrix's mathematical dimensions, storage dimensions and scale dimensions should appear together in every interface.

Use an asymmetric test: give B's first column values near one and its second values eight times larger. The correct scales follow each column's K blocks. A uniform matrix or square shape can conceal a swapped axis, while deliberately different magnitudes reveal it. Also test multiple K blocks with distinct maxima; one scale per entire row can otherwise appear to work.

docs.title: 5 — Packed bytes and blocked scales are separate layouts
docs.text:
Two four-bit codes fit in a byte. This exercise places the first logical code in the low nibble and the second in the high nibble. That convention must match the decoder; masking only byte & 15 duplicates the low value and discards half the operand.

If a row stores K logical values in K/2 bytes, its byte stride is K/2, not K. Derive row and column contributions in consistent units before forming an address. For odd K, specify padding and a logical valid-element count; never let a padding nibble become an extra reduction term. The reference requires an even code count and complete blocks so omissions cannot be hidden by implicit padding.

A blocked or swizzled scale tensor introduces another coordinate map. Flattening a permuted scale tensor does not make ordinary row-major indexing valid. Prove the producer and consumer maps agree for every logical scale coordinate, including padded regions. A hardware-required scale layout is specific to the chosen instruction and library interface, not a universal to_blocked() transformation or guaranteed speedup.

docs.title: Worked block: encode, pack, reconstruct, multiply
docs.text:
Use M=1, K=16 and N=2. Only the first six positions may be nonzero; positions 6 through 15 are zero. The original operands are:

K position 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 through 15 A row 1 2 3 4 0 6 All zero B column 0 1 −2 3 −4 12 0 All zero B column 1 4 −8 12 −16 48 0 All zero

The purpose is to see a complete representation path by hand, not to simulate Blackwell's scale storage. Use the CPU reference's exact Python-float scales and its low-nibble-first packing convention.

  1. Choose each K-block scale. A's maximum magnitude is six, so s_A=6/6=1. B's column maxima are 12 and 48, so their scales are two and eight. Logical S_B[block_k,n] is therefore [2,8] for the single K block. The helper stores these as rows of the transposed B view, [[2],[8]].
  2. Normalize and encode A. Its first six normalized values are 1,2,3,4,0,6, with E2M1 codes 2,4,5,6,0,7. For example, code 5 is floating-point value three, not integer five.
  3. Pack A pairs. Codes (2,4) become byte 0x42; (5,6) become 0x65; (0,7) become 0x70. The remaining ten zeros occupy five zero bytes. Sixteen values require eight bytes.
  4. Normalize and encode B. Both columns produce the same normalized values 0.5,-1,1.5,-2,6,0, but have different scales. Their first six codes are 1,A,3,C,7,0 in hexadecimal. The packed bytes begin A1 C3 07. Sign extension would incorrectly read code A as integer −6; the E2M1 decoder correctly returns −1.
  5. Reconstruct before multiplying. Column 0 becomes twice its decoded code values, restoring 1,-2,3,-4,12,0. Column 1 uses scale eight and restores four times column 0. No quantization error arises for these deliberately representable inputs.
  6. Calculate each dot. The normalized dot is 1×0.5 + 2×(-1) + 3×1.5 + 4×(-2) + 0×6 + 6×0 = -5. Restoring the scale products gives outputs 1×2×(-5)=-10 and 1×8×(-5)=-40.

You can reproduce the same steps using the complete reference rather than writing a second decoder. From the repository root:

import math
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "docs/examples/advanced")
from fp4_reference import quantize_rows, quantize_b_kn, pack

a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 0, 6] + [0] * 10
b0 = [1, -2, 3, -4, 12, 0] + [0] * 10
b1 = [4 * value for value in b0]
qa, sa, a_hat = quantize_rows([a])
qb, sb, b_hat = quantize_b_kn([list(pair) for pair in zip(b0, b1)])
print("A bytes:", pack(qa[0]).hex(" "))
print("B column 0 bytes:", pack(qb[0]).hex(" "))
print("A row scales:", sa)
print("B transpose-row scales:", sb)
print("Reconstructed dot products:", [
    math.fsum(a_hat[0][k] * b_hat[k][n] for k in range(16))
    for n in range(2)
])

The CPU calculation produces:

A bytes: 42 65 70 00 00 00 00 00
B column 0 bytes: a1 c3 07 00 00 00 00 00
A row scales: [[1.0]]
B transpose-row scales: [[2.0], [8.0]]
Reconstructed dot products: [-10.0, -40.0]

Check: the original-input dots also equal −10 and −40, and both B columns share codes while retaining different scales. Pitfall: swapping the two scale entries preserves every packed nibble but changes both outputs. With several K blocks, apply each block's own scale product before combining its partial dot; one final scale cannot generally replace all block scales. This worked result remains a CPU E2M1/exact-scale exercise, not evidence of E4M3 scale conversion or native NVFP4 execution.

docs.title: Keep codes, packed bytes and reconstructed values on separate rows
docs.text:
Read this panel downward for A's first six values. q denotes an E2M1 decoded numerical value; code is its unsigned four-bit representation. Hexadecimal digits below are codes, not ordinary integer quantization levels. A's scale is one in this deliberately exact example.

Logical k:        0       1       2       3       4       5
A original:       1       2       3       4       0       6
scale s_A:        1       1       1       1       1       1
q = A/s_A:        1       2       3       4       0       6
E2M1 code:       0x2     0x4     0x5     0x6     0x0     0x7
                   \     /         \     /         \     /
packed byte:        0x42             0x65             0x70
byte offset:          0                1                2
                 high|low         high|low         high|low

The first logical code goes in the low nibble: code0 | (code1<<4). To recover k=3, select byte 3//2=1, shift by four because 3%2=1, mask with fifteen and decode code 0x6 as numerical value four. Multiplying by scale one reconstructs A's original value four. The complete pack/unpack and decode functions perform these separate steps.

B's two columns illustrate why payload equality is not value equality:

K-block                 column 0                  column 1
first packed bytes      a1 c3 07                  a1 c3 07
first decoded values    0.5,-1,1.5,-2,6,0          0.5,-1,1.5,-2,6,0
block scale             2                         8
reconstructed values    1,-2,3,-4,12,0             4,-8,12,-16,48,0
normalized dot          -5                        -5
apply s_A*s_B           1*2*(-5)=-10               1*8*(-5)=-40

Each column's scale belongs to its reduction-axis K block. Keeping identical packed bytes but swapping the scales changes the outputs. This concrete panel models exact Python-float scales; it does not model E4M3 scale rounding, Blackwell's physical scale layout or native low-bit multiplication.

docs.title: Reproduce one nibble extraction with the actual reference API
docs.text:
Run this complete CPU snippet from the repository root with Python's standard library and the supplied reference module. It allocates only Python objects and launches no CUDA work:

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "docs/examples/advanced")
from fp4_reference import pack, unpack, decode

codes = [0x2, 0x4, 0x5, 0x6, 0x0, 0x7]
payload = pack(codes)
k = 3
byte_index, high_nibble = divmod(k, 2)
code = (payload[byte_index] >> (4 * high_nibble)) & 0xF
assert payload == bytes.fromhex("42 65 70")
assert code == 0x6 and decode(code) == 4.0
assert unpack(payload) == codes
print("byte=1 high=1 code=0x6 decoded=4.0")
  1. divmod(3,2) gives byte index one and nibble selector one. The selector is a position, not the sign bit.
  2. Byte one is 0x65. Shifting right by four discards low code 0x5, leaving high code 0x6.
  3. Masking with 0xF keeps the nibble. The decoder interprets code six as E2M1 value four; it does not return integer six.
  4. This A example has scale one. A different scale multiplies decoded four before the reconstructed value participates in a reference dot product.

Pitfall: reversing the high/low convention still creates valid nibbles, so a code-range check alone cannot detect the permutation. Compare reconstructed values at their original K coordinates.

docs.title: 6 — Keep error sources distinguishable
docs.text:
Let D_ref = A @ B and D_repr = A_hat @ B_hat, both evaluated by the reference arithmetic. Then D_repr - D_ref measures representation effects. D_kernel - D_repr includes implementation and accumulation differences. A correct kernel need not reproduce the unquantized matrix exactly, and a plausible total error does not prove its indexing is correct.

Test signed zeros, alternating signs, sparse values, outliers, block-boundary changes, nonuniform coordinates and nonmultiple dimensions where the kernel supports them. Measure maximum absolute error and a normwise relative error; handle a zero reference norm explicitly. Check finite outputs before applying tolerances. Record both worst-case coordinates and aggregate metrics so a local corruption cannot disappear in an average.

FP32 accumulation generally reduces reduction-rounding error relative to repeatedly storing partial sums in FP16. It does not remove input quantization error or guarantee a particular application's accuracy. “Proper scales prevent overflow” is also insufficient: the final dot product may exceed the output format even when each input block is well scaled. Define whether overflow fails, saturates or produces infinity, and validate that policy.

docs.title: Work a lossy rounding case and two distinct K-block scales
docs.text:
The previous packed example had no quantization loss by construction. To expose loss, choose a block containing the values 6 and 2.5 (and fourteen zeros). Its exact scale is one. The value 2.5 lies halfway between E2M1 magnitudes two (code 4) and three (code 5); nearest-even chooses code 4. Reconstruction yields two, so its signed representation error is 2-2.5=-0.5. The maximum value six remains exact. A successful code round trip therefore does not imply that arbitrary original real values round trip.

Now let a dot product have two K blocks, with normalized partial dots p0=3 and p1=-2. Suppose A's scales are [1,8] and B's are [2,4]. The reconstructed result is

D_repr = (1*2)*3 + (8*4)*(-2) = 6-64 = -58.

The general scalar formula is sum_b (S_A[m,b]*S_B[b,n])*p_b, where p_b reduces decoded codes only inside block b. Factoring out the first scale pair would give 2*(3-2)=2, a different result. This is why the scale coordinate must travel with every block contribution. These algebraic partial dots illustrate the contract; they are not an additional captured native GPU execution.

docs.title: Exercise: zero reference values and output overflow
docs.text:
Suppose one hypothetical reference output is zero and a kernel returns 1e-5. Dividing the error by the reference produces an undefined relative comparison. If the declared absolute tolerance is 1e-6, this element fails: abs(1e-5−0)>1e-6. The example's tolerance is a stated exercise choice, not a recommended universal threshold.

Now use exactly representable FP16 inputs A=[400,400], B=[100,100]. Their mathematical dot is 80000, which fits FP32 but exceeds FP16's largest finite magnitude 65504. Well-scaled finite inputs therefore do not guarantee finite FP16 output. A contract that requires finite output must reject or otherwise handle this case; a contract allowing infinity needs the reference and comparison to recognize it deliberately. The finite exact-scale CPU model and the H100 FP32-output lab do not establish a different format's overflow policy.

docs.title: 7 — Run the CPU representation oracle
docs.text:
The complete fp4_reference.py uses only Python's standard library:

python3 docs/examples/advanced/fp4_reference.py

It exhaustively checks all 16 code values and all 256 ordered nibble pairs. It checks signed zero, every adjacent positive-codebook midpoint, finite saturation, all-zero blocks, exact-scale reconstruction, separate K-block scales, B's scale axis and invalid-input diagnostics. The tests raise on failure; success is not printed after a skipped computation. Avoid Python's -O option because it disables the exercise's assertions.

The result establishes this decoder, packing convention and exact-scale model. It establishes neither FP8 scale rounding nor a native GPU path. To extend it, first add a separately specified E4M3 scale conversion and per-tensor scale, then compare intermediate codes and reconstructed values against a versioned vendor implementation before integrating a GEMM.

docs.title: 8 — Preserve the architecture boundary
docs.text:
Hopper supports FP16, BF16, TF32 and FP8 Tensor Core paths; its WGMMA and TMA machinery can feed supported operations efficiently. Blackwell introduces native microscaled low-bit operations and different programming mechanisms. A Hopper kernel may decode compressed storage into a supported operand type, but those unpacking and conversion costs remain real, and the multiplication is not native NVFP4.

A source-level layout idea can transfer between architectures. An MMA instruction, scale-fragment contract, memory descriptor or throughput figure cannot be transferred by changing an architecture flag alone. Native Blackwell studies need their own build configuration, scale layout, numerical checks and execution evidence. Until then, retain the representation exercise as CPU evidence and the Hopper GEMM as Hopper evidence.

For a worked review, explain why all-zero blocks require a policy, why B's physical last axis may differ from its reduction axis, and why matching A_hat @ B_hat says more about kernel correctness than matching an unexplained tolerance against A @ B. These three questions prevent most misleading low-bit demonstrations before performance tuning begins.

docs.title: Complete source and captured execution
docs.text:
Executed on November 18, 2026 (UTC). Scope: CPU-only Python arithmetic/format reference.

Tested source SHA-256: ffbaaa8cac5e92f51c4035b7e92ef6fab9a55537bd262c47d2fe9998fc766977. Exact source · System information · Workshop results.

The listing below matches the tested source. Its presentation is formatted at build time; downloads retain the captured bytes.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""CPU reference for E2M1 nibbles and exact block scaling, not native NVFP4.

Python float scales are deliberately NOT rounded to E4M3, and there is no
per-tensor FP32 scaling stage or Blackwell scale-layout implementation.
No dependencies, GPU operations, timing claims or model training are involved.
"""
import math

MAGNITUDES = (0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 6.0)


def decode(code):
    if not isinstance(code, int) or not 0 <= code < 16:
        raise ValueError("E2M1 code must be an integer nibble")
    return math.copysign(MAGNITUDES[code & 7], -1.0 if code & 8 else 1.0)


def encode(value):
    """Nearest E2M1 value; ties to even code LSB; finite saturation at +/-6."""
    if not math.isfinite(value):
        raise ValueError("This reference accepts finite values only")
    sign = 8 if math.copysign(1.0, value) < 0 else 0
    magnitude = abs(value)
    if magnitude >= 6.0:
        return sign | 7
    index = min(range(8), key=lambda i: (abs(magnitude - MAGNITUDES[i]), i & 1))
    return sign | index


def pack(codes):
    if len(codes) % 2:
        raise ValueError("Explicitly pad an odd code count before byte packing")
    for code in codes:
        decode(code)  # Validate before shifting.
    return bytes(codes[i] | (codes[i + 1] << 4) for i in range(0, len(codes), 2))


def unpack(data):
    return [code for byte in data for code in (byte & 15, byte >> 4)]


def quantize_rows(rows, block_size=16):
    """Independent last-axis blocks with exact Python-float amax/6 scales."""
    if block_size < 1 or not rows or not rows[0]:
        raise ValueError("Nonempty rows and positive block size required")
    width = len(rows[0])
    if width % block_size or any(len(row) != width for row in rows):
        raise ValueError("Use equal rows with complete blocks")
    codes, scales, reconstructed = [], [], []
    for row in rows:
        if any(not math.isfinite(x) for x in row):
            raise ValueError("Finite input required")
        row_codes, row_scales, row_values = [], [], []
        for start in range(0, width, block_size):
            block = row[start:start + block_size]
            amax = max(abs(x) for x in block)
            scale = amax / 6.0 if amax else 1.0
            if scale == 0.0:
                raise ValueError("Scale underflow: rescale the input before quantizing")
            encoded = [encode(x / scale) for x in block]
            row_codes.extend(encoded)
            row_scales.append(scale)
            row_values.extend(decode(c) * scale for c in encoded)
        codes.append(row_codes)
        scales.append(row_scales)
        reconstructed.append(row_values)
    return codes, scales, reconstructed


def transpose(rows):
    return [list(column) for column in zip(*rows)]


def quantize_b_kn(b, block_size=16):
    """Logical B[K,N]: block along K, by quantizing rows of B transpose."""
    if not b or not b[0] or any(len(row) != len(b[0]) for row in b):
        raise ValueError("Rectangular nonempty B required")
    codes_nk, scales_nk, values_nk = quantize_rows(transpose(b), block_size)
    return codes_nk, scales_nk, transpose(values_nk)


def run_checks():
    # Every nibble, including both signed zeros, survives decode/encode.
    for code in range(16):
        assert encode(decode(code)) == code
    assert math.copysign(1.0, decode(8)) < 0
    # All 256 ordered nibble pairs: low nibble first, high nibble second.
    for low in range(16):
        for high in range(16):
            assert unpack(pack([low, high])) == [low, high]
    for i in range(7):
        middle = (MAGNITUDES[i] + MAGNITUDES[i + 1]) / 2
        even = i if i % 2 == 0 else i + 1
        assert encode(middle) == even
        assert encode(-middle) == (even | 8)
    assert decode(encode(100.0)) == 6.0
    assert decode(encode(-100.0)) == -6.0
    assert decode(encode(1e308)) == 6.0
    _, scales, values = quantize_rows([[0.0] * 16, [-0.0] * 16])
    assert scales == [[1.0], [1.0]]
    assert all(x == 0.0 for row in values for x in row)
    assert all(math.copysign(1.0, x) < 0 for x in values[1])
    # E2M1-representable values at two exact scales: no quantization error.
    row = list(MAGNITUDES) * 2 + [x * 8 for x in MAGNITUDES] * 2
    codes, scales, values = quantize_rows([row])
    assert scales == [[1.0, 8.0]] and values == [row]
    assert unpack(pack(codes[0])) == codes[0]
    # Deliberately asymmetric B: K blocks must follow each column, not N rows.
    b = [[float((k % 8) - 4), float(8 * ((k % 8) - 4))] for k in range(32)]
    b_codes, b_scales, restored = quantize_b_kn(b)
    assert b_scales == [[4.0 / 6, 4.0 / 6], [32.0 / 6, 32.0 / 6]]
    for n in range(2):
        for k in range(32):
            assert restored[k][n] == decode(b_codes[n][k]) * b_scales[n][k // 16]
    # Invalid inputs and incomplete blocks are diagnosed, not silently padded.
    for operation in (lambda: encode(float('nan')), lambda: encode(float('inf')),
                      lambda: pack([0]), lambda: decode(16),
                      lambda: quantize_rows([[1.0] * 15]),
                      lambda: quantize_b_kn([[1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])):
        try:
            operation()
        except ValueError:
            pass
        else:
            raise AssertionError("Expected an invalid-input diagnosis")
    print("PASS: all 16 E2M1 codes, 256 nibble pairs and nearest-even ties")
    print("PASS: finite saturation, signed zero, zero blocks and exact-scale round trips")
    print("PASS: K-axis B scaling, independent block scales and invalid-input diagnoses")
    print("Scope: CPU format/layout reference; no E4M3 scale quantization, tensor scale or native NVFP4 GEMM")
    print("FP4 REFERENCE PASS: 3 CPU-only reference groups")


if __name__ == '__main__':
    run_checks()

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• E2M1 is a floating-point codebook, not signed INT4. Payload packing, scale representation, reduction axes and zero-block policy all belong to the interface.

  • The CPU exact-scale oracle does not implement a complete NVFP4 quantizer or execute native low-bit GPU arithmetic. Hopper and Blackwell paths retain separate evidence.

  • Compare against decoded operands before assessing original-input error, and include conversions and metadata in a reproducible performance experiment.

docs.title: 28. Benchmarking and Framework Integration Without Changing the Question
docs.text:
Scope of framework integration

This chapter supplies benchmarking examples and an integration contract, not a compiled PyTorch extension. A production wrapper must guard the input device, validate dtype/shape/strides/alignment with TORCH_CHECK, obtain at::cuda::getCurrentCUDAStream(device), allocate CUTLASS workspace through the framework allocator, call can_implement, and propagate initialization/run errors. Retain workspace until the stream finishes. A default-stream standalone program does not establish correct framework stream or graph-capture integration. The separately versioned CuTe DSL documentation is not evidence that its API matches this C++ v4.3.6 pin.

docs.title: Lesson 28 Companion Guide — Measure the Useful Operation and Preserve Framework Semantics
docs.text:
Your goal in this chapter

Define a fair correctness and timing contract, distinguish serial latency from concurrent throughput, and preserve device, stream and lifetime rules in integration. Read pipeline costs, fusion and precision first.

A kernel benchmark answers a narrow question about a particular operation on a particular system. A framework integration must additionally preserve layouts, numerical behavior, stream ordering and object lifetimes. Combining these tasks without an explicit contract can produce an impressive number for an operation the application never requested.

This chapter turns a verified Hopper GEMM into an experiment someone else can interpret. Its timing examples are arithmetic illustrations, not new measurements. The book's captured execution records remain the source of actual dates, systems, commands and outputs.

docs.title: 1 — Identify the implementation before comparing it
docs.text:
CUTLASS C++ is a collection of CUDA C++ templates and components. CuTe C++ supplies tensor and layout abstractions used within that ecosystem. CuTe DSL is a separate Python kernel-authoring interface in the CUTLASS Python stack; it generates device code while retaining explicit layout, copy, MMA and pipeline concepts.

Triton is another compiler and programming model. A function decorated with @triton.jit and written with triton.language remains Triton even if a surrounding Python class is named CuTeGEMM. Likewise, a handwritten WMMA kernel does not become a CUTLASS GEMM because its source includes a CUTLASS header. PyTorch tensor operations are a framework-level interface, whose backend depends on the operation, configuration, build and hardware.

These distinctions matter when recording dependencies and interpreting results. Pin a CUTLASS C++ checkout separately from any Python DSL package. The C++ revision used elsewhere in this book is not an automatic promise that a newer DSL wheel supports the same CUDA, Python or driver versions. Check the selected release's installation requirements. CUTLASS Python overview and Triton's programming model describe different interfaces, not successive performance tiers.

docs.title: 2 — Freeze an operation contract
docs.text:
Write an experiment record before tuning. Include M, N, K, batch dimensions, transpose operations, physical strides, storage order, input/output/accumulator types, alpha, beta, epilogue and output ownership. Also state whether inputs are already resident on the GPU and in the required format.

A dense FP16 GEMM and a compressed-input GEMM that first dequantizes to FP16 differ in preprocessing and memory traffic. A GEMM-plus-bias-plus-activation cannot be compared fairly against bare GEMM without naming the omitted work. Row-major and column-major interfaces may require different leading dimensions even when the mathematical matrix is unchanged.

Keep the baseline useful: choose a library implementation for the same contract, configure its precision behavior explicitly, and include its necessary workspace. If an implementation cannot represent that contract, report unsupported input rather than silently changing the operation. This is especially important for a fused epilogue, noncontiguous tensors or quantized scale layouts.

docs.title: 3 — Make correctness a prerequisite for timing
docs.text:
First run deterministic nonuniform inputs against an independent reference. Exercise nonsquare dimensions, padded leading dimensions, nonzero beta, distinct C and D buffers where supported, and values that expose transposition. Report failures with coordinates and expected/actual values. Test invalid alignment or unsupported shapes through the documented rejection path.

Then add randomized and representative application inputs with an explicit tolerance policy. A comparison should reject nonfinite values unless they belong to the stated contract. A normwise relative error needs a zero-norm policy; elementwise relative error is unstable near zero without an absolute tolerance. Exact equality is appropriate only when the chosen values and arithmetic make exact results a justified expectation.

Separate representation error from arithmetic error as Chapter 27 explains. For FP16 inputs accumulated in FP32, compare with a reference using the same rounded inputs, then separately assess the effect of converting the original data to FP16. Do not let a permissive quantization tolerance hide a layout bug. Only time cases whose correctness checks actually ran and passed.

docs.title: Keep repeated invocations mathematically identical
docs.text:
An in-place epilogue can change the input to the next repetition. With D=AB+C, scalar AB=2 and original C=1, the intended output is three. If D aliases C, the next invocation reads three and produces five; the following one produces seven. Warmup has already changed the timed problem before the first reported sample.

Choose distinct, unchanged C and D buffers where the implementation supports them, or reset the mutable input using a documented policy. State whether reset work is inside the timer. A multi-buffer rotation must preserve the same initial data and working-set assumptions for each method. Similarly, declare whether random input generation, quantization, workspace initialization or optimizer state updates occur once or per repetition. Correctness should check the operation actually timed, not only an earlier invocation with different state.

docs.title: 4 — Choose the timing scope explicitly
docs.text:
Three common scopes answer different questions:

Scope Includes Useful question Steady-state device work Scheduled kernel work between events How fast is this prepared operation? Prepared API invocation Host dispatch plus required device completion What does one ready-to-run call cost? End-to-end request Needed packing, transfers, allocation, compilation and computation What latency does this application receive?

Not every request needs compilation or allocation. Report cold-start and warmed reuse separately instead of charging setup arbitrarily to one implementation. If weights are packed once and reused many times, publish that assumption and the packing cost. If activations require a new conversion for every call, that conversion belongs on the recurring path.

For serial, nonoverlapping requests, a useful accounting model is T_total = T_setup + sum(T_request_i). Average amortized cost is T_total / R for R requests. In a concurrent pipeline, summing individual request intervals can double-count overlap. Instead measure the batch makespan from the defined batch start to completion of all R results, report throughput as R / makespan, and report individual request latency separately. State whether setup is inside that interval. Neither accounting method permits omitting synchronization dependencies or adding overlapping stages as if they executed serially.

docs.title: 5 — Place CUDA events around the actual dependency path
docs.text:
For one stream, record a start event, enqueue the intended operations, record a stop event on the same stream, wait for the stop event, and read elapsed time. Include warmup before this interval and check asynchronous errors at a synchronization boundary. Do not measure only the CPU duration of an asynchronous launch and call it kernel time.

For several streams, establish a start dependency in each participating stream and join all terminal work before the stop event. An event on the launcher's stream alone does not cover unrelated streams. The measured completion must mean the output is safe for the next consumer. CUDA event timing guidance explains the synchronization assumptions behind device timing.

A host wall-clock timer can measure application latency if it waits for the required completion. It will include host dispatch and other requested work, so label it accordingly. CUDA event timing and host wall-clock timing can both be correct while answering different questions. Avoid comparing one method's event interval with another method's end-to-end wall time.

docs.title: A timing interval, one API call at a time
docs.text:
The following is an excerpt pattern, not a standalone program. Assume stream, start and stop have been created, inputs are prepared, and launch_checked_gemm(stream) submits the already-validated operation while checking its CUTLASS status. Here check checks a CUDA return value, as in the complete overlap example from Chapter 14.

check(cudaEventRecord(
    start, stream)); // Mark the beginning on this stream.
launch_checked_gemm(
    stream); // Enqueue the operation on that SAME stream.
check(cudaGetLastError()); // Check the CUDA launch boundary too.
check(cudaEventRecord(
    stop, stream)); // This marker follows the operation.
check(cudaEventSynchronize(
    stop)); // Wait until the finish marker is reached.
float elapsed_ms = 0.0f;
check(cudaEventElapsedTime(&elapsed_ms, start, stop));
  1. Put the start in the queue. Recording an event submits a marker; it does not mean all queued work finished before the CPU returned.
  2. Submit the actual operation. The device stream orders the GEMM after start. A helper that launches on another stream would break this simple proof.
  3. Put the stop after the work. The same stream cannot reach stop until its earlier GEMM finishes.
  4. Wait for the result. Synchronizing stop makes the elapsed interval available and provides a boundary at which asynchronous errors can surface.
  5. Read the units. cudaEventElapsedTime returns milliseconds. An illustrative elapsed_ms=0.085 means 85 microseconds, not 85 milliseconds.

For two worker streams, the complete Chapter 14 program adds cudaStreamWaitEvent at the beginning and joins two completion events at the end. Trace those arrows before reusing the pattern; placing stop on an unrelated stream without the join measures a different interval.

docs.title: Draw the actual event join before trusting a stop event
docs.text:
For the Chapter 14 two-worker design, draw three queues. start, done[0], done[1] and stop are event markers, not four kernels. Arrows encode dependencies rather than elapsed milliseconds:

start (recorded on the timing stream)
  ├→ worker 0: wait start → even chunks × 8 → done[0] ─┐
  └→ worker 1: wait start → odd chunks × 8  → done[1] ─┤
                                                    v
timing stream:                 wait done[0] AND done[1] → stop
host:                          synchronize stop → read ms

Here even chunks are 0,2,...,14, odd chunks are 1,3,...,15, and ×8 means the eight workload repetitions. Each chunk includes its H2D, transform and D2H in that worker's stream order.

Read the drawing in four steps:

  1. Record start on the timing stream. Both workers enqueue cudaStreamWaitEvent(worker,start,0) before their measured operations.
  2. Each worker records its own completion event only after its final required operation, including any D2H needed for the useful result.
  3. The timing stream enqueues waits on both completion events before recording stop. These waits prevent the timing stream from racing ahead of an unfinished worker.
  4. Synchronize stop before reading elapsed time or consuming returned host data. A stop event recorded without the two waits could finish while a worker is still active.

This is the dependency structure implemented by the complete overlap program, not a separate copyable launch harness. Real execution can leave gaps between markers; the drawing alone predicts neither overlap nor its speedup. The single-stream timing snippet above needs no cross-stream join because all its measured work stays on one ordered stream.

docs.title: Work through amortization without hiding setup
docs.text:
Suppose, purely as a paper exercise, packing costs 4 ms once and each prepared request costs 0.2 ms. For ten serial requests:

  1. Recurring work is 10×0.2=2 ms.
  2. Total including setup is 4+2=6 ms.
  3. Average request cost including setup is 6/10=0.6 ms.
  4. The prepared request cost is still 0.2 ms. Report both quantities with their boundaries.
  5. At 100 requests the amortized cost becomes (4+100×0.2)/100=0.24 ms. Reuse changed the accounting, not the speed of the prepared kernel.

Put the units and timer boundaries on the same strip. These are the hypothetical serial costs just calculated, not the event intervals captured on H100:

Elapsed wall time (ms):  0          4                 6
                        | setup    | ten requests   |
Setup-inclusive timer:  [----------------------------]
Prepared-request timer:            [0.2] [0.2] ... [0.2]

4 ms setup + (10 × 0.2 ms/request) = 6 ms total
6 ms / 10 requests = 0.6 ms/request, including setup

The widths are schematic, not a plotting scale. The ten requests in this accounting example are serial, so the elapsed intervals add. A timer around just one prepared request answers a different question from the setup-inclusive batch timer. Neither quantity is the 0.085 ms GEMM arithmetic example in the next section; those are separate illustrative workloads.

Pause and check. If requests overlap, can you replace makespan with the sum of their individual durations? No: overlapping intervals would be counted twice. Time the actual joined completion boundary instead.

docs.title: Exercise: batch throughput is not individual latency
docs.text:
Use two hypothetical requests with measured boundaries A=[0.0,0.2] ms and B=[0.1,0.3] ms. These intervals are a paper model, not captured H100 samples.

  1. Each request's latency is 0.2 ms: subtract its own start from its own completion.
  2. The joined batch spans 0.0 through 0.3 ms, so its makespan is 0.3 ms, not the 0.4-ms sum of individual durations.
  3. Throughput is 2 / 0.0003 ≈ 6666.7 requests/s. Dividing batch time by request count gives 0.15 ms/request as an amortized batch cost, not either request's latency.
  4. A serial schedule with the same individual 0.2-ms work would take 0.4 ms for two requests, giving 5000 requests/s under that schedule. Concurrency changed the schedule's throughput; it did not make the individual 0.2-ms intervals become 0.15 ms.

Check: state which start/completion events define each request and the whole batch. Pitfall: timing only the first completion changes both the numerator and the useful-result boundary; it cannot support a claim that both requests finished.

docs.title: 6 — Calculate throughput in consistent units
docs.text:
A conventional dense GEMM work count is 2*M*N*K floating-point operations. This treats each multiply-add as two operations; epilogue operations usually are not included in that conventional count. State when a result is instead batched, sparse, quantized or counts a different workload.

For M=N=2048 and K=4096:

2*M*N*K = 34,359,738,368 FLOP, approximately 34.36 GFLOP.

At an illustrative, unmeasured time of 85 microseconds, throughput would be 34.359738368 / 0.085, or about 404.23 TFLOP/s. Dividing GFLOP by milliseconds produces TFLOP/s. Dividing by seconds instead requires the corresponding powers of ten. These are operation-count calculations, not a claim that this book's kernel achieved that time.

Compare with the matching hardware peak: datatype, accumulator mode, dense versus structured sparse execution and GPU variant must agree. Smaller stored operands do not justify using a native FP4 peak for a Hopper kernel that actually multiplies decoded FP16 values. Do not infer register or shared-memory bandwidth from a global-memory figure.

docs.title: 7 — Report variation and interference
docs.text:
Run enough repetitions to expose variation and publish the repetition count, warmup policy, median and an appropriate range or percentile. For tiny operations, time a documented batch to reduce event overhead, then divide by the operation count; recognize that a batch can change cache residency and scheduling compared with isolated requests.

Record GPU model and count, driver/toolkit/compiler versions, source revision, flags, input shape, workspace, schedule and clocks or power settings when relevant. Identify other GPU processes or communication traffic that affected the experiment. A favorable warm-cache result and a large working-set result are both useful if their conditions are named.

Use Nsight Systems to inspect stream gaps, launches and overlap, then Nsight Compute for a targeted kernel's resource and memory behavior. Profiling can perturb execution, so keep profiling results separate from the timing run. A larger tile or deeper pipeline is a hypothesis: resource pressure, occupancy and available work can reverse the expected benefit.

docs.title: Read a small timing distribution by hand
docs.text:
Suppose a paper exercise gives five elapsed times in milliseconds: 0.080, 0.081, 0.079, 0.082, 0.150. No hardware measurement is asserted here.

  1. Sort them: 0.079, 0.080, 0.081, 0.082, 0.150.
  2. The median is the middle sample, 0.081 ms. The observed range is 0.079–0.150 ms.
  3. Their mean is 0.0944 ms. The long sample affects the mean; silently removing it would conceal observed variation.
  4. Investigate a known interruption separately and publish any exclusion rule before selecting favorable samples. The minimum alone does not describe a typical request.
  5. Five samples are enough for this arithmetic exercise, not a stable tail-latency characterization. Collect an adequate sample set for the question and state the percentile convention if reporting percentiles.

Keep per-invocation statistics distinct from timings of repeated batches divided by batch size. The latter estimates amortized throughput under that batch's scheduling/cache conditions; it is not automatically the latency distribution of isolated calls.

docs.title: 8 — Respect the framework's stream and lifetime model
docs.text:
A PyTorch extension must select the input tensor's device and use the appropriate current CUDA stream for that device. Launching on an unrelated default stream can expose stale data or return an output whose producer is not ordered before its consumer. If a custom stream is necessary, establish explicit dependencies and follow the framework allocator's lifetime rules.

Validate device, dtype, shape, strides and alignment before obtaining raw pointers. Define whether noncontiguous inputs are accepted, copied or rejected. A hidden .contiguous() conversion changes the request cost and must be included when required. Keep inputs, outputs and workspace alive through asynchronous completion; returning from C++ does not mean device work has finished.

Use a documented integration layer rather than guessing opaque object or stream representations. PyTorch's C++ extension tutorial and CUDA semantics provide the framework context. Forward correctness alone does not implement autograd: training integration needs a defined backward path or an explicit inference-only interface.

docs.title: 9 — Preserve the CUTLASS launch lifecycle and fallback
docs.text:
The device adapter's lifecycle includes constructing arguments, checking can_implement, querying workspace, initializing and running on the selected stream. Match workspace sizing to those exact arguments. Check each returned status and subsequent CUDA completion; an accepted launch is not proof of a numerically correct result.

Define a fallback for unsupported dimensions, alignment, architecture or epilogue combinations. It should preserve the same mathematical operation and precision policy, or report a clear unsupported case. Do not catch every runtime error and silently retry: allocation failure, an invalid pointer or an asynchronous illegal access is not an ordinary shape-selection result.

Graph capture introduces additional requirements: avoid unexpected allocation or JIT work during capture, prepare supported workspace in advance, and ensure replay lifetimes remain valid. An inference wrapper, an autograd operator, a captured graph and a standalone benchmark are separate integration targets, each deserving its own test.

docs.title: 10 — A useful experiment ends with a reproducible decision
docs.text:
Publish what changed, the matching correctness evidence, the measured scope and the observed tradeoff. An efficient specialized kernel may win for repeated fixed shapes while losing when packing or compilation cannot be amortized. A library fallback may serve the remaining cases best.

The final deliverable is a validated dispatch decision with readable records, not a universal ranking of PyTorch, Triton, CuTe DSL and C++. Each can express different levels of control, and each can generate fast or slow implementations. The next workbook asks you to change one design choice at a time, predict its effect, verify correctness and explain the measurements that actually occur.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Freeze the operation, layout, precision and required preparation before comparing implementations; correctness is a prerequisite for timing.

  • Name timing boundaries, join actual dependencies, report variation and match throughput to the executed arithmetic. Concurrent request intervals do not add into a batch makespan.

  • Integration must preserve device selection, current-stream ordering, allocation lifetime and supported-input behavior. Turn these contracts into the workbook capstone.

docs.text: Continue to the renumbered chapter.

docs.title: 29. CuTe and CUTLASS Workbook — From Coordinates to Evidence
Lesson 29 Companion Guide — Progress from Coordinate Proofs to a Reproducible Capstone
docs.text:
Your goal in this chapter

Solve the beginner, intermediate and advanced labs, explain each worked answer, and submit a kernel comparison with reproducible correctness and measurement evidence. Use Chapters 15–19 for foundations and Chapters 20–28 for implementation and measurement.

This workbook turns the preceding chapters into problems you can solve, explain and extend. Start with a pencil and a small coordinate enumerator, then move to the GPU. The worked numbers below are derived exercise answers, not captured hardware measurements. For actual compilation dates, system information and program outputs, follow the book's execution records. A correct paper exercise does not establish that a new kernel compiled or ran.

Use the same pinned CUTLASS/CUDA environment as the preceding chapters. Preserve an unmodified working version before each experiment. Change one ownership rule, layout or schedule at a time; validate before timing. The beginner labs require arithmetic and small host-side checks. Intermediate labs require CUDA instruction and synchronization knowledge. Advanced labs combine the builder, precision and measurement chapters.

docs.title: Before you start — notation and checkpoints
docs.text:
Symbol or term Meaning in these labs M, N, K Output rows, output columns and reduction length in A[M,K] × B[K,N] L or l Batch count or one batch index; individual labs state whether batching is present BM, BN, BK Tile extents along those same axes, measured in elements Leading dimension / stride Physical spacing between selected coordinates; stated in elements unless a byte unit is explicit Lane / thread / CTA A lane within a warp, one CUDA thread, and a cooperating thread block Reference An independently calculated expected value, not a second copy of the implementation's indexing helpers

Work through labs 1–3 after the introductory sequence, labs 4–6 after copy ownership, MMA fragments and shared layouts, then labs 7–9 after pipelines, fusion, precision and measurement. Answer each problem before opening its worked derivation. Move on when you can explain why the tempting wrong answer fails, not merely repeat the final number.

docs.title: 1 — Beginner lab: distinguish a view from storage
docs.text:
Problem. A two-dimensional tensor has shape (3,4) and element strides (8,1). List its offsets, logical size, storage span and FP16 byte offset for coordinate (2,3). Does creating a compact view remove the padding from an existing allocation?

Worked answer. Its rows reference offsets 0..3, 8..11 and 16..19. There are 12 logical elements. A positive-stride allocation extending through the largest referenced element needs 20 elements; reserving three complete padded rows would instead need 24. Coordinate (2,3) maps to element 19, hence byte offset 38 for FP16. The gaps are real locations in the padded allocation, not additional tensor coordinates.

Constructing another layout changes the address interpretation. It does not copy the original rows into compact storage. A compact view over the same pointer would read different elements in rows one and two. To remove padding, perform a correctly indexed copy into a separate compact destination. Check both layouts against an array containing distinct coordinate-derived values; zeros cannot reveal this error.

Extension. Set the first stride to zero. Several rows now alias. Such a broadcast view can describe repeated reads, but independent parallel stores to those logical coordinates need an explicit ownership or reduction policy.

docs.title: Solve the first lab without skipping an address
docs.text:
If the answer above felt too quick, put the pieces on paper. A stride is measured in elements, not bytes:

  1. Read the domain. Shape (3,4) permits row i=0,1,2 and column j=0,1,2,3.
  2. Write the rule. Strides (8,1) mean offset(i,j)=8i+j. Advancing one row skips eight elements; advancing one column skips one.
  3. Expand the first row. With i=0, substitute j=0,1,2,3 to obtain offsets 0,1,2,3.
  4. Advance one row. With i=1, the row begins at 8×1=8, so its offsets are 8,9,10,11. Offsets 4..7 are not in this logical view.
  5. Finish the table. With i=2, the offsets are 16,17,18,19. Three rows times four columns give 12 logical coordinates; the span through offset 19 requires 20 element positions.
  6. Convert the selected address. At (2,3), 8×2+3=19 elements. FP16 occupies two bytes, so the address is base+38 bytes. Do not multiply only one term by two.
  7. Test the tempting shortcut. A compact row-major view would use 4i+j. Its (1,0) reads offset 4, while the padded source's (1,0) reads offset 8. A new view did not move any values.
logical row 0 →  0  1  2  3    gap:  4  5  6  7
logical row 1 →  8  9 10 11    gap: 12 13 14 15
logical row 2 → 16 17 18 19

Check yourself. At (1,2), the element offset is 8+2=10, and the FP16 byte offset is 20. If you obtained 6, you silently replaced the padded stride with a compact one. Return to the stride definition before continuing.

docs.title: 2 — Beginner lab: rectangular CTA origins and boundaries
docs.text:
Problem. Compute D[M,N] = A[M,K] B[K,N] with M=130, N=70, K=35. All matrices are compact row-major. Choose CTA tiles BM=64, BN=32, BK=16. For tile coordinates (tile_m,tile_n,tile_k)=(1,2,1), find the origins and offsets used by local coordinates m=3, n=2, k=5. Then describe the final boundary tiles.

Worked answer. The tile origins are (m0,n0,k0)=(64,64,16). The participating global coordinates are (m,n,k)=(67,66,21):

Operand Global coordinate Element offset FP16 byte offset A (67,21) 67×35+21 = 2366 4732 B (21,66) 21×70+66 = 1536 3072 D (67,66) 67×70+66 = 4756 9512

Do not use BM or BN as the global leading dimension. They describe local tiles, whereas global row strides here are 35 for A and 70 for B/D. If a CuTe GEMM interface represents B as (N,K) rather than the mathematical (K,N), the same row-major physical B is addressed by logical (n,k) with strides (1,70). Swapping a logical convention does not itself transpose the allocation.

Ceiling division gives ceil(130/64)=3 M tiles, ceil(70/32)=3 N tiles and ceil(35/16)=3 K iterations: nine output CTAs. The final output tile starts at (128,64) and contains only 2×6=12 valid outputs. The last K tile starts at 32 and contains three valid reduction positions. Predicate global loads/stores and supply the intended neutral values for invalid reduction elements; never replace the ceiling divisions with floor divisions and silently omit the edge.

docs.title: Draw every output tile, including the thin edge
docs.text:
For the problem above, each cell names a count of valid output elements, not their stored numerical values. Column boundaries and row boundaries are global logical coordinates:

                              output column n
                      0..31       32..63       64..69
                      tile_n=0    tile_n=1     tile_n=2
output row m      +------------+------------+------------+
0..63, tile_m=0   | 64×32=2048 | 64×32=2048 | 64×6=384   |
                  +------------+------------+------------+
64..127, tile_m=1 | 64×32=2048 | 64×32=2048 | 64×6=384   |
                  +------------+------------+------------+
128..129, tile_m=2|  2×32=64   |  2×32=64   |  2×6=12    |
                  +------------+------------+------------+

Tile-coordinate envelope: m=0..191, n=0..95
Logical output domain:  m=0..129, n=0..69
  1. Add the valid counts: 4×2048 + 2×384 + 2×64 + 12 = 9100, which equals M×N=130×70. This checks that the thin row and column edges were not lost.
  2. The nine full tile envelopes contain 9×64×32=18432 candidate positions. The other 18432−9100=9332 are not logical outputs, even though their tile-local indices exist.
  3. The final corner tile starts at (128,64). Local (1,5) maps to (129,69), the last valid output, at row-major element offset 129×70+69=9099.
  4. Local (0,6) maps to (128,70), which is invalid. Yet its naive row-major offset is 128×70+70=9030, the same physical offset as valid (129,0)! An allocation-bounds check alone would miss this logical error and could corrupt another row.

The K tail is a separate boundary; the output predicate does not protect operand loads automatically:

K tile 0: global k= 0..15   → 16 valid reduction positions
K tile 1: global k=16..31   → 16 valid reduction positions
K tile 2: global k=32..47   → only 32,33,34 are valid

Last tile's local kk:    0    1    2    3 ... 15
Global k:              32   33   34   35 ... 47
Load contribution:    real real real   0 ...  0

The final line describes a zero-fill reduction policy: three real contributions and thirteen neutral positions. It is not permission to read invalid global addresses and multiply the returned values by zero afterward. Predicate the load before accessing memory, then supply the neutral register/shared value.

docs.title: Add a batch without changing the local tile coordinates
docs.text:
As a separate extension, let L=2 and store independent, compact row-major outputs. Each batch has 9100 FP16 elements, so the output batch stride is 9100 elements, or 18,200 bytes:

Physical output element offsets (two packed batches)
batch l=0: [0 ..................................... 9099]
batch l=1: [9100 ................................. 18199]
             ^ same local tile grid begins at a new base

batch 1's last logical coordinate: (l,m,n)=(1,129,69)
element offset = 1×9100 + 129×70 + 69 = 18199
FP16 byte offset = 18199×2 = 36398

The (tile_m,tile_n) grid is the same in both batches. Only the allocation origin changes through the declared batch stride. The final FP16 element occupies byte offsets 36,398 and 36,399, so a 36,400-byte packed allocation covers both complete logical outputs. A padded or framework-strided output needs its actual batch/row strides instead; do not reuse 9100 merely because the logical shape matches.

docs.title: 3 — Beginner lab: build an adversarial reference
docs.text:
Problem. Why is an all-ones GEMM insufficient to validate a layout? Design a stronger test before optimizing the kernel.

Worked answer. Every output of a compatible all-ones product equals K. A permutation of output positions may therefore leave the result apparently correct. Use distinct, bounded, nonuniform inputs; calculate a reference independently of the kernel's layout helpers. Include rectangular and ragged dimensions, padded leading dimensions, mixed signs, nonzero alpha/beta and untouched guard regions. Compare every output and verify the guards.

Use small integers or exactly representable binary fractions for an initial indexing test. Then add floating-point stress cases with an explicit absolute/relative tolerance and finite-value checks. A reference that reuses the kernel's erroneous indexing function is not independent. For quantized operands, maintain both an original-input reference and a reference using reconstructed quantized inputs; they answer different questions.

docs.title: 4 — Intermediate lab: copy ownership and transactions
docs.text:
Problem. One warp copies 128 consecutive FP32 elements. Lane l owns elements 4l+v, for v=0..3. Does every element have one owner? Does a 16-byte-per-lane copy imply one memory transaction for the whole warp?

Worked answer. For any element x in 0..127, the unique owner is l=floor(x/4) and v=x mod 4. Coverage is complete and ownership is unique. With a suitably aligned base, each lane's four-element vector begins at byte offset 16l; the complete request spans 512 bytes. It cannot fit in one 32-byte sector. The address footprint covers 16 such sectors when sector-aligned; actual generated instructions, cache state and architecture determine the observed traffic.

Alignment of the original allocation does not guarantee alignment of every sliced tile pointer. Recheck the byte offset and bounds before assuming a vectorized copy is legal. In a TiledCopy exercise, enumerate thread/value coordinates, convert them to source and destination addresses, and verify coverage before evaluating performance. A correct partition is a proof about ownership; issuing the copy is a separate operation.

docs.title: 5 — Intermediate lab: an actual m16n8 accumulator mapping
docs.text:
Problem. For the FP32 accumulator fragment of floating-point mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k16, locate lane 13's four outputs. Which lane owns output (11,3)? Is this mapping also a WGMMA map?

Worked answer. For this instruction form, let g=lane>>2 and t=lane%4. Accumulator entries 0 and 1 occupy row g; entries 2 and 3 occupy row g+8. Their columns are 2t+(i mod 2). Lane 13 has g=3, t=1, so its entries are (3,2), (3,3), (11,2), (11,3). Output (11,3) belongs to lane 13, entry 3. Across 32 lanes, four entries per lane account for all 128 outputs.

This k16 exercise uses the same four-value accumulator-coordinate pattern as the k8 atom decoded in Chapter 21; its input fragments and K-depth are different. This is a specific warp-level accumulator mapping, not a universal “16×16 MMA” convention and not a Hopper WGMMA fragment map. Input fragments have their own mappings and packed-register rules. Verify an atom against the exact operand types, instruction shape and PTX fragment specification, then check what the CuTe atom encodes.

docs.title: 6 — Intermediate lab: derive a real bank conflict
docs.text:
Problem. Use the teaching model of 32 shared-memory banks with successive 32-bit words assigned to successive banks. What happens when lane l reads float tile[l][0] from tile[32][32]? What changes with a 33-element row stride?

Worked answer. With stride 32 words, lane l addresses word 32l; its bank is (32l) mod 32 = 0. The lanes request distinct words in one bank: a 32-way conflict in this model. With stride 33, the bank becomes (33l) mod 32 = l, distributing the accesses across all banks.

Conversely, tile[0][l] already distributes contiguous FP32 words across banks. Adding row padding is not a cure for that access pattern. Multiple lanes reading exactly the same word can use broadcast behavior rather than causing this distinct-address conflict. Wider, narrower and vector instructions need a more detailed model; an instruction-compatible swizzle must agree between producer and consumer. Treat the example as a derivation, then inspect the real instruction and profiler counters.

docs.title: 7 — Advanced lab: stage indices need generations
docs.text:
Problem. A three-stage pipeline handles eight K tiles numbered 0 through 7. Give each tile's stage and generation. When may tile 7 overwrite stage 1?

Worked answer. Use the abstract bookkeeping stage=t mod 3, generation=floor(t/3). The pairs are (0,0), (1,0), (2,0), (0,1), (1,1), (2,1), (0,2), (1,2). Tile 7 reuses the slot previously used by tiles 1 and 4.

Before overwriting it, the producer needs the empty/reuse permission for the preceding occupant, including completion of every asynchronous consumer that can still read that stage. A ready barrier says new input arrived; it does not by itself say old WGMMA reads are finished. Conversely, the consumer must wait for the correct current ready event, not merely observe a stale slot state. A parity bit may encode part of this progression, but its initial value and transition rules belong to the actual pipeline implementation; generation modulo two is not a substitute for its protocol.

Trace the prologue, all tile transitions and the drain. Repeat with one K tile and fewer K tiles than stages. Never bypass a wait just because the first large problem appeared to work. A final drain must complete outstanding operations before result use or storage teardown.

docs.title: 8 — Advanced lab: epilogue order changes the function
docs.text:
Problem. Compute D=ReLU(alpha×P + beta×C + bias) for P=-3, alpha=2, C=4, beta=0.5, bias=1. Is applying ReLU to P first equivalent?

Worked answer. The intended pre-activation is -6+2+1=-3, giving D=0. Applying ReLU to P first gives 0+2+1=3: a different result. Bias orientation, activation placement and conversion boundaries are part of the operation contract. An epilogue graph should implement that contract, not merely include operators with familiar names.

Keep accumulation and epilogue arithmetic in the specified precision, then convert at the documented boundary. Test nonzero beta; a beta-zero example cannot detect a broken C path. If the output aliases C, obey the operator's aliasing contract and ensure the reference preserves the original C values.

docs.title: 9 — Advanced lab: precision, metadata and honest timing
docs.text:
Problem. A and B have reduction extent 35 and use blocks of 16 values along K. Count unpadded scale groups for A with 130 rows and B with 70 columns. Estimate packed storage and explain the execution distinction between Hopper and Blackwell.

Worked answer. Each row of A and each mathematical column of B needs three K groups: 390 scales for A and 210 for B. Do not group B along N simply because its physical allocation is row-major. A rowwise A packing uses 18 bytes per row for 35 nibbles, or 2340 bytes. A columnwise B packing similarly uses 70×18=1260 bytes. Those are illustrative separate-row/column packing contracts, not a native CUTLASS scale-layout prescription. An instruction-specific representation can require padding, a different interleave and a defined scale layout. The complete CPU encoder in Chapter 27 deliberately requires complete blocks; K=35 here is a paper exercise in defining a tail contract, not a supported direct call to that encoder. To implement it, specify padding to complete blocks while retaining the logical reduction length 35, then test that padded elements contribute zero.

For NVFP4, account for E2M1 elements, E4M3 block scales and global FP32 scaling. Zero blocks, rounding, saturation and the unused nibble need explicit rules. At large aligned sizes, elements plus one byte per 16-value scale cost 0.5625 bytes/value, approximately 7.11× smaller than FP32 before global scales and padding. Hopper dequantization followed by FP16/BF16 GEMM is not native NVFP4 Tensor Core execution; native Blackwell experiments need separate compatibility and execution evidence. See NVIDIA's NVFP4 description.

For a separate hypothetical benchmark with FP16 A, B and D, beta zero, M=N=2048 and K=4096, the conventional GEMM count is 34,359,738,368 operations. At a hypothetical 85 microseconds, throughput is approximately 404.23 TFLOPS, not approximately 202.1. Reading A and B once and writing D once requires 41,943,040 bytes, excluding C reads, scales and extra passes. At one millisecond that minimum traffic implies 41.94 GB/s. With FP32 D instead, its output store costs twice as many bytes and the corresponding total becomes 50,331,648 bytes; state the output type rather than importing a traffic count from another kernel. These calculations are consistency checks, not measured bandwidth or peak-utilization claims.

docs.title: Exercise: account for padding before quoting a compression ratio
docs.text:
Return to M=130, N=70, K=35. Define a hypothetical serialized representation with complete 16-value K blocks: pad each logical K row/column to 48 codes, pack two codes per byte, store one byte per block scale and one four-byte global scale for each complete operand tensor. This is byte accounting for that stated representation, not a claim that the exact-scale Python oracle emits native NVFP4 storage.

  1. Each padded A row needs 48/2=24 payload bytes. A's payload is 130×24=3120 bytes, with 130×3=390 block-scale bytes.
  2. Each mathematical B column needs the same 24 payload bytes. B's payload is 70×24=1680 bytes, with 70×3=210 block-scale bytes.
  3. Two four-byte tensor scales add eight bytes. The subtotal is 3120+1680+390+210+8=5408 bytes before any further alignment or container metadata.
  4. The original compact FP32 operands use (130×35+35×70)×4=28000 bytes. For this small ragged case the ratio is 28000/5408≈5.18, not the aligned large-tensor estimate 7.11.
  5. Padding must retain the logical length 35. Codes added at K=35 through 47 contribute zero under the declared reconstruction policy and must not turn the operation into a different 48-term problem with arbitrary padded values.

Worked check: 390+210=600 local-scale groups, but their serialized bytes depend on the scale format. The Python exact-scale model uses Python-float objects and does not establish this one-byte storage cost. Pitfall: reporting only the nibble payload ignores scales and padding precisely where small or ragged shapes can make them important.

docs.title: 10 — Capstone: deliver a reproducible kernel comparison
docs.text:
Choose one supported operation and keep its semantics identical across the reference, baseline and tuned implementations. Submit:

  • The source revision, pinned dependencies, exact compile commands and architecture target.
  • A shape/stride/type table with aligned and ragged cases, numerical criteria and complete correctness results.
  • A diagram of ownership, stage lifecycle and epilogue order that matches the implementation.
  • Separate kernel-only and end-to-end timing boundaries, including quantization/layout conversion where relevant.
  • Raw timing samples, warmup/JIT policy, summary statistics, hardware/software information and a precise execution date.
  • A conclusion tied to measurements: what changed, why the evidence supports it, and which configurations remain outside the test.

Assess the submission in four passes. Mapping: reconstruct one nonuniform value's logical coordinate, owner and physical address. Safety: identify readiness and reuse edges, including tail/drain behavior. Numerics: distinguish representation, accumulation and epilogue errors. Measurement: reproduce the work count and timing boundary from the supplied record. A missing or failed check in one pass remains an open item even if the other three look convincing.

A convincing capstone can explain a slowdown. It need not promise a fixed fraction of peak. If a layout change reduces conflicts but increases register pressure or conversion cost, record that tradeoff. The final skill is connecting coordinates, numerical semantics and synchronization to evidence another reader can reproduce.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Trace coordinates through storage, thread/value ownership and instruction fragments before reasoning about bank conflicts or asynchronous stage reuse.

  • Preserve the mathematical epilogue and quantization contract, and check operation counts, metadata and timing units independently.

  • A capstone connects exact source and system records to full correctness checks, explicit timing scope and a measured conclusion. Derived exercise answers remain distinct from captured GPU results.

docs.title: Continue with an attention capstone
docs.text: Apply the same mapping, safety, numerics and measurement rubric to the attention derivation, then the pinned Hopper CUTLASS FMHA implementation. The two matrix products share an online-softmax dependency that makes attention a useful next step beyond a single GEMM.
