docs.title: Lesson 30 Companion Guide — From Two GEMMs to One Streaming Attention Contract
docs.text:
Your goal in this chapter

Compute a complete attention example before reading a fused kernel. Track its scores, mask, row maximum, denominator and weighted-value numerator; derive its layouts independently of its arithmetic. Read FlashAttention-3, strides, the GEMM adapter and pipeline ownership first. Chapter 31 connects this contract to pinned Hopper FMHA code.

The CUTLASS example studied here is examples/88_hopper_fmha in v4.3.6, commit 1afc6d355b8cb992398f17beb4425702f1d57ddd. Its README describes a forward GEMM–online-softmax–GEMM fusion and separate backward kernels. This chapter supplies the mathematical bridge. Its tiny d=2 problem is supported by the standalone SIMT CUDA reference below, but does not match the pinned Tensor Core FMHA runner's head-dimension specializations. Chapter 31 supplies the separate optimized CUTLASS implementation.

The accompanying complete CPU oracle uses Python binary64 arithmetic and the standard library. It independently compares a materialized reference with streaming updates. That checks the worked equations, masks and state transitions. It does not validate CUDA instruction ordering, FP16/FP8 rounding, the CUTLASS compiler interface or performance.

Complete runnable CUDA reference · Complete Python reference · Optimized CUTLASS CUDA source.

docs.title: 1 — Define the operation and every axis
docs.text:
For one batch and one attention head, write

S = (Q K^T) / sqrt(d)

P[i,j] = exp(S[i,j]) / sum_t exp(S[i,t])

O = P V.

Symbol Shape Meaning Q Nq × d One feature row per query K Nk × d One feature row per key V Nk × dv One output-value row per key S, P Nq × Nk Scores and row-normalized probabilities O Nq × dv Weighted value result per query

The reduction in Q K^T is over d. The reduction in P V is over Nk. Confusing those axes gives a plausible-shaped intermediate that computes another operation. The mathematical transpose K^T does not require physically copying K into a transposed allocation; a compatible tensor view/instruction layout can represent the needed access.

This mathematical chapter permits dv distinct from d. The pinned example runner instead uses one D for Q, K, V and O. Likewise, no dropout, bias, rotary-position transformation or output projection is present in the toy contract. Additions need an explicit placement and numerical reference; they are not implied by the word attention.

docs.title: 2 — Choose inputs whose softmax can be checked exactly on paper
docs.text:
Let a=sqrt(2)*ln(2), choose d=dv=2, and use:

Q = [ a  0 ]      K = [ 1  0 ]      V = [ 1  0 ]
    [ 0  a ]          [ 0  1 ]          [ 0  2 ]
                      [ 1  1 ]          [ 3  4 ]

Here Nq=2, Nk=3. The numbers are a mathematical construction, not exactly representable FP16 inputs. Python approximates the transcendental constants in binary64, so its checks use an explicit 1e-12 relative/absolute tolerance. The hand derivation treats the equations over real numbers.

  1. Query row zero dotted with key zero gives a; key one gives zero; key two gives a.
  2. Scaling by 1/sqrt(2) yields score row zero [ln(2),0,ln(2)].
  3. Query row one produces [0,ln(2),ln(2)].
  4. The unshifted exponentials are [2,1,2] and [1,2,2]. Each row sums to five.

Therefore the noncausal probability rows are [2/5,1/5,2/5] and [1/5,2/5,2/5]. Each has sum one and nonnegative entries. A sum-one check is necessary but cannot detect every key permutation; the nonuniform V values make that permutation observable at the output.

docs.title: 3 — Finish the second GEMM by hand
docs.text:
For output row zero, weight all three V rows:

(2/5)*[1,0] + (1/5)*[0,2] + (2/5)*[3,4] = [8/5,2].

For output row one:

(1/5)*[1,0] + (2/5)*[0,2] + (2/5)*[3,4] = [7/5,12/5].

The expected matrix is thus O=[[1.6,2],[1.4,2.4]]. The first component of row zero includes 2/5+6/5=8/5; the second includes 2/5+8/5=2. These are different weighted sums, not copies of the same softmax denominator.

Pitfall: multiplying every score row by V before normalizing would give unnormalized numerators [8,10] and [7,12]. Dividing by five is essential. Another wrong shortcut is normalizing each key tile independently and adding its outputs; tile-local denominators do not equal the complete row denominator.

docs.title: 4 — Use a stable maximum without changing the function
docs.text:
Subtracting one common value from a row of logits leaves its softmax unchanged. Choose row maximum m:

exp(s_j)/sum_t exp(s_t) = exp(s_j-m)/sum_t exp(s_t-m).

For row zero, m=ln(2). The stable exponential weights are [1,1/2,1], denominator l=5/2, and weighted-value numerator z=[4,5]. Then z/l=[8/5,2] as before.

The denominator l is a scalar; z is a vector of length dv. Their magnitudes depend on the chosen maximum, but the normalized output does not. Save LSE=m+ln(l) if the implementation's contract requires natural-log log-sum-exp. Both noncausal rows have LSE=ln(5) in this example.

Some kernels evaluate exponentials with base two. The equivalent expression is exp(s)=exp2(s*log2(e)); it changes the scaling constant and the meaning of an internal maximum, not the requested function. Never mix a base-two maximum with a natural-exponential rescaling formula. Consult the selected implementation's units before comparing internal traces.

docs.title: 5 — Derive the online recurrence, including the numerator
docs.text:
A fused forward pass need not store the full P or S matrix in global memory. For one query row, retain (m,l,z) for all keys processed so far. Initially m=-infinity, l=0, z=0. For a new block of valid keys J:

m_new = max(m, max_{j in J} s_j)

alpha = exp(m-m_new)

l_new = alpha*l + sum_{j in J} exp(s_j-m_new)

z_new = alpha*z + sum_{j in J} exp(s_j-m_new)*V[j,:].

  1. Every old contribution was scaled relative to m.
  2. The new state is scaled relative to m_new.
  3. Multiplying the old denominator and numerator by alpha converts them to that new reference.
  4. New contributions can then be added under one scale.
  5. After the final actual key block, divide z by l once to produce O.

The first nonempty block uses alpha zero explicitly in the oracle, avoiding an undefined -infinity-(-infinity) calculation. A block containing no valid keys is skipped. An entirely masked row is rejected by this oracle rather than inventing a universal GPU convention for zero outputs or LSE.

docs.title: 6 — Follow every state through two real key blocks
docs.text:
Split keys into block zero {0,1} and block one {2}. The second block is shorter; its third key is real, while nonexistent padding keys must not gain softmax weight.

Query row / block m alpha for old state l z Row 0, keys 0–1 ln(2) 0 1.5 [1,1] Row 0, key 2 ln(2) 1 2.5 [4,5] Row 1, keys 0–1 ln(2) 0 1.5 [0.5,2] Row 1, key 2 ln(2) 1 2.5 [3.5,6]

For row zero's first block, stable weights one and one-half give z=1*[1,0]+0.5*[0,2]=[1,1]. Key two contributes [3,4] at stable weight one, so the final numerator is [4,5]. Divide by 2.5 to obtain [1.6,2].

For row one, the first two stable weights are one-half and one. Its first numerator is [0.5,2]; adding key two yields [3.5,6]. Dividing by the same denominator gives [1.4,2.4]. Equal denominators do not make the two output vectors equal.

Check: the sequential trace and the materialized full-row reference agree. The CPU oracle also checks different valid partitions and traversal orders. Floating-point results need not be bit-identical under reassociation; matching within this stated tolerance is the criterion for these binary64 inputs.

docs.title: 7 — Force a maximum change so rescaling cannot be omitted
docs.text:
The previous order never increased m after the first tile. That cannot expose a missing rescale. Process row zero's key one first, then keys zero and two:

  1. Key one has score zero and V row [0,2]. State is m=0,l=1,z=[0,2].
  2. The new block has scores ln(2),ln(2), so m_new=ln(2).
  3. Old-state factor is alpha=exp(-ln(2))=1/2.
  4. Rescale old l to 0.5 and old z to [0,1].
  5. Add two new weights of one: l_new=0.5+1+1=2.5.
  6. Add new weighted vectors [1,0]+[3,4] to [0,1], producing [4,5].
  7. Final output remains [1.6,2].

If only l is rescaled, z incorrectly becomes [4,6], giving [1.6,2.4]. If neither is rescaled, l becomes three and z [4,6], giving [4/3,2]. A correct-looking component or normalized row is insufficient; check the whole vector against the independent reference.

docs.title: 8 — Define causal positions before applying a mask
docs.text:
The pinned CausalFusion::before_softmax demonstrates top-left causal alignment: a key is excluded when its logical index j exceeds query index i. For Nq=2,Nk=3, the Boolean mask is:

                key j=0  j=1  j=2
query i=0          yes    no   no
query i=1          yes   yes   no
  1. Row zero retains only key zero, so its normalized weight is one and output is [1,0].
  2. Row one retains scores [0,ln(2)], whose exponentials are [1,2].
  3. Its weights are [1/3,2/3,0] and output is [1/3,4/3].
  4. The corresponding natural-log LSE values are ln(2) and ln(3).

Mask logits before softmax: an excluded entry contributes zero weight and does not enter the row maximum or denominator. Setting an excluded logit to zero is wrong because exp(0)=1. The CPU helper represents masking with a separate Boolean allowed list while retaining finite logits; it does not accept literal infinity/NaN score inputs. Thus the mathematical negative-infinity mask and the helper's input representation are different. An entirely masked block is skipped, and an entirely masked row is rejected under its stated contract. Zero-filling an out-of-range K tile similarly does not automatically mask its score; it can create a false zero logit with positive softmax mass.

Rectangular attention makes the position convention visible. If the two queries represent the last two positions of a three-key sequence, use absolute query positions i+1. The valid test becomes j<=i+1, and the outputs are [[2/3,2/3],[1.4,2.4]]. This is a separate oracle contract, not what the pinned causal functor silently does. Its own comments explain where such an offset would be introduced. Head sharing, cached decode and unequal lengths require explicit positions and ownership, not merely causal=true.

docs.title: 9 — Separate memory offsets from score coordinates
docs.text:
A score coordinate (i,j) names a query/key pair, whereas a Q/K element coordinate names one feature. For compact row-major views use:

Q(i,c): i*d+c, K(j,c): j*d+c, V(j,v): j*dv+v, O(i,v): i*dv+v.

View coordinate Element offset FP16 byte offset, if E=2 Q(1,1) 1*2+1=3 6 K(2,1) 2*2+1=5 10 V(2,0) 2*2+0=4 8 O(1,0) 1*2+0=2 4

This byte column illustrates a hypothetical FP16 allocation; it does not claim that the CPU oracle used half storage or reproduced half rounding. With eight-byte binary64 elements, multiply the same offsets by eight instead. K's mathematical transpose in QKᵀ does not change its row-major (j,c) storage formula.

For two batches and three heads, choose illustrative mode order (sequence,feature,(batch,head)) with Q strides (d,1,(H*Nq*d,Nq*d)). At (i,c,b,h)=(1,1,1,2), offset is 1*2+1+1*12+2*4=23 elements, or 46 bytes for FP16. The last valid element occupies bytes 46–47 of the 48-byte Q allocation. K/V use Nk instead of Nq, so their batch/head strides are different.

The pinned sixteen-bit runner uses the same mode order, with StrideQ/StrideK represented as tuple<int,_1,tuple<int,int>>. Its FP8 V specialization uses a different stride pattern; do not transplant the sixteen-bit V map into the byte-element path. Supported TMA alignment and head dimensions impose additional restrictions beyond this affine address calculation.

docs.title: 10 — Map the mathematics to the pinned implementation
docs.text:
The pinned runner’s file comment describes four layers:

Layer What to locate Mathematical obligation Runner/reference Inputs, strides, checks and timing Same operation and numerical criterion Device operation Workspace and launch orchestration Correct pointers, shapes, lifetimes and completion Kernel Scheduling and roles Complete query/output coverage Collectives QK, softmax state, PV and epilogue Correct reductions, rescaling and output

A small type excerpt from the actual forward runner exposes the construction boundary:

// Excerpt: aliases/headers/template parameters come from the complete runner.
using Operation = cutlass::device::Universal<
    typename cutlass::fmha::kernel::FmhaBuilder<
        Element,
        ElementAccumulatorQK,
        ElementAccumulatorPV,
        TileShape,
        StrideQ,
        StrideK,
        StrideV,
        ActiveFusion,
        DispatchPolicy,
        KernelOptions...>::Kernel>;

This is not an ordinary GEMM builder with a different activation tag. Softmax is between two matrix products, and both row statistics and output numerators persist across key tiles. The implementation uses FMHA-specific collective/kernel/device components. The runner's problem tuple is (B,H,Q,K,D); Q and K in that tuple are sequence lengths, not tensor pointers. Compare the tuple with the data and stride arguments before constructing a launch.

The pinned README lists forward FP16/BF16 head dimensions 32,64,128,256 and FP8 dimensions 128,256; backward is separately FP16 with dimensions 32,64,128. These are advertised example paths, not proof of all arbitrary shapes, masks and strides. The toy d=2 belongs only to this mathematical chapter. A successful address calculation is not a supported launch.

The customization hook before_softmax receives score accumulators and their logical positions. ResidualFusion masks keys beyond Nk; CausalFusion applies the demonstrated causal comparison. Inspect the selected fusion's complete behavior rather than assuming every mask automatically combines every kind of tail. A real ragged causal configuration must be checked against its exact specialization and reference.

docs.title: 11 — Keep intermediate lifetime and arithmetic separate
docs.text:
A fused implementation still needs Q/K/V delivery, safe buffer reuse, complete WGMMA participation and valid output stores. The online recurrence proves how to combine mathematical contributions; it does not establish TMA arrival or asynchronous-reader completion. Conversely, correct barriers do not repair a wrong rescaling formula.

Map one physical stage to its logical key interval. Record when K/V become ready, which query rows consume them, when asynchronous readers finish, and which producer may next overwrite the stage. A probability fragment may be converted before PV; that conversion changes numerical error even if the state recurrence is algebraically correct. Match the reference to the selected accumulator/conversion policy.

Avoid claiming that streaming attention reads each input from HBM exactly once. Query tiling, cache residency and schedule affect requested and physical traffic. The important storage difference is that a full Nq×Nk score/probability matrix need not be materialized in global memory. Benchmark only after specifying dtype, mask, lengths, heads, position alignment, work count and useful-result boundary.

docs.title: 13 — Exercises with worked answers
docs.text:
The complete runnable versions follow these exercises: CUDA reference and Python reference.

Exercise 1: move one V row

Keep Q/K unchanged, but replace key two's V row by [0,0]. What are the noncausal outputs?

Answer: The probabilities stay unchanged. Row zero becomes [2/5,2/5]; row one becomes [1/5,4/5]. Masking key two instead would change the denominator and is a different operation.

Exercise 2: identify a bad mask

At causal query zero, an implementation replaces excluded scores by zero. What does it compute?

Answer: Its exponentials are [2,1,1], so probabilities are [1/2,1/4,1/4]. Output becomes [1.25,1.5], rather than [1,0]. Excluded entries must contribute no softmax mass.

Exercise 3: why save two row statistics?

Can a streaming implementation retain only l and omit m?

Answer: Not with this recurrence and arbitrary logits. l is defined relative to m. A new maximum changes that reference and requires alpha to rescale old l and z. Another algorithm could store other equivalent information, but it still needs a well-defined stable representation.

Exercise 4: count full-matrix storage

A separate example has Nq=Nk=1024 and materializes both S and P in FP32. How many bytes do just those two matrices occupy per head?

Answer: 2*1024*1024*4=8388608 bytes, or 8 MiB. This excludes Q/K/V/O, temporary storage, extra heads/batches and allocator overhead. Avoiding that materialization is not a claim that all other memory traffic disappears.

docs.title: 14 — Complete runnable CUDA reference
docs.text:
Download attention_online.cu.

This complete program implements the chapter's online recurrence with one CUDA thread per query row. It owns m, l and the numerator vector locally, skips excluded keys before updating any statistic, and writes O and natural-log LSE. A separate CPU implementation materializes a score row in binary64 and checks every result using the actual FP32 inputs; the small worked cases also check their closed-form results. No external CUDA helpers or CUTLASS headers are required.

This is a correctness-oriented SIMT reference, not a high-performance FlashAttention-3 or Tensor Core kernel. It deliberately supports the chapter's d=2 case. Q/K/V/O use separate, packed row-major allocations; d and dv may differ. The bounded contract is 1<=Nq,Nk<=1024, 1<=d<=64, 1<=dv<=16, query offset 0–1024, and finite input magnitudes at most eight. With positive key length and nonnegative causal offset, every query has at least key zero available. Dropout, finite bias, arbitrary strides, multiple heads and fully masked rows are outside this small program's interface.

From the repository root on Hopper:

nvcc -std=c++17 -O2 -arch=sm_90a \
  docs/examples/attention/attention_online.cu -o attention_online
./attention_online
compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --error-exitcode 3 ./attention_online

The tests cover the worked noncausal case, top-left causal alignment, offset-one alignment, reordered keys/values that force a maximum update, and three nonuniform rectangular cases with Nq=17, Nk=23, d=8 and dv=5. The last shapes also exercise a partial CUDA block. Every O and LSE value must be finite and satisfy abs(error)<=1e-4+1e-4*abs(reference); initialization uses NaN sentinels so an unwritten output cannot pass. Those thresholds are the acceptance criteria for the seven recorded cases, not a proven error bound for every input in the permitted range or every attention datatype/distribution.

Inside online_row, read the operations in the same order as Sections 5–7: compute and scale one score, find next_m, rescale both l and z, add the new weighted value, then update m. The final division happens after all valid keys. This CUDA implementation treats each key as a singleton block; the Python walkthrough groups keys into larger blocks for its printed trace. Their intermediate states therefore need not appear at the same iteration boundaries. The CUDA host reference starts from the actual rounded FP32 Q/K/V values, while the Python mathematical example constructs its constants in binary64; compare each program against its stated reference and tolerance. The GPU reference does not allocate the full Nq-by-Nk score/probability matrix; reusing K/V across different query threads can still generate repeated memory traffic.

// Educational FP32 online attention: one CUDA thread per query row.
// No CUTLASS, Tensor Cores, dropout, bias or performance claim.
// CPU-only check: clang++ -x c++ -std=c++17 -O2  (continued)
//   -DATTENTION_HOST_ONLY attention_online.cu -o attention_host
// Hopper: nvcc -std=c++17 -O2 -arch=sm_90a attention_online.cu -o attention_online
#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#ifndef ATTENTION_HOST_ONLY
#include <cuda_runtime.h>
#define ATTENTION_HD __host__ __device__
#else
#define ATTENTION_HD
#endif

constexpr int MAX_DV = 16;

struct Shape {
    int nq, nk, d, dv;
    bool causal;
    int query_offset;
};

// Q/K/V/O are packed row-major float arrays. Each row owns its z/l/m state.
ATTENTION_HD void online_row(const float* q,
                             const float* k,
                             const float* v,
                             float* out,
                             float* lse,
                             Shape s,
                             int i) {
    float m = -INFINITY, l = 0.0f;
    float z[MAX_DV] = {};
    const float scale = 1.0f / sqrtf(static_cast<float>(s.d));
    for (int j = 0; j < s.nk; ++j) {
        if (s.causal && j > i + s.query_offset)
            continue;
        float score = 0.0f;
        for (int c = 0; c < s.d; ++c)
            score += q[i * s.d + c] * k[j * s.d + c];
        score *= scale;
        const float next_m = fmaxf(m, score);
        const float alpha = l == 0.0f ? 0.0f : expf(m - next_m);
        const float weight = expf(score - next_m);
        l = alpha * l + weight;
        for (int c = 0; c < s.dv; ++c)
            z[c] = alpha * z[c] + weight * v[j * s.dv + c];
        m = next_m;
    }
    for (int c = 0; c < s.dv; ++c)
        out[i * s.dv + c] = l > 0.0f ? z[c] / l : NAN;
    lse[i] = l > 0.0f ? m + logf(l) : NAN;
}

#ifndef ATTENTION_HOST_ONLY
__global__ void attention_kernel(const float* q,
                                 const float* k,
                                 const float* v,
                                 float* out,
                                 float* lse,
                                 Shape s) {
    const int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i < s.nq)
        online_row(q, k, v, out, lse, s, i);
}

void check_cuda(cudaError_t status) {
    if (status != cudaSuccess)
        throw std::runtime_error(cudaGetErrorString(status));
}

struct DeviceBuffer {
    float* data = nullptr;

    explicit DeviceBuffer(size_t count) {
        check_cuda(cudaMalloc(reinterpret_cast<void**>(&data),
                              count * sizeof(float)));
    }

    DeviceBuffer(const DeviceBuffer&) = delete;
    DeviceBuffer& operator=(const DeviceBuffer&) = delete;

    ~DeviceBuffer() {
        if (data)
            cudaFree(data);
    }

    void release() {
        float* allocation = data;
        data = nullptr;
        check_cuda(cudaFree(allocation));
    }
};
#endif

void validate(const Shape& s,
              const std::vector<float>& q,
              const std::vector<float>& k,
              const std::vector<float>& v) {
    if (s.nq < 1 || s.nq > 1024 || s.nk < 1 || s.nk > 1024 ||
        s.d < 1 || s.d > 64 || s.dv < 1 || s.dv > MAX_DV ||
        s.query_offset < 0 || s.query_offset > 1024 ||
        q.size() != size_t(s.nq * s.d) ||
        k.size() != size_t(s.nk * s.d) ||
        v.size() != size_t(s.nk * s.dv))
        throw std::invalid_argument(
            "Unsupported shape, offset or storage extent");
    for (const auto* input : {&q, &k, &v})
        for (float x : *input)
            if (!std::isfinite(x) || std::fabs(x) > 8.0f)
                throw std::invalid_argument(
                    "Inputs must be finite with |x| <= 8");
}

// Independent materialized binary64 reference from the ACTUAL float inputs.
void reference(const Shape& s,
               const std::vector<float>& q,
               const std::vector<float>& k,
               const std::vector<float>& v,
               std::vector<double>& out,
               std::vector<double>& lse) {
    for (int i = 0; i < s.nq; ++i) {
        std::vector<double> scores(s.nk, -INFINITY);
        double m = -INFINITY;
        for (int j = 0; j < s.nk; ++j) {
            if (s.causal && j > i + s.query_offset)
                continue;
            double dot = 0;
            for (int c = 0; c < s.d; ++c)
                dot += double(q[i * s.d + c]) * k[j * s.d + c];
            scores[j] = dot / std::sqrt(double(s.d));
            m = std::max(m, scores[j]);
        }
        double sum = 0;
        for (double& score : scores) {
            score = std::exp(score - m);
            sum += score;
        }
        for (int c = 0; c < s.dv; ++c) {
            double value = 0;
            for (int j = 0; j < s.nk; ++j)
                value += (scores[j] / sum) * v[j * s.dv + c];
            out[i * s.dv + c] = value;
        }
        lse[i] = m + std::log(sum);
    }
}

void compare(const std::vector<float>& actual,
             const std::vector<double>& expected,
             const char* label) {
    if (actual.size() != expected.size())
        throw std::runtime_error("Result size mismatch");
    for (size_t i = 0; i < actual.size(); ++i) {
        const double tolerance =
            1e-4 + 1e-4 * std::fabs(expected[i]);
        if (!std::isfinite(actual[i]) ||
            !std::isfinite(expected[i]) ||
            std::fabs(double(actual[i]) - expected[i]) > tolerance)
            throw std::runtime_error(std::string(label) +
                                     " mismatch at " +
                                     std::to_string(i));
    }
}

void run_case(const char* name,
              Shape s,
              std::vector<float> q,
              std::vector<float> k,
              std::vector<float> v) {
    validate(s, q, k, v);
    std::vector<float> out(s.nq * s.dv, NAN), lse(s.nq, NAN);
    std::vector<double> expected(out.size()),
        expected_lse(lse.size());
    reference(s, q, k, v, expected, expected_lse);
#ifdef ATTENTION_HOST_ONLY
    // Executes the shared FP32 row function on the CPU; not a CUDA run.
    for (int i = 0; i < s.nq; ++i)
        online_row(q.data(),
                   k.data(),
                   v.data(),
                   out.data(),
                   lse.data(),
                   s,
                   i);
#else
    DeviceBuffer dq(q.size()), dk(k.size()), dv(v.size());
    DeviceBuffer dout(out.size()), dlse(lse.size());
    check_cuda(cudaMemcpy(dq.data,
                          q.data(),
                          q.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    check_cuda(cudaMemcpy(dk.data,
                          k.data(),
                          k.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    check_cuda(cudaMemcpy(dv.data,
                          v.data(),
                          v.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
    check_cuda(
        cudaMemset(dout.data, 0xff, out.size() * sizeof(float)));
    check_cuda(
        cudaMemset(dlse.data, 0xff, lse.size() * sizeof(float)));
    attention_kernel<<<(s.nq + 127) / 128, 128>>>(
        dq.data, dk.data, dv.data, dout.data, dlse.data, s);
    check_cuda(cudaGetLastError());
    check_cuda(cudaDeviceSynchronize());
    check_cuda(cudaMemcpy(out.data(),
                          dout.data,
                          out.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    check_cuda(cudaMemcpy(lse.data(),
                          dlse.data,
                          lse.size() * sizeof(float),
                          cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));
    dq.release();
    dk.release();
    dv.release();
    dout.release();
    dlse.release();
#endif
    compare(out, expected, "O");
    compare(lse, expected_lse, "LSE");
    if (std::string(name) == "worked-full" ||
        std::string(name) == "worked-reordered") {
        compare(out, {1.6, 2.0, 1.4, 2.4}, "Closed-form O");
        compare(
            lse, {std::log(5.0), std::log(5.0)}, "Closed-form LSE");
    } else if (std::string(name) == "worked-causal") {
        compare(
            out, {1.0, 0.0, 1.0 / 3.0, 4.0 / 3.0}, "Closed-form O");
        compare(
            lse, {std::log(2.0), std::log(3.0)}, "Closed-form LSE");
    } else if (std::string(name) == "worked-offset-1") {
        compare(
            out, {2.0 / 3.0, 2.0 / 3.0, 1.4, 2.4}, "Closed-form O");
        compare(
            lse, {std::log(3.0), std::log(5.0)}, "Closed-form LSE");
    }
    std::printf(
        "PASS %s: all %zu O values and %zu LSE values checked; first O=[",
        name,
        out.size(),
        lse.size());
    for (int c = 0; c < std::min(s.dv, 2); ++c)
        std::printf("%s%.7g", c ? ", " : "", out[c]);
    std::puts("]");
}

int main() {
    try {
#ifndef ATTENTION_HOST_ONLY
        int count = 0;
        const cudaError_t status = cudaGetDeviceCount(&count);
        if (status != cudaSuccess || count == 0) {
            std::fprintf(stderr,
                         "BLOCKED: CUDA device unavailable (%s)\n",
                         cudaGetErrorString(status));
            return 2;
        }
        check_cuda(cudaSetDevice(0));
#endif
        const float a = std::sqrt(2.0f) * std::log(2.0f);
        const std::vector<float> q = {a, 0, 0, a};
        const std::vector<float> k = {1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1};
        const std::vector<float> v = {1, 0, 0, 2, 3, 4};
        run_case("worked-full", {2, 3, 2, 2, false, 0}, q, k, v);
        run_case("worked-causal", {2, 3, 2, 2, true, 0}, q, k, v);
        run_case("worked-offset-1", {2, 3, 2, 2, true, 1}, q, k, v);
        run_case("worked-reordered",
                 {2, 3, 2, 2, false, 0},
                 q,
                 {0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1},
                 {0, 2, 1, 0, 3, 4});
        Shape s{17, 23, 8, 5, false, 0};
        std::vector<float> q2(s.nq * s.d), k2(s.nk * s.d),
            v2(s.nk * s.dv);
        for (size_t i = 0; i < q2.size(); ++i)
            q2[i] = (int(i * 7 % 19) - 9) * 0.03125f;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < k2.size(); ++i)
            k2[i] = (int(i * 3 % 17) - 8) * 0.0625f;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < v2.size(); ++i)
            v2[i] = (int(i * 5 % 23) - 11) * 0.0625f;
        run_case("rectangular-full", s, q2, k2, v2);
        s.causal = true;
        run_case("rectangular-causal", s, q2, k2, v2);
        s.query_offset = 1;
        run_case("rectangular-offset-1", s, q2, k2, v2);
#ifdef ATTENTION_HOST_ONLY
        std::puts(
            "HOST ROW CHECK PASS: shared FP32 arithmetic versus binary64 reference; CUDA compilation/execution not performed.");
#else
        std::puts(
            "CUDA ATTENTION PASS: seven cases; complete O/LSE checks; no performance claim.");
#endif
        return 0;
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::fprintf(stderr, "FAIL: %s\n", e.what());
        return 1;
    }
}

docs.title: 15 — Complete runnable Python reference
docs.text:
Download attention_walkthrough.py. This is the full program used by the dated mathematical checks in Section 12. It runs with Python's standard library and prints each online state; no GPU or Python CUDA package is needed.

python3 docs/examples/advanced/attention_walkthrough.py

The input mask is the Boolean allowed list described in Section 8. Keep logits finite; represent excluded positions through the mask instead of passing literal negative infinity into this helper. Its all-masked-row rejection is intentional. Compare its binary64 arithmetic with the GPU reference's FP32 arithmetic rather than expecting identical last bits.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""CPU binary64 attention/online-softmax oracle, not a CUTLASS/GPU execution.

The tiny d=2 example is mathematical; pinned Hopper FMHA kernels require their
supported larger head dimensions, datatype/stride and launch contracts.
"""
import math


def require(condition, message):
    if not condition:
        raise ValueError(message)


def check_close(actual, expected):
    if isinstance(expected, (list, tuple)):
        require(len(actual) == len(expected), 'Result shape mismatch')
        for a, e in zip(actual, expected):
            check_close(a, e)
    elif not math.isfinite(actual) or not math.isclose(actual, expected,
                                                     rel_tol=1e-12, abs_tol=1e-12):
        raise AssertionError(f'{actual!r} != {expected!r}')


def score_rows(q, k):
    require(q and k and q[0], 'Nonempty Q/K required')
    d = len(q[0])
    require(all(len(row) == d for row in q + k), 'Q/K head dimension mismatch')
    require(all(math.isfinite(x) for row in q + k for x in row), 'Finite inputs required')
    scale = 1.0 / math.sqrt(d)
    return [[math.fsum(x * y for x, y in zip(qi, kj)) * scale for kj in k]
            for qi in q]


def reference_row(logits, values, allowed):
    """Materialized stable row reference; all-masked rows are explicitly rejected."""
    keys = [j for j, valid in enumerate(allowed) if valid]
    require(keys, 'All-masked row is outside this oracle contract')
    maximum = max(logits[j] for j in keys)
    weights = [math.exp(logits[j] - maximum) if allowed[j] else 0.0
               for j in range(len(logits))]
    denominator = math.fsum(weights)
    probabilities = [p / denominator for p in weights]
    output = [math.fsum(p * v[c] for p, v in zip(probabilities, values))
              for c in range(len(values[0]))]
    return output, maximum + math.log(denominator), probabilities


def online_row(logits, values, blocks, allowed=None):
    """Return output, natural-log LSE and every block's (m,l,z,alpha) state."""
    count = len(logits)
    require(count > 0 and len(values) == count and values[0], 'Nonempty matching K/V required')
    width = len(values[0])
    require(all(len(v) == width for v in values), 'Ragged V rows')
    require(all(math.isfinite(x) for x in logits), 'Finite unmasked score inputs required')
    require(all(math.isfinite(x) for v in values for x in v), 'Finite V required')
    allowed = list(allowed) if allowed is not None else [True] * count
    require(len(allowed) == count, 'Mask width mismatch')
    flat = [j for block in blocks for j in block]
    require(sorted(flat) == list(range(count)), 'Blocks must cover each key exactly once')
    maximum, denominator, numerator = -math.inf, 0.0, [0.0] * width
    trace = []
    for block in blocks:
        valid = [j for j in block if allowed[j]]
        if not valid:
            trace.append(dict(keys=list(block), skipped=True, m=maximum,
                              l=denominator, z=numerator[:], alpha=None))
            continue
        new_maximum = max(maximum, max(logits[j] for j in valid))
        alpha = 0.0 if maximum == -math.inf else math.exp(maximum - new_maximum)
        weights = [(j, math.exp(logits[j] - new_maximum)) for j in valid]
        denominator = alpha * denominator + math.fsum(p for _, p in weights)
        numerator = [alpha * numerator[c] + math.fsum(p * values[j][c] for j, p in weights)
                     for c in range(width)]
        maximum = new_maximum
        trace.append(dict(keys=list(block), skipped=False, m=maximum,
                          l=denominator, z=numerator[:], alpha=alpha))
    require(denominator > 0.0, 'All-masked row is outside this oracle contract')
    return [z / denominator for z in numerator], maximum + math.log(denominator), trace


def evaluate(q, k, v, causal=False, query_offset=0, blocks=None):
    logits = score_rows(q, k)
    require(len(k) == len(v), 'K/V sequence mismatch')
    require(isinstance(query_offset, int) and query_offset >= 0, 'Nonnegative position offset required')
    blocks = blocks if blocks is not None else [list(range(0, min(2, len(k)))), list(range(2, len(k)))]
    outputs, traces = [], []
    for i, row in enumerate(logits):
        allowed = [not causal or j <= i + query_offset for j in range(len(k))]
        reference, ref_lse, probabilities = reference_row(row, v, allowed)
        output, lse, trace = online_row(row, v, blocks, allowed)
        check_close(output, reference)
        check_close(lse, ref_lse)
        check_close(math.fsum(probabilities), 1.0)
        outputs.append(output)
        traces.append(trace)
    return outputs, traces


def pretty(values):
    return '[' + ', '.join(f'{x:.12g}' for x in values) + ']'


def main():
    ln2 = math.log(2.0)
    q = [[math.sqrt(2.0) * ln2, 0.0], [0.0, math.sqrt(2.0) * ln2]]
    k = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]]
    v = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]
    scores = score_rows(q, k)
    check_close(scores, [[ln2, 0.0, ln2], [0.0, ln2, ln2]])
    full, traces = evaluate(q, k, v)
    check_close(full, [[1.6, 2.0], [1.4, 2.4]])
    print('NONCAUSAL O:', '; '.join(pretty(row) for row in full))
    for i, trace in enumerate(traces):
        for step, state in enumerate(trace):
            print(f'ROW {i} BLOCK {step} keys={state["keys"]}: '
                  f'm={state["m"]:.12g} alpha={state["alpha"]:.12g} '
                  f'l={state["l"]:.12g} z={pretty(state["z"])}')
    causal, _ = evaluate(q, k, v, causal=True)
    check_close(causal, [[1.0, 0.0], [1.0 / 3, 4.0 / 3]])
    print('TOP-LEFT CAUSAL O:', '; '.join(pretty(row) for row in causal))
    shifted, _ = evaluate(q, k, v, causal=True, query_offset=1)
    check_close(shifted, [[2.0 / 3, 2.0 / 3], [1.4, 2.4]])
    print('OFFSET-1 CAUSAL O:', '; '.join(pretty(row) for row in shifted))
    # A new maximum must rescale the old numerator AND denominator.
    reordered, reordered_trace = evaluate(q, k, v, blocks=[[1], [0, 2]])
    check_close(reordered, full)
    check_close(reordered_trace[0][1]['alpha'], 0.5)
    print('RESCALE row0:', f'alpha={reordered_trace[0][1]["alpha"]:.12g}',
          f'l={reordered_trace[0][1]["l"]:.12g}',
          f'z={pretty(reordered_trace[0][1]["z"])}')
    for blocks in [[[0], [1], [2]], [[2, 0], [1]], [[0, 1, 2]], [[2], [1], [0]]]:
        check_close(evaluate(q, k, v, blocks=blocks)[0], full)
    for row in scores:
        shifted_logits = [x + 1000.0 for x in row]
        check_close(online_row(shifted_logits, v, [[0, 1], [2]])[0],
                    reference_row(row, v, [True] * 3)[0])
    # An initially empty masked tile is skipped, not exp(-inf - -inf).
    check_close(online_row(scores[0], v, [[2], [0, 1]], [True, False, False])[0], [1, 0])
    for operation in [lambda: online_row(scores[0], v, [[0, 1], [1, 2]]),
                      lambda: online_row(scores[0], v, [[0, 1], [2]], [False] * 3)]:
        try:
            operation()
        except ValueError:
            pass
        else:
            raise AssertionError('Invalid contract accepted')
    print('PASS: materialized/online references; causal positions; rescaling; partitions; shift stability; masked/invalid diagnostics')
    print('ATTENTION WALKTHROUGH PASS: CPU binary64 mathematics; no CUTLASS compilation or GPU execution')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Define the Q/K and P/V reduction axes, positions, mask and conversion policy before choosing an FMHA kernel.
  • Online attention carries a row maximum, scalar denominator and vector numerator. A new maximum rescales both accumulated quantities; mask before contributing to any statistic.
  • Layouts map feature coordinates to storage independently of score coordinates. A logical transpose, valid address map or tiny correct equation does not establish a supported Hopper launch.
  • The CPU oracle checks the mathematics, and the standalone CUDA reference passed seven H100 cases against its binary64 reference plus memcheck. Continue to the optimized pinned implementation and its separate forward/backward record in Chapter 31.

docs.title: Chapter 31: Building Fused Attention with CUTLASS on Hopper
From two GEMMs to a complete attention kernel
docs.text:
Goal and prerequisites

Connect Chapter 30's online-softmax arithmetic to a complete, pinned NVIDIA implementation. You will trace tensor layouts, TMA loads, WGMMA consumers, normalization, output/LSE stores and the verification boundary. Read tensor views, copy ownership, MMA fragments and pipeline lifetimes first; this chapter uses their objects rather than replacing them with pseudocode.

The implementation is CUTLASS v4.3.6 example 88, pinned to commit 1afc6d355b8cb992398f17beb4425702f1d57ddd. It supplies forward and backward FMHA implementations. The lab below starts with FP16 forward and can additionally collect two FP16 backward cases. This is an official CUTLASS C++ implementation using CuTe; it is neither a Triton kernel nor the separate FlashAttention-3 software package. The upstream README relates its design to the FlashAttention-3 paper, while explicitly qualifying backward performance.

H100 validation complete: the pinned FP16 target compiled and passed six forward cases and two backward cases, covering all 17 expected verified variant results. D=64 forward/backward memchecks also reported zero errors. The dated record below is separate from the earlier workshop and identifies the exact sources, system, commands and outputs. It does not establish performance or correctness for untested extensions.

Jump to the complete CUDA listing · Download .cu · Download source and local headers.

The plain-TMA variants use KernelTma in kernel/fmha_kernel_tma.hpp and collective/fmha_collective_tma.hpp; they are distinct from the warp-specialized TMA path. Trace the exact printed variant before selecting a source file.

docs.title: 31.1 Establish the shape and storage contract
docs.text:
For each batch/head, attention computes O = softmax(Q*K^T / sqrt(D) + mask)*V. Here Q has Q rows and D columns, K/V have K rows and D columns, and O has Q rows and D columns. The identifier K therefore denotes the key sequence length here; it is not the reduction dimension of the first GEMM, which is D.

The runner's problem tuple is (B,H,Q,K,D). Its CuTe tensor views group batch/head into a hierarchical third mode: Q/O use (Q,D,(B,H)), K/V use (K,D,(B,H)). In the default FP16 executable, the head element is contiguous. For Q/O, the initialized stride is (D,1,(H*Q*D,Q*D)) when D is already aligned. Allocation code rounds storage D upward to a multiple of eight; the lab uses D in {32,64,128,256} so this padding does not obscure the example.

Take B=1,H=2,Q=K=128,D=64:

  1. Q, K and V each hold 1*2*128*64=16384 half elements: 32768 bytes each. O has the same count and storage width.
  2. Q coordinate (query=3,head_element=5,batch=0,head=1) maps to element offset 3*64+5+1*(128*64)=8389, or byte offset 16778. This is an address calculation, not a score value.
  3. LSE has one FP32 value per query/head: 1*2*128=256 values, 1024 bytes, with view (Q,(B,H)). It records the natural-log normalizer log(sum_j exp(score_ij)) under the applied mask.
  4. A hypothetical global FP32 score array would contain B*H*Q*K=32768 values, or 131072 bytes. The fused kernel avoids materializing that full global intermediate. This is not the total memory footprint: inputs, outputs, reference allocations, shared memory, registers and any workspace remain real resources.

Check: reconstruct an address using the actual strides before changing layout. The FP8 target uses a different V stride orientation; copying these FP16 stride assumptions into FP8 is incorrect. Although the README describes broader FP16/BF16 building-block support, the default runner explicitly selects cutlass::half_t; it has no BF16 command-line switch.

Exercise: double the number of heads

Keep all other values fixed and set H=4. What happens to Q and LSE storage?

Worked answer: Q becomes 65536 bytes; LSE becomes 2048 bytes. A single query's softmax still ranges over 128 keys, not over all four heads.

docs.title: Share KV heads without aliasing query outputs
docs.text:
The pinned README explains that MHA, grouped-query attention (GQA) and multi-query attention (MQA) can be expressed through different tensor views. That does not make them command-line modes of the default runner. The collected baseline remains FP16 ordinary MHA; it has no GQA, MQA or BF16 CLI switch.

As a mathematical storage exercise, choose four query heads and two KV heads, with group size Hq/Hkv=2. Query head h reads KV head floor(h/2):

Query head h 0 1 2 3 KV head 0 0 1 1
  1. Q and O still have four distinct head outputs. Softmax is computed separately for each query head using its own Q values; sharing K/V does not average those queries together.
  2. For Nq=2,Nk=3,D=4, hypothetical packed FP16 Q uses 4*2*4*2=64 bytes. K and V each use 2*3*4*2=48 bytes, rather than the 96 bytes each needed for four independently stored KV heads.
  3. Write the K offset in half elements as floor(h/2)*(Nk*D)+j*D+c. At key j=2 and feature c=1, query heads 0 and 1 both read offset nine (byte 18); heads 2 and 3 both read offset 21 (byte 42). This is intentional read sharing.
  4. Output storage must retain the query-head identity. Reusing the shared-KV head index for O would cause two different query heads to overwrite the same output. Training also requires the appropriate accumulation of gradient contributions into shared K/V heads.
  5. MQA is the limiting one-KV-head case: all four queries read KV head zero. With the same Nk/D/type, each K or V allocation becomes 24 bytes; Q/O still retain four query heads.

CuTe can represent the duplicated read view through hierarchical/broadcast layout modes. For a compact head mode (2,2), CuTe linearizes its first coordinate fastest: stride (0,12) produces offsets [0,0,12,12], matching floor(h/2)*12. Stride (12,0) instead produces [0,12,0,12], an interleaved grouping. A reordered query-head view can use that ordering, but its consumers must agree. The exact head ordering, strides, query-to-KV grouping and derivative contract must agree between loader, reference and consumers. The offset formula above is a paper contract, not an implemented or executed GQA extension of this lab. Changing only H in the existing runner changes its MHA head count; it does not enable KV sharing.

docs.title: 31.2 Read the source in dependency order
docs.text:
Use the pinned runner as the entry point, then follow this map:

Layer Source/object to inspect Question it answers Host runner Options, FwdRunner, run_fwd_64 Which shapes, strides, datatype and kernel variants are instantiated? Device adapter device/device_universal.hpp How are support checks, workspace, initialization and launch connected? Kernel builder kernel/fmha_kernel_builder.hpp, FmhaBuilder Which mainloop, epilogue and kernel match the dispatch policy? Kernel orchestration kernel/fmha_kernel_tma_warpspecialized.hpp Which participants load, compute and retire work? Load/mainloop collective/fmha_collective_load.hpp, fmha_collective_tma_warpspecialized.hpp How do TMA stages feed the two matrix products? Softmax/fusion fmha_collective_softmax.hpp, fmha_fusion.hpp Which rows are reduced, rescaled and masked? Final stores collective/fmha_epilogue.hpp Which participants store O and one LSE per query?

For D=64, the default executable instantiates three variants: TMA 64x128x64, cooperative 128x64x64, and ping-pong 128x64x64. These triples mean (query tile,key tile,head tile). They do not mean (B,H,D) or three different requested attention problems. The first query tile of a 128x64x64 variant covers queries 0–127; with K=128 it consumes two 64-key blocks. At B=1,H=2, both heads require their own computation and outputs.

The lifecycle is the familiar CUTLASS pattern: construct arguments containing pointers/strides and hardware information, request workspace, call can_implement, initialize, launch, then wait before validation. Do not skip support checking merely because D appears in the README. A listed head size does not promise arbitrary user pointers, strides, masks or resource settings are valid.

docs.title: 31.3 Follow one query tile through the fused mainloop
docs.text:
The warp-specialized mainloop uses PipelineTmaAsync stage state for Q and K/V storage. Its CollectiveLoadTma helpers build global views from TMA descriptors and the current tile coordinates. This turns the preceding CuTe layout lessons into actual copy ownership.

  1. Acquire storage and load operands. A producer must acquire a reusable stage before issuing its TMA transaction. Consumers wait for that generation's completion. The Q tile supplies a block of queries; the K tile supplies a block of keys. Reusing a physical stage does not mean its previous generation is finished automatically.
  2. Form QK accumulators. WGMMA computes dot products with FP32 QK accumulation in the default FP16 runner. Accumulator fragments are distributed among participating threads. Their logical query/key coordinates, not register order, determine mask and row-reduction semantics.
  3. Apply fusion and update row state. before_softmax can change scores using those coordinates. Softmax maintains row maxima and denominator state. When a later key block raises the maximum, both the old denominator and old PV accumulator must be rescaled. The implementation uses base-two exponential instructions with a converted scale_softmax_log2; this implements the same mathematical exponential as Chapter 30, subject to its numerical approximation and precision choices.
  4. Multiply probabilities by V. The second matrix product accumulates weighted value vectors. It shares the key-block progression with QK, but has different operand roles and fragment layouts. A QK fragment cannot be treated as an arbitrary row-major matrix without the associated CuTe mapping/conversion.
  5. Normalize and store. The softmax finalization normalizes the accumulated output and produces LSE. FmhaFwdEpilogue uses the output partition/store path for O and the corresponding row ownership for LSE. Storing a row statistic from every lane would create redundant or conflicting writers; the code selects the appropriate participants.

Keep the implementation's maximum in its actual units. Chapter 30 defines mathematical scores s=raw_QK/sqrt(D) and tracks their maximum m. In the pinned default FP16 collective, s_max instead retains the unscaled QK maximum. The rescale is exp2((old_s_max-new_s_max)*scale_softmax_log2), where scale_softmax_log2=log2(e)/sqrt(D). Final natural-log LSE is s_max*scale_softmax+log(sum), with scale_softmax=1/sqrt(D). These are equivalent conventions when used consistently; copying only m+log(l) with an unscaled s_max is wrong.

The before_softmax hook receives those raw QK accumulators. Zero/minus-infinity masking is invariant under the positive scale, but a finite additive bias is not. At D=64, scale is 1/8: a desired bias of two after scaling would require raw bias 16 if inserted before that scaling, or application at an appropriate later stage. Dropout, finite bias and absolute causal positions each change the operation contract; this baseline does not enable a dropout mask or implement such extensions automatically.

Expected check: every logical output coordinate and its row's LSE correspond to the same query/head. A correct-looking O with a misplaced LSE can break backward even when a forward-only application never reads LSE. Pipeline stage release must follow the last operand consumer, not simply TMA issue or QK issue. The chapter explains dependencies; the figure is not a measured overlap timeline.

docs.title: 31.4 Specify masks before testing tails or decoding
docs.text:
The pinned CausalFusion masks a score when query index < key index. This is a top-left causal convention. With Q=2,K=3, allowed key sets are {0} and {0,1}. An incremental-decode interpretation placing these queries at the end of a three-token context instead needs an offset: allowed sets {0,1} and {0,1,2}. The source comments discuss this distinction; --mask=causal does not apply the offset automatically.

ResidualFusion is a separate noncausal key-boundary mask. TMA zero padding is not equivalent to a softmax mask: a padded zero score has exponential one and can change the denominator. DefaultFusion does not exclude such scores, and CausalFusion is not a composition with ResidualFusion. Therefore this lab uses aligned sequence lengths for full and causal runs. It makes no blanket claim that arbitrary unequal/ragged Q/K combinations work just because allocations are padded. A later tail test must choose a supported residual-mask path, verify its precise boundary behavior and check O and LSE; it is separate from these baseline cases.

All-masked rows require an explicit application contract. Do not infer one from the usual nonempty softmax formula. The pinned implementation has its own zero/NaN-denominator handling; the CPU arithmetic lesson rejects undefined all-masked cases instead of silently declaring them equivalent.

Exercise: locate the two queries in a three-key context

Q=2,K=3. Which keys can query row zero attend under the pinned top-left mask, and under an explicit query offset of one?

Worked answer: top-left permits only key 0. With offset one, the query is at absolute position 1 and may use keys 0 and 1. Changing the offset changes the operation, not just a memory address; compare against the matching reference.

docs.title: 31.5 Build exactly the intended executable
docs.text:
Follow Getting Started for a compatible driver, CUDA toolkit and host compiler. This additional CMake lab also needs CMake; on the supported Ubuntu host:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install --no-install-recommends cmake
bash tools/fetch_cutlass.sh /tmp/cutlass-attention-v436
python3 tools/run_cutlass_attention.py --cutlass /tmp/cutlass-attention-v436 \
  --output artifacts/attention-hopper-01

The last command prints a plan, including the pin, source/collector hashes and commands. It creates no execution evidence and launches no GPU work. The pinned source has a CUDA 12.0 minimum guard; this book's established Hopper toolchain is CUDA 12.8.93. Compile for 90a, as the implementation uses architecture-specific SM90a paths. An A100, or a Blackwell device accepting some Hopper-compatible code, does not satisfy this example's exact runtime guard: it specifically checks compute capability 9.0.

To collect the separate GPU record on a suitable Hopper host:

python3 tools/run_cutlass_attention.py --cutlass /tmp/cutlass-attention-v436 \
  --output artifacts/attention-hopper-01 --execute

The collector archives the exact Git commit into a new evidence directory, hashes its source files, captures tool/system information, configures CMake with CUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS=90a, and builds only target 88_hopper_fmha. The separate target 88_hopper_fmha_fp8 defines FP8; this collector does not build or validate it. The official CMake recipe adds --use_fast_math on its supported non-Windows/non-Clang-host path, so record that build configuration when interpreting error and timing results.

Baseline cases cover D=32/64/128/256 with explicit B/H/Q/K/D/iterations, including aligned full and causal D=64/128 cases. Explicit dimensions matter: upstream defaults couple H to D and B to K. Each run selects the same problem for all variants instantiated at that D. Use a new output directory for every execution; the collector refuses to overwrite a previous record.

docs.title: 31.6 Understand exactly what verification proves
docs.text:
Pass --verify. Upstream FwdRunner::verify compares O and LSE to its device reference. For FP16 it requires maximum absolute difference below 1e-2 and mean absolute difference below 1e-3, separately for both outputs. These are the pinned example's absolute thresholds, not universally justified tolerances for every model distribution.

The reference is a GPU kernel, not a CPU/FP64 oracle. It forms one query row's scores in dynamic shared memory and includes FP16 intermediate rounding; it does not materialize a complete global score matrix. Chapter 30's CPU arithmetic walkthrough independently checks the mathematical recurrence on tiny inputs. It does not consume this runner's random device inputs or independently certify the optimized kernel. A stronger new-input audit would export the exact Q/K/V and compare each O/LSE coordinate to a higher-precision reference under the identical mask/scale/layout contract.

Upstream prints [OK] only for a passed verified variant; [--] means execution without verification, and [FAIL] indicates failure. The upstream main discards the return value of main_single and returns zero, including on its reported failure paths. Architecture guards can also exit zero. The collector therefore requires the expected count and exact names/order of [OK] variants, one launch header matching requested B/H/Q/K/D, direction and mask, finite reported rates and positive finite verbose timings, no failure diagnostics and successful process status. A duplicated success row, wrong problem header or nonfinite timing cannot become PASS merely because the row count matches. A skipped or missing kernel is SKIP/INCOMPLETE, never PASS; one successful variant cannot hide another variant's failure.

Logs retain argv, UTC start/end, separate stdout/stderr, source hashes and system information in results.json and sibling files. Those timestamps become execution dates only after an actual run. The host parser tests exercise false-success cases without claiming GPU validation:

python3 -m unittest discover -s tools/tests -p test_cutlass_attention.py -v
Exercise: a zero exit with incomplete verification

A D=64 run exits zero and prints two [OK] rows plus one [--] row. Is the complete case verified?

Worked answer: no. This runner instantiates three variants at D=64, and [--] indicates an unverified result. The collector returns INCOMPLETE rather than PASS. A numerical failure instead returns FAIL, even if another variant succeeded.

docs.title: 31.7 Read the backward path as a new dependency graph
docs.text:
The library also implements FP16 backward for head dimensions 32,64,128. It is not an automatic derivative of a black-box forward launch. Given upstream gradient dO and softmax probabilities P, the mathematical relations per head are:

  • dV = P^T*dO and dP = dO*V^T;
  • delta_i = sum_j P_ij*dP_ij = dot(dO_i,O_i);
  • dS_ij = P_ij*(dP_ij-delta_i) for the scaled, masked score S;
  • dQ = dS*K/sqrt(D) and dK = dS^T*Q/sqrt(D).

Walk one row: P=[1/4,3/4], V rows [1,0], [0,2], and dO=[2,3]. Then O=[1/4,3/2] and dP=[2,6]. Delta is (1/4)*2+(3/4)*6=5, also dot(dO,O)=1/2+9/2=5. Thus dS=[-3/4,3/4], whose sum is zero. This row contributes dV rows [1/2,3/4] and [3/2,9/4]. The dQ/dK products then use the actual Q/K and the same score scale. The numbers demonstrate derivative bookkeeping, not a vendor-supported head size of two.

Follow BwdRunner, device/fmha_device_bwd.hpp, the backward mainloop, the sum_OdO kernel and conversion stage. Reconstructing probability tiles from scores/LSE avoids storing the whole probability matrix, but creates dependencies on the exact forward normalization and mask convention. The optimized gradients are compared against reference/fmha_bwd_reference.hpp; the pinned thresholds are again max <1e-2, mean <1e-3, separately for dQ, dK and dV.

Add --include-backward to the collector plan or execution command to request aligned D=64 full and causal backward cases. Each case expects two verified variant rows. The published Hopper record includes both of these D=64 backward cases and all four expected variant results; it neither validates every backward head size nor claims FA3-equivalent performance. The upstream README explicitly says backward kernels are more limited in performance than FA3.

Exercise: detect an incorrect softmax backward correction

For the worked row P=[1/4,3/4],dP=[2,6], someone uses delta=4 rather than five. What check exposes the error?

Worked answer: the wrong dS is [-1/2,3/2], whose sum is one. The correct delta gives [-3/4,3/4], summing to zero. A softmax score-gradient row sums to zero in exact arithmetic; use an appropriate tolerance for floating-point checks.

docs.title: 31.8 Profile only after preserving the numerical contract
docs.text:
The small B=1,H=2 cases above are correctness configurations, not throughput benchmarks. Two heads and short query lengths provide only a few logical query tiles and can leave most of an H100 idle. Their captured TFLOP/s must not be presented as a peak-performance result. A throughput study needs a separately stated larger workload and adequate independent work, while preserving the same numerical contract.

--verbose prints per-variant elapsed milliseconds and shared-memory bytes. The upstream timer surrounds repeated device operations; initialization and reference checking lie outside that timed region. Its forward FLOP numerator is approximately 4*B*H*Q*K*D, halved for causal mode. That convention omits softmax/masking work and approximates the causal triangle; it is not a count of every executed instruction. Compare kernels using the same shape, dtype, mask, precision, warmup and timing boundary.

Use Nsight Systems to inspect launch/overlap and Nsight Compute to investigate shared-memory/register pressure, pipeline stalls and Tensor Core activity. A profile or sanitizer run perturbs timing and is not the normal throughput record. The following are commands to run after a real build, not captured profiling results. Set the binary to the separately collected run directory. The symbol filter follows the actual device_kernel<...FmhaKernel...> launch type in the pinned adapter; inspect the profiler's kernel list if a tool version reports no match.

ATTENTION_BIN="$PWD/artifacts/attention-hopper-01/build/examples/88_hopper_fmha/88_hopper_fmha"
mkdir -p artifacts/attention-profiles
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=none \
  --output=artifacts/attention-profiles/d64-full \
  "$ATTENTION_BIN" --b=1 --h=2 --q=128 --k=128 --d=64 \
  --mask=no --iterations=3 --verify --verbose
ncu --set basic --kernel-name-base demangled \
  --kernel-name 'regex:.*FmhaKernel.*' --launch-count 1 \
  --export artifacts/attention-profiles/d64-one-kernel \
  "$ATTENTION_BIN" --b=1 --h=2 --q=128 --k=128 --d=64 \
  --mask=no --iterations=3 --verify --verbose

Nsight Systems includes all selected variants and reference launches. Nsight Compute's one-launch filter examines one matching kernel, not the complete application timing or all variants. Choose new report names for another capture. Profiling requires the site's permitted performance-counter access; missing permissions or no matching kernel is not a successful profile. See the Nsight Systems CLI and Nsight Compute CLI.

Keep optimization experiments in a new checkout/run directory: changing stage count, schedule or probability conversion can alter resource limits and numerical behavior. Recheck O, LSE and, when applicable, all three gradients before accepting a speed improvement.

docs.text:
Download the complete .cu file · Download the example with every local kernel/reference header · Source manifest · BSD license.

The full translation unit below is the exact pinned NVIDIA example, including main, argument parsing, allocation, forward/backward dispatch and numerical verification. Its local collective/, device/, kernel/ and reference/ headers contain the implementations it instantiates; all are included in the project download. CUTLASS/CuTe library headers still come from the pinned checkout, just as the GEMM chapters use library headers. The standalone .cu download therefore needs those dependencies; it is not a skeleton with missing kernel bodies.

Read the complete warp-specialized kernel, QK/PV mainloop, online softmax and output epilogue alongside the runner.

docs.title: Build this listing and run its checks
docs.text:
From the book repository root on the Hopper host, use a fresh scratch checkout. The copy below puts the exact downloadable project into the official example's build location:

bash tools/fetch_cutlass.sh /tmp/cutlass-attention-page-v436
cp -R docs/examples/attention/88_hopper_fmha/. \
  /tmp/cutlass-attention-page-v436/examples/88_hopper_fmha/
cmake -S /tmp/cutlass-attention-page-v436 \
  -B build/attention-page \
  -DCUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS=90a -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_TESTS=OFF -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_PROFILER=OFF \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_EXAMPLES=ON -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_CUBLAS=OFF \
  -DCUTLASS_ENABLE_LIBRARY=OFF
cmake --build build/attention-page --target 88_hopper_fmha --parallel 1
./build/attention-page/examples/88_hopper_fmha/88_hopper_fmha \
  --b=1 --h=2 --q=128 --k=128 --d=64 --mask=no \
  --iterations=3 --verify --verbose
./build/attention-page/examples/88_hopper_fmha/88_hopper_fmha \
  --b=1 --h=2 --q=128 --k=128 --d=64 --mask=causal \
  --iterations=3 --verify --verbose --bwd

Use the collector in Section 31.5 when recording formal evidence: it also checks every expected result row and preserves system information, dates, hashes and logs. Direct invocation above is useful for studying this source, but exit zero alone is insufficient. Expected verified-variant counts are three for the D=64 forward call and two for its backward call. The dated Hopper execution record in Section 31.6 reports the actual results for this exact source.

The upstream banner's large all-2048 usage example is not this lab's command: D=2048 has no instantiated kernel in this pin. Use the explicit supported D=64 commands above. /*! \file
    \brief Example implementation of fused multi-head attention for Hopper using CUTLASS 3.

    This example showcases the use of CUTLASS to build forward and backward fused
    multi-head attention (FMHA) collectives from existing CUTLASS collectives targeting
    the NVIDIA Hopper architecture.

    Background and motivation
    -------------------------
    CUTLASS is a highly flexible library that provides open-source building blocks
    for tensor core programming for GEMM or GEMM-like problems. Fused multi-head
    attention (FMHA) is a foundational kernel for large language models (LLMs) since it
    makes long sequence lengths feasible from a memory-usage perspective. It also
    improves computational efficiency since it transforms an outer-product-like and
    a matrix-vector-like GEMM into a fused operation with much higher arithmetic
    intensity. For more details, see Dao et al, 2022; Dao, 2023.
    Implementing this kernel in CUTLASS enabled easy customization and high
    performance.

    Introduction
    ------------
    The example targets the NVIDIA Hopper architecture, and takes advantage of
    warpgroup-wide tensor cores, the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), just like
    GEMMs do. It provides both a forward and a backward pass (often abbreviated
    fwd and bwd in the code), and an optional FP8 mode for the forward pass.
    The code is structured into four layers: The runner (and the reference kernels)
    takes care of initialization, measurement, and testing; the device layer
    orchestrates kernel calls and partitions workspace; the kernel layer (just
    like the CUTLASS kernel layer); and the collective layer (most of the logic
    of FMHA is implemented here).

    Details
    -------
    This example contains a considerable amount of code. For a more detailed
    look at it, please refer to the README.md.

    Example usage:
      $ ./examples/88_hopper_fmha/88_hopper_fmha \
            --b=2048 --h=2048 --d=2048 --q=2048 --k=2048
*/

#include <iostream>

#include "cute/tensor.hpp"

#include "cutlass/cutlass.h"

#include "cutlass/util/command_line.h"
#include "cutlass/util/distribution.h"
#include "cutlass/util/host_tensor.h"
#include "cutlass/util/tensor_view_io.h"
#include "cutlass/util/reference/device/tensor_fill.h"

#include "collective/fmha_fusion.hpp"
#include "device/fmha_device_bwd.hpp"
#include "device/device_universal.hpp"
#include "kernel/fmha_kernel_builder.hpp"
#include "reference/fmha_reference.hpp"
#include "reference/fmha_bwd_reference.hpp"
#include "reference/reference_abs_error.hpp"

using namespace cute;
using namespace cutlass::fmha::kernel;
using namespace cutlass::fmha::collective;
using namespace cutlass::fmha;

// Uncomment for FP8
// #define FP8

///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

/// Command line options parsing
struct Options {

    bool help;
    bool error;

    int b, h, q, k, d;
    int iterations;
    bool verify;
    bool verbose;
    bool causal;
    bool residual;
    bool bwd;

    Options()
        : help(false), error(false), b(16), h(16), q(1024), k(1024),
          d(128), iterations(3), verify(false), causal(false),
          residual(false), bwd(false), verbose(false) {
    }

    // Parses the command line
    void parse(int argc, char const** args) {
        cutlass::CommandLine cmd(argc, args);

        Options defaults;

        if (cmd.check_cmd_line_flag("help")) {
            help = true;
            return;
        }

        cmd.get_cmd_line_argument("d", d, defaults.d);
        cmd.get_cmd_line_argument("h", h, -1);
        if (h == -1)
            h = 2048 / d;

        cmd.get_cmd_line_argument("q", q, -1);
        cmd.get_cmd_line_argument("k", k, -1);
        if (q == -1)
            q = k;
        if (k == -1)
            k = q;
        if (q == -1 && k == -1)
            q = k = defaults.q;

        cmd.get_cmd_line_argument("b", b, -1);
        if (b == -1)
            b = 16384 / k;
        if (b == 0)
            b = 1;

        cmd.get_cmd_line_argument(
            "iterations", iterations, defaults.iterations);
        verify = cmd.check_cmd_line_flag("verify");
        verbose = cmd.check_cmd_line_flag("verbose");

        std::string mask;
        cmd.get_cmd_line_argument<std::string>("mask", mask, "");
        if (mask == "no" || mask == "") {
            causal = residual = false;
        } else if (mask == "causal") {
            residual = false;
            causal = true;
        } else if (mask == "residual") {
            residual = true;
            causal = false;
        }

        bwd = cmd.check_cmd_line_flag("bwd");
    }

    /// Prints the usage statement.
    std::ostream& print_usage(std::ostream& out) const {

        out << "88_hopper_fmha\n\n"
            << "  This example showcases the use of CUTLASS's collective operation builders to easily construct\n"
            << "  fused multi-head attention forward-pass kernels targeting NVIDIA's Hopper architecture.\n\n"
            << "Options:\n\n"
            << "  --help                      If specified, displays this usage statement\n\n"
            << "  --b=<int>                   Sets the B extent\n"
            << "  --h=<int>                   Sets the H extent\n"
            << "  --q=<int>                   Sets the Q extent\n"
            << "  --k=<int>                   Sets the K extent\n"
            << "  --d=<int>                   Sets the D extent\n"
            << "  --iterations=<int>          Benchmarking iterations\n"
            << "  --verify                    Verify results\n"
            << "  --verbose                   Print smem and execution time per kernel\n"
            << "  --mask=<no|residual|causal> Enables masking\n"
            << "  --bwd                       Runs the backwards pass\n"
            << "\n";

        return out;
    }
};

/// Helper to initialize a block of device data
template <class Element>
bool initialize_block(cutlass::DeviceAllocation<Element>& block,
                      uint64_t seed = 2023,
                      bool init_one = false) {

    if (init_one) {
        cutlass::reference::device::BlockFillRandomUniform(
            block.get(),
            block.size(),
            seed,
            (Element)1,
            (Element)1);
    } else {
        cutlass::reference::device::BlockFillRandomGaussian(
            block.get(),
            block.size(),
            seed,
            (Element)0,
            (Element)1);
    }

    return true;
}
