template <bool kIsVarlen,
          class TileShape,
          class DispatchPolicy,
          class ActiveMask,
          class... KernelOptions>
struct FwdRunner {

#ifdef FP8
    using Element = cutlass::float_e4m3_t;
#else
    using Element = cutlass::half_t;
#endif

    using ElementAccumulatorQK = float;
    using ElementAccumulatorPV = float;
    using ElementOut = cutlass::half_t;

    // Q K D ((H_R, H_K) B)
    using ProblemShapeRegular =
        cute::tuple<int,
                    int,
                    int,
                    cute::tuple<cute::tuple<int, int>, int>>;
    using ProblemShapeVarlen =
        cute::tuple<VariableLength,
                    VariableLength,
                    int,
                    cute::tuple<cute::tuple<int, int>, int>>;
    using ProblemShapeType =
        std::conditional_t<kIsVarlen,
                           ProblemShapeVarlen,
                           ProblemShapeRegular>;

    using StrideQ =
        cute::tuple<int,
                    _1,
                    cute::tuple<cute::tuple<int, int>,
                                int>>; // Q D ((H_R, H_K), B)
    using StrideK =
        cute::tuple<int,
                    _1,
                    cute::tuple<cute::tuple<_0, int>,
                                int>>; // K D ((H_R, H_K), B)
    using StrideV = StrideK;
    using StrideO = StrideQ;
    using StrideLSE =
        cute::tuple<_1,
                    cute::tuple<cute::tuple<int, int>,
                                int>>; // Q ((H_R, H_K), B)

    static constexpr bool kIsPersistent =
        find_option_t<Tag::kIsPersistent,
                      true_type,
                      KernelOptions...>::value;
    using TileScheduler = std::conditional_t<
        kIsPersistent,
        cutlass::fmha::kernel::PersistentTileScheduler,
        cutlass::fmha::kernel::IndividualTileScheduler>;

    using Mainloop = cutlass::fmha::collective::
        Sm100FmhaFwdMainloopTmaWarpspecialized<Element,
                                               ElementAccumulatorQK,
                                               ElementAccumulatorPV,
                                               TileShape,
                                               StrideQ,
                                               StrideK,
                                               StrideV,
                                               ActiveMask>;
    using Operation = cutlass::fmha::device::FMHA<
        cutlass::fmha::kernel::Sm100FmhaFwdKernelTmaWarpspecialized<
            ProblemShapeType,
            Mainloop,
            cutlass::fmha::collective::
                Sm100FmhaFwdEpilogueTmaWarpspecialized<
                    ElementOut,
                    ElementAccumulatorPV,
                    typename Mainloop::TileShapePV,
                    StrideO,
                    StrideLSE>,
            TileScheduler>>;

    //
    // Data members
    //

    /// Initialization
    StrideQ stride_Q;
    StrideK stride_K;
    StrideV stride_V;
    StrideO stride_O;
    StrideLSE stride_LSE;
    uint64_t seed = 0;

    struct DeviceBuffer {
        DeviceAllocation<Element> block_Q;
        DeviceAllocation<Element> block_K;
        DeviceAllocation<Element> block_V;
        DeviceAllocation<ElementOut> block_O;
        DeviceAllocation<ElementAccumulatorPV> block_LSE;
        DeviceAllocation<ElementOut> block_ref_O;
        DeviceAllocation<ElementAccumulatorPV> block_ref_LSE;
        DeviceAllocation<int> device_cumulative_seqlen_q;
        DeviceAllocation<int> device_cumulative_seqlen_kv;

        DeviceBuffer() = default;
        DeviceBuffer(const DeviceBuffer&) = delete;
        DeviceBuffer& operator=(const DeviceBuffer&) = delete;

        size_t get_storage_size() const {
            return block_Q.get_storage_size() +
                   block_K.get_storage_size() +
                   block_V.get_storage_size() +
                   block_O.get_storage_size() +
                   block_LSE.get_storage_size() +
                   block_ref_O.get_storage_size() +
                   block_ref_LSE.get_storage_size() +
                   device_cumulative_seqlen_q.get_storage_size() +
                   device_cumulative_seqlen_kv.get_storage_size();
        }
    };

    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<DeviceBuffer>> buffers;

    std::vector<int> cumulative_seqlen_q;
    std::vector<int> cumulative_seqlen_kv;

    //
    // Methods
    //
    bool verify(const ProblemShapeType& problem_shape,
                DeviceBuffer& buffer) {
        Tensor mQ = make_tensor(make_gmem_ptr(buffer.block_Q.get()),
                                select<0, 2, 3>(problem_shape),
                                stride_Q);

        Tensor mK = make_tensor(make_gmem_ptr(buffer.block_K.get()),
                                select<1, 2, 3>(problem_shape),
                                stride_K);

        Tensor mV = make_tensor(make_gmem_ptr(buffer.block_V.get()),
                                select<1, 2, 3>(problem_shape),
                                stride_V);

        Tensor mO =
            make_tensor(make_gmem_ptr(buffer.block_ref_O.get()),
                        select<0, 2, 3>(problem_shape),
                        stride_O);

        Tensor mLSE =
            make_tensor(make_gmem_ptr(buffer.block_ref_LSE.get()),
                        select<0, 3>(problem_shape),
                        stride_LSE);

        auto [Q, K, D, HB] = problem_shape;

        auto problem_shape_ref = cute::make_tuple(Q, K, D, D, HB);

        fmha_reference(
            problem_shape_ref, mQ, mK, mV, mO, mLSE, ActiveMask{});

        cudaError_t result = cudaDeviceSynchronize();
        if (result != cudaSuccess) {
            std::cerr
                << "Reference kernel failed. Last CUDA error: "
                << cudaGetErrorString(result) << std::endl;
            return false;
        }

        const double kMaxDiffThresh =
            sizeof(Element) == 1 ? 1e-1 : 1e-2;
        const double kMeanDiffThresh =
            sizeof(Element) == 1 ? 1e-1 : 1e-3;

        // Check if output from CUTLASS kernel and reference kernel are equal or not
        double max_diff = 0;
        double mean_diff = 0;
        reference_abs_diff(buffer.block_O,
                           buffer.block_ref_O,
                           max_diff,
                           mean_diff);

        bool passed_O = (max_diff < kMaxDiffThresh) &&
                        (mean_diff < kMeanDiffThresh);
        if (!passed_O) {
            std::cerr << "failed O: max diff " << max_diff
                      << " mean " << mean_diff << std::endl;
        }

        reference_abs_diff(buffer.block_LSE,
                           buffer.block_ref_LSE,
                           max_diff,
                           mean_diff);

        bool passed_LSE = (max_diff < kMaxDiffThresh) &&
                          (mean_diff < kMeanDiffThresh);
        if (!passed_LSE) {
            std::cerr << "failed LSE: max diff " << max_diff
                      << " mean " << mean_diff << std::endl;
        }

        return passed_O && passed_LSE;
    }

    template <class ProblemShape>
    auto initialize_varlen(const Options& options,
                           const ProblemShape& problem_size,
                           const bool kVarlenSame = true) {

        int num_batches = get<3, 1>(problem_size);

        // generate Q as --b times
        //    gaussian (--Q, --Q / 2) sampled positive
        //    track cumulative
        std::mt19937 rng(0x202305151552ull);
        std::normal_distribution<double> dist_q(
            get<0>(problem_size), get<0>(problem_size) / 2);
        std::normal_distribution<double> dist_kv(
            get<1>(problem_size), get<1>(problem_size) / 2);
        std::cout << "N: " << num_batches
                  << ", Q: " << get<0>(problem_size)
                  << ", KV: " << get<1>(problem_size) << std::endl;

        auto generate_positive_int = [](auto& dist, auto& gen) {
            int result = 0;
            do {
                result = static_cast<int>(dist(gen));
            } while (result <= 0);
            return result;
        };

        cumulative_seqlen_q = {0};
        cumulative_seqlen_kv = {0};

        int total_seqlen_q = 0;
        int total_seqlen_kv = 0;
        int max_seqlen_q = 0;
        int max_seqlen_kv = 0;

        for (int i = 0; i < num_batches; i++) {
            int seqlen_q =
                (!options.varlen_q.empty()) ? options.varlen_q.at(i)
                : kVarlenSame               ? get<0>(problem_size)
                              : generate_positive_int(dist_q, rng);
            int seqlen_kv =
                (!options.varlen_k.empty()) ? options.varlen_k.at(i)
                : kVarlenSame               ? get<1>(problem_size)
                              : generate_positive_int(dist_kv, rng);

            total_seqlen_q += seqlen_q;
            total_seqlen_kv += seqlen_kv;

            max_seqlen_q = std::max(max_seqlen_q, seqlen_q);
            max_seqlen_kv = std::max(max_seqlen_kv, seqlen_kv);

            cumulative_seqlen_q.push_back(
                cumulative_seqlen_q.back() + seqlen_q);
            cumulative_seqlen_kv.push_back(
                cumulative_seqlen_kv.back() + seqlen_kv);
        }
        std::cout << "Q max: " << max_seqlen_q
                  << " total: " << total_seqlen_q << " vs even "
                  << num_batches * get<0>(problem_size)
                  << std::endl;
        std::cout << "KV max: " << max_seqlen_kv
                  << " total: " << total_seqlen_kv << " vs even "
                  << num_batches * get<1>(problem_size)
                  << std::endl;

        ProblemShape problem_size_for_init = problem_size;
        get<3, 1>(problem_size_for_init) = 1;
        get<0>(problem_size_for_init) = total_seqlen_q;
        get<1>(problem_size_for_init) = total_seqlen_kv;

        ProblemShapeType problem_size_for_launch;

        get<0>(problem_size_for_launch) =
            VariableLength{max_seqlen_q, nullptr, total_seqlen_q};
        get<1>(problem_size_for_launch) =
            VariableLength{max_seqlen_kv, nullptr, total_seqlen_kv};
        get<2>(problem_size_for_launch) = get<2>(problem_size);
        get<3>(problem_size_for_launch) = get<3>(problem_size);

        return cute::make_tuple(problem_size_for_init,
                                problem_size_for_launch);
    }

    /// Initialize operands to be used in the GEMM and reference GEMM

    ProblemShapeType initialize(const Options& options) {
        int h_r = options.h / options.h_k;
        assert(options.h % options.h_k == 0);
        auto problem_shape_in = cute::make_tuple(
            options.q,
            options.k,
            options.d,
            cute::make_tuple(cute::make_tuple(h_r, options.h_k),
                             options.b));

        ProblemShapeType problem_shape;
        decltype(problem_shape_in) problem_size;

        if constexpr (kIsVarlen) {
            auto [problem_shape_init, problem_shape_launch] =
                initialize_varlen(options, problem_shape_in);
            problem_shape = problem_shape_launch;
            problem_size = problem_shape_init;
        } else {
            problem_size = problem_shape_in;
            problem_shape = problem_shape_in;
        }

        get<2>(problem_size) =
            cutlass::round_up(get<2>(problem_size), 8); // alignment

        auto shape_QO = select<0, 2, 3>(problem_size);
        auto shape_KV = select<1, 2, 3>(problem_size);
        auto shape_LSE = select<0, 3>(problem_size);

        int SQ = size<0>(problem_size);
        int SK = size<1>(problem_size);
        int D = size<2>(problem_size);
        int H = size<3, 0>(problem_size);
        int H_K = size<3, 0, 1>(problem_size);
        int H_Q = size<3, 0, 0>(problem_size);
        int B = size<3, 1>(problem_size);

        stride_Q = make_stride(
            H * D,
            _1{},
            make_stride(make_stride(D, H_Q * D), H * D * SQ));
        stride_O = stride_Q;
        stride_K = make_stride(
            H_K * D,
            _1{},
            make_stride(make_stride(_0{}, D), H_K * D * SK));
        stride_V = stride_K;
        stride_LSE = make_stride(
            _1{}, make_stride(make_stride(SQ, SQ * H_Q), SQ * H));

        if (kIsVarlen) {
            get<2, 1>(stride_Q) = 0;
            get<2, 1>(stride_K) = 0;
            get<2, 1>(stride_V) = 0;
            get<2, 1>(stride_O) = 0;
            get<1, 1>(stride_LSE) = 0;
        }

        auto buffer_init_fn = [&](auto& buffer) {
            buffer.block_Q.reset(size(shape_QO));
            buffer.block_K.reset(size(shape_KV));
            buffer.block_V.reset(size(shape_KV));
            buffer.block_O.reset(size(shape_QO),
                                 kIsVarlen ? D * SQ * H : 0);
            buffer.block_LSE.reset(size(shape_LSE));
            buffer.block_ref_O.reset(size(shape_QO),
                                     kIsVarlen ? D * SQ * H : 0);
            buffer.block_ref_LSE.reset(size(shape_LSE));

            initialize_block(
                buffer.block_Q, seed + 2023, options.init_style_q);
            initialize_block(
                buffer.block_K, seed + 2022, options.init_style_k);
            initialize_block(
                buffer.block_V, seed + 2021, options.init_style_v);

            if (!cumulative_seqlen_q.empty()) {
                buffer.device_cumulative_seqlen_q.reset(
                    cumulative_seqlen_q.size());
                buffer.device_cumulative_seqlen_q.copy_from_host(
                    cumulative_seqlen_q.data(),
                    cumulative_seqlen_q.size());
            }
            if (!cumulative_seqlen_kv.empty()) {
                buffer.device_cumulative_seqlen_kv.reset(
                    cumulative_seqlen_kv.size());
                buffer.device_cumulative_seqlen_kv.copy_from_host(
                    cumulative_seqlen_kv.data(),
                    cumulative_seqlen_kv.size());
            }
        };

        buffers.push_back(std::make_unique<DeviceBuffer>());
        buffer_init_fn(*buffers.back());

        int tensor_ring_buffers = options.tensor_ring_buffers;
        for (int i = 1; i < tensor_ring_buffers; i++) {
            buffers.push_back(std::make_unique<DeviceBuffer>());
            buffer_init_fn(*buffers.back());
        }

        if constexpr (kIsVarlen) {
            get<0>(problem_shape).cumulative_length =
                buffers[0]->device_cumulative_seqlen_q.get();
            get<1>(problem_shape).cumulative_length =
                buffers[0]->device_cumulative_seqlen_kv.get();
        }

        return problem_shape;
    }

    auto get_arguments(const ProblemShapeType& problem_shape,
                       const cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo& hw_info,
                       int buffer_index) {
        auto problem_shape_ = problem_shape;
        if constexpr (kIsVarlen) {
            get<0>(problem_shape_).cumulative_length =
                buffers[buffer_index]
                    ->device_cumulative_seqlen_q.get();
            get<1>(problem_shape_).cumulative_length =
                buffers[buffer_index]
                    ->device_cumulative_seqlen_kv.get();
        }
        typename Operation::Arguments arguments{
            problem_shape_,
            {buffers[buffer_index]->block_Q.get(),
             stride_Q,
             buffers[buffer_index]->block_K.get(),
             stride_K,
             buffers[buffer_index]->block_V.get(),
             stride_V},
            {buffers[buffer_index]->block_O.get(),
             stride_O,
             buffers[buffer_index]->block_LSE.get(),
             stride_LSE},
            hw_info};
        return arguments;
    }

    ExampleResult run(const Options& options,
                      const cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo& hw_info) {

        ProblemShapeType problem_shape = initialize(options);

        int buffer_index = 0;
        typename Operation::Arguments arguments =
            get_arguments(problem_shape, hw_info, buffer_index);

        Operation op;

        ExampleResult example_result;

        example_result.smem_size =
            Operation::Kernel::SharedStorageSize;

        size_t workspace_size = 0;
        workspace_size = Operation::get_workspace_size(arguments);
        DeviceAllocation<uint8_t> workspace(workspace_size);

        cutlass::Status status = cutlass::Status::kSuccess;
        status = op.can_implement(arguments);
        if (status != cutlass::Status::kSuccess) {
            std::cerr
                << "This kernel is not supported. Last CUDA error is: "
                << cudaGetErrorString(cudaGetLastError())
                << std::endl;
            return example_result;
        }

        status = op.initialize(arguments, workspace.get());
        if (status != cutlass::Status::kSuccess) {
            std::cerr
                << "Failed to initialize the CUTLASS kernel. Last CUDA error is: "
                << cudaGetErrorString(cudaGetLastError())
                << std::endl;
            return example_result;
        }

        // Run
        for (int i = 0; i < options.warmup_iterations; i++) {
            status = op.run();
            if (status != cutlass::Status::kSuccess) {
                std::cerr
                    << "Failed to launch the CUTLASS kernel. Last CUDA error is: "
                    << cudaGetErrorString(cudaGetLastError())
                    << std::endl;
                return example_result;
            }
            buffer_index = (buffer_index + 1) % buffers.size();
            arguments =
                get_arguments(problem_shape, hw_info, buffer_index);
            status = op.update(arguments, workspace.get());
            if (status != cutlass::Status::kSuccess) {
                std::cerr
                    << "Failed to update the CUTLASS kernel's parameters. Last CUDA error is: "
                    << std::endl;
                return example_result;
            }
        }

        cudaError_t result = cudaDeviceSynchronize();
        if (result != cudaSuccess) {
            std::cerr
                << "Error running the CUTLASS kernel. Last CUDA error is: "
                << cudaGetErrorString(result) << std::endl;
            return example_result;
        }

        //
        // Construct events
        //

        cudaEvent_t events[2];

        for (auto& event : events) {
            result = cudaEventCreate(&event);
            if (result != cudaSuccess) {
                std::cerr << "cudaEventCreate() failed: "
                          << cudaGetErrorString(result)
                          << std::endl;
                return example_result;
            }
        }

        // Record an event at the start of a series of GEMMs
        result = cudaEventRecord(events[0]);
        if (result != cudaSuccess) {
            std::cerr << "cudaEventRecord() failed: "
                      << cudaGetErrorString(result) << std::endl;
            return example_result;
        }

        for (int i = 0; i < options.iterations; i++) {
            status = op.run();
            if (status != cutlass::Status::kSuccess) {
                std::cerr
                    << "Failed to launch the CUTLASS kernel. Last CUDA error is: "
                    << cudaGetErrorString(cudaGetLastError())
                    << std::endl;
                return example_result;
            }
            buffer_index = (buffer_index + 1) % buffers.size();
            arguments =
                get_arguments(problem_shape, hw_info, buffer_index);
            status = op.update(arguments, workspace.get());
            if (status != cutlass::Status::kSuccess) {
                std::cerr
                    << "Failed to update the CUTLASS kernel's parameters. Last CUDA error is: "
                    << std::endl;
                return example_result;
            }
        }

        //
        // Stop profiling loop
        //

        // Record an event when the GEMMs are complete
        result = cudaEventRecord(events[1]);
        if (result != cudaSuccess) {
            std::cerr << "cudaEventRecord() failed: "
                      << cudaGetErrorString(result) << std::endl;
            return example_result;
        }

        // Wait for work on the device to complete.
        result = cudaEventSynchronize(events[1]);
        if (result != cudaSuccess) {
            std::cerr << "cudaEventSynchronize() failed: "
                      << cudaGetErrorString(result) << std::endl;
            return example_result;
        }

        // Measure elapsed runtime
        float runtime_ms = 0;
        result =
            cudaEventElapsedTime(&runtime_ms, events[0], events[1]);
        if (result != cudaSuccess) {
            std::cerr << "cudaEventElapsed() failed: "
                      << cudaGetErrorString(result) << std::endl;
            return example_result;
        }

        runtime_ms /= static_cast<float>(options.iterations);

        double flops;
        if (kIsVarlen) {
            flops = 0.0;
            for (int i = 0; i < size<3, 1>(problem_shape); i++) {
                flops += (cumulative_seqlen_q[i + 1] -
                          cumulative_seqlen_q[i]) *
                         1.0 *
                         (cumulative_seqlen_kv[i + 1] -
                          cumulative_seqlen_kv[i]);
            }
        } else {
            flops = 1.0;
            flops *= static_cast<double>(size<0>(problem_shape));
            flops *= static_cast<double>(size<1>(problem_shape));
            flops *= static_cast<double>(size<3, 1>(problem_shape));
        }
        flops *=
            4.0 *
            (std::is_same_v<ActiveMask, CausalMask<true>> ||
                     std::is_same_v<ActiveMask, CausalMask<false>>
                 ? 0.5
                 : 1.0);
        flops *= static_cast<double>(size<2>(problem_shape));
        flops *= static_cast<double>(size<3, 0>(problem_shape));
        double tflops_s =
            flops * 1e-12 /*tera*/ / (runtime_ms * 1e-3 /*ms*/);
        example_result.tflops_tc_s = tflops_s;
        example_result.runtime_ms = runtime_ms;

        result = cudaDeviceSynchronize();
        if (result != cudaSuccess) {
            std::cerr
                << "Error running the CUTLASS kernel. Last CUDA error is: "
                << cudaGetErrorString(result) << std::endl;
            return example_result;
        }

        // Verify that the result is correct
        bool passed = true;
        if (options.verify) {
            passed = verify(problem_shape, *buffers[0]);
            if (passed)
                example_result.verified = true;
        }

        if (!passed) {
            std::cerr << "Reference check failed" << std::endl;
            return example_result;
        }

        example_result.passed = true;

        return example_result;
    }
};

int main_result = 0;

/// Helper to print a description of the example run and its result
void print_result(const std::string& description,
                  ExampleResult result,
                  bool verbose) {
    std::ios fmt(nullptr);
    fmt.copyfmt(std::cout);
    std::cout << (result.passed
                      ? (result.verified ? " [OK]  " : " [--] ")
                      : "[FAIL] ");
    if (!result.passed) {
        main_result = -1;
    }
    std::cout << std::setw(32) << std::left << description;
    std::cout.copyfmt(fmt);
    std::cout << " : " << result.tflops_tc_s << " TFLOPS/s"
              << std::endl;
    if (verbose) {
        std::cout << "       t=" << result.runtime_ms
                  << "ms, "
                     "smem="
                  << result.smem_size << "b" << std::endl;
    }
}

template <class Mask>
void run_fwd_128(Mask fusion,
                 Options const& options,
                 cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo const& hw_info) {
    auto run = [&](auto shape,
                   const char* name,
                   auto... kernel_options) {
        if ((!options.kernel_filter.empty()) &&
            (!std::regex_search(
                name, std::basic_regex(options.kernel_filter)))) {
            return;
        }
        if (options.varlen) {
            FwdRunner<true,
                      decltype(shape),
                      void,
                      Mask,
                      decltype(kernel_options)...>
                runner;
            auto result = runner.run(options, hw_info);
            print_result(name, result, options.verbose);
        } else {
            FwdRunner<false,
                      decltype(shape),
                      void,
                      Mask,
                      decltype(kernel_options)...>
                runner;
            auto result = runner.run(options, hw_info);
            print_result(name, result, options.verbose);
        }
    };

    using HeadDim = _128;

    if (options.persistent) {
        // Persistent Tile Scheduler
        run(Shape<_256, _128, HeadDim>{},
            "tma ws 256x128 acc fp32 persistent",
            Option<Tag::kIsPersistent, true_type>{});
    } else {
        // Individual Tile Scheduler
        run(Shape<_256, _128, HeadDim>{},
            "tma ws 256x128 acc fp32 individual",
            Option<Tag::kIsPersistent, false_type>{});
    }
}

// Book adaptation of CUTLASS v4.3.6 example 77: only FP16 fixed-length
// forward, D=64/128, individual scheduling, full/top-left-causal masks.
// Kernel implementations and their GPU reference verifier remain upstream.
template <int D, class Mask>
void run_book_forward(Options const& options,
                      cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo const& hw_info) {
    using Tile = Shape<_256, _128, Int<D>>;
    using Schedule = Option<Tag::kIsPersistent, false_type>;
    FwdRunner<false, Tile, void, Mask, Schedule> runner;
    print_result("book sm100 FP16 forward",
                 runner.run(options, hw_info),
                 options.verbose);
}

int main_single(int argc, char const** args) {

    cudaDeviceProp props;

    cudaError_t error = cudaGetDeviceProperties(&props, 0);
    if (error != cudaSuccess) {
        std::cerr << "cudaGetDeviceProperties() returned an error: "
                  << cudaGetErrorString(error) << std::endl;
        return -1;
    }

    if (__CUDACC_VER_MAJOR__ < 12 || props.major != 10) {
        std::cout
            << "This example requires a GPU of NVIDIA's Blackwell Architecture "
            << "(compute capability major 10) and CUDA 12.8 or greater.\n";
        return 0;
    } //
    // Parse options
    //

    Options options;

    options.parse(argc, args);

    if (options.help) {
        options.print_usage(std::cout) << std::endl;
        return 0;
    }

    if (options.error) {
        std::cerr << "Aborting execution." << std::endl;
        return -1;
    }

#if defined(CUTLASS_ARCH_MMA_SM100_SUPPORTED)

    //
    // Run examples
    //

    // The KernelHardwareInfo struct holds the number of SMs on the GPU with a given device ID. This
    // information is used by the underlying kernel.
    cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo hw_info;

    // Change device_id to another value if you are running on a machine with multiple GPUs and wish
    // to use a GPU other than that with device ID 0.
    hw_info.device_id = 0;
    if (options.sm_count == 0) {
        hw_info.sm_count = cutlass::KernelHardwareInfo::
            query_device_multiprocessor_count(hw_info.device_id);
    } else {
        hw_info.sm_count = options.sm_count;
    }

    std::cout << "###### B " << options.b << " H " << options.h
              << " H_K " << options.h_k << " Q " << options.q
              << " K " << options.k << " D " << options.d << " ";
    std::cout << "Forward" << " "
              << (options.causal
                      ? "Causal"
                      : (options.residual ? "Residual" : "None"))
              << " ";
    std::cout << "#SM " << hw_info.sm_count << std::endl;

    if (options.varlen || options.persistent || options.residual ||
        !options.causal_q_begin ||
        (options.d != 64 && options.d != 128) || options.b < 1 ||
        options.h < 1 || options.h_k < 1 ||
        options.h % options.h_k != 0 || options.q < 1 ||
        options.k < 1 || options.q % 128 || options.k % 128 ||
        !options.verify || options.iterations < 1 ||
        options.warmup_iterations < 0 ||
        !options.kernel_filter.empty()) {
        std::cerr
            << "Book scope: FP16 fixed-length D=64/128, positive B/H/H_K, H divisible by H_K, "
               "Q/K multiples of 128, mask=no or top-left causal, individual scheduler, "
               "--verify, iterations>=1, no kernel filter.\n";
        return 2;
    }
    if (options.causal) {
        if (options.d == 64)
            run_book_forward<64, CausalMask<>>(options, hw_info);
        else
            run_book_forward<128, CausalMask<>>(options, hw_info);
    } else {
        if (options.d == 64)
            run_book_forward<64, NoMask>(options, hw_info);
        else
            run_book_forward<128, NoMask>(options, hw_info);
    }

#endif

    return main_result;
}

int main(int argc, char const** args) {
    std::vector<std::string> full_arguments(args, args + argc);

    bool recursed = false;
    for (size_t i = 1; i < full_arguments.size(); i++) {
        if (full_arguments[i].find(',') != std::string::npos) {
            auto arg = full_arguments[i];
            size_t eq_pos = arg.find('=');
            std::string prefix = eq_pos == std::string::npos
                                     ? ""
                                     : arg.substr(0, eq_pos + 1);
            std::string rest = eq_pos == std::string::npos
                                   ? arg
                                   : arg.substr(eq_pos + 1);
            for (;;) {
                size_t comma_pos = rest.find(',');
                std::string current = rest.substr(0, comma_pos);
                full_arguments[i] = prefix + current;
                std::vector<const char*> next_args;
                for (auto& elem : full_arguments) {
                    next_args.push_back(elem.data());
                }
                main(argc, next_args.data());
                if (comma_pos == std::string::npos)
                    break;
                rest = rest.substr(comma_pos + 1);
            }
            recursed = true;
            break;
        }
    }

    if (!recursed) {
        int status = main_single(argc, args);
        if (status != 0)
            main_result = status;
    }

    return main_result;
}

docs.title: 11 — Exercises with worked answers
docs.text:
1. Why did the older register-resizing binary fail although the B200 supports register resizing? The first build used the wrong target: generic sm_100 rejected the architecture-specific instruction; a Hopper sm_90a fallback was not compatible with B200. Recompilation for sm_100a passed both 128-value producer/consumer checks. See the compatibility result.

2. How many bytes do the logical FP16 A/B tiles consume for (128,128,64)? A is 128*64*2=16384 bytes and B is 64*128*2=16384 bytes, totaling 32,768 operand bytes per logical stage. This is not the total shared-memory reservation; stage count, descriptors and epilogue storage must also be considered.

3. Why can a zero-filled output hide a bad store? A legitimate result can be zero. The examples poison every output with NaN bits and check every coordinate, so an untouched element fails the finite-value test.

4. In the GQA case, do both K/V and Q/O halve? Only K/V halve when Hkv changes from two to one while Hq stays two. Each query head still owns its query and output rows.

5. Does [--] establish reference correctness? No. The upstream printer uses [OK] for a verified passing result; [--] is an unverified result. An architecture guard can also return zero without launching a kernel. The recorded checks require the matching verified result.

6. Does TMEM remove the need for barriers? No. It changes storage and completion mechanisms. The producer/consumer proof still needs operand readiness, completion of asynchronous readers and a safe lifetime for the accumulator storage.

docs.text: Preserve the equation and coordinate proof, but rebuild the instruction/storage/schedule contract for the target architecture. The recorded single-device B200 tests cover native FP16-to-FP32 GEMM, fused ReLU and four FP16 forward-attention configurations. docs.title: Follow the native accumulator lifetime
docs.text:
The pinned one-SM builder selects a 128×128 SM100 MMA and six shared-memory stages; its shared storage is 230400 bytes, below the B200 per-CTA 232448-byte limit. This is a source-derived resource calculation, not a SASS capture. The tested builder uses one-SM UMMA, not a demonstrated two-SM kernel.

  1. Allocate accumulator columns in tensor memory (TMEM). These are not Hopper’s per-thread FP32 accumulator registers.
  2. Acquire a shared-memory input stage and submit its TMA transfers. Wait for the stage’s transaction barrier before MMA reads it.
  3. Issue the selected tcgen05.mma operation through the pinned CuTe UMMA wrapper. Descriptor and TMEM-address operands have Blackwell-specific contracts.
  4. Commit its asynchronous completion to the appropriate barrier. Do not treat instruction issue as completed accumulation.
  5. Wait for completion before loading accumulator values out of TMEM for epilogue conversion and stores. Release input stages only after their asynchronous readers finish.
  6. Deallocate TMEM only after its readers have finished; reuse requires the complete allocation/ownership protocol.

Two-SM forms coordinate a CTA pair and change operand, allocation and completion contracts. They cannot be obtained by launching twice as many independent one-SM CTAs. Consult the pinned UMMA wrappers and Blackwell functionality guide linked in Step 2 for the exact instruction forms. No handwritten tcgen05 listing or two-SM execution is claimed here.

The unused historical -DFP16 flag is absent from the suggested command above; raw commands remain unchanged. Attention verification uses the same build’s GPU reference under --use_fast_math, not an independent float64 CPU oracle.

In the dated execution below, the portable Chapter 11 TP=2 × PP=2 × DP=2 teaching program completed on eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs, compiled for sm_80. This is a separate architecture-specific supplement; the original one-H100 and final two-H100 datasets remain unchanged. It is not an eight-H100 run. Hopper-specific WGMMA and TMA examples are not validated by this A100 execution.

  • Run captured: 2026-11-18T00:03:00.400131+00:00 (UTC).
  • Finished: 2026-11-18T00:03:13.511354+00:00 (UTC).
  • Compiler / process exit: 0 / 0.
  • Program result: All-rank training validation: PASS.
  • Executed source SHA-256: 9a8dfd7c3904304b8cc1f344d6c91f4bb8748491a96cd6699455f9f012818cb2.

The revised program uses distinct DP inputs and checks all 16,384 final weight values against an independent CPU serial reference, plus all 16 per-step replica loss values and four DP replica-pair comparisons. The reference follows the same DP averaging and per-TP-shard gradient-clipping semantics, with explicit numerical tolerances. This is a reference comparison of the teaching program, not a training-quality or throughput benchmark, cross-node RDMA test, or validation on B200. Loss is checked against the reference for each step; changing inputs do not imply a monotonic loss trajectory.

Download the exact executed source, manifest, compiler log, raw run log, and system/topology log. The complete raw log is authoritative; thread print order is run-specific.

The captured compiler command, with only the remote source and output paths shortened, is:

nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_80 -O2 ex13_hybrid_parallel_training.cu -o ex13_hybrid_parallel_training -lnccl -Xcompiler -pthread -lcublas
./ex13_hybrid_parallel_training

The manifest preserves the exact original absolute-path commands and UTC stage timestamps. Verify the immutable hashes and current chapter-source match with:

python3 tools/verify_eight_gpu_audit.py

The complete validation summary combines the 26 successful H100 program runs with this eight-A100 training result: all 27 complete programs compiled and executed successfully across the recorded hosts.

docs.text: CI verifies the successful H100/A100 records, captured logs and statuses, and verifies the four corrected revisions against the November 18 execution dataset. docs.title: Getting Started & Installation
docs.text:
This guide takes you from a terminal to the book's first verified GPU result. You can read and preview the website on a machine without an NVIDIA GPU. Run the Hopper-specific programs on a compatible NVIDIA GPU host, locally or over SSH.

What was actually tested

Historical records cover 26 H100 program revisions and the revised training program on eight A100 GPUs. Current post-review source changes still need GPU revalidation. On November 17, 2026, the original validation used one H100 PCIe: all 27 complete programs compiled and 24 single-GPU workloads passed. The follow-up audit used two H100 80GB HBM3 GPUs connected through NV18, compiling all 27 programs and executing 26 workloads, including peer transfer and NCCL AllReduce. Both hosts used Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, driver 580.105.08, CUDA Toolkit 12.8.93, GCC 13.3.0, C++17, -O2, and sm_90a. On November 18 (UTC), the revised portable training program passed on eight A100 GPUs, targeting sm_80, with full final-weight and per-step loss comparisons against a CPU reference. This was not an eight-H100 run.

The SSH client instructions describe standard usage; the linked system records identify the exact execution configurations. System record · Execution manifest · Preflight JSON.

The four barrier-ordering corrections in Chapters 3–5 passed the November 18 two-H100 rerun and memory checks. Sixteen original-program revisions retain matching execution records; eleven corrected revisions need GPU revalidation across the H100 and eight-A100 hosts. The additional H100 record includes fresh compilation dates, execution times, system information and sample outputs.

Select a diagram to open its full-size SVG.

B200 architecture targets

Every command using -arch=sm_90a produces Hopper-specific GPU code and cannot be run on B200. Portable examples must be rebuilt for the actual supported Blackwell target. Architecture-specific WGMMA kernels require a native implementation, not only a flag change. See the compatibility scope and native appendix.

November 21 corrections: historical executions apply to their archived source hashes. Some current examples have subsequent fixes and require fresh GPU validation; see the repair record. An evidence-verifier pass is an offline consistency check, not a GPU rerun.

docs.title: 1 — Choose the right machine
docs.text:
What you have What you can do Where the GPU commands run Any ordinary laptop or desktop with Python Read the book, build the website, inspect sources and check evidence hashes No GPU required for these activities Apple Silicon Mac or a computer without a suitable NVIDIA GPU Use the machine as an SSH client to a Linux GPU host In the remote Linux shell, not the local terminal One H100 PCIe or H100 SXM Run the single-GPU examples; H100 PCIe is the tested SKU On that GPU host Another Hopper GPU, such as H200 The sm_90a architecture target is relevant, but this is a different hardware configuration Re-run the checks and record your own results Two or more suitable NVIDIA GPUs Attempt the relevant Chapter 11 P2P/NCCL examples after checking topology On the multi-GPU host; count alone does not establish peer access Eight suitable GPUs Attempt the TP=2 × PP=2 × DP=2 teaching workload Completed separately on eight A100 GPUs with sm_80; see the supplement A100 or Blackwell Read the material, but do not assume the Hopper WGMMA programs will run A100 lacks WGMMA; Blackwell needs a different Tensor Core implementation

The a in sm_90a enables architecture-specific features. It does not mean “this GPU and every later GPU.” Use a provider image with a suitable CUDA toolkit already installed when possible. No GPU rental is required just to read or preview the book.

docs.title: 2 — Connect from your computer
docs.text:
If you are already logged into the GPU machine, skip to Step 3. Otherwise use the host address and private key supplied for your instance. Keep the key on your own machine; it does not belong in the book repository.

On Linux or macOS:

chmod 400 /path/to/your-key.pem
ssh -i /path/to/your-key.pem ubuntu@YOUR_INSTANCE_IP

Windows users can run the same ssh -i ... command in a terminal with OpenSSH installed, using the Windows path to the key. The POSIX chmod command above is for Linux/macOS; Windows key-file permissions use Windows access controls. See Microsoft's OpenSSH client documentation.

On the first connection, compare the server's host-key fingerprint with your provider's trusted information before accepting it. Once connected, the prompt should refer to the remote Linux host. All remaining GPU commands in this guide belong there. CPU-only website commands can also run locally.

docs.title: 3 — Check the driver and toolkit separately
Choose the installation path
docs.text:
The commands below target Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, x86-64, on a Linux GPU host, with CUDA 12.8. Ubuntu 24.04 is the book's recorded host family. Run them in Bash on that host, not on an Apple Silicon laptop. For ARM/Grace, WSL, containers or another distribution, use the corresponding NVIDIA CUDA installation instructions; the repository and driver steps differ.

Starting point Follow this path Provider image already runs nvidia-smi and nvcc --version reports a suitable toolkit Keep the provider's driver; install only missing libraries/tools and select the intended toolkit. Working driver, missing compiler Install the CUDA toolkit below; a toolkit-only package does not replace the driver. Fresh Ubuntu GPU host without a driver Install prerequisites, register the repository, install the driver, reboot, then install CUDA and libraries. Container Install the driver on the host; use the provider's GPU-enabled container runtime and a CUDA development image. Do not install kernel drivers inside the container.

Record the starting environment:

cat /etc/os-release
uname -m
uname -r
nvidia-smi
command -v nvcc
nvcc --version

On a fresh host, missing nvidia-smi or nvcc at this stage is the reason to continue installation. On a managed image, first check its documented environment modules/toolkit paths. Conda activation is not a universal CUDA installation step.

docs.title: Install Ubuntu prerequisites
docs.text:
On a fresh Ubuntu host:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y build-essential python3 python3-venv python3-pip \
    git wget ca-certificates pciutils

build-essential supplies GCC/G++, Make and the basic linker toolchain. CUDA also constrains supported host-compiler versions: use the selected toolkit's host compiler support table. The captured Ubuntu 24.04 runs used GCC 13.3. A generic Python CUDA wheel is not a replacement for this C++ build environment.

docs.title: Register the matching NVIDIA repository
docs.text:
Use this only if the matching NVIDIA APT repository is not already configured. It selects Ubuntu 22.04 versus 24.04 from the actual OS; it stops for other systems. The subshell keeps its temporary variables local.

(
    set -eu
    . /etc/os-release
    case "$ID:$VERSION_ID:$(uname -m)" in
        ubuntu:22.04:x86_64) cuda_repo=ubuntu2204 ;;
        ubuntu:24.04:x86_64) cuda_repo=ubuntu2404 ;;
        *) echo "Use NVIDIA's instructions for this OS/CPU." >&2; exit 1 ;;
    esac
    keyring_dir=$(mktemp -d)
    trap 'rm -rf "$keyring_dir"' EXIT
    wget -O "$keyring_dir/cuda-keyring.deb" \
        "https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/$cuda_repo/x86_64/cuda-keyring_1.1-1_all.deb"
    sudo dpkg -i "$keyring_dir/cuda-keyring.deb"
    sudo apt-get update
)

Stop if this block fails. Do not continue with a repository for a different Ubuntu release, or mix a runfile driver installation with unrelated package-manager driver packages. NVIDIA documents the keyring and repository setup.

docs.title: Install a driver only when needed
docs.text:
Preconfigured cloud image: retain its working, compatible driver. If it needs an upgrade, use the provider's supported procedure. The recorded driver was 580.105.08. For CUDA 12.8 Update 1, this guide selects the release's corresponding 570.124.06 or newer driver baseline. CUDA 12.x minor-version compatibility permits some applications on older drivers, with feature and PTX/JIT limitations; it is a different compatibility path, not the setup baseline used here. See NVIDIA's release compatibility tables.

Fresh Ubuntu host you administer: if Secure Boot requires module-key enrollment, arrange the distribution/provider console access before rebooting. After repository setup, install kernel headers and NVIDIA's open-module driver package. H100 and A100 are supported by the open-module driver family. These commands are for the host, not a container:

sudo apt-get install -y "linux-headers-$(uname -r)"
sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-open
sudo reboot

The reboot disconnects SSH. Reconnect with your original SSH command, then run:

nvidia-smi
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version --format=csv

Continue only when the driver sees the intended GPU(s). A custom cloud kernel may need provider-specific headers. With Secure Boot, follow the distribution's module-signing/key-enrollment prompts, which can require console access; do not bypass a failed module load by blindly reinstalling CUDA. The nvidia-open package follows the repository's selected driver branch; it does not pin the recorded 580.105.08 patch. See NVIDIA's driver installation and reboot steps.

docs.title: Install CUDA 12.8 and cuBLAS
docs.text:
Skip installation if this toolkit and its development libraries already work. Otherwise:

sudo apt-get install -y cuda-toolkit-12-8

This versioned toolkit-only package supplies nvcc, CUDA Runtime development files, the Driver API headers/link stubs, cuBLAS headers/libraries, Compute Sanitizer and CUDA tools. It does not install a kernel driver. NCCL is separate. Avoid the unversioned cuda meta-package when you intend to keep the 12.8 toolkit and the provider's driver. The distribution package nvidia-cuda-toolkit can be a different CUDA release; it is not this recipe.

APT may install newer patches within the 12.8 line; inspect actual versions rather than expecting an exact historical environment. NVIDIA's toolkit package definitions distinguish toolkit, runtime and driver bundles.

docs.title: Select the toolkit and library paths
docs.text:
Choose one layout; these are alternatives, not consecutive export blocks.

NVIDIA APT toolkitProvider toolkit under /usr 
export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-12.8
export CUDA_INCDIR="$CUDA_HOME/include"
export CUDA_LIBDIR="$CUDA_HOME/lib64"
export PATH="$CUDA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$CUDA_LIBDIR${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:+:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH}"
hash -r
command -v nvcc
nvcc --version

Use this layout when the provider's working nvcc is /usr/bin/nvcc and its CUDA headers/libraries are under /usr/include and /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu, as on the recorded Lambda image.

export CUDA_HOME=/usr
export CUDA_INCDIR=/usr/include
export CUDA_LIBDIR=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu
export PATH="$CUDA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$CUDA_LIBDIR${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:+:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH}"
hash -r
command -v nvcc
nvcc --version

For another layout, use the site's module or its real install prefix. Confirm the selected headers and libraries belong to the intended compiler; the multi-GPU collector accepts CUDA_HOME, CUDA_INCDIR and CUDA_LIBDIR explicitly.

APT normally registers its shared libraries with the loader; the explicit toolkit path above also makes the intended 12.8 libraries visible for this shell. For a custom install, substitute its real path. Never add $CUDA_HOME/lib64/stubs to the runtime library path: libcuda.so.1 at execution time must come from the installed host driver, not a link-time stub.

To persist this selection in interactive Bash sessions, add these exports once to ~/.bashrc, then run source ~/.bashrc or open a new shell. In scheduler jobs and noninteractive SSH sessions, load the site's module or set these exports explicitly in the job script; those sessions may not read ~/.bashrc. The conditional expansion avoids an empty trailing library-path entry.

docs.title: Install NCCL runtime and development files
docs.text:
NCCL is needed by the collective examples. Install both the runtime and development package with the same CUDA-compatible version. For the documented NCCL 2.26.2/CUDA 12.8 installation baseline (the original H100 capture did not record an NCCL package version), first confirm package availability:

apt-cache madison libnccl2 libnccl-dev

When both list 2.26.2-1+cuda12.8:

sudo apt-get install -y \
    libnccl2=2.26.2-1+cuda12.8 \
    libnccl-dev=2.26.2-1+cuda12.8

These versions were present in NVIDIA's Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 x86-64 repositories when this guide was checked on November 18, 2026. If unavailable, select a matching pair built for CUDA 12.x from NVIDIA's repository/archive and record the actual version. Do not silently install the default CUDA 13 build or pass --allow-downgrades over a provider-managed stack. An existing compatible NCCL installation can be retained; its headers and runtime must resolve consistently. NVIDIA's NCCL installation guide explains explicit package-version selection.

docs.title: Check fabric setup on NVSwitch servers
docs.text:
On a native HGX/DGX NVSwitch server, the GPU driver and CUDA toolkit alone are not the entire fabric setup. DGX OS normally supplies Fabric Manager; a fresh HGX installation needs the compatible Fabric Manager components for its platform and driver. Use NVIDIA's bare-metal Fabric Manager procedure to choose the packages. Package/version rules differ by NVSwitch generation, and Fabric Manager versioning changed with driver release 620; do not copy a branch number from an unrelated server.

After installing the matching components on the host that owns the fabric, enable/start the service and inspect its state:

sudo systemctl enable nvidia-fabricmanager
sudo systemctl start nvidia-fabricmanager
systemctl is-active nvidia-fabricmanager
nvidia-smi -q -i 0 | grep -i -A 3 Fabric

For Hopper NVSwitch systems, check that fabric registration completes successfully before relying on NVLink peer paths. On a managed cloud instance or guest/container, the provider/host administrator may own this service; its absence inside the guest is not an instruction to install or restart it there. PCIe-only and direct-NVLink setups do not universally need Fabric Manager. Do not restart an active fabric service as a routine troubleshooting step.

docs.title: Verify files, versions and topology
docs.text:
nvcc --version
gcc --version
python3 --version
nvidia-smi
nvidia-smi topo -m
ls "$CUDA_INCDIR/cuda_runtime.h" "$CUDA_INCDIR/cuda.h"
ls "$CUDA_INCDIR/cublas_v2.h"
dpkg-query -W libnccl2 libnccl-dev
dpkg -L libnccl-dev | grep '/nccl.h$'

The driver supplies GPU access; the toolkit supplies compilation; cuBLAS and NCCL supply libraries. nvidia-smi's “CUDA Version” is driver compatibility, not the installed nvcc version. A topology listing describes connectivity, not a measured bandwidth or a successful peer-transfer test. Finish with the book's actual compile, launch and numerical checks below.

docs.title: 4 — Download the source and run preflight
docs.text:
git clone --branch main https://github.com/MaximumBeings/programming-the-h100.git
cd programming-the-h100
python3 tools/h100_preflight.py
python3 tools/h100_preflight.py --json > preflight.json

The clone explicitly selects the source branch. If already cloned, check git branch --show-current: gh-pages contains generated HTML rather than the source/build tools.

The checker uses the CUDA Driver API to count CUDA-visible devices, including the effect of CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. It checks Hopper capability, the compiler, and the availability of optional inspection tools. It needs Python's standard library, not PyTorch. It does not prove that a kernel is correct or that multiple GPUs have a suitable interconnect.

Selected fields rendered from the validation host’s preflight JSON (not a verbatim terminal capture):

H100 book preflight: PASS
Visible GPUs: 1; nvcc: 12.8.93
  NVIDIA H100 PCIe; CC 9.0; 81079.1 MiB

CUDA-visible memory can be lower than the board's nominal capacity or the management tool's physical-memory report because of reserved resources. Use the actual runtime capacity when allocating buffers.

For a particular distributed exercise, require its actual device count:

python3 tools/h100_preflight.py --minimum-gpus 2
python3 tools/h100_preflight.py --minimum-gpus 8

The eight-GPU training program passed on eight A100 GPUs, including comparisons of every final weight and per-step loss against an independent CPU reference. See the captured execution and system record.

For Chapter 4/11 development-library linkage, this optional check compiles the relevant current programs without launching their GPU workloads:

python3 tools/validate_examples.py --compile-only 04-cutensormap 11-multi-gpu

It checks Driver API, NCCL and cuBLAS links through the examples' complete commands. A successful compile/link is not an execution result. The eight-GPU training workload still requires eight suitable GPUs for its full run. MPI, NVSHMEM, PyTorch and cuDNN are not required to build the 27 named CUDA programs; the separate attention-reference script uses PyTorch.

If you downloaded only the website, the standalone preflight utility is also available. Save it, inspect it, then run it on your Linux GPU host.

docs.title: 5 — Compile and execute your first verified program
docs.text:
From the repository root, copy the exact tested source to a scratch build directory:

mkdir -p build/first-run
cp docs/validation/2026-11-17/02-clusters-inline-ptx/ex01_cluster_inspect/ex01_cluster_inspect.cu build/first-run/
cd build/first-run
nvcc -std=c++17 -arch=sm_90a -O2 ex01_cluster_inspect.cu -o ex01_cluster_inspect
./ex01_cluster_inspect
echo $?

This is the complete cluster-inspection program from Chapter 2, not a placeholder fragment. In the captured H100 PCIe run it reported:

DSMEM Exchange Tests: 4/4 passed

Cluster Metadata Verification:
  ✓ All cluster metadata correct

ALL TESTS PASSED — Clusters working correctly!

The program's exit status was 0. GPU printf ordering and the device name may differ on another host. Compare the checks and final pass status, not incidental line ordering. Exact tested source · Full captured output.

Learning checkpoint: For a one-dimensional cluster of two blocks, predict the local rank of global block 3 and its partner block. Check the cluster/rank fields in the program output. The prediction is rank 1 with partner global block 2: global numbering and rank-within-cluster are different quantities. This is a reasoning exercise, not an additional recorded GPU run.

Return to the repository root after this example:

cd ../..

For later examples, use the full command beside that example. Some need -lcuda, -lnccl, -lcublas or additional compilation options; the baseline nvcc command is not a universal link command.

docs.title: 6 — Install optional profiling tools
docs.text:
Check what the image already provides:

ncu --version
nsys --version
compute-sanitizer --version
cuobjdump --version

For the CUDA 12.8 toolkit installed through the repository above, missing inspection tools can be installed with:

sudo apt-get install -y cuda-nsight-compute-12-8 cuda-nsight-systems-12-8 cuda-sanitizer-12-8
ncu --version

The earlier captured Lambda session installed the image's nsight-compute package and reported 2025.1.1.0; the versioned toolkit package above can supply a newer 2025.1.x patch. Record ncu --version on your host. If ncu is outside PATH, inspect dpkg -L cuda-nsight-compute-12-8 and its nsight-compute-2025.1.1 dependency for the installed executable, then use its full path or add that directory to PATH. The first ordinary-user profile reported ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM; profiling with elevated permissions succeeded on the instance we administered. Chapter 13 shows both logs and the exact successful invocation. Do not change system-wide counter permissions merely to imitate a screenshot.

docs.title: Optional Systems and CUTLASS extension
docs.text: Chapter 14 adds Nsight Systems CLI capture and timeline analysis; record nsys --version separately from ncu --version. Chapter 24 pins CUTLASS v4.3.6 and supplies a separate collector for the new layout, GEMM and overlap exercises. Follow those chapters for their additional setup and current validation scope.

docs.title: CUTLASS fused-attention extension
docs.text: Chapter 30 adds a standard-library CPU attention walkthrough. Chapter 31 builds the pinned CUTLASS Hopper FMHA example with CMake and supplies a separate, opt-in evidence collector. Its published H100 GPU results are separate from the existing 27-program and CuTe/CUTLASS workshop records. The CUDA reference passed seven cases and memcheck; the pinned FMHA target passed six forward/two backward invocations, with 17 verified variants and additional clean D=64 memory checks. Use a new output directory for your own execution record.

docs.title: Optional attention-reference dependency
docs.text:
The 27 named CUDA programs do not require PyTorch. To reproduce the separate Chapter 12 recurrence check from the repository root, use an isolated environment and the recorded CUDA-enabled PyTorch version:

python3 -m venv .venv-attention
.venv-attention/bin/python -m pip install torch==2.7.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
.venv-attention/bin/python tools/validate_attention.py

This script runs 12 GPU reference cases; it is not the FA3 skeleton or a performance benchmark. PyTorch's CUDA wheel does not replace the system compiler or driver. See the official PyTorch 2.7 installation commands.

docs.title: 7 — Build and read the website locally
docs.text:
These steps need Python, not a GPU. From the repository root:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python3 tools/verify_validation_records.py
mkdocs build --strict
python3 tools/verify_site_links.py
mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 on the same machine. Stop the server with Ctrl+C. On Windows, virtual-environment activation has a different path; you can instead invoke the environment's Python directly to install packages and run MkDocs.

If the preview server is on a remote host, keep it bound to localhost and forward it from your own computer:

ssh -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 -i /path/to/your-key.pem ubuntu@YOUR_INSTANCE_IP

Start mkdocs serve in that remote shell, then open the local address above in your own browser. Alternatively, clone and preview on your laptop so the GPU instance is not needed for documentation work.

The evidence checker compares chapter sources, downloadable sources and recorded hashes. It can detect stale execution records after a code edit, but it does not execute CUDA on a CPU-only CI runner. A strict MkDocs build checks site construction and treats build warnings as errors; tools/verify_site_links.py separately checks built internal links and anchors. These checks do not replace the GPU reference checks.

docs.title: 8 — Troubleshoot the first failing step
docs.text:
Work through the rows for the first error you actually see. Preserve the full compiler/runtime message and the exact command before changing the environment.

What happens What to check next nvidia-smi is missing or finds no devices Confirm you are in the GPU host's shell. Check the provider's driver setup and, inside a container or scheduler job, its GPU allocation/exposure. A missing management command alone does not prove CUDA is unavailable; use the preflight's Driver API diagnostic too. nvidia-smi lists GPUs but preflight sees fewer or none Check CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, the job/container allocation and CUDA driver-library access in the same shell that will run the example. Management-tool visibility and CUDA-process visibility can differ. nvcc: command not found Check the selected toolkit, environment module and PATH; the driver alone is not a compiler. Run nvcc --version after selecting the toolkit. Unsupported sm_90a target Check which nvcc your shell selects and its version. Use a toolkit supporting the example's architecture and instructions; CUDA 12.8.93 is the recorded compiler. Do not remove the a to silence a WGMMA assembly error. no kernel image is available or architecture mismatch Check the CUDA-visible GPU and rebuild the intended source with its full command. Rule out a stale executable or shared library. Hopper-specific sm_90a/compute_90a code is not forward- or backward-compatible with other architectures. Undefined cuTensorMap..., NCCL or cuBLAS symbols while linking Use the example's complete link command: driver API calls need -lcuda, NCCL needs -lnccl, and cuBLAS needs -lcublas. Check matching headers and libraries from the selected installation. The executable cannot load libnccl.so, libcublas.so or another shared library This is runtime library discovery, distinct from compilation. On Linux, inspect ldd ./your_example and use the library-path setup documented for the installed toolkit/library. Preflight says BLOCKED Read its specific error: driver discovery, visible count, Hopper capability or compiler availability/version. Preflight does not test topology, peer access or NCCL; check those separately for multi-GPU work. Its Hopper requirement also means an A100 can fail this checker while still being suitable for the separately documented portable training example. Illegal memory access Keep the first CUDA error and reproduce in a fresh process. Use the current corrected listing, then run Compute Sanitizer memcheck before performance tuning. An earlier dated source is useful for reproducing that exact record, not for undoing a documented correction. Wrong numerical results Compare the exact problem shape, data type, input initialization, layout and numerical tolerance with the example's reference check. A clean memory-check report does not establish numerical correctness. Timeout or stalled barrier Check required GPU/rank counts, launch dimensions, participant arrival counts, expected transfer bytes and buffer ownership. Use the chapter's synchronization protocol and stop a hung test rather than treating it as a performance measurement. Sanitizer coverage depends on the tool, version and instructions; a clean report does not prove every asynchronous ordering rule. ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM Read Chapter 13 and the administrator's profiling policy. This is a performance-counter permission problem, not evidence that the kernel is incorrect. Your times differ from the captured output Compare shape, SKU, clocks, timing scope, warmup, interconnect and profiler settings. A single-CTA correctness demo is not a peak-throughput benchmark.

For the unchanged first program from Step 5, run this from the repository root, after compiling it:

compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --error-exitcode 1 ./build/first-run/ex01_cluster_inspect

--error-exitcode 1 makes detected sanitizer errors produce a nonzero status even if the application itself exits successfully. Instrumented runtime is not ordinary benchmark timing. For the four barrier-ordering corrections in Chapters 3–5, use the current chapter listings and read their revision-specific validation status; their earlier logs cover the archived revisions.

References: NVIDIA's Hopper compatibility guide, Compute Sanitizer guide, and performance-counter permission guidance.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Choose a learning path. For the first pass, work through Chapter 1, then the complete examples in Chapter 2. Each chapter now has learning goals and self-checks with worked answers. Keep your own environment report with every result you want to reproduce.

docs.title: Native B200 extensions
docs.text: The Hopper sm_90a WGMMA/GEMM kernels are architecture-specific. For B200, use the separately tested native SM100 appendix, including its sm_100a build commands and pinned CUTLASS version. The B200 compatibility report distinguishes completed original examples from architecture-guard exits. This does not turn the Hopper instructions elsewhere in the book into Blackwell instructions.

The changed complete sources were compiled and executed on November 21 on a two-H100 host. docs.title: Critical finding dispositions
docs.text: Review ID Correction B2-Ch02-1 Both DSMEM programs rendezvous before remote storage owners exit. Current sources passed the November 21 H100 rerun and applicable sanitizer checks. B2-Ch02-2 Multicast sketch distinguishes cluster initialization, per-destination transaction barriers, mask and completion waits. B2-Ch03-1 Named barriers count all 192 participating producer/consumer threads and separate ready/release generations. B2-Ch04-1 128-byte-swizzled BF16 example uses a 64-element contiguous extent; descriptor, byte budget and walkthrough agree. B3-Ch07-1 BF16-input Hopper WGMMA requires FP32 accumulation; FP16 conversion belongs in the epilogue. B3-Ch07-2 FP8 pair conversion uses the two-argument intrinsic, raw-half pair and storage return type. CUDA compilation still pending. B3-Ch10-1 CUTLASS fragments are traversed backwards, distinct from the paper's tile-start-owner protocol. The small role demo does not test that scheduler. B4-Ch11-1 Optional NVLS is distinguished from ring/tree and does not make eight-endpoint AllReduce a guaranteed one-peer transfer. B4-Ch11-2 Per-endpoint traffic is separated from aggregate fabric traffic; the false O(N)-to-O(1) claim is removed. B4-Ch11-3 Ring bandwidth and tree latency characteristics are corrected; selection is per collective. B4-Ch11-17 Top-K activates K experts; equal-sized top-2 experts cost approximately twice one dense FFN, independent of expert count. B4-Ch11-18 Tuning starts with NCCL's defaults and observed selection; invented SHARP settings and reversed protocol advice are removed. B4-Ch12-1 Pending PV completes before O rescaling or V-slot release; the final PV contribution is drained. This is a protocol sketch, not a newly executed FA3 implementation.

• Architecture/ISA: occupancy, bandwidth allocation, FP64/INT32 explanations, TMA swizzle/subsampling/OOB/alignment, reduction operation/type combinations, WGMMA descriptors and operand precision, FP8 rounding/scaling/loading, and asynchronous buffer ownership.

  • Teaching chapters: chapter-number mappings, composition-domain distinction, explicit limitations of the Python arithmetic models, cooperative/ping-pong timelines, Hopper FP8 scaling and accumulation policies, correctness-build serialization warnings and framework integration scope.
  • Evidence/presentation: historical source labels, base-commit versus working-tree identity, B200 CPU/GPU counts and build targets, importer path, Nsight command syntax, TOC targets, worked SVG corrections and diagram viewer navigation.

Framework integration is documented as a contract, not a compiled extension. The Python workbooks remain limited teaching models and are no longer cited as concurrent-protocol tests. docs.title: H100-book compatibility checks on eight B200 GPUs
docs.text:
November 19, 2026. This is a separate architecture-compatibility pass, not a replacement for the recorded H100 runs. The host supplied eight NVIDIA B200 GPUs, CC 10.0, driver 580.105.08 and NVCC 12.8.93 on Ubuntu 24.04.5.

The pass covered 41 source cases: 27 original examples, eight workshop CUDA translation units (not all use CuTe or CUTLASS), four Python references and two attention sources. 36 exited successfully: seven CPU-only checks and 29 GPU-using programs. The CPU checks were four Python scripts and three CuTe host enumerators. GPU use is not synonymous with a numerical kernel oracle. Five cases did not execute their intended Hopper kernels: two WGMMA builds were rejected for sm_100 and their Hopper fallback binaries were incompatible; two Hopper CUTLASS GEMMs and example 88 exited at architecture prerequisites. No CUTLASS kernel ran in this compatibility set; cute_copy was its one CuTe GPU kernel. The native appendix below is a separate successful CUTLASS test set. Nsight workload runs here did not collect profiling traces.

The native B200 replacements are in the Blackwell appendix: checked SM100 GEMM, fused ReLU, and a scoped forward-attention adaptation. They have their own evidence and are not counted as unchanged Hopper executions.

Raw system probes · Raw collector results · Capture hashes. The original collector mistakenly labeled the upstream Hopper FMHA prerequisite exit as completed; the architecture message in its raw log establishes that no attention kernel ran. The table below corrects that interpretation. Raw logs are unchanged.

docs.title: Architecture guards are not successful numerical runs
docs.text:
The two raw WGMMA examples require Hopper. The two Hopper CUTLASS GEMMs also check CC 9.0 before launching. Upstream example 88 prints its Hopper prerequisite and exits before attention work on B200—even though that exit is zero. Replacing a guard without changing its architecture-specific MMA/storage implementation is not a port. The appendix instead uses native SM100 collectives and a separate Blackwell attention implementation.

The original nsys_overlap source completed both serial and overlap modes. Its two raw workload logs are preserved; no profiling trace was captured during this short rental window.

docs.title: Limits of these records
docs.text:
All printed -arch=sm_90a book commands produce Hopper-specific GPU code that cannot run on B200. This pass rebuilt applicable sources for sm_100, using sm_100a for architecture-specific register resizing. Changing a flag alone does not port WGMMA. The setmaxnreg example checks value preservation, not measured register redistribution.

The source/hash/log inventories check internal consistency, not independent hardware attestation or proof that a log is genuine. Evidence tarballs and some ad hoc follow-up drivers were not committed. The committed command arrays preserve those actual invocations; the compatibility runner log lacks its final summary line, so use the per-command records and exits. The original WGMMA build diagnostics and fallback outcomes are distinct; the linked run outputs alone do not prove the compiler diagnostics.

The ex11 capture includes warning #549-D from the historical self-initializing macro. Its zero exit does not validate that error path. The four archived source copies are immutable evidence of that defect, not current recommended sources. See the current corrections and completed H100 reruns.

docs.title: Exercises for Chapters 14–29
docs.text:
Actual November 18 H100 results provide the source-specific commands, system information, dates and outputs. The original 27-program suite has separate historical records. This workshop uses eight CUDA translation units and two Python reference programs, with 11 workload invocations: the overlap program runs in both serial and two-stream modes. Three CuTe executables enumerate layouts/traits on the CPU; five programs launch CUDA workloads; both Python programs are CPU-only references.

Prepare the pinned dependency from Chapter 15, then run the collector from the book repository root:

export CUTLASS_ROOT="$HOME/cutlass-v4.3.6"
bash tools/fetch_cutlass.sh "$CUTLASS_ROOT"
python3 tools/run_advanced_validation.py \
  --cutlass "$CUTLASS_ROOT" \
  --output "$HOME/h100-workshop-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)" \
  --execute --profiles

Omit both --execute and --profiles for a side-effect-free plan. A fresh output directory is required. The collector records exact source copies/hashes, the real toolchain and hardware, stage UTC timestamps, commands, exit codes, explicit numerical pass markers and optional Nsight Systems reports. Python byte-compilation is recorded as Python validation, not CUDA compilation. A profiler capture is accepted only with a passing workload and an actual captured transform kernel summary.
